indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent or guardian, teacher or other school staff and employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Identify safety hazards that could potentially be encountered during the work placement experience.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Compose a list of questions related to workplace hazards and safety to ask of the work placement employer such as:
- What physical, chemical, ergonomic or biological hazards should I be aware of in my work placement?
- When will I receive job safety training and orientation before I begin work?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear or other clothing am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify employment standards (e.g., use of a uniform) that may pertain to one’s work placement.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on one’s right to know, right to participate and right to refuse while in the work placement.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop personal and learning goals for the work placement in consultation with the parent or guardian, teacher or other school staff member and employer.

outcomes.statement:
Examine the significance of God's covenantal relationship with humanity through the stories of:
- Moses
- David
- selected prophets of the Old Testament.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Interpret lessons learned about hearing and heeding the call of God through the stories of:
- Moses (e.g., God commissions us to do His work)
- David (e.g., the smallest or seemingly least can be great with God) prophets of the Old Testament (e.g., Miriam – courageously live and celebrate your faith in God, Jonah - you cannot run from the call of God, Samuel - sometimes we need others to help us discern God is calling us).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Give examples of how individuals within the Catholic community, including oneself, respond to the revelation of God's commitment through covenant.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the significance of the name of God revealed to Moses (i.e., "I am"), and collaborate to examine the significance of other key faith experiences of Moses.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify ways the story of Moses foreshadows the story of Jesus including Passover for the Paschal mystery.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Examine Catholic perspectives on the Davidic covenant such as:
- David's rise to and loss of power (e.g., trust in God)
- the role of Jerusalem in salvation history (e.g., capital city uniting the northern and southern tribes of Israel)
- the importance of the Temple in salvation history (e.g., physical reminder of the covenants with Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses and David giving added significance to Mt. 12:6).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify how David fulfills the roles of priest, prophet and king, and discuss one's own call to such roles within the covenant.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine connections between David and the Messiah as presented through various prophets (e.g., Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Represent how the prophets play the role of bridge from Moses to Messiah within salvation history.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text:
Discuss various ways the prophets describe the Eucharistic covenant of the Messiah such as:
- new covenant (e.g., Jeremiah)
- everlasting covenant (e.g., Isaiah)
- covenant of peace (e.g., Ezekiel).

outcomes.statement: Examine the history of the development of the four Gospels and consider implications for faith formation.
outcomes.printedWith: [KG]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Outline and explain the three stages of Gospel formation including:
- life and teaching of Jesus Christ
- oral tradition
- written Gospels.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain why the Gospels were not written immediately following the death and resurrection of Jesus (e.g., expectation of impending Second Coming, prevalence of oral tradition, literacy rates, etc.).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the influence of oral teachings (i.e., stage two of Gospel formation) on the written Gospels (i.e., stage three of Gospel formation).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the impact on personal faith of skepticism concerning the historical accuracy of the Gospels (e.g., accuracy of oral traditions, limited historical documents on the life and teaching of Jesus).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the target audiences of all four Gospels and discuss implications for the writing style, content, and sequencing of the Good News according to each of the four evangelists (i.e., Matthew, Mark, Luke and John).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Discuss how understanding Gospel formation and intent influences the development of faith using examples such as:
- the development of the synoptic gospels
- the theory of a potential Q-source
- presence of unique content within John's Gospel
- conflicting interpretations of scripture (e.g., contextualists vs. Bible literalists).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain key uses of the Gospels after they were written (e.g., prayer, liturgy, catechesis, evangelization) and examine their influence on communal and personal faith development.

outcomes.statement: Contrast the Mosaic Law perspective on morality and sin with a contemporary Christian perspective of relationship building with God.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, DHP, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the place of the Ten Commandments within Mosaic Law.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the shift in understanding the Ten Commandments as laws (e.g., enforced by scribes and Pharisees) to a relationship with God in the spirit of the law (e.g., Jesus as fulfillment of the law).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Contrast how each of the Ten Commandments was understood from a legal perspective and a contemporary relational context through discussions such as:
- keep holy the Sabbath (e.g., adherence to Sabbath laws moving towards relationship building with God)
- honour mother and father (e.g., moving from honouring parents towards honouring parents and other elders within the community)
- do not commit adultery (e.g., rules and punishment pertaining to extra-marital sex moving towards personal responsibility for sexual morality)
- do not covet (e.g., person as possession moving towards recognition of the dignity of the person).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Distinguish the difference between merely avoiding evil and doing good using examples from Mosaic law and relational perspectives (e.g., the parable of the Good Samaritan).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Discuss legalistic and relational considerations in making a moral judgement including:
- the moral object (i.e., action)
- the moral intention (i.e., motive)
- the moral circumstance (i.e., context and consequence).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Collaborate with peers to represent the Catholic teaching that a good intention can never justify an evil act.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss examples of diminished responsibility for immoral acts (e.g., conditions for mortal sin).

outcomes.statement: Express Catholic perspectives on forgiveness, mercy, generosity, justice and joy within the ongoing nature of salvation history.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Examine Catholic connections between:
- original sin and forgiveness, mercy, generosity, justice and joy
- personal sin and forgiveness, mercy, generosity, justice and joy

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Respond to Christian religious artworks and writings pertaining to forgiveness, mercy, generosity, justice and joy such as:
- Rembrandt's The Prodigal Son
- Michaelangelo's The Creation of Adam
- various Byzantine icons such as Christ the Pantocrator or The Mother of Perpetual Help
- local church art such as stained glass and statues
- excerpts from Pope Francis's Joy of the Gospel
- The Jesus Prayer (i.e. Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner)
- Gospel parables such as The Prodigal Son, The Good Samaritan, The Workers in the Vineyard
- various poems in honour of Saint Mother Teresa

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Create a representation (e.g., visual, written, digital) incorporating distinguishing features of forgiveness from a Catholic perspective such as:
- forgiveness does not excuse an act
- forgiveness does not remove responsibility of the offender to repair damage done by an act
- forgiveness desires positive change, not revenge
- forgiveness does not have limitations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Investigate why and how one should forgive or seek forgiveness when forgiveness is difficult in situations such as:
- genocide and terrorism (e.g., Holocaust, Holodomor, Rwanda, recent terrorist acts such as 9/11)
- racial segregation including First Nations residential school experiences and others (e.g., Apartheid and slavery)
- abuse and violence (e.g., sexual, emotional, domestic)
- bullying (e.g., cyber, physical, emotional, mental, spiritual)
- betrayal by a friend or family member.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Recognize conversion as a process involving contrition, confession and correction.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss ways that sacramental reconciliation involves forgiveness, mercy, generosity, justice and joy.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Express how humility can lead to:
- joy
- generosity
- a Magnificat moment (i.e., modest recognition of one's talents as gifts from the Creator)
- social justice.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Examine how individuals, although flawed, can exemplify characteristics of:
- forgiveness lived (e.g., Immaculée Ilibagiza, Rev. Dale Lang)
- mercy lived (e.g., Sister Helen Prejean, Oskar Schindler)
- generosity lived (e.g., St. Vincent de Paul, St. Marguerite d'Youville)
- justice lived (e.g., Malala Yousafzai, Ovide William Mercredi of the Cree Nation, Aung San Suu Kyi, Gabriel Dumont of the Métis Nation)
- joy lived (e.g., St. André Bessette, St. Thérèse of Lisieux , St. Philip Neri).

outcomes.statement:
Investigate the existence, source, and purpose of miracles through examples from:
- the Old Testament
- the New Testament
- the historical era of the past 200 years.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize the value of wonder and awe in relation to the beauty of miracles of life, Creation, and all works of an omnipotent God.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare secular and religious perspectives on miracles including the Catholic emphasis on a miracle's source and purpose (e.g., message or resulting teaching).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Explain the Catholic understanding of the source, purpose and validity of various miracles such as those involving:
- Moses (e.g., burning bush, plagues, parting of the Red Sea)
- Jesus (e.g., water to wine, healing, commanding weather, casting out demons, raising the dead)
- Pentecost (e.g., the miracle of the tongues)
- Church authenticated miracles in modern history (e.g., Fatima, Lourdes, St. Padre Pio, Our Lady of Guadalupe and the tilma of St. Juan Diego).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Investigate the Church's approach to claims of miracles including:
- canonization of saints (e.g., venerable to blessed to saint)
- validation processes (e.g., use of research and science)
- examination for purpose (e.g., a discernable message from God)
- authentication of a miracle, deeming it worthy of belief but not a requisite of faith.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss various motives of fraudulent claims of miracles (e.g., power, money, fame, religious zealotry/fanaticism).

outcomes.statement: Evaluate the essential Christian conviction of Jesus as the Messiah.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the concept of Messiah as developed within Jewish history and prophesized within the Old Testament.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the implications of naming John the Baptist as the last prophet and the prophet of the Most High.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide examples of how God spoke to people prior to and following the Word becoming flesh and living among humanity in Jesus.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Analyze how events from Scripture support the conviction of Jesus as Messiah such as:
- the Incarnation (e.g., the Word became flesh, Jn. 1: 1-14)
- infancy narratives of Jesus including the role of Mary
- baptism of Jesus
- temptation of Jesus
- statements made by Jesus indicating his messianic nature such as Mt. 12: 6 and Luke 4: 16-21
- Transfiguration of Jesus
- Institution of the Eucharist at the Last Supper
- Agony in the Garden
- death and Resurrection.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Analyze how the miracles of Jesus in Scripture support a claim of Jesus as Messiah including miracles such as:
- curing the sick
- casting out demons
- controlling nature
- raising the dead.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Outline beliefs and discuss motives of those who do not view Jesus as Messiah including followers of the new atheism, Jews and Muslims.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Assess arguments naming Jesus as the Messiah from Catholic teaching authorities such as:
- the magisterium (e.g., John Paul II's Redemptoris Missio #5 and Dives In Misericordia #3)
- saints (e.g., St. Augustine, St. Teresa of Avila)
- theologians (e.g., Joseph Ratzinger/Pope Benedict XVI, Dr. Josephine Lombardi)
- apologists (e.g., C.S. Lewis, Peter Kreeft).

outcomes.statement: Investigate Catholic evangelization as a call from God.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain how the call to evangelize is both individual and communal in nature.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Distinguish between examples of evangelization (e.g., involving zeal, respect for freedom) and proselytization (e.g., involving coercive indoctrination, unjust use of force and power).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Examine how effective evangelization incorporates the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops' five important actions of the Catholic Church in pursuit of her mission:
- Proclaim Jesus Christ
- Worship Christ through the sacraments
- Form a communion of people
- Give witness, and
- Serve.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate how individual Catholics, although flawed, have led others into a relationship with God through their example (e.g., Catholics in the community and well known individuals such as Pope John Paul II, Saint Mother Teresa, Jean Vanier, Saint Kateri Tekakwitha, Chiara Lubich, Catherine Doherty, Father Athol Murray).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate how proselytization may lead to societal challenges such as assimilation practices or religious extremism.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Role play the evangelization of those who oppose Christianity (e.g., atheistic scientist, agnostic, secular humanist or moral relativist).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Demonstrate connections among:
- the call to evangelization in contemporary society
- the Scriptural question: 'Am I my brother's keeper?'
- Pope Francis' concepts of a "culture of encounter" (e.g., Evangelii Gaudium 3) and "missionary disciples" (e.g., Evangelii Gaudium 120).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze what is meant by the 'new evangelization' of the Catholic Church and propose methods to achieve it.

outcomes.statement: Examine the benefits, challenges and responsibilities of being both a member of a church and an engaged citizen.
outcomes.printedWith: [KG, DHP, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain Jesus' statement to "Give back to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's" (Mk. 12:17).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Contrast Peter's words: "we must obey God rather than any human authority" (Acts 5:29) with Paul's writings on submitting to governing authority (e.g., Romans 13: 1-7).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Debate issues of the primacy of conscience versus the authority of church and government (e.g., misuse of power, civil disobedience, conscientious objection, other issues addressed in the Pastoral Letter on Freedom of Conscience and Religion, April, 2012 - CCCB).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine Christian perspectives on political themes such as globalization, economic inequality and self-interest.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Discuss benefits and challenges of the ten responsibilities of a good government identified by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, 2001 including:
- respect the dignity of the person
- accept the rule of law
- promote the common good and good order
- protect the family
- safeguard the right to life of every person
- be responsible for the economy and well-being of citizens
- give access to work and just wages
- ensure religious freedom
- look after the health of citizens
- defend the country.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Discuss benefits and challenges of the six responsibilities of citizens to the country identified by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, 2001 including:
- obey civil authority
- vote
- participate in public life
- pay taxes
- welcome immigrants and refugees
- defend the country.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the obligation of a Catholic to assist those who are politically marginalized by governmental policies including First Nations and Métis peoples and others (e.g., veterans, refugees).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Construct meaning for the expression 'politically active', and inquire into how living according to the Gospel is a political act (e.g., called to transform culture).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine how a Christian life may lead to supporting the work of Canadian social movements and organizations (e.g., Chalice, Christian Near East Welfare Association, Development and Peace, World Wildlife Fund Canada, Métis Nation - Saskatchewan).

outcomes.statement:
Examine Catholic social teachings and actions involving:
- reverence for life
- treatment of the marginalized
- social sin.
outcomes.printedWith: [DHP, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Discuss effects, culpability and individual responsibility resulting from:
- original sin (i.e., Adam and Eve)
- personal sin (i.e., actual sin)
- social sin (i.e., structures of sin).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Contrast Catholic teachings on reverence for life, treatment of the marginalized and social sin with moral relativist examples.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Use scripture to support understanding and application of Catholic social teachings on reverence for life, treatment of the marginalized and social sin.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Use the experiences of Mary to deepen understanding of Catholic social teachings regarding issues such as:
- reverence for life (e.g., "yes" to the angel Gabriel, mourning of Jesus)
- treatment of the marginalized (e.g., Mary as widow, as refugee, as homeless, as poor)
- social sin (e.g., Mary living in a male-dominated society).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Explain how Scripture and Church teachings influence personal views on:
- life issues (e.g., abortion, euthanasia, palliative care, Dr. assisted-suicide, suicide, capital punishment)
- the treatment of the marginalized (e.g., the poor, elderly, disabled, those suffering from discrimination, human trafficking)
- social sin within contemporary society (e.g., pornography, prostitution, gambling).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the cause and effects of various poverties (e.g., economic, relational, spiritual) in the world and how the Catholic community seeks to address them.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Analyze and discuss how a person's views might be challenged when presented with Church teaching regarding the 'Preferential Option for the Poor' supported in Scripture and Tradition such as:
- Ex. 22:20-26, Is. 58: 5-7, Mt. 25:34-40, Lk. 4:16-21
- Pope Paul VI's encyclical Populorum Progressio #23, Pope John Paul II's encyclical Centesimus Annus #58.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Discuss the marginalization of First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples of Canada through topics such as:
- the Truth and Reconciliation process and Calls to Action
- Jordan's Principle (e.g., First Nations and Métis children disadvantaged due to conflicts involving federal and provincial bureaucracy)
- treaties that remain unfulfilled.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text:
Apply to societal issues such as sanctity of life, marginalization and social sin the five steps of effective social action identified by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops:
- Be present to the poor.
- Develop understanding of the causes of suffering.
- Judge the situation in light of Gospel values and Church teaching.
- Think and act creatively, guided by the vision of the kingdom of God.
- Act together (in solidarity) to transform unjust situations.

outcomes.statement: Analyze Catholic prayer teachings and reflect on their influence on one's prayer life.
outcomes.printedWith: [KG, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Analyze and discuss how one's prayer life may be influenced by Catholic teachings regarding:
- why pray
- how to pray
- what to pray for
- when to pray
- to whom a person should direct prayer (e.g., God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit)
- through and with whom a person may be encouraged to pray (e.g., Mary, saints, the angelic host).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Discuss relationships among and benefits of:
- personal prayer (i.e., prayers dealing with personal issues)
- private prayer (i.e., prayers made by oneself)
- communal prayer (i.e., praying with others).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Create an arts expression in response to the five types of prayer listed within the Catechism of the Catholic Church including:
- petition (e.g., asking for what one wants)
- intercession (e.g., prayer for others)
- thanksgiving (e.g., gratitude for gifts of life and love, moving away from selfishness, enjoying what life brings)
- praise and worship (e.g., respect for God, celebrates everything coming from and belonging to God, results in bringing God's love to others)
- blessing and adoration (e.g., recognition of the nature of God, leads to being 'poor in spirit', recognizes everything comes from and belongs to God and therefore everything can be used for the glory of God).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate similarities and differences in prayer among Christian, Jewish, First Nations and Métis traditions (e.g., mealtime prayers, prayers of thanksgiving, praise and worship, petition and intercession).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the infusion of cultural traditions within Catholic ecclesial prayer rituals including First Nations traditions (e.g., smudging ceremonies within the Catholic church, Way of The Cross events incorporating cultural art works, Theophany Water Blessing, diverse Holy Week cultural traditions such as Catholic Filipino and Ukrainian Catholic).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the Catholic view that prayer should be affective in nature (e.g., causing personal change or growth) and thereby leads to acts of goodness (e.g., being an instrument of God's will, deepening one's connection to God).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Construct a plan for personal prayer and action using Jesus as a model (e.g., prayed in solitude, led others in prayer, fasted).

outcomes.statement: Express personal beliefs about life after death and spiritual beings considering Catholic perspectives and other views.
outcomes.printedWith: [KG, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship between scientific inquiry and spiritual and religious beliefs (e.g., physical evidence for spiritual claims).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Pose questions for inquiry regarding the spiritual nature of one's existence through the use of examples such as:
- creation stories and myths
- beliefs about the Creator
- the eternal nature of spirit or soul
- Elders' knowledge of vision quests and spiritual ways of knowing
- spiritual beings such as angels, demons, animal spirits, ghosts
- spiritual apparitions and supernatural experiences.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Investigate concepts of life after death from various spiritual and religious viewpoints considering perspectives such as:
- Christian views about heaven, hell and purgatory
- Byzantine and Orthodox understandings of the journey of theosis
- First Nations, Métis and Inuit traditions
- Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism traditions
- Atheism.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the role of saints in Catholic tradition and contrast this to other approaches to prayer related to the deceased including traditional First Nations' ceremonies and others (e.g., Catholic prayer with and through the saints, Catholic prayer for and through the dearly departed, Eastern Christian concept of eternal memory, the Hindu cycle of rebirth).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Assess how one's exposure to varying spiritual and religious viewpoints influence personal beliefs about life, death and spiritual beings considering concepts such as:
- personal ethics and morality
- sin and forgiveness
- obedience and freedom
- hope.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Contrast Catholic teachings (CCC 1673, 1237, 2116, 2117) about exorcism and acts of divination (e.g., séance, Ouija boards, astrology, palm reading) with pop culture views (e.g., dismissive harmless games, portrayals in horror films).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Examine perspectives on life after death and spiritual beings by responding to arts expressions such as:
- Traditional Powwow dances
- On Eagle's Wings by Michael Joncas (Psalm 91 and Isaiah 40:31)
- The First Nation Art Garden (Toronto Zoo's Turtle Island Conservation Program)
- the murals of Berthold Imhoff in St. Peter's Cathedral at Muenster, Saskatchewan.
- The Ecstasy of St. Teresa of Avila sculpture by Bernini
- The Fall of the Rebel Angels painting by Pieter Bruegel
- The Ladder of Divine Ascent, St. John Climacus
- excerpts from Dante's Inferno or John Milton's Paradise Lost
- other contemporary works (e.g., music, literature, cartoons, visual art, film).

outcomes.statement: Examine principles, benefits and challenges of interfaith dialogue.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, DHP, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Examine key principles of interfaith dialogue such as commitment to:
- accept others as equal partners
- learn and share rather than teach
- respect diversity within and among religions
- include all religious and spiritual communities who wish to be engaged in dialogue
- seek to understand what is true and holy in other religions (e.g., Nostra Aetate)
- challenge the misuse of religion for political gain or to justify violence or coercion
- critique one's own tradition and seek to understand criticisms of that tradition
- critically appraise online materials and conversations about diverse religious and spiritual traditions
- collaborate on common goals (e.g., peace, environment, poverty, human dignity).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss Jewish, Christian and Muslim views on the role of key religious historical figures such as Abraham, Isaac, Ishmael, Noah, Moses, Mary, Jesus and Mohammed.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare rituals of worship, forms of prayer, development of moral codes, and religious artistic expression of Jews, Christians and Muslims.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the effects of persecution on interfaith dialogue throughout history faced by Jews (e.g., anti-Semitism), Christians (e.g., martyrdom) and Muslims (e.g., Islamophobia).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Investigate how interfaith dialogue is supported by understanding historic events and movements such as:
- genocidal acts (e.g., the Holocaust, Holodomor, the Kurdish Genocide: Al-Anfal Campaign)
- the Crusades
- religious extremism within Judaism (e.g., the Kingdom of Israel/Tzrifin Underground)
- religious extremism within Christianity (e.g., Ku Klux Klan)
- religious extremism within Islam (e.g., Al-Qaeda).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research case studies where interfaith dialogue results in positive change among Jews, Christians and/or Muslims (e.g., Albania's Muslim and Christian populations, Pope Paul VI's Nostra Aetate, the work of Saskatchewan born Sister Rosaleen Zdunich B.Ed. M.Sc. ).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Describe the relationships between interfaith dialogue and Pope Francis' concepts of:
- building a 'culture of encounter' (e.g., Evangelii Gaudium - The Joy of the Gospel)
- 'care of our common home' (e.g., Laudato Si' – Praise be to You).

outcomes.statement: Describe how one's experience in a Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat affects one's life and understanding of the call to evangelize.
outcomes.printedWith: [DHP, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create, in collaboration with one's peers and teacher, a plan for participation in a Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how the planned Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat might affect one's life, faith development and call to evangelize.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the impact of faith-motivated service and communal endeavors on individuals and communities.

allEvidence.observation: The “Outcomes and Indicators” table lists the Catholic Studies 10 outcomes as one numbered sequence under a single heading, with no unit, strand, theme or module headings.

outcomes.statement: Examine the fullness of God's covenant through Jesus and how it applies to one's life.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify key events from the breaking of the covenant by Adam and Eve to the fulfillment of God's covenant with humanity through Jesus including Luke 22-24 and Acts 1-2.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Explain how the Resurrection reveals core Catholic beliefs such as:
- new life after death
- hope (CCC 1817-1821)
- Jesus as Lord, pointing to the heart of the Christian faith
- the possibility of transformation throughout one's life.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the nature of love including its prominence within the Eucharistic covenant and examples of signs of love in society (e.g., agape/unconditional, eros/romantic, philia and philio/brotherly and sisterly, encyclical Deus Caritas Est – God is Love).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Collaborate with peers to explore compelling questions about how the Eucharistic covenant affects one's everyday life involving core concepts such as grace, salvation, forgiveness, hope, love and joy.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Represent the Catholic understanding of Eucharist as a source of joy and hope supporting the call to live joyfully within a covenant relationship with Christ.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the following concept: Good works don't bring salvation, but the joy of salvation reveals itself in good works through God's grace.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reassess one's response to Jesus' call to a personal relationship with him through the Eucharistic covenant.

outcomes.statement: Examine the Christian conviction of Jesus as Lord.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe how belief in Jesus as Lord affects one's life and community (e.g., joy, hope, forgiveness, generosity).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Evaluate Church doctrine relating to Jesus as Lord, second person of the Trinity, such as:
- Creator of all
- pre-existent Word made flesh
- divinity and humanity of Jesus (i.e., Hypostatic Union).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Evaluate Church doctrine relating to Jesus as Lord of humanity through Mary, the bearer of God (i.e., Theotokos), such as:
- The Immaculate Conception (i.e., Mary preserved from the stain of Original Sin in St. Anne's womb)
- The Incarnation / The Annunciation (i.e., the Word made flesh)
- The Nativity – virgin birth (i.e., Jesus conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the identity of Jesus as Lord through the use of C.S. Lewis' "liar, lunatic, or Lord" apologetic argument.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Support the Christian conviction of Jesus as Lord using scriptural examples such as:
- teachings of Jesus (e.g., parables, Sermon on the Mount)
- Peter's declaration about Jesus at Caesarea Philippi, Jesus' response and subsequent renaming of Peter (i.e., Mt. 16: 13-20)
- The Passion, resurrection and ascension
- the experience of the centurion at the foot of the cross (i.e., Mk. 15:39)
- Jesus being:
- the pre-existing Word (i.e., John1:1-5),
- the way, the truth, and the life (i.e., John 14: 6)
- the son of David, the son of Abraham (i.e., Mt.1:1)
- "I am" through multiple personal identity statements in the gospel of John.

outcomes.statement: Assess how living the Beatitudes of Christ affects individuals and society.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, DHP, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Discuss understanding of the Beatitudes including:
- 'poor in spirit' – recognizing one's spiritual poverty and powerlessness to save oneself
- 'those who mourn' – acknowledging wounded relationships and the need for God's grace
- 'the meek' – keeping one's power or strength under control; curbing selfish desires to be obedient to God's will
- 'those who hunger and thirst for righteousness' – desiring to learn and do the will of God; seeking to live in right relationships
- 'the merciful' – showing forgiveness and/or compassion in a time of need
- 'the pure in heart' – setting one's mind and will to God's call abiding in faith, hope, and love
- 'peacemakers' – reconciling broken relationships
- 'those persecuted for the sake of righteousness' – suffering for following the will of God, living the Beatitudes with courage.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate the concept of joy from happiness and explain how one's joy results from living the Beatitudes.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Support the concept that living the Beatitudes is a pursuit of goodness involving more than the avoidance of evil.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how the Beatitudes call individuals to assume personal responsibility within society (e.g., support cultural understanding, environmental and social sustainability, and the marginalized).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Represent the joys and challenges of living out the Beatitudes (e.g., role play, short story, cartoons).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Discuss how individuals and movements, although flawed, can impact society by demonstrating characteristics of one or more of the Beatitudes:
- 'poor in spirit' (eg., Saint Mother Teresa, Saint. Paisios of Mount Athos)
- 'those who mourn' (e.g., Lieutenant-General Roméo Dallaire, marches for missing and murdered Aboriginal women)
- 'the meek' (e.g., Moses, Rosa Parks, Saint Pope John XXIII)
- 'those who hunger and thirst for righteousness' (e.g., Blessed Oscar Romero, Wangari Maathai, Anne Cools, environmental activist groups)
- 'the merciful' (e.g., Irena Sendler, Nelson Mandela, Tommy Douglas, Venerable Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky)
- 'the pure in heart' (e.g., Mary and Joseph as the parents of Jesus, Joseph Chiwatenhwa , Mary Ellen (Bellelle) Guerin)
- 'peacemakers' (e.g., Betty Williams and Mairead Corrigan, Jimmy Carter, Fr. Albert Lacombe, Pîhtokahanapiwiyin/Poundmaker)
- 'those persecuted for the sake of righteousness' (e.g., Agnes MacPhail, Saints Felicity and Perpetua, Louis Riel).

outcomes.statement: Examine how the Paschal Mystery, as the foundation of the Catholic faith, shapes views on suffering, death and resurrection.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, DHP, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the struggles and joy of the Paschal Mystery (i.e., Jesus' suffering, death and resurrection).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine how Jesus' suffering, death and resurrection reveals the depth of God's love and power to bring life from death and light from darkness.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how arts expressions may challenge, clarify and develop religious and spiritual understanding of the mysteries of suffering, death and resurrection (e.g., hope-filled imagery, icons, expressions of joy, concepts of compassion).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Construct personal views on the nature of suffering by comparing Catholic views of 'redemptive suffering' in light of the joy of the Gospel with:
- traditional First Nations and Métis beliefs
- various worldviews (e.g., Viktor Frankl, Helen Keller, the Buddha).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain or represent personal viewpoints on how one knows that the Creator God understands his or her suffering (e.g., physical, mental, emotional, spiritual domains of the medicine wheel, the suffering of Jesus as the second person of the Trinity).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how the Church calls the faithful to respond in hope to people suffering from grief, end-of-life challenges, and illness (e.g., St. Pope John Paull II's Apostolic Letter On Human Suffering).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine how one's personal faith impacts wellness (e.g., physical, mental, emotional, spiritual domains of the medicine wheel).

outcomes.statement: Investigate how Tradition complements Scripture as a form of Revelation in the Catholic church.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss Tradition (i.e., Apostolic or Holy Tradition) and Scripture as the two complementary forms of Revelation (see CCC 80-83).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between Apostolic Tradition and ecclesial traditions within the Catholic Church.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Discuss ecclesial traditions within the Church such as:
- meditations involving stained glass windows such as Blessed are the Pure in Heart and others at St. Augustine's Church in Wilcox, Saskatchewan.
- cultural music including First Nations drumming within Catholic masses
- pilgrim events such as:
- Byzantine celebrations at the Shrine of the Venerable Nun Martyrs Olympia and Laurentia in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan
- events at Saint-Laurent de Grandin established by Fransaskois and Métis peoples
- the annual Shrine of Our Lady of Lourdes Pilgrimage at St. Peter's Colony, Saskatchewan.
- sacramentals (e.g., blessings) as distinct from sacraments.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the role of Peter within Tradition (e.g., the founding of the Church, Apostolic succession).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Distinguish between acts of veneration and worship from a Catholic religious perspective and show how acts of veneration (i.e., devotions) to the Virgin Mary and the saints are part of the Tradition of the Catholic Church.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine liturgy and the Mass within Tradition and their role in Revelation.

outcomes.statement: Examine the Church's mission and its actualization.
outcomes.printedWith: [CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Review the mission of the Church (CCC773) and recognize how the Church is to be a gift to the world especially in the ways of love, joy, peace and service (e.g., Jn. 15:10-12).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Explain how the evangelical mission of the Church is supported by the five actions identified by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops including:
- Proclaiming Jesus Christ
- Worship Christ through the sacraments
- Form a communion of people
- Give witness
- Serve.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Describe how evangelization is supported by models of Church proposed by Cardinal Avery Dulles including:
- Sacrament
- Institution
- Servant
- Herald
- Community of disciples.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how the mission of the Church is supported through the celebration of sacraments in various Catholic churches through their rites (e.g., Roman, Byzantine, Chaldean, Coptic).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Contrast the communal nature of the Church with the individualism of modern society.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Examine how joyful involvement in the mission of the Church is assisted by traditions and practices such as:
- use of the liturgical calendar (e.g., feast days, memorial days, liturgical seasons)
- Church pilgrimages or reverence of holy sites
- seeking grace through the sacraments and everyday life
- patronage of the arts throughout Church history
- honouring of Canonized Saints and other Catholic holy men and women
- Church youth groups.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss challenges faced by the Church as she strives to fulfill her mission (e.g., political and social challenges).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze how the faith and works relationship impacts the mission of the Church (e.g., an action-oriented mission).

outcomes.statement: Contrast Catholic teachings with secular views regarding human sexual morality and reproductive ethics.
outcomes.printedWith: [DHP, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Analyze key themes within Blessed Pope Paul VI's encyclical Humanae Vitae such as:
- humanity belongs to God rather than everything belonging to humanity (e.g., my body, my life, my choices)
- sex as a gift from God
- sex cannot be separated from its purpose (i.e., a unitive act conveying committed love with openness to life).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Analyze key themes within Saint Pope John Paul II's Theology of the Body such as:
- the body expresses the person (e.g., the power and symbolism of body language in our actions including sexual acts)
- sex is an expression of love and a gift from God (e.g., chastity aids in understanding the positive purpose and basic 'goodness' of sex, a reflection of Christ's love relationship with the Church)
- the contradictory natures of love and lust
- discerning the value of self and others including the call to love throughout one's life
- a sacramental worldview (e.g., invisible realities, grace influencing ethics).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess the ethical implications of Natural Family Planning as a form of birth control and other birth avoidance techniques (e.g., various forms of artificial contraceptives, sterility-inducing surgical procedures).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Evaluate implications of Catholic, secular and scientific views on issues of sexual behaviour and contraception methods (e.g., chastity, promiscuity, direct vs. indirect sterilization or contraception).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate implications of Catholic, secular and scientific views on moral issues of reproductive ethics (e.g., in-vitro fertilization, designer babies, gender selection practices and eugenics).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Examine the relationship between sexual morality and:
- human dignity
- free will
- power dynamics.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Debate complexities surrounding the issue of clear personal consent including popular culture terminology (e.g., culture of sexual consent, no means no, silence is not consent, or rape culture).

outcomes.statement: Examine how Catholic social teachings influence personal views regarding issues of labour and the environment.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, DHP, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Investigate moral issues and consequences for individuals and society relating to:
- labour (e.g., foreign labourers, forced labour, child labour, humane working conditions, employment equity, dishonest accounting practices)
- the environment (e.g., privatization of water, sustainability issues, deforestation, resource extraction, food production practices such as use of animal growth hormones and genetic engineering).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Contrast Catholic, relativistic and Indigenous views of justice concerning labour, the environment and globalization (e.g., legal and moral considerations).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss perspectives on the private, communal or government ownership of water, land and resources from Catholic and various worldviews including those of First Nations and Métis peoples.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess one's opinions and actions concerning various labour and environmental issues (e.g., human trafficking, child labour, climate change).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Investigate how issues of labour and the environment connect to:
- the Creation accounts of Genesis
- the Beatitudes of Christ
- the concept of stewardship.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Discuss contributions of individuals, although flawed, who served as leaders in the field of the environment such as:
- David Schindler and Ronald Reagan for their respective scientific and political leadership surrounding acid rain
- St. Kateri Tekakwitha as patron saint of the environment and ecology
- Pope Francis for his encyclical Laudato Si'.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Discuss contributions of individuals and movements, although flawed, that served as leaders in the field of labour such as:
- Dorothy Day and the Catholic Worker Movement
- Fr. Moses Coady and the Antigonish Movement
- Iqbal Masih as a child labour victim, activist and political martyr
- St. Joseph as patron saint of workers.

outcomes.statement: Assess the value and examine challenges of a life of service in the model of Jesus.
outcomes.printedWith: [KG, DHP, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the Catholic understanding of servant leadership including the relationship between service and power (i.e., the ability to create change).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe how Jesus is a model of service within Scripture.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize how Jesus, by his nature, teachings and actions, is at the root of Catholic social teachings (e.g., the value of solidarity stems from the Incarnation, the preferential option for the poor is reflected in the Beatitudes , the call for social justice is rooted in Jesus' ministry).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship between service and the call to 'love as Jesus loved'.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine personal and communal challenges of corporal and spiritual works of mercy within a model of Christ-like service.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Conduct an inquiry into the impact of service on individuals and society considering how service brings:
- joy to an individual
- hope to a community
- peace and justice to a society
- God's grace to humanity.

outcomes.statement: Explain the implications of choosing to live as a "disciple of Christ".
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG, CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine implications of the Lord's Prayer for individuals and society.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss challenges and value of living a contemporary Christian life of prayer.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Examine ways the Church fosters discipleship such as:
- teachings and support for living out the 7 virtues (i.e., the 3 theological virtues of faith, hope and charity and the 4 cardinal virtues of prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance)
- liturgical seasons as guide to prayer
- Mass/ Divine Liturgy
- liturgy (i.e., the work of the church)
- service
- veneration of saints and Marian devotion
- Scripture study courses
- retreat opportunities.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how one's identity as a disciple of Christ within the community of the church is influenced by statements in the Creed including "one, holy, catholic and apostolic" church.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Collaborate with peers to explore and contribute ideas about the statement: Going to church does not make one a good Christian, but a good Christian will want to go to church.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine one's understanding of and response to a personal call to sainthood using the lives of canonized saints as models of discipleship for contemporary living.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Construct an argument for Mary as a model of discipleship to be valued and emulated through merits such as:
- faithful obedience
- joy
- modelling the Beatitudes (e.g., poor in spirit, meek, pure of heart).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe characteristics of being a disciple of Christ and reflect upon ways of developing these attributes in one's life (e.g., joy in times of tragedy, a spirit of service during times of apathy, gentleness in times of frustration).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text:
Explain how being a disciple of Christ involves courage to live the Gospel in ways such as:
- being 'counter-cultural'
- 'living in the world but not being of the world'
- building a 'culture of encounter'
- being a 'steward of Creation'.

outcomes.statement: Investigate effects of infusion, suppression and rejection of Christian values and teachings on society.
outcomes.printedWith: [CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss factors that influence cultural and personal identity (e.g., gospel values, various religious, spiritual, moral and legal views).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify how positive and negative portrayals of Christ and Christian teachings affect contemporary society (e.g., portrayals in fictional writing, music, film, academic discourse, architecture, political campaigns).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe effects of the suppression and rejection of Christ and Christian teachings on contemporary individuals, family and society (e.g., the rise of atheism and idolatry, moral relativity or ambiguity, family dysfunction, persecution of Christians, religious extremism, diminished joy in life).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine ways in which Christ and Christian teachings are purposefully and effectively infused in contemporary society (e.g., contemporary worship music, Catholic charitable organizations, Natural Family Planning, Christian corporate philanthropy, Christian prayer at family mealtime, Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, World Youth Day).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify similarities among Church teachings, the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss and represent interpretations of 'the family as the domestic church' (e.g., St. Pope John Paul II's Apostolic Exhortation Familiaris Consortio – The Role of the Family in the Modern World).

outcomes.statement: Examine the benefits and challenges of ecumenical dialogue.
outcomes.printedWith: [CH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss effects on Christianity of the Great Schism of 1054.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate influences of the Protestant Reformation and Catholic counter-reformation on Christianity and inter-denominational relations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Contrast Catholic and Protestant teachings such as:
- Revelation (e.g., Martin Luther's "Bible alone")
- interpretation of Scripture (e.g., literalists and contextualists)
- the presence of Christ in the Eucharist (e.g., real or symbolic presence)
- the role, training, gender and marital status of the clergy
- the nature of salvation by faith alone vs. the union, by grace, of faith and works
- the theological or scriptural basis for varying number of sacraments.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the impact of influential events in modern Church history, including the Second Vatican Council on the Christian call to unity (e.g., Restoration of Unity, 1964).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Discuss examples of Christian churches coming together, seeking to be faithful to Christ's desire that his disciples be one, through:
- common mission or service (e.g., the Anglican rite in communion with Catholics of North America, two or more local Christian denominations working together to feed the hungry, shelter the homeless, provide warm clothing to those need)
- joint witness (e.g., joint communion where appropriate, pro-life rally)
- common prayer (e.g., peace vigils, Week of Prayer for Christian Unity)
- a chance to learn from each other (e.g., The Common Witness Project).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Discuss wounds to Christian unity such as:
- historical divisions (e.g., Church heresies such as Gnosticism, Arianism)
- modern divisions (e.g., the emergence of new sects, churches and cults)
- cultural conflicts including First Nations residential school experiences and others (e.g., misrepresentations of various Christian identities in media and popular culture, pro-life groups pitting church against society).

outcomes.statement: Analyze the personal and societal effects of an imperfect Church institution and imperfect individuals responding to the call for holiness.
outcomes.printedWith: [CH, DHP, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Contrast holiness with perfection using John 8:1-11.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Collaborate to interpret what it means for the Church to be holy and what it means for people, as individuals, to be holy.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine impacts of sin, acknowledgment of sin, reconciliation and conversion on personal and societal relationships.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Analyze and discuss how a person's faith and religious views may be impacted by religious role models who struggle with issues such as:
- addictions (e.g., drugs, alcohol, gambling, pornography)
- crises of personal faith
- sexual abuse (e.g., as victims or perpetrators).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Analyze effects of the Church's holy missionary work including First Nations residential school experiences and other examples such as:
- World Youth Day
- the establishment and maintenance of holy pilgrimage sites
- the Crusades
- Catholic education throughout the world
- Catholic health care
- Catholic social services.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the relevance of the Beatitudes for those seeking to heed the call to holiness.

outcomes.statement: Describe how one's experience in a Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat affects one's life and understanding of Catholic identity.
outcomes.printedWith: [DHP, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create, in collaboration with one's peers and teacher, a plan for participation in a Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how the planned Christian Action Project, rally and/or retreat might affect one's life, faith development and understanding of Catholic identity.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the impact of faith-motivated service and communal endeavors on individuals and communities.
