outcomes.statement: Explore tree growth and lumber production.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Wood (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the structure and growth of common lumber trees including concepts such as pith, heartwood and annual rings.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Classify common woods as softwoods or hardwoods and open- or closed-grained.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the creation process of dimensional lumber from falling a tree to retail sales in a lumber yard.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe common wood defects such as warp, check, cup and bow.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the effects of moisture on dimensional lumber.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess current logging practices in Saskatchewan and Canada and express an opinion about the sustainability of the wood product industry.

notes: The Ministry CSV words it: “Demonstrate an understanding of tree growth and lumber production.”.

outcomes.statement: Describe how a variety of wood products are manufactured.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Manufactured Building Products (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare the manufacturing processes and categories for various engineered structural wood panels (i.e. plywood, oriented strand board, and composite panels).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Classify the common uses of non-structural panels such as hardwood, plywood, medium density fibreboard (MDF), hardboard and particleboard.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Summarize the advantages of glued-laminated timber (glulam) over conventional timber beams.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Justify the use of wood I-joists and floor trusses over traditional joists in residential construction.

notes: The Ministry CSV words it: “Demonstrate an understanding of how a variety of wood products are manufactured.”.

outcomes.statement: Determine the cost of material for a small project.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4A: Project Estimating A (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the difference between the nominal size and the actual size of lumber.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Utilize the appropriate formula to calculate the number of board feet in a small project.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Calculate the cost of a small project given a material list and the cost of the lumber and hardware.

outcomes.statement: Calculate the cost of material in a cabinet-making project.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4B: Project Estimating B (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 4A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Utilize the appropriate formula to calculate the number of board feet for a given cabinet making project.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Calculate material quantities and cost for advanced cabinet-making projects based on project specifications and design plans.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Estimate labor hours for various tasks involved in advanced cabinet-making projects, considering factors such as complexity, skill level and efficiency.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify and factor in additional costs such as hardware, finishes and miscellaneous expenses for a project estimate.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Utilize relevant software tools or traditional methods to generate comprehensive project material and cost estimates.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify and mitigate potential risks and uncertainties that may affect project cost estimates.

outcomes.statement: Apply advanced calculation skills to determine the cost of a cabinet making project.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4C: Project Estimating C (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 4B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze project blueprints and designs to extract essential information to translate conceptual ideas into actualized building costs.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Critically assess and revise project estimates based on feedback, changing project requirements and unforeseen challenges.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate adaptability and problem-solving skills in the estimation process.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate strategic decision-making in aligning project choices with individual capabilities, goals and available resources.

outcomes.statement: Execute the calculation of material for a construction project.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4D: Project Estimating D (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 4A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate the ability to read a blueprint.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a lumber material list for the floor of a structure.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a lumber material list for the walls of a structure, including windows, doors and backing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a material list for the roof of a structure including rafters, trusses and finished roofing materials.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Calculate the overall cost of the construction project based on the material lists.

outcomes.statement: Explore advanced calculation skills to determine the cost of a revised construction project.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4E: Project Estimating E (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Advance · Prerequisite: Module 4D

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research how different construction trades in Saskatchewan price their jobs.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between hourly rate, square footage pricing, linear footage, day rates, per job pricing and when they should be used.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Calculate the cost of construction material (e.g., lumber for house framing, roofing material, insulation, exterior finishes and drywall) using a blueprint.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate the ability to give a quote in various construction trades based on material and labour costs.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the advantages and disadvantages of various alternative building materials and processes over wood and wood products.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5A: Alternative Building Materials and Processes A (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate recent innovations in residential building (e.g., low-E argon windows, insulated concrete forms, recycled plastic decking), and compare them to traditional products and methods.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research energy and resource efficient alternatives in residential construction.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the efficiency advantage (e.g., lifespan, reduction of waste, recycling of materials) of manufacturing building materials to traditional materials.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the benefits and drawbacks of metal framing versus traditional wood framing.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the growing trends of residential construction in Saskatchewan such as using straw bales.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate proficiency in the use of alternative cabinet making materials and processes.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5B: Alternative Building Materials and Processes B (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 5A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Assess the suitability of alternative materials for specific cabinetmaking projects, taking into consideration factors such as durability, costeffectiveness and aesthetic appeal.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate the use of a diverse range of alternative building materials suitable for cabinetmaking such as engineered wood products, recycled materials and sustainable options.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop practical skills in working with alternative building materials through hands-on experiences, including cutting, shaping, joining and finishing processes.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Implement rigorous quality control measures to ensure the longevity and durability of cabinetmaking projects constructed with alternative materials.

outcomes.statement: Execute advanced methods of using alternative cabinet making materials and processes.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5C: Alternative Building Materials and Processes C (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 5B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore material limitations, address compatibility issues, and develop effective solutions to ensure the successful completion of cabinetmaking projects.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Make informed recommendations in utilizing alternate materials for a cabinetmaking project.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Integrate alternate building materials creatively into project designs, showcasing innovation and an ability to push the boundaries of traditional cabinetmaking, while ensuring structural integrity and functionality.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate proficiency in the use of alternative construction materials and processes.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5D: Alternative Building Materials and Processes D (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 5A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between SPF and pressure treated lumber and when to use each when manufacturing a structure.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the pros and cons between OSB sheathing and plywood sheathing and when to use each.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the use of a variety of exterior finishes including their price points, advantages, disadvantages and installation.

outcomes.statement: Explore advanced methods of using alternative construction materials and processes.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5E: Alternative Building Materials and Processes E (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 5D

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate construction materials (e.g., concrete with forms, concrete with ICF blocks, cinderblocks and wood) that can be used to create a structural foundation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Execute how to frame a building using a variety of materials such as timber, steel stud, LVL and steel beams.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Practice the use of a variety of construction finishing materials and when to appropriately use them.

outcomes.statement: Show proficiency and accuracy when measuring materials.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6A: Measuring and Layout A (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Illustrate accurate measurements to 1/16” or 1-2 millimetres with a pocket tape measure.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Operate a combination square to draw a line parallel to a board’s side.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Calculate area, perimeter, and volume using simple formulas and a tape measure.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Illustrate how to draw a line at 90 and 45 degrees using a framing square.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Practice how to check for level and plumb using a carpenter’s level.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate several other measurement devices (e.g., plumb bob, sliding T-bevel, tramel points, dividers).

outcomes.statement: Use advanced precision and accuracy skills when measuring materials for a cabinet making project.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6B: Measuring and Layout B (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 6A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Apply an understanding of grain direction, moisture content, and potential movement to make informed decisions during the measuring and layout processes.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Incorporate measurement tools and technology, such as laser measuring devices, angle finders, and calipers, to enhance accuracy and efficiency in the measuring and layout phases of cabinetmaking.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate advanced techniques to ensure accuracy, efficiency and quality of a cabinet making project.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6C: Measuring and Layout C (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 6B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Apply mathematical principles to calculate and adjust measurements for joinery, allowances, and other factors critical to the precision and functionality of cabinetmaking projects.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Integrate efficient measuring and layout practices into the broader workflow of cabinetmaking, ensuring a seamless transition from design and planning stages to the actual construction of projects.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Implement quality assurance measures to inspect and verify measurements at key stages of cabinet construction, ensuring adherence to project specifications.

outcomes.statement: Practice advanced precision and accuracy skills when measuring materials for a construction project.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6D: Measuring and Layout D (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 6A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Apply a blueprint to a project.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Complete the layout of a wall and floor that are 12” and 16” on center using standard SPF/PT lumber.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a 24” on center roof layout using manufactured rafters or trusses.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Lay out a wall with a door or window on a small structure like a shed or tiny home.

outcomes.statement: Explore advanced techniques to ensure accuracy, efficiency and quality of a construction project.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6E: Measuring and Layout E (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 6D

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine how to read a blueprint.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Layout a floor system 19.2” on center.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how to read a window and door rough opening plan.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Layout an exterior wall, including windows and doors, using jack studs, king studs, cripples and headers.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Calculate and layout the angles to accommodate rake walls and vaulted ceilings in a construction project.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate proficiency with a variety of hand tools to accomplish cutting, shaping, smoothing and boring wood.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7A: Hand Tools A (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 6A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the hand tools in the shop and describe their function.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Utilize hand tools best suited to accomplish a task.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Perform the correct technique in using a hand tool.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe safety precautions for each hand tool used in the class including correct PPE.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate proficiency with a variety of hand tools for a cabinet making project.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7B: Hand Tools B (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Select appropriate hand tools for specific cabinet making tasks.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Achieve finished surfaces utilizing the correct hand tool for a specific objective.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Implement safe practices when operating hand tools, including the use of personal protective equipment.

outcomes.statement: Develop proficiency using a variety of hand tools for a construction project.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7C: Hand Tools C (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify basic tools used to construct a building (e.g., hammer, speed square, tape measure, cats paw and level)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Use hand tools required to construct a building.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain when a hand tool is more appropriate to use instead of a portable power tool when constructing a building.

outcomes.statement: Develop proficiency using a variety of portable power tools.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8A: Portable Power Tools A (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 7A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate the correct use of a jigsaw including cutting curves and replacing the blade.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Illustrate the proper use of a drill including selecting and changing bits, batteries, and bit direction.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify several common bits and their cuts (e.g., rabbet, dado, cove, flush trim).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use a router safely including changing a bit, setting the depth.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Use a biscuit joiner including marking stock and adjusting for the size of biscuit.

outcomes.statement: Develop increasing proficiency using a variety of portable power tools.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8B: Portable Power Tools B (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7B, 8A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate the safe setup, operation and maintenance procedures for a variety of portable power tools while following shop safety standards and personal protective equipment (PPE) requirements.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Use appropriate portable power tools to accurately complete measuring, cutting, drilling, fastening, and finishing tasks in cabinet making projects.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Use portable power tools in producing projects that meet required specifications, quality standards and workplace expectations.

notes: The Ministry CSV words it: “Develop increasing proficiency with a larger number of portable power tools.”.

outcomes.statement: Develop advanced proficiency using a variety of portable power tools.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8C: Portable Power Tools C (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7C, 8B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate advanced competency in the safe setup, operation, troubleshooting, and maintenance of an expanded range of portable power tools while consistently adhering to workplace safety standards and PPE requirements.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Use appropriate portable power tools to complete detailed cabinet making tasks requiring precision, accuracy, and efficient workflow management.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate confidence, efficiency and professional-level craftsmanship in the use of portable power tools for projects that consistently meet industry specifications, tolerances and quality expectations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Execute precise and accurate cuts, contours and edges using portable power tools.

outcomes.statement: Develop increasing proficiency using a variety of portable, jobsite power tools.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8D: Portable Power Tools D (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7C, 8A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate the safe setup, operation, and maintenance procedures for a variety of portable jobsite power tools while consistently following workplace safety standards and PPE requirements.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Operate appropriate portable jobsite power tools to accurately complete cutting, fastening, shaping and assembly tasks in construction projects.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate increasing proficiency, efficiency and control in the use of portable jobsite power tools in producing projects that meet required specifications, quality standards and workplace expectations.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Perform cuts with a reciprocating saw.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Install a reciprocating saw blade.

indicators.text: Use of a pneumatic nailer and/or stapler.

indicators.text: Connect and disconnect the air hose (if applicable) when loading nails or staples in a pneumatic nailer and/or stapler.

outcomes.printedWith: Module 8E: Portable Power Tools E (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 8D

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate advanced competency in the safe inspection, setup, operation, troubleshooting and maintenance of an expanded range of portable jobsite power tools while consistently applying industry safety standards and PPE requirements.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select, calibrate, and operate portable jobsite power tools with a high degree of precision and efficiency to complete detailed and complex construction and carpentry applications.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Illustrate professional-level proficiency, productivity, and craftsmanship in the use of portable jobsite power tools by producing projects that consistently meet industry specifications, tolerances, and workplace quality standards.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Utilize advanced techniques for making crosscuts, rip cuts and cutting panel products with a circular saw.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate advanced techniques for cutting with a reciprocating saw.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore advanced use of a pneumatic nailer and/or stapler.

outcomes.statement: Operate a variety of stationary power tools.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Install the correct saw blade for a specific application.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Illustrate the safe use of a table saw and/or radial arm saw including setting the fence, setting the depth of cut, and selecting and installing the correct blade.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the safe use of a mitre saw including adjusting the angle of the cut and changing the blade.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use a bandsaw to make straight and irregular cuts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Illustrate the proper use of a drill press including how to adjust the depth of the hole, the tilt of the table, and the speed of the bit.

notes: The Ministry CSV words it: “Develop proficiency with operating a variety of stationary power tools.”.

outcomes.statement: Operate complex stationary power tools.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Set up proper tooling for stationary power tools.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select the appropriate tool for specific tasks based on material, design, and project requirements.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate safety procedures and protocols related to the use of stationary power tools.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Execute precise and accurate cuts, contours and edges using stationary power tools.

notes: The Ministry CSV words it: “Demonstrate increasing proficiency with an increasing number of complex stationary power tools.”.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate, when interpreting oral and written texts, knowledge of Dakota language concepts including basic context-specific vocabulary, word order and linguistic conventions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the similarities between the Dakota and English alphabets.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the letters and accents on letters that produce particular sounds in the Dakota alphabet. Please refer to Appendix A for a complete list of sounds.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Practise reading basic Dakota vocabulary (e.g., forest, water and air) and simple sentences.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize numbers from 0 to 100 when spoken and written in contexts related to the land (e.g., number of birds in a flock).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the difference when using the number one to count or to describe a quantity (i.e., one book – waɳji; 1, 2, 3, – waɳc̀a).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore how the pronunciation of some words affects their meaning.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Recognize singular and plural versions of basic nouns in environments beyond the classroom (e.g., lake and lakes).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Identify male and female ways of speaking, such as:
- the greeting for “Hello” is pronounced “haɳ” by a female and “hau” by a male; and,
- the word for “yes” is pronounced “haɳ” by a female and “hau” by a male.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Comprehend present-tense verbs in first, second and third person singular (e.g., dancing, hunting and gathering).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explore, with guidance, the inverted phrase structure of the Dakota language when listening to and reading complete sentences.

outcomes.statement: Respond critically and constructively to dance compositions, in progress and complete, using form-specific terminology and rationale.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and organize criteria, individually or collectively-developed, to analyze and assess dance compositions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Articulate goals and intentions for dance, using discipline-specific terminology.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide rationale for contextual and environmental production decisions (e.g., lighting, staging, sets, props in a theatre; site-specific permits, safety considerations, sound, technical requirements).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Seek and apply feedback from others during dance-making process.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Critique own, peers’ and others’ dance compositions, in progress and finished, identifying and articulating strengths and areas for improvement.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Using a framework appropriate to the dance type and style, assess dance compositions (e.g., footwork in Fancy dance, movement of roach in Grass dance, isolations in hip hop, use of turnout in ballet).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Respond to dance compositions on an emotional, associative and formal intellectual level.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify potential for extended growth or future work based on feedback from self, peers and others (e.g., guest dancer/choreographer).

outcomes.statement: Analyze how dance challenges and influences personal and collective thinking about Canadian social, environmental and/or political issues.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine Canadian social, environmental and political issues and their influence on current dance compositions (e.g., dance as social or political commentary).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare personal and collective thinking, perspectives and biases about societal issues before and after viewing and responding to dance.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research and reflect on ways that dance raises awareness, challenges thinking and inspires change with regard to issues such as treaty rights, land usage, immigration, diversity, war, ethics, human rights, water rights, disease, racism, gender and sexual diversity, suicide.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Transfer understanding of a dance maker’s work related to a Canadian social, environmental and/or political issue into own dance compositions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: View, analyze and respond to dances that reflect Canadian social, environmental and/or political issues.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Take part in, analyze and respond to dances that reflect Canadian social, environmental and/or political issues.

outcomes.statement: Examine the issues, questions and concerns of appropriation of voice in dance and the arts.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the boundaries of cultural appropriation (e.g., what dances and/or elements of dances are appropriate?).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate questions concerning appropriation of voice in dance and the arts

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research examples of controversy in dance and the arts regarding appropriation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Survey students, community members and artists regarding their perspectives on the issues.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Debate and/or discuss questions surrounding appropriation (e.g., When does portrayal cross the line into perpetuating stereotypes? Who can participate in culture-specific dances? When does borrowing become cultural appropriation in dance? When can culturally specific elements such as regalia designs be incorporated in dance? Is hip hop dancing cultural appropriation?).

outcomes.statement: Investigate how Indigenous perspectives and ways of knowing, including local cultural knowledge, impact the creation of traditional and contemporary dance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Engage, digitally or in-person, with Indigenous Elders, Knowledge Keepers, community leaders and/or dancers to understand the impact of Indigenous practices and perspectives related to dance making.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine Indigenous perspectives on traditional and contemporary dance, drawing where possible/appropriate on the experience of students and expertise community members.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the ways of knowing and learning (e.g., dances passed down/gifted) that are applied to learning traditional and contemporary First Nations and Métis dances.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze how the work of contemporary and traditional First Nations dances and dance makers (e.g., Michael Greyeyes, Floyd Favel Starr) and Métis dances and dance makers (e.g., Scott Dance 10, 20, 3049Duffee, Krystle Pederson) are influenced by relationships to land, tradition, community and impacts of colonization (e.g., Truth, Dance and Reconciliationdocumentary, treaty education outcome SI12 -investigate the values and beliefs of self, family, community, and society in relation to the importance of honouring the Spirit and Intent of treaties).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how dance and dance makers influence and respond to social, political and cultural contexts.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how Saskatchewan and other Canadian Indigenous peoples’ experiences and worldviews are expressed through dance.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine protocols related to the teaching, learning and presenting of dances of Saskatchewan and other Canadian Indigenous peoples.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine topics related to gender and sexual diversity (e.g., two-spirit individuals) in dance.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Conduct research (e.g., digital, live, interview) on a contemporary First Nation, Inuit or Métis dancer or dance maker in Canada and report on such things as: philosophy or focus, subject or themes presented, discipline specific or interdisciplinary work, and the potential influence of traditional practices (e.g., ask questions such as Do traditional practices and/or Elders influence the work you create? Does your culture influence the subject matter or themes of your work?).

outcomes.statement: Develop understanding of dance within a Canadian social context.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine choreographers who investigate specific social ideas through dance.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine choreography that is reflective of social commentary and make connections with development of own work.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate choreographers’ approaches to creating social activism.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use social commentary in a way that reflects the idea of a professional artist.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe how dance can transmit or question values and beliefs.

outcomes.statement: Develop understanding of dance within a Canadian historical context.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze how social messages are communicated through time, identify what makes them memorable and use this information in own work.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the significance of the evolution of dance types, styles and specific choreography throughout history and discuss how the work is connected to social activism.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the synergies and evolutions of dance in response to current cultural globalization.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate choreographers as activists throughout history, and identify how own dance composition relates to these ideas.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine dance rituals and ceremonies in a variety of Canadian belief systems.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the role of dance within Indigenous societies across Canada, specifically pre-contact and post-colonial.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Pose questions about how different belief systems view dance (e.g., repression, affirmation).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate why certain dance compositions were considered to be controversial at different times in Canadian history.

outcomes.statement: Analyze and explore ways that skills and competencies learned from dance apply to careers one is interested in pursuing.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate and identify careers that would suit one’s strengths, beliefs and interests.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss transferable skills learned from dance to the career students are interested in pursuing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore a dance/movement opportunity one might pursue in one’s own life.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Establish a plan for lifelong participation in dance or movement.

outcomes.statement: Explore design studies and the stages of a design process.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Introduction to Design Studies (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
b
c
indicators.text:
Examine how the design process is non-linear and recursive, and includes:
- communication of the problem or need by the end user to the designer; and,
- clarification of perception of end user expectation by the designer; or need held by the designer; provided (i.e., test, refine and improve, test again).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a visual representation (e.g., flow chart, concept map, story board) of the stages of a design process.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply the steps of the design process to a simple design challenge.

outcomes.statement: Explore common principles and elements of design.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Principles and Elements of Design (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
b
c
indicators.text: Investigate how designers apply the elements of design, using the principles of design.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the role of modelling and prototyping in the design process.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: The Modelling and Prototyping Process (Optional) · Suggested Time: 7-12 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Define the term model and explain the purpose for modelling in the design process.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify critical attributes that differentiate a prototype from a model.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe situations in which either a model or a prototype is an important aspect of the design process.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate between a physical and an analytical prototype.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Speculate on reasons for creating either a comprehensive prototype (e.g., similar in appearance and including most components and attributes of a final product), or a focused prototype (e.g., implementing and testing one or two components and attributes of a final product).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Create a prototype from a given scenario to illustrate a design process, including:
- an annotated sketch of a solution to a design problem;
- two-dimensional and three-dimensional models of the solution to the design problem using digital tools; and,
- a variety of prototypes to test different elements within the design.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critically evaluate the efficacy of design decisions made within the prototype.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Adapt and refine the design to reflect data gleaned from the testing of prototypes.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Elicit feedback for a prototype using the terminology of the design process.

c

b

b
indicators.text: Differentiate between user-centred design and universal design.

indicators.text: Research ways in which design has resulted in exclusion of individuals from accessing objects or spaces.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify individuals, groups and organizations that have advocated for change in design thinking and individual and systemic dispositions toward design.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine ethical and economic reasons for inclusion of universal design in all design processes.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how universal design facilitates empowerment and self sufficiency among individuals and organizations encountering designed spaces, objects or events.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe ways in which universal design is beneficial to all individuals regardless of life stage or physical abilities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create an inventory of universal design features in school and community spaces.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the benefits of universal design applications such as levered doorknobs, taps in sinks and tubs, strategically placed assisted lifts and grab bars, governors on water heaters, adjustable height cupboards and tables, no barrier entries to buildings in single family dwellings and multi-unit residential dwellings.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Propose universal design improvements that would enhance user experiences with a variety of private and public spaces and products.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Suggest considerations required in the design process to develop products and places that are accessible to people with a wide range of abilities, to the greatest extent possible.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain why universal design is important to include in all spaces, not just industrial, commercial or publicly accessed buildings and spaces.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the design process in a design improvement scenario.

indicators.text: Examine existing products (e.g., a pencil, a pen, a backpack) or procedures (e.g., the process of moving from classroom to classroom for various classes, the process for borrowing library books) and critically evaluate their form, function(s) and limitations, including universal design considerations.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Hypothesize why decisions regarding form and function were made in the original design process.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine what problems or opportunities for modification exist to improve or broaden the application of products or procedures to achieve a desired outcome.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify modifications to improve a current design.

d

outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Aesthetics and Function in Design (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define aesthetics (i.e., that which is considered beautiful or tasteful), form (i.e., an object’s shape, size and material from which it is made), and function (i.e., the purpose of an object or what it helps people do) as they relate to design.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the relationship between function and aesthetics, and function and form.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess the aesthetic choices used to convey the intended functionality of a variety of products.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore the impacts of aesthetics and function on the human psyche.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore alternative materials and processes that might be used in creating a product.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify a variety of products that share a function but use a variety of aesthetic choices, such as colour, shape, size and surface texture.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe how the aesthetic choices of form can detract from or enhance the functionality of a variety of products (e.g., a convertible rooftop on a car may look attractive but is not functional to heat the interior of the car in cold temperatures).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore how form impacts the way we interact with a product, leading to preference of one product over another (e.g., clothing, washroom fixtures).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Speculate how differing cultural contexts can change the way that certain aesthetic features are perceived (e.g., clothing, universal design norms).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create norms for assessing work and providing feedback in a respectful and professional manner.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify potential sources of critique for improvement, emphasizing the importance of communication with the end user or client as essential to the work of professional designers.

indicators.text: Examine methods of critique for both individual and collaborative design processes.

indicators.text: Differentiate between constructive and nonconstructive criticism.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Critique design solutions using a process that includes the following stages:
- Describe: What do you see (e.g., colour, shape, form)?
- Analyze: What did the producer intend?
- Interpret: Is the product successful in conveying the message or achieving its purpose? Is the product successful using elements and principles of visual design? and,
- Evaluate: What changes would I suggest? What factors need to be considered in assessing the feasibility of the potential changes?

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

outcomes.statement: Research the specifics of working in theatre and/or film, including performance and career opportunities in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research (e.g., in person, written or recorded interview) a theatre and/or film artist about the “real life” concerns of a working artist (e.g., pay, contracts, hours, health, professional unions and safety).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Improvise a variety of realistic and absurd scenarios related to working in theatre and/ or film (e.g., terrible auditions, “what not to do” scenarios, inequitable power relationships, interviews, rehearsal conflicts, technical malfunctions, securing an agent or position backstage).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Volunteer or job shadow, where possible, in a professional or community theatre, theatre school or film production company.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a presentation to represent own skills and experiences in theatre and/or film (e.g., portfolio, CV, artist statement, cover letter, audition piece, pitch for a show).

outcomes.statement: Examine, and explore in own work, one or more theatre traditions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss connections between Indigenous artistic traditions (e.g., song, dance, stories) and the land, identity and worldview.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Recognize that artistic practices may be specific to a treaty territory, cultural and/or language group in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine theatre traditions representing various cultures and worldviews and explain how they are specific to place and time (e.g., Indigenous storytelling, Greek Theatre, Karagozi shadow puppetry, Talchum mask dance, Kathakali, Theatre of the Oppressed, mummers in Newfoundland).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Provide examples of how theatre traditions continue to evolve.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Present work inspired by a theatre era or tradition (e.g., perform scenes from different eras, present design elements).

outcomes.statement: Examine the influence of social, cultural, environmental and personal contexts on drama.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize the various ways that dramatic works arise from and respond to contemporary issues within society (e.g., gender-based or racially-motivated violence, causes and effects of climate change, impacts of economic disparity, youth mental health).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze the various social, cultural and environmental conditions that inform the creation of dramatic work.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify, examine, and practically explore the ways that diverse theatre styles have influenced society from the past and in the present.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Consider the ways that Saskatchewan theatre productions (e.g., Paper Wheat, Operation Big Rock Story of Mistaseni by SUM Theatre, The Weyburn Project) represent a time and place.

outcomes.statement: Explore how Indigenous perspectives and ways of knowing, including local cultural knowledge, impact the creation of dramatic work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Engage, where possible, with an Elder, Knowledge Keeper or community leader to listen to experiences or stories and use as inspiration for a creative response involving own drama work.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Use various sources of inspiration (e.g., image, sound, story) and research to explore reconciliation-related issues (e.g., racism, healing, treaty negotiations, privilege, relationship building, language loss and revitalization) through dramatic work (e.g., treaty education outcome TR11, indicator -- apply the principles of Canadian treaty making as a means for resolving conflict and represent in drama work).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research Saskatchewan Métis, First Nations and Inuit theatre artists and their work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: View and/or read plays created by Indigenous artists.

outcomes.statement: Use world theatre traditions to inspire ideas for own dramatic work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate how performance styles (e.g. mask, storytelling, shadow puppetry, naturalism, commedia) inform ideas.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate how different styles have been applied to traditional plays (e.g., Macbeth adaptation to Pawâkan Macbeth).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Organize and document ideas for possible exploration (e.g., portfolio, journal, digital media).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Devise and perform dramatic work inspired by world theatre traditions.

outcomes.statement: Create dramatic work demonstrating use of genre and style.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research style or genre and share learning (e.g., design a student-led workshop, act out a scene).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Incorporate and justify the use of genre and style in own devised work.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Select an aspect of theory and/or style and apply to own work through, for example:
- improvised play
- performance art
- monologue
- scene
- video

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Juxtapose unlike genre and style (e.g., use puppets to explore a political issue, create a Victorian ‘drawing room play’ using social media as script).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Design the look and sound of a scene to reflect a genre or style (e.g., director’s notebook, sketches, production notes, maquette, set list).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the strengths of the drama work and/or performance and reflect on the collaborative approaches, challenges, and individual contributions encountered in the creative process.

outcomes.statement: Express a multiplicity of voices and perspectives (e.g., self, family, community, marginalized individuals, silenced people in history, powerful figures, celebrities, extraterrestrials, fictional characters) through works of dramatic art.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Assume roles in order to represent a variety of voices and perspectives.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: When preparing a scene, monologue or play, consider questions such as: whose voice and perspective is being heard? Who is left out of the story? How does voice impact the story? How does the perspective impact the audience?

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze and describe how personal identity and cultural lens affects creation of the work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore ways of expressing power, status and perspective through drama work (e.g., Image Theatre, Forum Theatre, contextual drama).

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate directorial choices for a performance that utilizes oral or written text and/or devised material.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Collaborate with peers, Elders or community experts to decide on the merits of various creative processes for building a specific drama work (e.g., play, collective creation, devised theatre, performance art).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Work with peers to select a creative process and make a production plan (e.g., roles, budget, timelines, expectations).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop source material (e.g., analyze and/or decode text, image, sound, movement, research, story, idea) and build the drama work within the selected process.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Construct and revise the rehearsal process according to the style and needs of the production.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Engage, where possible, with Saskatchewan directors about their own creative processes (e.g., interview, research, email, view or listen online).

outcomes.statement: Present and sustain a performance for an audience (e.g., peers, invited guests, public) that demonstrates innovation (e.g., aesthetic and technical).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Purposefully use the language of theatre in selected creative processes.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Practically explore the director’s toolbox (e.g., communication of vision, interpretation of oral or written text, analysis and planning, creating a rehearsal plan) for artistic purpose.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Reinterpret or imagine a scene or dramatic work through innovative use of various theatrical toolboxes (e.g., director, designer, actor).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use a specific technical component (e.g., light, costume, sound, digital technologies) for symbolic purposes as a mode for communicating ideas.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Change the point of view of a scene or dramatic work by amplifying a technical or artistic aspect (e.g., incorporate contact improv, actor and audience interaction, replace the actor with an object or technical component, project digital images on moving actors, use social media conventions in performance).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate willingness to take creative risks.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Justify decisions made by various roles (e.g., director, actor, designer) to achieve intent.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on problems, surprises or challenges that arose in the performance and how they might be resolved.

outcomes.statement: Respond critically, using appropriate theatrical language, to directorial choices in a variety of performance experiences (e.g., live, digital).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: View and reflect on a live or recorded performance and discuss the role of the audience in various types of performances (e.g., conventional Western theatre, children’s theatre, forum theatre, site specific).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the differences and similarities between staged theatre and plays adapted to film.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Review and reflect on directorial choices in various genres of recorded and/or live theatre.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: View a filmed adaptation of a play and identify the qualities specific to film that cannot be replicated on stage and the qualities of staged performance that cannot be replicated through film.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss considerations a director makes when creating a film adaptation such as location, setting, directing the viewer’s focus through camera angles and shots, special effects, computer generated imagery (CGI) and editing.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Reflect on the impact of directorial choices on an audience and one’s own experiences viewing plays.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Recognize the effect the location of the theatre has on the audience, such as outdoor theatre, theatre in the round, site-specific theatre, historical theatres.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore several different ways to critique (e.g., written, verbal, collage, multimedia, journal, monologue) using language specific to theatre or film.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss how viewing theatre shapes future decisions in making theatre.

outcomes.statement: Examine the purpose of theatre in societies.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Interview a member of a professional or community-based theatre company about their vision, focus and process (e.g., How do you determine your season? How do you promote your work? How do you get funding? How do you develop a budget? How do you recoup costs?).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a vision and focus for an imagined theatre company.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop an outline to describe an imagined theatre company (e.g., name, company members, season schedule, budget and location).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a proposal, including sponsorship and funding plan (e.g., social media, PR and publicity, logo).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Pitch a proposal for a production, season or grant and defend the proposal to a panel of peers.

outcomes.statement: Research and experiment with contemporary theatre practices.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss connections between Indigenous artistic traditions (e.g., song, dance, stories) and the land, identity and worldview.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Recognize how artistic practices can be specific to a treaty territory, cultural and/or language group in Saskatchewan and Canada (e.g., examine drama and theatre traditions of newcomer students’ communities, treaty education outcome TPP12 - represent personal understanding of the concept, We Are All Treaty People).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research and examine how past traditions inform contemporary theatre.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a maquette or theatrical diagram of modern production choices for a play.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the impact and contributions of contemporary theatre practitioners working within various theatre roles (e.g., writers, dramaturge, performers, directors, stage managers, designers of set/costume/lighting/sound, choreographers of fight/dance, music directors/musicians, technicians).

outcomes.statement: Examine the role of the theatre and artists as potential agents of social change.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze and practically explore a theatre movement that arose in response to social conditions (e.g., Paper Wheat in response to the creation of farming cooperatives in Saskatchewan, Native Earth Performing Arts in response to colonialism, Theatre of the Absurd in Europe and Butoh in Japan in response to WWII, Guerrilla Theatre in response to radical social movements of the 1960s, Bread and Puppets in the 1970s in response to social activism in USA).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Practically explore a current social issue of interest (e.g., treaty education outcome TR12, indicator - analyze how the media currently depicts the treaty relationship and determine the effects this has on public perception, marginalized groups, issues identified in the media) and consider how one might respond through dramatic work.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how theatre artists use their art form to question the status quo and empower others to influence change (e.g., challenging perspectives on gender equity).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry to examine Saskatchewan theatres and theatre artists (e.g., Gordon Tootoosis Nikaniwin Theatre, SUM Theatre, Persephone Theatre, Globe Theatre, Dancing Sky Theatre, Troupe du Jour, Curtain Razors, Listen to Dis, Deaf Crows, Live Five) whose work addresses local and/or global issues (e.g., food security, water access, health, migration, colonization, reconciliation, climate change, gender and sexual diversity, ethics and technologies, economic disparity, economic, social and environmental sustainability).

outcomes.statement: Research contemporary and/or current theatre practices of First Nations, Inuit and Métis artists in Canada.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss questions concerning the relationship between identity and art-making practices (e.g., Does culture influence the subject matter or themes of dramatic work? How might traditional practices inform the work of specific artists?).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Conduct research on a contemporary First Nations, Inuit or Métis theatre company in Canada and report on such things as company philosophy or focus, subject or themes presented, discipline specific or interdisciplinary approaches and/or the potential influence of local cultural practices.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research (e.g., in person interviews, written information, recorded or online interview) an Indigenous theatre artist and examine what impacts his or her work, considering questions such as What is the role of Indigenous theatre in the local community and society? Is it important to distinguish Indigenous theatre separately from non-Indigenous theatre? Does cultural identity influence the work?

evidence.observation: The outcomes page groups the outcomes under 9 unit headings.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate effective communication skills.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Communication (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare and contrast various communication styles.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe how professional communication differs from other types of communication (e.g., personal social media posts, personal cell phone use).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe verbal (e.g., calling someone by their first name) and non-verbal communication (e.g., body language, touch, silence, eye contact, shaking hands) that vary among cultures.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore effective communication methods (e.g., paraphrasing, empathetic listening, asking closed questions, asking open-ended questions, clarifying).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the barriers to effective communication (e.g., vision problems, loud noises, lack of privacy, distractions).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) tools to reduce barriers to communication.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: List common defense mechanisms (e.g., denial, displacement, passive-aggressiveness, projection, rationalization, suppression) and explain how they interfere with effective communication.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain how messages can be misinterpreted when conveyed electronically.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Practise using effective communication techniques for telephone conversations and text messages.

outcomes.statement: Describe ways to respect the privacy and confidentiality of care recipients.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Privacy and Confidentiality (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the importance of maintaining confidentiality in caregiving environments.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the role and significance of various forms used in caregiving environments such as medical release forms, parental permission forms, incident reports and consent to release information forms.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify situations or types of communication which may compromise the privacy and confidentiality of a care recipient (e.g., taking pictures, using the carbon copy or blind carbon copy function in emails).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine strategies used to protect or respect privacy and confidentiality of care recipients, their families and employees in caregiving environments.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify laws and protocols that regulate privacy and confidentiality in caregiving environments.

outcomes.statement: Discuss characteristics of professional conduct.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Professional Conduct (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-4 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify professional qualities such as being attentive, respectful, resourceful, diligent, responsible and ethical.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the role of professional organizations in setting and monitoring codes of conduct.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Discuss professional appearance in various professional caregiving environments.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the use of personal devices while at work in caregiving roles.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore the necessity of establishing personal and professional boundaries.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain what to do if boundaries have been crossed between the care recipient, their family and the caregiver.

outcomes.statement: Research workplace safety principles, practices and relevant legislation required for employees in the workplace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Workplace Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine how provincial Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) legislation outlines the rights and responsibilities of workers and employers.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how hazardous materials in the workplace should be identified, managed and stored according to the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore human rights legislation that protects workers’ basic human rights (e.g., being free from discrimination based on ethnic background, gender, sexual orientation, religion, age or disability).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research injury prevention and safety certifications (e.g., First Aid, CPR, and AED training) in caregiving environments that prepare for employment.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify risks and potential hazards in work area in caregiving environments (e.g., space, location and storage of equipment, ergonomics, electrical cords) and strategies to mitigate risks.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss how employers can support employee mental health as a part of workplace safety.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research the roles and responsibilities of the worker, employer and supervisor in ensuring workplace safety.

outcomes.statement: Explore the worldviews of health and well-being of Métis, First Nations and Inuit people in Canada.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Indigenous Worldviews of Health and Well-Being (Core) · Suggested Time: 7-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the nehiyaw concepts of miyo pimâtisiwin (i.e., living the good life) and wâhkotowin (i.e., we are all related).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the importance of achieving balance between the physical, emotional, mental and spiritual dimensions of being.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine traditional life stages.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate similarities and differences between various understandings of health (e.g., western and Indigenous).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research matotisân, or the Sweat Lodge, as a traditional Indigenous method of healing.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore how Indigenous medicinal knowledge has influenced Western medicinal practices.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate ways traditional Indigenous beliefs, rituals and ceremonies can be incorporated into western health care systems (e.g., smudging, traditional medicines).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the connection between a healthy environment and individual and community health.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the structure of First Nations and Métis families and communities and their role in supporting health and well-being (e.g., extended family members providing critical care).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research Métis or First Nations care facilities in Saskatchewan (e.g., All Nations Healing Hospital, Round Prairie Elders’ Lodge, Sturgeon Lake First Nation Health Centre) and their approach to holistic care.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss the gathering, harvesting and uses of traditional medicines and healing practices with an Elder or Knowledge Keeper.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Investigate protocols to follow when seeking traditional knowledge from Elders and Knowledge Keepers about traditional life stages, Sweat Lodges, and uses of traditional medicines.

outcomes.statement: Investigate principles related to ethical practice in caregiving environments.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Ethical Practice (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define ethical values and responsibilities.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between personal ethics and professional ethics.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine a code of ethics for a profession or practice related to health care and/or early learning.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Outline the professional and legal consequences and penalties for violating professional standards and ethics in health care and/or early learning environments.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine steps to take when professional standards and code of ethics have been violated.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate effective collaboration skills for managing conflict, providing and receiving feedback and making decisions in the workplace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7: Collaboration (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the concept of conflict and why it occurs in work settings.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the importance of dealing with conflict.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate problem-solving processes, including talking circles, to identifying the problem, analyzing the problem and devising a plan.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate alternative approaches to problem solving that are inclusive of different cultural backgrounds.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe ways to provide constructive feedback.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine strategies for receiving feedback from others.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Practise using active listening strategies to receive feedback from others.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Use collaboration skills when working with others.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate the use of talking circles to solve problems and collaborate.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate consensus building strategies to make decisions.

outcomes.statement: Explain key aspects of human development and growth.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Human Growth and Development (Core) · Suggested Time: 7-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate different historical and contemporary theories of human growth and development by various authors such as Erikson, Vygotsky, Bronfenbrenner, Bandura and Piaget.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the domains of development (i.e. physical, social-emotional, spiritual and intellectual).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the physical, social-emotional, intellectual and spiritual development of infants, toddlers, preschoolers and school-aged children.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss a-typical physical, social-emotional, intellectual and spiritual development of infants, toddlers, preschoolers and school-aged children.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the development of human growth for different age groups in early childhood, middle childhood, late childhood, adolescence, young adulthood, middle adulthood, and late adulthood.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore traditional Indigenous perspectives of life cycles and human growth.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate how interaction with nature affects wellness in individuals.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Nature and Wellness (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-4 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the impact of nature on stress and mood.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Evaluate how interactions with nature affects personal well-being, mood and behaviour.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the link between lack of exposure to nature and depression.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how nature encourages pro-social behaviours.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate how time spent in nature can impact personal connection to community.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research opportunities to bring nature indoors.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the benefits of images and sounds of nature in indoor environments.

outcomes.statement: Explore ways to provide culturally safe care in caregiving environments.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Culturally Safe Care (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-4 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between cultural awareness and cultural sensitivity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Recognize personal cultural perspectives on caring for others such as the very young or older adults.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate alternative worldviews related to caregiving.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify and analyze how personal biases may affect professional relationships in caregiving environments.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify ways to support home languages in caregiving environments.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe signs of ageism and age discrimination.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify ways to respect diversity (e.g., using respectful accommodations) in caregiving environments.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the physical environment (e.g. visual décor, sounds, access to nature) of a culturally safe caregiving environment.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the legal ramifications of accommodating or declining to accommodate cultural preferences in caregiving environments.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss ways to improve employee understanding of various cultures present in caregiving environments.

outcomes.statement: Examine the benefits of volunteering in caregiving environments in the community.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Volunteering (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify reasons to volunteer (e.g., to learn more about a career, to contribute to the community, to help others).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the characteristics of an effective volunteer (e.g., respectful, on task, punctual, enthusiastic).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the social benefits of volunteering in caregiving environments for individuals and the community.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how volunteering improves community wellness.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore how volunteers support care recipients in health care and early learning environments.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss how volunteering may contribute to future employment opportunities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research local volunteering opportunities in caregiving environments in the community.

outcomes.statement: Examine caregiving approaches for infants.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: Caring for Infants (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate how early learning and child care environments must meet the nutritional needs of infants (e.g., bottle feeding, using breast milk, formula, introduction to solid foods).
