outcomes.statement: Assess approaches used by emergency services personnel in supporting diverse populations in the community.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Relationships in the Community (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze the diversity in the local community, Saskatchewan and Canada, including cultural and linguistic needs.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect on the importance of building positive relationships within the local community as emergency services personnel.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss ways in which to build positive relationships in the community as emergency service personnel.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research the potential impact of discrimination based on factors such as ancestry, nationality, creed, gender, sexual orientation and age on the provision of emergency services.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore strategies (e.g., technology, subscribing to interpretation and translation services) used by emergency services personnel to effectively assist and communicate with individuals from diverse backgrounds and needs.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the challenges and opportunities (e.g., cost, availability of translators, time to provide service) that occur when communicating with community members who speak English as an additional language.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of utilizing inclusionary practices when serving the public.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the application of effective communications during an emergency.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7: Emergency Communications (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of effective communication during an emergency.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine strategies for communicating effectively during an emergency.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the interpersonal skills required of those working or assisting at an emergency.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the methods (i.e., radio/telecommunications, interpersonal, written/data) of emergency communications.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Justify the most appropriate communication method for a variety of given emergency situations.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the history and current usage of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) phonetic alphabet in emergency communications.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Converse with others using the NATO phonetic alphabet.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore tips for basic etiquette (e.g., introduce oneself immediately, speak clearly, listen intently) that contribute to effective communication.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the components of a Location, Conditions, Actions, Needs (LCAN) report.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Describe instances when an LCAN report could be used in emergency communications.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine the history, usage and coverage of the Provincial Public Safety Telecommunications Network (PPSTN).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Examine procedures for sending and receiving radio messages while using the PPSTN.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Describe the purpose and components of a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) in an emergency situation.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Examine reasons why basic common language rather than 10 codes are used in interagency emergency communication.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Investigate the purpose of public safety alert systems (e.g., SaskAlert, Amber Alert, Silver Alert) in Saskatchewan and Canada.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the use of social media as a communication tool during an emergency.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Social Media (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 7

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify examples of emergency communications using common social media platforms.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages (e.g., instantaneous messaging; supporting various media such as text, video and audio; audience reach) and disadvantages (e.g., short, concise messages may be misunderstood; loss of control of a message after it is sent; limited audience reach) associated with using social media to communicate with the public during an emergency.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the implications (e.g., to self, others and community) of misuse of social media by bystanders in an emergency situation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research ways that social media could be used effectively to manage communications during an emergency.

outcomes.statement: Assess the purpose and importance of professionalism in all areas of emergency services.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Professionalism in Emergency Services (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain deportment as it relates to the professionalism of emergency services personnel.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Summarize professional skills (e.g., respect for all individuals, groups and people; punctuality; integrity; ability to contribute positively to a team with diverse members; responsible use of social media) that contribute to good deportment.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Justify the personal and professional importance of deportment for those who work in emergency services.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop and implement a plan for developing and demonstrating additional professional skills required for a successful career in emergency services.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the use of uniform and dress, including ceremonial attire, associated with various areas of emergency services.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the origin, symbolism and use of badges such as the Maltese Cross, in emergency services.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Outline reasons to maintain confidentiality in the provision of emergency services.

outcomes.statement: Examine basic first aid used by all emergency services personnel.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Basic First Aid (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define the terms first aid and first aider.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Discuss the three P’s or aims of first aid to:
- preserve life;
- prevent the injury or illness from getting worse; and,
- promote recovery.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Examine the ABCD basics of basic first aid including:
- Airway – Does the patient have an open airway?
- Breathing – Is the patient breathing? Is it effective breathing?
- Circulation – Does the patient have a pulse?
- Deadly bleeding – Is the patient bleeding, and if so, how badly?

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify potential actions (e.g., calling 911) and equipment used to assist in providing the ABCD basics of basic first aid.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Identify the characteristics of non-time-critical emergencies (e.g., minor cuts or bruises, rash, sprain).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Participate in mock emergency situations to practise appropriate initial responses to scenarios where first aid is required.

outcomes.statement: Investigate strategies for assessing a patient during an emergency.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Assessment of a Medical Patient (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 10

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the purpose of medical identification jewellery (e.g., bracelet, neckpiece).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess the importance of searching a patient’s wrist and neck for medical identification jewellery.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe elements of an initial general assessment (e.g., posture, facial expression, sitting position, breathing that interferes with the ability to speak) that might provide diagnostic clues to the patient’s condition or illness.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Examine the AVPU (i.e., Alert, Verbal, Pain, Unresponsive) scale that helps determine a patient’s level of consciousness.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Assess the vital signs (i.e., consciousness, breathing, pulse, skin temperature, pupils) to be monitored while treating an injured person, and the frequency (e.g., every 5 to 10 minutes) for doing so.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Examine elements of the LOCPRESS acronym for monitoring vital signs, including
- LOC – level of consciousness
- P – pulse
- R – respiration;
- E – eyes;

indicators.text: Discuss the importance of the IMIM/Use of Force Model in policing and ways in which the model changes a police officer’s response.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Consider scenarios (e.g., physical threats, verbal threats, addictions, mental health) and responses using the IMIM/Use of Force model.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine ethical and moral situations police encounter daily in community policing (e.g., respecting confidentiality of community members, policing friends and family).

outcomes.statement: Assess the purpose and importance of drill and deportment in policing.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 34: Drill and Deportment in Policing (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 32

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze the similarities and differences in drill and deportment between different police forces (e.g., federal, provincial, municipal and First Nations).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the use of drill and deportment as a training tool in police training programs (e.g., enforcing attention to detail, self-discipline).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the evolution of personal grooming standards in policing, such as allowing long hair, beards and tattoos.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the process of learning about drill structure as an RCMP recruit at Depot.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the traditions and uses of events, such as the Seargent Major’s Parade, Sunset Ceremony and Musical Ride in the RCMP.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the history of the use of drill in the RCMP, including dismounted cavalry drill.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate ways foot drill is utilized in community events (e.g., Remembrance Day, parades) when different organizations (e.g., municipal police, RCMP, Canadian Forces) march together.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Practise or describe basic foot drill movements.

outcomes.statement: Assess the use of personal protective equipment and clothing in policing.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 35: Personal Protective Equipment and Clothing in Policing (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 4B and 32

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify hazards (e.g., bodily fluids, broken glass, harmful chemicals, animals) commonly faced by police officers.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate common pieces of personal protective equipment (PPE) (e.g., Kevlar vest, duty belt with full operational gear, uniform, search gloves, CSA certified footwear, first aid kit, Naloxone) police officers are required to wear.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the evolution of PPE technology utilized in past and present policing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe situations in which specific pieces of police PPE (e.g., body armor, gas mask, search gloves) are used based on situational tasks.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the characteristics and features of police PPE and clothing that provide protection to officers.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess problems (i.e., restricted visibility, weight, maneuverability, comfort, weather conditions) associated with a variety of police PPE and clothing.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research the different types of uniforms available to police officers, such as general duty, plain clothes and ceremonial dress.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine situations in which police officers select work uniforms based on assigned work situations such as general duty or special task.

outcomes.statement: Investigate preparation for, and use of, the Police Fitness Assessment and the Police Officer Physical Abilities Test in police training.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 36: Fitness Assessments in Police Training (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-6 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 32

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze the components of the Police Fitness Assessment (PFA).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze the components of the Police Officer Physical Abilities Test (POPAT).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the reasons for the requirement of the PFA/POPAT assessment in police training programs.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the evolution of the use of the PFA/POPAT assessment in policing training.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore reasons why police recruits must pass the PFA/POPAT assessment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the preparations (e.g., training plan) and requirements (e.g., doctor’s physical assessment) for the PFA/POPAT assessment.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the benchmarks required to pass the PFA/POPAT assessment in police training programs.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create a plan to train for the components of the PFA/POPAT assessment.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in a practice PFA/POPAT assessment.

outcomes.statement: Examine rural and remote policing realities in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 37: Rural and Remote Policing (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 32

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the geographic areas which are considered to be rural and remote policing jurisdictions in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate scenarios (e.g, one person responding to a call for service, shift work, working nights) common to rural and remote policing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the skill set required for first on the scene emergency response (e.g., administering first aid, securing the scene, directing traffic, communicating with operations center) for police officers.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore ways in which RCMP/police interact and communicate with local fire and EMS services during scene calls.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify ways which demographics and local culture influence policing response.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore unique situations (e.g., responding to a call individually, no immediate back up, geographical distance) which police officers may encounter while responding to calls for service.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the importance of police officers understanding threat cues and perceived dangers to inform decision making to protect the safety of themselves and the community.

outcomes.statement: Assess the skills and procedures required to manage a scene call as a police officer.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 38: Incident Management and Response in Policing (Optional) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 32

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate situations (e.g., collisions, human crime, property crime) in which police secure and manage the scene.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Determine procedures to secure and preserve evidence at a scene (e.g., photographing evidence, assist collision reconstructionist, etc.).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the basic procedures of documentation, note taking and photographing evidence after an emergency and/or crime scene has been secured.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify challenges and barriers to evidence preservation (e.g., weather, human interference, time).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the roles and responsibilities of specialized police officers (e.g., forensic analyst, collision reconstructionist) at scene calls.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify situations in which interagency response is required.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the role of the Division Emergency Operations Centre (DEOC) when Incident Command System (ICS) is initiated.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate or describe the procedures of scene call management for a mock collision and/or crime scene.

outcomes.statement: Explore the responsibilities of police officers post-incident.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 39: Post-incident Management and Response in Policing (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-8 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 32

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the basics of report writing (e.g., writing style, components to include in reports) in policing.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the components taking of statements (e.g., witness, victim, suspect).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the differences between custodial and non-custodial interviews.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the psychology (e.g., creating a safe space) of obtaining statements.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the requirements of legally obtaining statements.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the importance of accurate and quality investigations.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the benchmarks of the investigative processes.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the consequences of incomplete investigative processes.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the role of Victim Services in assisting police and victims after crime, tragedy and throughout the criminal justice process.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the importance of the victim impact statement in investigations.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Assess reasons why the investigative processes may be delayed (e.g., time for forensic lab to complete analysis, time to conduct interviews).

outcomes.statement: Explore various career options available in policing.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 40: Career Options in Policing (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 32

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the various career options available in policing in the field setting, such as general duty, police dog and marine services.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the various career options available in policing in the office setting, such as computer crime, financial crime and identification.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research ways in which police officers can advance into other career options in the policing field once they have trained and gained experience in the general duty setting.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate civilian career positions (e.g., forensics lab, legal, analysts) that support police services.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the rank structure of policing services.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the promotion processes in the rank structure (e.g., examinations, competencies, years of service) within police organizations.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe recognition of individual achievement (e.g., medals, badges) in policing.

outcomes.statement: Investigate search and rescue services in Saskatchewan and Canada.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 41: An Introduction to Search and Rescue (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the purpose of Search and Rescue (SAR) services.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the organizational structure, implementation and operation of SAR services in Saskatchewan and in Canada, including the roles of the Search and Rescue Saskatchewan Association of Volunteers (SARSAV) and the Search and Rescue Volunteer Association of Canada (SARVAC).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the origins of SARSAV and SARVAC.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify SAR chapters in Saskatchewan and the communities they serve, including those that serve First Nations communities (e.g., Prince Albert Grand Council Search, Rescue and Recovery; Southern Saskatchewan First Nations SAR; La Loche Dene Trackers).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the support that the Canadian Rangers provide to SAR in Northern and other areas of Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the general responsibilities associated with the three levels of searchers (i.e., searcher, team leader, manager) involved in a search and rescue (SAR) mission.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the skills and abilities (e.g., team player, communication skills, professionalism, responsibility) required of a basic level search and rescue volunteer.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the physical and psychological demands associated with being a basic level searcher.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Assess hazards (e.g., environment, animals, insects) associated with SAR.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the process for becoming a volunteer searcher in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explore the process of searching for a missing person in the local community.

outcomes.statement: Analyze elements of a search and rescue mission.

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Identify SAR technology tools (e.g., GPS, Family Radio Systems, Personal Location Beacons, Night Vision Goggles).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate correct use of GPS or compass commonly equipment used by searchers.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare the supplies and personal and protective equipment (PPE) required for SAR missions in various locations (e.g., northern, rural, urban, remote) and at various times of the year in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the items typically found in a 24-hour SAR kit.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify practical steps for maintaining field health and hygiene for SAR missions of varying durations and in a variety of locations.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Demonstrate proper procedures for radio communication for a SAR mission.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the importance of relationships with the local First Nations community (e.g., knowledge of the land, community, people and language) can make to a SAR mission on First Nations land or for a First Nation’s individual.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain protocols that are required to conduct a SAR mission on First Nations land or for a First Nations individual.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss typical procedures for call-out and check-in associated with a SAR mission.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Describe the purpose and process of an After Action Review (AAR).

outcomes.statement: Examine the relationship between an understanding of lost person behaviour and successful search and rescue efforts.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 43: Lost Person Behaviour (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 41

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe scenarios when an individual may be considered lost (e.g., a small child wanders away from a farmyard; a hunter does not return home at the anticipated time; a lone skier on a remote hill breaks a leg in a fall and cannot move).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research facts about lost person behaviour pertaining to factors such as age (e.g., toddler, child, teenager, adult), mental conditions (e.g., suffering from dementia or mental illness) and reason for being outdoors (e.g., hiker, hunter, nature photographer).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine strategies and ways that individuals who are lost can make it easier for searchers to find them.

outcomes.statement: Create a public awareness campaign that addresses a community safety concern.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 44: Public Awareness Campaign (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the purpose of a public awareness campaign.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate local, provincial and federal public safety awareness campaigns from various branches of emergency services (e.g., fire, police, EMS).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the characteristics (e.g., clearly defined goal(s) or outcomes; a well-defined target audience; specific actions requested of the target audience; plans for measuring success) of a successful awareness campaign or program.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify a community safety concern (e.g., proper installation and use of car seats, sun safety, snowmobile safety, pedestrian crossing safety, texting and driving, vehicle or home emergency kits, fire extinguishers in the home).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore different media methods utilized for public safety campaigns, such as social media, newspaper and radio advertising and billboard advertising.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create a public awareness campaign that address a community safety concern.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: Modules 5A and 9

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Examine the diversity and impact of Saskatchewan’s energy and mining sectors.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Introduction to Energy and Mines (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Review forms and sources of energy (e.g., chemical, mechanical and potential) in the context of human activity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the principles of energy release, conversion and utilization.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the fundamental differences between matter and energy.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the renewable and non-renewable energy and mineral resources found in Saskatchewan and the local area.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the main stages of the exploration, mining and drilling processes.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the role of government ministries and Indigenous peoples in the energy and mining sectors.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate some of the commercial enterprises that engage in mining, drilling and support activities in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the impact of the energy and mining on society (e.g., communication technology, manufacturing, agriculture and consumer products and services).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the history of the hiring practices in the energy and mining sectors to include diverse groups (e.g., women, Indigenous peoples and immigrants).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explore recruitment and retention strategies for diverse groups in the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify local energy and mineral companies.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Discuss local, national and global current events in the energy and mining sectors.

outcomes.statement: Explore the safety standards of the energy and mining industries.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2A: Workplace Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze the historical safety statistics on injuries in the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify strategies to mitigate risks and potential safety hazards in energy, petroleum and mining operations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the use of zero energy state and lockout tagout features of equipment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how the Globally Harmonized System (GHS) is used.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the reliance on basic safety policies when using advanced technology.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe ways to reduce personal injury because of unsafe work activities (e.g., lifting heavy objects, travelling underground and blasting) or environments (e.g., working around large and noisy equipment, radiation exposure and working underground).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate ways to mitigate damage to equipment because of unsafe work activities or environments.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the safety regulations, procedures, equipment and personnel at local or regional mining, drilling and power generation sites.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the use of personal protective equipment (PPE) (e.g., masks, ear plugs, safety goggles and footwear) for respiratory, hearing, sight and body protection.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the hierarchy of controls including elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative controls and PPE.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify potential fire hazards and prevention procedures in underground mines, well sites and processing plants.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain the importance of emergency response teams, drills and procedures at a mine site.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Assess the consequences of failure of one or more worker safety programs or controls, whether through accident or not following established procedures.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Explore the chief hazards and risks (e.g., high voltage power lines, turbines and ground falls) faced by workers in energy and mining industries.

outcomes.statement: Explore the safety standards of the energy and mining industries.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2B: Workplace Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze the historical safety statistics on injuries in the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify strategies to mitigate risks and potential safety hazards in energy, petroleum and mining operations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the use of zero energy state and lockout tagout features of equipment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how the Globally Harmonized System (GHS) is used.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the reliance on basic safety policies when using advanced technology.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe ways to reduce personal injury because of unsafe work activities (e.g., lifting heavy objects, travelling underground and blasting) or environments (e.g., working around large and noisy equipment, radiation exposure and working underground).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate ways to mitigate damage to equipment because of unsafe work activities or environments.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the safety regulations, procedures, equipment and personnel at local or regional mining, drilling and power generation sites.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the use of personal protective equipment (PPE) (e.g., masks, ear plugs, safety goggles and footwear) for respiratory, hearing, sight and body protection.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the hierarchy of controls including elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative controls and PPE.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify potential fire hazards and prevention procedures in underground mines, well sites and processing plants.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain the importance of emergency response teams, drills and procedures at a mine site.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Assess the consequences of failure of one or more worker safety programs or controls, whether through accident or not following established procedures.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Explore the chief hazards and risks (e.g., high voltage power lines, turbines and ground falls) faced by workers in energy and mining industries.

outcomes.statement: Explore Saskatchewan's landforms and natural environments and their relationship to the location of renewable and non-renewable resources.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Physical Geography of Saskatchewan (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define physical geography.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how the geological processes of weathering, evaporation and erosion transform the Earth's land surface over time.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide specific examples from Saskatchewan’s landscape that illustrate the numerous branches of physical geography (e.g., geomorphology, hydrology, glaciology, biogeography, climatology and geomatics).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the impact of continental glaciation in shaping Saskatchewan’s key topographic features (e.g., Qu’Appelle valley).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the variance of current vegetation zones of Saskatchewan and why some areas are devoid of resource production (e.g., forestry in central Saskatchewan and environmentally protected areas).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the difference between and provide local examples of renewable and non-renewable resource.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe how the physical geography and climate of Saskatchewan are unique to the rest of Canada and other parts of the world.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify where the most prominent natural resources are geographically located (e.g., clay and potash in southern regions and uranium in northern Saskatchewan).

outcomes.statement: Investigate the scientific theories and principles that explain the formation of landforms on Earth and their relationship to the location of renewable and non-renewable resources.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Saskatchewan Geology and Geological History (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the relationship between geology and physical geography.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the three rock types, the fundamental cycles of matter in the Earth's mantle, crust and atmosphere (e.g., hydrologic, mineral and rock cycles, subduction and carbon/carbonate cycle) and their role in the formation of mineral and energy resources.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the significance of the fundamental scientific principles of geology (e.g., principle of uniformitarianism, principle of superposition, principle of faunal succession and theory of plate tectonics) in understanding the present nature of Earth's surface, crust and sedimentary strata.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the formation of sedimentary strata in terms of origin of sedimentary material, transportation, deposition and lithification.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the role of sedimentary strata in the preservation of fossil materials, including fossil fuels (e.g., folding and hydrocarbon traps).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the purpose of a stratigraphic chart and its importance to the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore the Phanerozoic eon including its age, eras and formations and its relevance to modern day Saskatchewan geology.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the types of resources and commodities that are utilized from different formations (e.g., Bakken formation produces light oil).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify mine locations, types of deposits and estimated reserves of natural resources (e.g., uranium, other metals, helium, diamonds, coal, oil, natural gas and potash) in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain why geology and geological history are important in the energy and mining industries.

outcomes.statement: Investigate groundwater and how it is extracted.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5A: Introduction to Groundwater (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define groundwater.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the importance of groundwater based on its uses and availability locally and worldwide.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the hydrologic cycle with a focus on groundwater components.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the process of infiltration.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Create a diagram of the subsurface configuration of hydrogeological layers containing groundwater.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore how groundwater is extracted and the purpose of different types of wells (e.g., drilled vs. bored, withdrawal vs. monitoring and domestic vs. industrial).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore the similarities and differences between saturated and unsaturated zones.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the extraction of groundwater and the advantages and disadvantages on the environment and community at large (e.g., animals, vegetation, land subsidence and sinkhole formation, and the people of our province including surrounding Indigenous communities).

outcomes.statement: Explore the movement of groundwater.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5B: Groundwater Movement (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 5A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the mechanism, forces, and material properties that result in and control groundwater movement.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the evolution of groundwater flow along a path in terms of flow path (length), residence time and groundwater quality (fresh, brackish and saline).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the connection between groundwater and surface streams.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the effects of pumping on a water table, surface water and water levels in general including the formation of a drawdown cone.

outcomes.statement: Investigate treaty relationships with First Nations peoples as they relate to the energy and mining industries.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Treaties and Traditional Territory (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the history of numbered treaties in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a map of treaty boundaries and Indigenous communities in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the impact The Saskatchewan Treaty Land Entitlement Framework Agreement on the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how First Nations and Métis people use storytelling to convey knowledge about the land (e.g., the impact on Indigenous communities, families, traditional foods and medicines).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare treaty relationships and the spirit and intent of the treaties, where both parties benefit, to other relationships found within the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the past and current relationship crown and private corporations have with Indigenous peoples when developing energy and mining resources.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine how treaty rights and traditional territories impact energy and mining.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the positions of First Nations and government agencies responsible for the management and stewardship of energy and mining resources (e.g., duty to consult process).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect on how energy and mining relationships can support necessary and ongoing efforts of reconciliation.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explore the impact of the Natural Resources Transfer Agreements on both the Indigenous peoples and the resource industry.

outcomes.statement: Examine the sustainability of the energy and mining industries.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7: Sustainability (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Interpret data comparing Canadian energy and resource consumption to the rest of North America and the world to determine the sustainability of Canadian resources.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Critique the implications of Saskatchewan’s current and sustainable levels of energy use, in the context of climate change, global economic demand and available resources.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe actions that can be taken to live and work more sustainably with non-renewable resources today and into the future.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Propose a plan to sustain the energy sector when non-renewable resources are gone.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the pressure placed on non-renewable mineral resources (e.g., silver and lithium) due to developments in technology (e.g., microchips).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of continuing to explore and mine mineral and petroleum resources.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the role of social media in the spreading of information and how to determine fact versus fiction.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate how Saskatchewan’s energy and mining industries provide increased national supply chain security.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research sustainable practices in the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain how conservation relates to sustainability and long-term planning.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explore the impact of renewable energy sources on the sustainability of the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Investigate sustainable practices in energy and mining to maintain water resources.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Reflect on land sustainability from First Nations and Métis worldviews (e.g., keepers of the land).

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Examine how different worldviews (e.g., First Nations and Métis and Western) impact human interaction with the land.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Explore the direct connection and importance of the relationship Indigenous people have with the land.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the short- and long-term environmental impacts of the energy and mining industries.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Environmental Impact (Core) · Suggested Time: 6-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 6

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the acts and regulations in place to protect the environment in energy and resource industries and how they are applied in practice.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess the consequences of failure of one or more environmental safety programs or controls (e.g., oil well fire, natural gas leak and mining tailings dam failure), whether through accident or not following established procedures.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Complete a case study of the environmental impact and resulting fines of past accidents in Saskatchewan (e.g., Husky pipeline leak into North Saskatchewan River and Nexen oil spill at Long Lake).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine provincial policy on communication with Indigenous peoples including The First Nation and Métis Consultation Policy Framework (which includes the duty to consult) and federal or international policies like the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) and The Indian Act.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the relationship between The Natural Resources Transfer Acts and The Saskatchewan First Act and its impact on both Indigenous peoples and resource industry stakeholders.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the duty to consult and the consultation process with local communities and Indigenous stakeholders on the environmental impact of an energy or mining project (e.g., mining, drilling, refinery, alternate energy and transportation of resources).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify specific safety, prevention and environmental protection procedures normally observed at a drilling, mining or processing site.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the factors (e.g., land, forests and waterways) considered when conducting an environmental impact study.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Compare the environmental scores of the resource industry in Saskatchewan to the rest of the world.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the innovation and green solutions (e.g., Mcllvenna Bay in Northern Saskatchewan, the world’s first carbon neutral copper project) that have been developed and implemented in the energy and mining sectors.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss the sustainability and environmental impact (e.g., bio fuels cause deforestation) of different green solutions.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explore the environmental protection measures in place to ensure proper decommissioning and reclamation of energy and mining projects.

outcomes.statement: Examine the advancements in technology in the energy and mining industries.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Introduction to Technology (Core) · Suggested Time: 6-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Explain how the energy and mining sectors gather data and why the data compiled through exploration and other energy and mining processes must be credible to be useful in technology and in other areas.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore how development of technology in other industries is adaptable to the energy and mining sectors.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare the technology used for hard and soft rock mining.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how technology is used in preventative and predictive maintenance programs.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate Canadian organizations involved in research and development of technology in the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Trace the advancement in technology of different types of equipment (e.g., drilling, robotic vehicles and surveying) including changes being suggested for the future.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the processes involved in planning for exploration of natural resources in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10A: Natural Resource Exploration Planning (Core) · Suggested Time: 6-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 6

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the differences in permits (e.g., environmental, exploration and seismic), land permission, First Nations and Métis consultation and accommodations and not disturbing historic land (e.g., former settlements) that are required to explore for different natural resources (e.g., coal, potash, petroleum and uranium).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the impact of duty to consult on both Indigenous peoples and resource industry stakeholders.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the government acts (e.g., Mineral Resources Act) and regulations (e.g., the Mineral Tenure Registry and the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulations) that govern the exploration for natural resources.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the distinction between mineral, surface and access rights for landowners.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate land rights, land acquisition, landowner consent and engagement with communities as important parts of exploration.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify potential consequences of natural resource exploration including the impact on the environment (e.g., land, forests and waterways), conservation and sustainability.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the reasons mining companies conduct feasibility studies and environmental impact assessments prior to engaging landowners in a pre-mining process.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the three main methods of oil/gas exploration.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the similarities and differences in the methods of exploration for oil/gas and mineral deposits.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze the difference in timelines of the general development processes of an oil/gas well and a mine.

outcomes.statement: Explore the general processes involved in the exploration of natural resources in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10B: Natural Resource Exploration (Core) · Suggested Time: 6-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 10A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the types of tools (e.g., 3D seismic, core samples, satellite imagery) used to explore for resources.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how the geology of an area and type of resource determines the exploration methods used.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how the search for one natural resource may result in the discovery of another.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how hole logging is used to map the geology of an area to identify targets, hydrocarbon traps and potash deposits.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze wireline logs with different horizons shown on them.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how databases are used to openly share information about the exploration of natural resources.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain how the development of software to analyze data helps locate new natural resource deposits.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare the critical minerals that occur and are mined in Canada with those currently mined and produced in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Compare the exploration methods for critical minerals to traditional methods used for coal and diamonds.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze maps comparing lakes, forests, towns, villages, treaty areas and First Nations communities with staked claims and current mining or drilling projects.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Analyze the impact that clear cutting of the natural forest can have on people (e.g., Indigenous peoples’ traditional medicines and food sustainability) and animals.

outcomes.statement: Examine the processes involved in the decommissioning and reclamation of mines and orphaned wells.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Decommissioning and Reclamation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 6-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 8

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the concept of decommissioning and its importance.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the historical development of decommissioning and reclamation of mines and orphaned wells, including the involvement of First Nations and Métis peoples.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the impact of orphaned mines and wells on the natural water supply (i.e., sustainability of the animals, plants and the health of communities including the Indigenous peoples).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the current government acts and regulations overseeing the end-of-life process for mining and drilling operations.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the role of organizations (e.g., Saskatchewan Environmental Quality Committee) in quality control of decommissioning and reclamation projects.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify the elements of a decommissioning and reclamation plan.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe how an end-of-life plan is developed to determine the real cost and what needs to be done for each project.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore environmental elements (e.g., replacing the soil and aggregate, planting trees and having proper runoff for lakes and streams) in decommissioning and reclaiming a site.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain the importance of continuous monitoring of a reclaimed site.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the role of Indigenous partnerships, resource companies and The Saskatchewan First Act in reestablishing sites.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explore how native prairie grasses, wetland and forested areas are re-established.

indicators.label: l
m
indicators.text: Investigate other uses (e.g., hydrogen or carbon dioxide gas storage and tourism) of underground mine formations and petroleum reservoirs.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Discuss when a mining or petroleum company can officially be released from responsibility of a site.

outcomes.statement: Examine the principles of effective communication skills in energy and mines.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: Effective Communication in Energy and Mines (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of effective communication skills (e.g., speaking, writing, listening and reading) for those employed in energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the characteristics (e.g., specific language choice, simple instructions and concise answers) of effective verbal and written communication.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the types of communication (e.g., reading and interpreting products and manuals, discussing equipment needs with suppliers and managing employees) required in energy and mining sectors.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain why communication is a critical component of safety procedures.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the role that negotiation plays in effective business communication.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research negotiation strategies used to acquire better business deals within the energy and mining industries.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify communication tools (e.g., video conferencing, broadcast media and social media), the skills required to effectively use them and when they might be used.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of communication between industry, suppliers (e.g., equipment manufacturers), consumers and the public about energy and mining practices.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify learning resources (e.g., Sask Mining, Student Energy and Petroleum Technology Research Center) specific to energy and mining topics.

outcomes.statement: Explore the royalty structure in the energy and mining industries.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13: Royalties (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 6 and 12

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship between surface and mineral (sub surface) rights.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how mine mouth value and royalty holidays affect royalty payments.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the change in royalties paid by the resource industry to the provincial government from the 1970s to now.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the difference between Crown royalty payments and freehold production tax.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe how the base rate and marginal rate for royalties are applied.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the past and current resource revenue sharing processes followed by crown and private corporations with Indigenous peoples in Canada.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the difference in percentage of revenue sharing in energy and natural resource sectors.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the impact Saskatchewan Treaty Land Entitlement Act has on the royalty structure in the mining industry.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify the average percentage of workers on mining projects that are from the First Nations peoples on traditional territories.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain the impact of The Natural Resources Transfer Acts and The Saskatchewan First Act on royalty structure.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the characteristics and formation of oil, gas and coal deposits in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14: Oil, Gas and Coal Formation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 4

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare the different types of oil (e.g., heavy and light crude) and gas (e.g., sweet and sour natural gas).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the physical and chemical characteristics of different samples of crude oil.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the different types of coal (e.g., lignite, bituminous and anthracite).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Summarize the physical and chemical characteristics of different samples of coal.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the natural processes that produced oil, gas and coal in Saskatchewan during the Carboniferous period.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare oil, gas and coal deposits in Saskatchewan with other provinces and countries.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain how the type of deposit formation (e.g., porous rock and oil sands, and shallow versus deep coal seams) will determine the type of extraction used.

outcomes.statement: Investigate oil and gas exploration in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15: Petroleum Exploration (Optional) · Suggested Time: 6-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 6, 10B and 14

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify historical and everyday uses of oil and gas.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate how oil and gas were discovered in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Outline major events in the history of oil and gas exploration in Saskatchewan, Canada and globally.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the permits (e.g., environmental, exploration and seismic), land permission, First Nations and Métis consultation and accommodations and not disturbing historic land (e.g., former settlements) that are required to explore for petroleum.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the relationship between the large-scale geology of an area and the process of locating oil and gas.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe the theory and process of traditional seismic and subsurface imaging exploration.

indicators.label: g
h
indicators.text: Investigate how petroleum and other fluids move within the Earth’s crust.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the effect of rock porosity and permeability on the extraction of oil and gas.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate how exploration technology and processes collect data about oil and gas deposits.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explain how data is used to map the specific location of oil and gas deposits.

outcomes.statement: Explore oil and gas extraction.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16: Petroleum Extraction (Optional) · Suggested Time: 8-12 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the importance of oil and gas companies conducting feasibility studies and environmental impact assessments prior to establishing a drilling site.

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j

indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.
