indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess the effect of new understandings and strategies on self and others.

outcomes.statement:
View, listen to, read, comprehend, and respond to a variety of grade-appropriate international, including indigenous, texts that address:
- identity (e.g., Sense of Self)
- social responsibility (e.g., Social Criticism), and
- social action (agency) (e.g., Addressing the Issues).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore topics and contemporary and traditional visual, oral, written, and multimedia (including digital) texts that present different viewpoints and perspectives on issues related to identity, diverse personal identities, worldviews, and backgrounds (e.g., culture, socio-economic status, ability, age, gender, language).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: View, listen to, read, and respond to a variety of historical and contemporary literary and informational (including business and technological communication) texts by authors from a variety of cultures, backgrounds, and time periods.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Make connections between the ideas in texts and personal knowledge, experiences, and insights; between other texts; and between texts and the world.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Consider how historical, cultural, political, and social contexts influence the presentation of ideas, themes, and issues in texts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze texts in terms of messages, ideas, information, universal questions, themes, and issues; provide evidence from the texts to support analysis.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how informational and literary texts contribute to an understanding of human nature and of self, and raise awareness about a range of topics, ideas, cultures, events, people, and issues.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify ways in which informational and literary texts might promote social and personal change.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate appreciation for a variety of texts.

outcomes.statement: View, comprehend, and evaluate critically a variety of visual and multimedia texts by international, including indigenous, artists and authors from various cultural communities, and identify how the texts address beliefs, values, and power.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: View, respond to, and interpret visual and multimedia texts created by artists and authors from various cultural communities including indigenous peoples.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select deliberately and use effectively a variety of before (page 27), during (page 28), and after (page 29) strategies to construct and confirm meaning when viewing texts.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Use language cues and conventions (page 25) from a variety of informational and literary texts to construct and confirm meaning when viewing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Demonstrate critical viewing behaviours to evaluate how effectively information, ideas, issues, and opinions are communicated in visual and multimedia texts and whether the texts achieve their intended purpose:
- Determine what the text is representing
- Identify and analyze how the text was constructed
- Identify and analyze the artist's/author's intent
- Identify the intended audiences and points of view in the text
- Determine the historical context of the text and its impact on the text
- Identify and explain the overt and implied messages conveyed
- Infer the assumptions, interests, beliefs, and values embedded in the text and the credibility and purpose of the author
- Identify and analyze artist's/author's tone, attitude, and bias
- Analyze how the text uses argument, images, placement, and/or music for effect and impact
- Evaluate and critique the persuasive techniques including emotion and propaganda.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain how visual and multimedia texts are created to suit particular purposes and audiences.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain why the same visual or multimedia texts might prompt different responses from different audiences.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify characteristics, conventions, and/or techniques used in a variety of media forms, and explain how they shape content, convey meaning, and influence their audience(s).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify the perspectives and/or biases evident in visual and multimedia texts and comment on questions the texts may raise about beliefs, values, and power.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify the aesthetic effects of media presentations and evaluate the techniques used to create them.

outcomes.statement: Listen to and comprehend grade-appropriate informational and literary texts created by international, including indigenous, speakers and authors, and analyze the perspectives, biases, beliefs, values, identities, and power presented in each text.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to and develop interpretations of oral and multimedia texts created by international speakers and authors from various cultural communities.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select deliberately and use effectively a variety of before, during, and after strategies to construct and confirm meaning when listening to texts.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Use language cues and conventions of a variety of informational and literary texts to construct and confirm meaning when listening.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Adopt and demonstrate critical listening behaviours to analyze the overall effectiveness of oral presentations:
- Focus attention on the speaker's message
- Filter distractions and recognize factors that interfere with effective listening, including personal biases
- Identify the thesis of a speech and determine the essential elements that support it
- Analyze explicit and implicit messages/concepts, viewpoints, values, theme, and tone
- Recognize overall plan or organization including transitional expressions
- Distinguish between emotional appeal and reasoned argument
- Evaluate and verify facts and arguments, and identify fallacies in oral arguments
- Identify key allusions and symbols
- Use effective note making strategies and a variety of written or graphic forms to organize and share ideas acquired from what was listened to
- Identify and analyze the effect of artistic elements (e.g., imagery, language, character development) within texts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the purpose of a variety of listening tasks and set goals for specific tasks (e.g., comprehension, collaboration, facilitation, persuasion, mediation, empathy, evaluation).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Use evidence from the texts to support interpretations.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify and analyze the perspectives and/or biases evident in oral texts.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Listen to, discuss, interpret, and evaluate spoken texts in terms of their structure and their social, cultural, political, and historical contexts.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze historically significant speeches (e.g., Gettysburg Address, Mandela's Hope and Glory, Churchill's speeches) to find rhetorical devices and features that make them memorable.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Describe and analyze potential sources of bias in oral presentations including those that attempt to persuade.

outcomes.statement: Read and demonstrate comprehension of a range of contemporary and classical grade-appropriate informational (including position papers, magazine and newspaper articles, and electronic communications) and literary (including drama, novels, poetry, short stories, essays, biographies, and autobiographies) texts from various international, including indigenous, cultures and analyze the philosophical, ethical, and social influences that have shaped information, issues, characters, plots, and themes.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Read and interpret a range of literary and informational texts written by international authors including indigenous authors.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select deliberately and use effectively a variety of before, during, and after strategies to construct and confirm meaning when reading texts.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Use language cues and conventions of a variety of informational and literary texts to construct and confirm meaning when reading.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Demonstrate critical reading behaviours to analyze meanings, ideas, language, and literary quality in a range of contemporary and historical texts:
- Establish a purpose for reading such as to learn, interpret, and enjoy
- Skim, scan, and read closely
- Identify the main ideas and supporting details of informational texts
- Identify and analyze explicit and implicit messages, viewpoints, and concepts
- Analyze the ways in which a text's organizational structure and elements support or confound its purpose
- Identify and analyze persuasive techniques
- Evaluate the accuracy (e.g., differentiate fact from opinion) and usefulness of information presented
- Differentiate between literal and figurative statements and recognize satire, parody, and irony
- Interpret allusions and symbols and symbolic patterns in literary texts
- Test ideas and values.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Use knowledge from texts as a basis to understanding self and society by using literary texts for understanding individual and social issues.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Read historical and contemporary literary and informational texts to understand, appreciate, and respond to international and global perspectives.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Contrast major text forms and characteristics of major literary periods in world history.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Interpret, evaluate, and discuss a range of texts, identifying their language and literary qualities and considering the personal, social, cultural, political, and historical contexts in which the texts were created.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Read silently with comprehension for a sustained period of time.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Use note making and outlining to better understand texts.

outcomes.statement:
Create a range of visual, multimedia, oral, and written texts that explore:
- identity (e.g., Sense of Self)
- social responsibility (e.g., Social Criticism), and
- social action (agency) (e.g., Addressing the Issues).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop and articulate defensible positions on individual, community, national, and world issues.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate originality and inventiveness in work.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique the effectiveness of a piece of satire as a commentary on current events.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use spoken, written, and other forms of representing to achieve specific purposes (e.g., for learning, enjoyment, persuasion, and the exchange of information).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Research a global social issue and develop a problem scenario and position paper to teach others about this issue:
- Consider own and others' expertise and knowledge to explore breadth and depth of knowledge and focus inquiry or research based on parameters of task
- Formulate inquiry or research questions and refine them through reflection and discussion of topic, purpose, and context
- Develop and select from a repertoire of inquiry strategies, and adjust plan according to needs (audience, purpose, context, topic parameters, time available)
- Evaluate and select ideas and information from prior knowledge of inquiry or research topic appropriate for audience, purpose, and perspective or focus
- Identify and examine diverse information sources relevant to particular inquiry or research needs
- Evaluate factors that affect the credibility, authenticity, accuracy, and bias of information sources for inquiry or research
- Synthesize information, ideas, and perspectives from a variety of sources to solve problems, answer questions, and seek solutions; document sources accurately
- Evaluate information for completeness, accuracy, currency, historical context, relevance, balance of perspectives, and bias
- Access information efficiently and effectively, evaluate information critically and competently, and use information accurately and creatively for the issue
- Use technology as a tool to research, organize, evaluate, and communicate information, and demonstrate a fundamental understanding of the ethical and legal issues surrounding the access and use of information.

outcomes.statement: Create a visual or multimedia presentation that suits the topic, purpose, and audience; teaches others about a global social issue; and persuades them to act on the issue in a responsible manner.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Prepare and present visual and multimedia presentations:
- Exhibit logical structures appropriate to audience, purpose, and context
- Have a central foci and strong messages
- Organize ideas in logical and appropriate sequences
- Include smooth transitions
- Use a variety of forms and technologies such as sound, photographs, models and understand how ideas are communicated through elements of design (e.g., colour, shape, line, texture, placement) and principles of design (e.g., proximity, alignment, repetition, and contrast)
- Provide logical and convincing conclusions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select, use, and evaluate deliberately a wide variety of before, during, and after strategies to communicate meaning when representing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Apply accurately and effectively the language cues and conventions to construct and communicate meaning when representing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Create and present a visual or multimedia presentation persuading an audience to act on an issue using presentation techniques most appropriate to audience and purpose:
- Identify and establish that a problem exists (e.g., crime in a community)
- Analyze the problem (e.g., what are the causes?)
- Provide possible solutions (What has been tried? What has not been tried?)
- Select a solution (What's best? What are possible future obstacles?)
- Persuade audience to implement solution
- Use digital presentation tools or other media to highlight the problem and point to possible solutions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Select a media form to suit the topic, purpose, and audience for a visual or multimedia text, and explain why it is an appropriate choice.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify a variety of conventions and/or techniques appropriate to a visual or multimedia form, and explain how these will help communicate specific aspects of intended meaning.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Use appropriately a variety of audio-visual aids to support and enhance oral presentations and to engage an audience.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Use a visual as a basis for creating an analysis of recurrent themes and variations in a piece of text.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze how media messages are constructed, for what purposes, and using which tools, characteristics, and conventions.

outcomes.statement: Create and defend an informed critical response to a global issue in formal (including a workshop presentation, a debate, and an oral reading of poetry or a prose passage related to the issue) and informal (including discussion and collaborative group work) situations.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Function both as a group member and a group leader, and demonstrate effective group interaction skills and strategies:
- Demonstrate commitment and flexibility in a group
- Monitor own and others' contributions
- Build on others' strengths to achieve group goals
- Collaborate and consult effectively with others in completing communications tasks
- Represent and promote respect for contributions of other team members
- Apply a variety of strategies including formal decision-making techniques and consensus-building skills to solve problems and achieve group goals
- Exercise flexibility and willingness to be helpful in making necessary compromises to accomplish a common goal
- Assume shared responsibility (including roles) for collaborative work
- Demonstrate ability and commitment to work effectively with diverse teams
- Work effectively in a climate of ambiguity and changing priorities.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select, use, and evaluate deliberately a wide variety of before, during, and after strategies to communicate meaning when speaking.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Apply accurately and effectively the language cues and conventions to construct and communicate meaning when speaking.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Create and present oral presentations:
- Communicate orally in a clear, coherent manner, using a structure and style appropriate for a variety of purposes, subject matters, and intended audiences
- Employ a logical structure appropriate to the context, audience, and purpose
- Group related ideas and maintain a consistent focus
- Include smooth transitions
- Support judgements with sound evidence and well-chosen details
- Make skillful use of rhetorical devices
- Provide engaging introductions and coherent conclusions
- Identify a variety of vocal strategies, including tone, pace, pitch, and volume, and use them appropriately and with sensitivity to audience needs and cultural differences
- Identify a variety of non-verbal cues, including facial expression, gestures, and eye contact, and use them appropriately to help convey meaning and sensitivity to audience needs and cultural differences
- Recognize and adjust oral presentation elements (i.e., articulation, pronunciations, volume, tempo, pitch, stress, gestures, eye contact, facial expression, and poise) in keeping with purpose, audience needs, and individual cultural and linguistic background.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Plan and lead a workshop/seminar presentation:
- Define topic, goals, and specific objectives for workshop
- Determine who the participants will be and what their knowledge of the topic is
- Determine the appropriate subject matter, format, presentation method, and venue that will best meet workshop objectives
- Introduce the group members to self and each other
- Outline the objectives and agenda
- Provide relevant and practical information (speaker gives address) and resources (e.g., handouts)
- Select and use appropriate technology
- Plan for and encourage active participation, and allow for skill acquisition, problem solving, and small group discussion
- Summarize session and feedback.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Prepare and participate in a debate (structured argumentation) on an international issue:
- Focus on a defensible position
- Participate on the affirmative team or the opposing or negative team
- Engage in necessary research and demonstrate understanding of topic and related concepts
- Defend or attack given proposition
- Demonstrate organization and forethought
- Adhere to procedural and parliamentary rules
- Make relevant, well-researched, and accurate statements in a clear and concise manner without too much reliance on notes
- Respond with rebuttal statements that are appropriate and that demonstrate comprehension and understanding of the opposing positions.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Demonstrate an understanding of a variety of interpersonal speaking strategies and adapt them to suit the purpose, situation, and audience, exhibiting sensitivity to and respect for cultural differences.

outcomes.statement: Compose and create narrative, descriptive, expository, and persuasive writings that include a position paper, a comparative essay, a letter of inquiry, a critique of an author's style, and a short story or essay that uses parody, satire, and/or irony.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Create a variety of written communications using various elements of discourse (e.g., purpose, speaker, audience, form) in narrative, expository, persuasive, informative, and/or descriptive texts:
- Address audience needs, stated purpose, and context
- Develop a thesis statement
- Create an organizing structure appropriate to purpose, audience, and context
- Include relevant information and exclude extraneous information
- Provide facts and details, describe or analyze subject, explain benefits or limitations, compare or contrast, or provide graphics or illustrations
- Clarify and defend positions with relevant evidence, including facts, expert opinions, quotations, and/or expressions of commonly accepted beliefs and logical reasoning
- Use a variety of rhetorical devices to support assertions (e.g., appeal to logic through reasoning, case study, and analogy)
- Anticipate potential misunderstanding, problems, or mistakes that might arise for audience
- Structure drafts using standard forms and predictable structures (e.g., headings, white space, and graphics) and customary formats (including proper salutations, closing, and signature when writing a letter)
- Provide a coherent conclusion.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Select, use, and evaluate deliberately a wide variety of before, during, and after strategies to communicate meaning when writing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Apply accurately and effectively the language cues and conventions to construct and communicate meaning when writing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Write a position paper (convincing argument):
- Address an issue the writer feels strongly about
- Introduce topic and state position in beginning
- Support writer's position with the most important facts, details, and logical reasons arranged in a coherent and convincing order
- Defend position against an important objection
- End with a strong restatement of the writer's position
- Defend position well and compel reader to act
- Create confidence in position through a clear and strong voice
- Use inclusive and respectful language
- Use "fair" words and qualifiers
- Ensure all parts work together to build a thoughtful convincing position.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Write a comparative essay:
- Reveal new insights about topic because of the comparison
- Capture reader's attention and provide details that lead up to thesis or focus statement in a well-developed introduction
- Discuss each topic point by point in the body
- Sum up, reflect on, or comment on the comparison in a coherent, convincing conclusion.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Write a letter of inquiry (or request):
- Explain adequately what the inquiry is about and what the reader is to do in response to the letter (e.g., advice; information from a government agency; information on a product or service; copy of an official document; request for credit; application materials; estimates or bids)
- Make letter courteous and clear
- State who the writer is and give status or position
- State what the inquiry is about and explain specifically what the recipient should do
- Include the necessary details (e.g., date information is needed, services, etc.)
- Thank the recipient for his/her time
- Follow a standard letter format.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Write a story or essay using parody, satire, and/or irony:
- Choose one scene from a print text
- Use a tone that seems straightforward but leads the reader to know that the real intention is to criticize or ridicule and, in the end, illuminate a problem.
- Use exaggeration and/or understatement.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Write a critique of an author's style:
- Consider purpose and intended audience
- Address author's treatment of subject (specific, concrete, direct, general, abstract, philosophical)
- Analyze form chosen to express ideas: tone (e.g., informal, conversational, professional critical, satirical, amused, encouraging, pensive); point of view (e.g., first person or third person); arrangement and organization of ideas; sentence structures; diction (e.g., formal or informal; colloquial or technical); images and symbols; use of rhetorical devices; other distinctive mannerisms
- Identify the writer's overall, distinctive approach or "style."

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Experiment with different forms and formats (e.g., proposal, script, letter to government officials advocating change) and techniques, and explain their appeal.

outcomes.statement: Assess own and others' work for precision, clarity, and artistry.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Review and analyze own and others' work for content, organization, delivery, audience response, and style.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify a variety of skills and strategies in viewing, listening, reading, representing, speaking, and writing; and explain how the skills and strategies improve communication.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify appropriate steps and implement plans to improve comprehension and communication skills.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Select a range of products that clearly reflect own growth as a communicator, and explain the reasons for choices.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess the effect of new understandings and strategies on self and others.

outcomes.statement: Reflect on and assess understanding of self as a self-directed, self-appraising, and strategic learner.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Review and analyze own and others' work for content, organization, delivery, audience response, and style.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify a variety of skills and strategies in viewing, listening, reading, representing, speaking, and writing; and explain how the skills and strategies improve communication.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify appropriate steps and implement plans to improve comprehension and communication skills.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Select a range of products that clearly reflect own growth as a communicator, and explain the reasons for choices.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess the effect of new understandings and strategies on self and others.

evidence.observation: The curriculum document lists its outcomes under a single heading (“Outcomes and Indicators”).

footnotes: *Full-length texts include novels, plays and longer non-fiction works (e.g., memoir, autobiography).

items.text: Evaluate how authors/creators construct character, conflict (e.g., character vs. self, character vs. character, character vs. society, character vs. nature), setting and point of view in fiction and non-fiction texts to reveal, reflect, or critique worldviews and specific cultural, historical or ideological contexts.

Interpret fiction and non-fiction texts by inferring multiple plausible, nuanced meanings that are informed by authorial perspective and cultural and social context using specific and varied evidence while considering alternative interpretations.

Evaluate how fiction and non-fiction texts use structure, evidence, tone and rhetorical devices (e.g., appeals, repetition, direct address) to inform, provoke thought, persuade or position audiences toward specific interpretations, beliefs or actions.
Analyze how an author’s/creator’s stance, bias, context and assumptions influence interpretation and privilege particular viewpoints.
Synthesize connections among ideas, observations, opinions, themes and emotions across a variety of texts from diverse voices.

Evaluate how different text forms (e.g., poem, article, documentary) explore similar social issues or themes, analyzing how conventions and constraints of each form impact audience interpretation and emotional resonance.

Evaluate how the mode of communication influences the message and impacts the audience’s understanding, perception, emotional response and engagement (see Appendix A). Explain how texts raise questions or offer insights about identity, social responsibility, or social agency (action).
Apply comprehension and metacognitive strategies (e.g., previewing, questioning, visualizing) to support the construction of meaning across modalities and text types (see Appendix B and Appendix C).
Reflect on how texts raise questions or offer insights about identity, social responsibility or social agency (action).

Develop original descriptive, narrative, poetic, expository and persuasive compositions that demonstrate understanding of genre-specific purposes, structures and language features (see Appendices D-H).
Experiment with various modalities (e.g., written, oral, visual, multimodal) to determine which one(s) best supports the purpose, audience and message of the composition.
Compose both fiction and non-fiction texts, thoughtfully considering the elements of each form, such as fact-based development in non-fiction and imaginative techniques in fiction.
Integrate multimodal elements (e.g., sound, image, movement, visual design) thoughtfully when composing in hybrid formats to enhance the delivery of the intended message.
Develop compositions that explore personal and collective identities, promote social responsibility and inspire social agency (action).
Revise compositions for clarity, coherence and impact, considering how effectively genre and form are aligned to audience and purpose.
Develop composition stamina by creating a longer-form text that sustains ideas, organization, purpose and audience engagement across the whole composition.

Integrate genre-specific strategies (e.g., juxtaposing poetic imagery with expository explanation, combining persuasive appeals with narrative pacing) to shape the composition’s tone, structure and impact (see Appendices D-H).
Evaluate how form, genre, audience and purpose shape the creative choices made throughout the composition process.
Reflect on how stories, narratives and oral traditions can challenge assumptions, including pan-Indigenous and pan-cultural generalizations.
Explain how stories, narratives and oral traditions convey knowledge, values, and teachings within specific cultures or communities.
Analyze how the structure (e.g., cyclical, linear) and delivery (e.g., relational/ community/ cultural context) of stories, narratives and oral traditions are connected to the worldview they express.

Analyze how specific cultural stories, narratives and oral traditions (e.g., creation stories, family histories, land-based teachings) can resist stereotyping, cultural erasure or generalized representations.
Examine the impact of pan-Indigenous and pan-cultural generalizations in literature, media and education.

Explore how stories, narratives and oral traditions with specific and local contexts can preserve cultural knowledge, strengthen identity and sustain relationships to land, language, community or place.
Reflect on the significance of understanding cultural context before interpreting, sharing or representing a story, narrative or oral tradition (e.g., protocols, accountability).
Analyze how engaging with specific stories, narratives and oral traditions can challenge assumptions and deepen understanding of perspectives, experiences and ways of knowing.

Analyze how specific stories, narratives and oral traditions from diverse cultures can challenge broad assumptions about cultural groups by revealing distinct worldviews, values, teachings, histories or social contexts.
Reflect on how personal experiences, social contexts and cultural backgrounds influence both the interpretation of texts and creation of compositions.
Reflect on how one’s lived experiences, values or worldview influence decisions about form, tone, genre and audience in original compositions.
Explore how cultural background or social context can influence an author’s/creator’s choices in themes, perspectives or representations within texts.
Examine how texts by authors/creators with diverse backgrounds or lived experiences can expand or shift personal or collective viewpoints on social issues, cultural practices or historical events.
Reflect on the responsibility authors/creators hold when representing identities, cultures and experiences that differ from their own.
Analyze how interpretations of a text are shaped, challenged or reconsidered across cultural, social, political or historical contexts.
Explain how understanding an author’s/creator’s personal, social, or cultural context can inform, complicate or challenge interpretation of a text.
Integrate personal, cultural, or social context with control and purpose to strengthen insight, voice, or meaningful engagement with the audience when developing original compositions.
Evaluate how authors/creators strategically integrate elements in multimodal texts to communicate ideas and engage the audience.
Analyze how audience interpretation of multimodal compositions may shift based on individual experiences, context (e.g., platform, cultural moment, target audience) or familiarity with various modes.
Analyze how multimodal elements foreground, intensify or complicate perspectives, biases or calls to action (see Appendix K).
Evaluate how multimodal compositions use symbolism, irony, satire or juxtaposition across modes to convey complex or contradictory meanings.

Evaluate whether creators have demonstrated ethical responsibility (e.g., crediting authors/creators, respectful representations, considering privacy and consent) in the creation of multimodal compositions (e.g., propaganda, social media posts, AI-generated elements), including how images, sound or movement may influence emotional response, perception of truth or public understanding.
Evaluate how the interaction between elements (e.g., how audio complements visuals, how text layout affects pacing) creates cohesion, tension or complexity in the overall message (see Appendix K).
Analyze how genre conventions are reinforced (e.g., documentary voiceover, rhythmic spoken word) or subverted (e.g., experimental silence, monotone delivery) through multimodal elements.

Evaluate how multimodal creators use, adapt, or disrupt design choices (e.g., withholding information, shifting point of view, disrupting expected sequencing, using silence) to shape the audience’s role, interpretation or response.
Synthesize insights from multiple multimodal compositions to construct a critical stance on how form influences audience understanding, accessibility, interpretation and response.
Combine multimodal elements strategically to convey messages with clarity, emotion and intention.

Plan multimodal compositions by selecting and intentionally combining elements (e.g., text, visuals, sound, movement) in ways that support purpose, audience, message and tone across modes (see Appendix K).

Combine or intentionally disrupt design expectations (e.g., withholding information, disrupting expected sequencing, contrasting sound with image, using silence, changing pace abruptly) to influence audience understanding and create a purposeful emotional effect (see Appendix K).
Combine design features (e.g., colour palettes, font size and style, white space, transitions, image placement) to create emphasis, rhythm or emotion (see Appendix K).
Reflect on how changes in one element (e.g., altering tone of voice, background visuals) influence the interpretation of other elements and the overall cohesion of the composition.
Revise compositions to improve the relationship between elements, ensuring that each serves a clear purpose within the whole.

Apply accessibility strategies when combining modes (e.g., using captions with video, high contrast visuals with clear text, alt-text for images) to ensure clarity, usability and inclusion for all audiences (see Appendix K).
Consider cultural diversity, emotional safety and audience perspectives when making design choices, reflecting on how language, imagery and form may include, exclude or impact audiences.
Analyze how form, style, tone, structure, purpose and language features of different genres can shape meaning and enhance audience impact.
Analyze the purpose and functions of descriptive, narrative, expository, poetic and persuasive genres (see Appendices D-H).

Evaluate how structural choices (e.g., spatial order in descriptive, cause-effect in expository) shape the clarity and emotional impact of each genre in relation to purpose and audience (see Appendices D-H).
Examine how language features such as imagery, rhetorical appeals, figurative language, sentence variety and diction serve different purposes within and across genres.

Examine how perceived neutrality in genres, such as expository or informational writing, may still reflect an author’s/creator’s bias, framing choices or selective evidence that influence audience interpretation.
Explain genre-specific strategies in mentor texts and how they connect to the message, theme or argument.
Evaluate how genres engage audiences differently through mood, tone, voice and stylistic conventions (see Appendices D-H).
Analyze how genre language features adapt to different formats (e.g., oral retellings, multimodal representations, digital compositions) while maintaining core genre characteristics.
Synthesize how similar thematic topics (e.g., Canadian identity, diversity) are explored through different genres and how genre-specific choices affect audience interpretation and impact.
Analyze how genre expectations can be deliberately followed, blended or subverted to enhance impact, convey complex meaning or challenge audience expectations.
Experiment with form, style, tone, structure and language features in original descriptive, narrative, expository, poetic and persuasive compositions to suit different purposes and audiences.

Experiment with different perspectives (e.g., shifting between first-person, second-person, or third-person point of view; retelling an event from another character’s perspective; using limited, omniscient or unreliable narration) to explore how voice shapes audience engagement and interpretation.
Disrupt conventional structures (e.g., using nonlinear timelines, in medias res openings, cliffhangers, fragmented or reverse order) to test how sequencing affects tension, pacing and clarity.

Transform an existing text or idea into a new form (e.g., found poem from a news article; personal story retold in dramatic monologue; visual collage from an essay) to explore meaning-making across genre and modes.
Experiment with multimodal or non-verbal storytelling techniques to express ideas when language is limited, absent or intentionally minimized.
Transform language creatively (e.g., vernacular, repetition, dialect, sensory imagery, unexpected word pairings) to evoke tone, mood, or emotion appropriate to genre and audience.
Incorporate elements like dialogue, inner monologue, or contrasting character voices to build tension, reveal motivation or develop complex conflict.
Explore form and style with low-stakes composition tasks (e.g., timed creative writes, collaborative genre mashups, character improvisations) without the pressure of perfection.
Reflect on how experimentation helped clarify intention, shift audience impact or open new possibilities for voice and genre.
Analyze how authors/creators intentionally use or subvert craft techniques to enhance meaning and impact.

Analyze how authors/creators conform to or subvert (e.g., use an unreliable narrator in memoir; create a nonlinear structure in persuasive essay) genre expectations to shape interpretation and impact.
Analyze how authors/creators intentionally manipulate craft elements (e.g., fragmented syntax, disrupted chronology) to evoke tension, ambiguity or surprise.

Examine how the subversion of familiar craft techniques (e.g., reversing a traditional character arc, omitting a climax, using atypical tone shifts) challenges audience expectations or invites new ways of understanding characters, themes or issues.
Evaluate the strategic use of silence, omission or ambiguity (e.g., unresolved endings, minimalism, ellipses) as intentional choices that shape emotional tone, audience response or thematic emphasis.

Interpret how authors/creators manipulate multimodal elements (e.g., disruptive white space, shifting font, abrupt cuts in film, jarring sound transitions) to reinforce, complicate or clarify meaning.
Assess how cultural, historical or political context can influence an author’s/creator’s decision to either uphold or resist dominant literary conventions or genre norms.
Analyze how understanding author/creator intent (e.g., social critique, satire, parody, reclamation) shapes the reader’s interpretation and emotional response.

Analyze how authors/creators use, withhold, or disrupt oral and non-verbal craft techniques (e.g., silence, pacing, stillness, eye contact, shifts in volume) to shape tone, tension, meaning or audience response.
Critique how creators’ design choices (e.g., sequencing, layout, white space, sound, visual composition) enhance or detract from clarity, atmosphere or argument strength.

Analyze how authors/creators intentionally use, manipulate, or subvert sentence- and word-level craft techniques (e.g., parallelism, grammatical disruption, strategic simplicity or density, syntactic repetition) to reinforce, complicate, or challenge meaning and audience interpretation.

Critique texts in which authors/creators approach similar themes or ideas but make contrasting stylistic and structural decisions (e.g., poetic repetition versus stark simplicity), evaluating the effect of those decisions on audience engagement and message clarity.

Analyze how authors/creators intentionally use alternative and assistive communication systems (e.g., sign language, captions, visual supports, audio description) to shape meaning, emotion, accessibility and audience engagement in compositions.
Use craft techniques to enhance the quality, style and impact of original compositions.
Apply or intentionally subvert specific craft techniques from mentor texts to suit audience, genre and purpose (see Appendices D-H).

Apply descriptive techniques (e.g., sensory detail, figurative language, spatial or chronological structure, selective focus) to evoke emotion, create atmosphere or highlight significance (see Appendix D).
Apply narrative techniques (e.g., character and plot development, point of view, dialogue, flashbacks, setting, pacing) to immerse the audience and build narrative tension (see Appendix E).
Apply poetic techniques (e.g., line breaks, stanza structure, repetition, rhythm, figurative language, imagery, sound devices) to create tone, emotion and emphasis (see Appendix F).
Apply expository techniques (e.g., organizational structure, text features, rhetorical questions, anecdotal examples, tone) to clarify complex ideas and guide reader understanding (see Appendix G).
Apply persuasive techniques (e.g., rhetorical appeals, direct address, repetition, tone, purposeful sentence structure) to influence thinking and action (see Appendix H).
Apply oral delivery strategies (e.g., inflection, pacing, volume, pausing, emphasis) to enhance clarity, rhythm and emotional impact in original compositions.
Apply non-verbal strategies (e.g., facial expressions, gestures, posture, eye contact) to reinforce tone, clarify meaning and strengthen audience engagement in original compositions.
Justify which craft techniques were most effective in achieving the intended impact of original compositions.

Apply sentence- and word-level craft techniques (e.g., parallelism, rule of three, sentence length and variety, repetition, strategic word choice, syntactic variation) to strengthen emphasis, rhythm, clarity, tone and meaning in original compositions.
Apply comprehension and metacognitive strategies that deepen understanding and analysis when reading, listening and viewing.
Apply global, problem-solving and support strategies to monitor learning and deepen comprehension when reading, listening and viewing (see Appendix B and Appendix C).
Make and refine predictions before and during reading, listening, or viewing by drawing on titles, genre features, prior knowledge and contextual clues.

Establish a specific purpose before reading, listening, and viewing (e.g., understanding argument, identifying genre features, evaluating author's stance) and adjust strategies (e.g., shifting from skimming to close reading when a key argument or tone shift appears) as new information is encountered.
Identify when understanding breaks down and use strategies (e.g., re-reading, summarizing, slowing down pace, asking questions for clarification) to improve comprehension.
Apply morphology strategies by analyzing word parts (i.e., roots, prefixes, suffixes) to decode unfamiliar vocabulary and enhance comprehension.

Engage with texts multiple times for distinct purposes (e.g., first encounter for basic comprehension, second for analyzing structure or language features, third for interpreting author’s/creator’s craft, tone or deeper meanings).

Analyze how recognizing genre-specific craft techniques during reading, listening or viewing (e.g., narrative suspense, persuasive appeals, poetic repetition) supports more precise interpretation of purpose, audience, impact and meaning across complex texts.
Use support strategies during and after reading, listening or viewing (e.g., annotating texts, posing questions, taking structured notes, using graphic organizers) to map key ideas and analyze texts.
Visualize complex descriptions or abstract ideas that enhance understanding of challenging sections.
Reflect on the effectiveness of personal comprehension strategies post-task by identifying what worked, what was challenging and setting specific future goals.
Use a variety of writing and design processes to thoughtfully plan, develop, revise and refine original compositions.
Explore multiple ideas, forms and craft techniques through a variety of low-stakes composition processes (e.g., quick writes, spoken brainstorms, imitation writing).

Plan original written, oral, visual and multimodal compositions using strategies (e.g., brainstorming, mind-mapping, sketching, discussion or inquiry questions) to generate ideas, clarify purpose and consider audience.

Organize ideas intentionally during planning by selecting appropriate structures, modalities, and design elements suited to the intended genre (e.g., sensory details, narrative pacing, logical organization, figurative language), purpose (e.g., to entertain, to persuade) and audience.
Experiment with early drafts by using a variety of design processes (e.g., storyboard, speech annotations, Venn diagram) to test ideas, structures and genre techniques.
Revise original compositions meaningfully by reworking content, structure, form, style or mode based on self-assessment, peer feedback and evolving clarity of purpose.
Refine original compositions by polishing language, improving coherence, fine-tuning transitions, clarifying key ideas, and aligning form and tone precisely to purpose and audience.
Revise titles in original compositions to align with purpose and genre and enhance the audience's engagement or interpretation.
Finalize original compositions for the intended audience, considering how final design, medium, and presentation choices impact meaning, accessibility and emotional resonance.

Reflect on feedback and creative intentions to determine which suggestions enhance clarity, strengthen purpose, or improve audience impact, and make intentional decisions about what to revise, retain, or reject based on creative vision.
Revise recursively by revisiting ideas, structure and techniques at multiple stages to refine meaning and expression over time.
Apply appropriate spelling, grammar, punctuation and language conventions according to genre, purpose and audience.
Apply grammar, syntax, punctuation and spelling conventions to enhance clarity and coherence in original compositions.
Adjust use of language conventions based on purpose, audience and genre (e.g., formal conventions for academic essays; strategic flexibility for creative, spoken word, or informal compositions).
Use morphological strategies (i.e., analyzing roots, prefixes and suffixes) to spell complex words accurately and to expand academic vocabulary.
Edit drafts purposefully to correct errors in spelling, punctuation and grammar, focusing on patterns of strength and recurring areas for improvement.
Utilize punctuation and syntax intentionally to control pacing, emphasis and tone in compositions (e.g., varied sentence lengths, line breaks, strategic use of commas, dashes, pauses).

Organize ideas into cohesive sections (e.g., paragraphs, scenes, stanzas, frames, slides) that reflect purposeful shifts in focus, topic, speaker, time, or tone to support clarity, coherence and audience understanding in original compositions.
Reflect on how choices in tone, formality and language precision affect audience perception and comprehension.

Recognize and discuss the evolving nature of language conventions across different cultural, social and digital contexts (e.g., how African American Vernacular English has grammatical rules distinct from Standard American English; how professional vs. peer dialogue changes in tone, formality and structure; how emojis, hashtags, or acronyms can shift meaning and tone).

Use appropriate citation styles in formal writing (e.g., MLA for literary and artistic analysis; APA for research, informational, or social science-related texts), selecting format based on context, discipline and audience.
Evaluate the reliability, credibility and effectiveness of information presented in a range of texts, including media and digital texts.

Evaluate factors that contribute to credibility (e.g., author expertise, institutional affiliation, purpose, transparency of sourcing) and reliability (e.g., accuracy of information, use of evidence, consistency across sources).

Evaluate factors that contribute to a lack of credibility (e.g., unclear authorship, lack of expertise, missing source information, obvious bias, lack of transparency, misleading intent) and reliability (e.g., inaccurate information, unsupported claims, limited evidence, outdated information, inconsistency across sources).

Analyze how medium, modality, platform and publication context (e.g., independent journalism vs. sponsored content, news article vs. influencer post, date of publication) influence the credibility, reliability and perceived objectivity of a text.

Analyze how persuasive techniques (e.g., loaded or emotional language, selective use of statistics, repetition, jargon, propaganda, oversimplification) can distort facts, influence perception or compromise the objectivity of information.
Analyze how visual or multimodal elements (e.g., image selection, layout, sound design, captioning) shape the perceived trustworthiness and tone of a source.
Evaluate conflicting or ambiguous sources by assessing the strength of evidence, source transparency and logical reasoning used to support claims.
Analyze how personal interest, prior knowledge, bias or media habits may influence one’s evaluation of a source and take action to approach information more critically.
Synthesize insights across multiple perspectives to draw conclusions about a topic, considering the credibility and context of each source.
Analyze how power and social context influences production, dissemination and reception of information (e.g., media ownership, algorithmic influence, censorship).
Synthesize diverse, credible and reliable evidence with precision to support complex arguments and positions.
Synthesize insights from diverse, credible and reliable sources to develop complex arguments that show connected reasoning, recognize nuance or address contradictions across perspectives.

Introduce evidence with framing language that clarifies its relevance:
• “According to…”
• “As shared in the interview with…”
• “The author suggests...”
• “The situation shows...”
• “The actions of the character demonstrate...”.

Evaluate the function and impact of selected evidence by explaining how it strengthens reasoning, addresses complexity or contradiction, and enhances the precision or persuasiveness of the central message, theme or argument.

Integrate the most relevant and impactful evidence from a range of credible sources (e.g., scholarly articles, interviews, media, statistics, expert commentary, novels, poems) to preserve originality and avoid over-reliance on source material.

Apply different strategies for tracking and attributing sources (e.g., primary, secondary, print, scholarly, AI) depending on context:
• In academic or research-based compositions, use appropriate citation styles (e.g., MLA for literary analysis, APA for informational texts).
• In informal, creative, or oral compositions, attribute ideas through oral acknowledgments, captions, credits, or notes in accompanying materials.
Revise compositions to strengthen evidence integration, clarity and reasoning through precise word choice, purposeful language and thoughtful explanation of evidence.
Embed counter-evidence or alternative viewpoints into the composition and respond with thoughtful rebuttal, concession or contextualization.
Synthesize multiple pieces of evidence addressing the same topic or claim to identify patterns, contradictions or gaps in reasoning.
Explain the significance, credibility and reliability of each source and its unique contribution to the overall argument or position.
Inquire into a topic by developing essential questions and narrowing the scope to create a central message, argument or theme.
Formulate essential questions that connect personal inquiry to larger cultural, historical, or philosophical issues.
Refine inquiry by identifying emerging patterns, tensions, gaps, contradictions or perspectives across contexts (e.g., literature, current events, sources, lived experiences)

Analyze underlying complexities, contradictions, or evolving insights across multiple sources, texts, or compositions that can inform a complex central message, theme or argument that considers multiple perspectives or tensions.

Select a genre and form that best align with a narrowed focus, considering how structure, modality and voice can amplify the intended impact (e.g., argument in editorial form, theme in short story, message in visual collage).

Integrate evidence, symbols or aesthetic devices with intentionality, using them not only to support meaning but also to provoke thought or reinterpretation (e.g., using shifts in tone or point of view to unsettle audience expectations).
Evaluate how sections, paragraphs or design elements work together to sustain coherence, manage complexity and strengthen the central message, theme or argument.
Explain how the central message has evolved through the process and how aesthetic or craft techniques challenge assumptions, expand audience interpretation or clarify meaning.

Reflect on how cultural, social, historical and personal lenses can shape how audiences interpret the central message, theme or argument and revise to strengthen clarity, relevance, or resonance across diverse contexts.
Facilitate in-depth, collaborative discussions that promote critical engagement and deepen comprehension of texts.
Lead or co-facilitate discussions using a clear purpose, guiding questions and strategies to deepen collective understanding of complex texts or issues (See Appendix I).
Foster critical dialogue by encouraging multiple interpretations and drawing connections to broader social, historical or cultural contexts.

Model discussion norms (e.g., encouraging evidence-based contributions, acknowledging contradictions, inviting participants to respond, prompting reflection) in collaborative discussions formats (e.g., Socratic seminar, fishbowls, collaborative inquiry).
Model respectful disagreement by balancing critique with empathy and maintaining an atmosphere of inclusive language and intellectual curiosity.
Contribute to and guide collaborative discussions by synthesizing others’ contributions, asking clarifying questions and connecting multiple perspectives.
Demonstrate respect for diverse perspectives by validating differing opinions and lived experiences, using inclusive language and maintaining a constructive tone during disagreement.
Demonstrate awareness of group dynamics by encouraging contributions, mediating tensions and adapting communication to support productive, inclusive and critical dialogue.
Facilitate dialogue that helps participants examine feedback, disagreement or new insights to deepen interpretations of complex texts or issues.
Reflect on how facilitating collaborative dialogue shapes, expands or challenges personal thinking or comprehension.
Collaborate with others to generate ideas, organize and revise original compositions, contributing feedback and experimenting to improve clarity, effectiveness and impact.

Generate and build ideas with various brainstorming strategies (e.g., mentor-text inspired exercises, low-stakes compositions tasks, sketching) identifying possibilities for genre, voice, or structure.
Provide thoughtful, question-driven feedback that highlights strengths, identifies gaps and invites deeper thinking about clarity, nuance or artistic intention.

Engage in conferences to discuss creative choices, offering specific suggestions about structure, language, tone, multimodal integration or genre alignment to strengthen the logical flow and impact of original compositions.

Experiment with peer-suggested feedback (e.g., altering genre, reworking perspective, shifting modality), documenting changes and analyzing how revisions improve meaning and overall effectiveness of compositions.
Experiment with new techniques or structures suggested through dialogue (e.g., trying a different opening move, adjusting pacing, reordering sections) to strengthen personal compositions.
Reflect on how giving and receiving feedback shapes understanding and informs decisions or goals for future compositions.

Collaborate with others to generate and refine ideas for individual compositions (written, oral, visual, multimodal), evaluating how audience, genre and purpose influence form, style, and stance (See Appendix J).
Refine compositions by intentionally following or subverting craft techniques drawn from mentor texts to shape meaning, disrupt conventions, or deepen audience interpretation.

Provide insightful, inquiry-driven feedback (e.g., noting confusions, emotions and curiosities) to others on ways to enhance clarity, effectiveness, emotional resonance, or coherence in their original compositions (see Appendix J).
Evaluate how compositional risks can enhance sophistication, originality or audience engagement.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the role and contributions of entrepreneurship and intrapreneurship to personal, school and community life.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe what entrepreneurship is and what entrepreneurs do.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Identify examples of entrepreneurship and entrepreneurs within the local community and province.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Discuss opportunities and challenges associated with being intrapreneurial and entrepreneurial within the school and community.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Analyze statistics related to the contributions made by entrepreneurs to the local, provincial and Canadian economics.

outcomes.statement: Investigate factors that define and contribute to entrepreneurial success.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Entrepreneurial Success (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate among for-profit, not-for-profit and social enterprises within the community and province.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the meaning of success within the contexts of profit, not-for-profit and social enterprises.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how culture and worldviews, including those of First Nations and Métis people in Saskatchewan, inform the definition of success for an entrepreneurial venture.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess entrepreneurial success as defined by the Seventh Generation Principle.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Debate the role of failure in entrepreneurship.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Generate a list of questions that could be asked of entrepreneurs to gain insight into their ventures and to understand what success means to them. Sample questions include:
- How did you come up with your business idea?
- What problem does your business solve?
- What makes your business unique?
- Why did you choose entrepreneurship?
- What is the biggest challenge you have overcome?
- What is your greatest achievement?
- What mistakes have you made in your business, and how did you handle them?
- Do you consider yourself successful as an entrepreneur? Why or why not?
- As an entrepreneur, what advice would you give your younger self?

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Interview or research local and Saskatchewan entrepreneurs to gain insight into the broad range of entrepreneurial ventures within the community and province.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Communicate interview or research findings related to local and Saskatchewan entrepreneurs through a multi-media (e.g., video and presentation), print (e.g., brochure and magazine) or oral presentation.

outcomes.statement: Assess characteristics and skills important for entrepreneurial success.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Entrepreneurial Characteristics and Skills (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between characteristics and skills.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research characteristics (e.g., confidence, passion and motivation) and skills (e.g., leadership, teamwork and networking) common to successful entrepreneurs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate between characteristics that are innate and those that are learned and gained through time and experience.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the relationship among personal financial competence and confidence, personal credit score and entrepreneurial progress and success.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss what it means to have an entrepreneurial mindset.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Debate the statement, “Entrepreneurs are born.”

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the role of creativity in entrepreneurship.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe interpersonal skills (e.g., verbal and non-verbal communication, listening, negotiation, decision-making and assertiveness) that contribute to entrepreneurial success.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify traits (e.g., self-doubt, perfectionism and being easily distracted) that may hinder entrepreneurial success.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect on personal characteristics, skills, interest in, and suitability for, entrepreneurship as a career pathway of choice or for intrapreneurship within a company or organization.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Propose ways (e.g., using a team approach, formal and informal education and volunteering) to overcome personal shortcomings necessary for entrepreneurial success.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Commit to a personal plan for utilizing personal characteristics and skills and for overcoming shortcomings necessary for entrepreneurial success.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Recognize and affirm the characteristics and skills possessed by classmates.

outcomes.statement: Examine entrepreneurial opportunities at home, at school and in the community.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Seeking Opportunities (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe an entrepreneurial opportunity (i.e., a need, a want or a problem that needs to be solved).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the view that change causes entrepreneurial opportunities and that entrepreneurial opportunities cause change.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: List potential sources of entrepreneurial opportunities (e.g., technological change, changing demographics, shortages, surpluses and shifts in demand).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess the impact of PESTLE factors (i.e., political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental) on entrepreneurial opportunities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate between a trend and a fad and their impacts on entrepreneurial opportunities.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Propose ways (e.g., being optimistic, accepting challenges, searching for opportunities and researching) that entrepreneurs discover and take advantage of opportunities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Differentiate between an opportunity (i.e., the problem) and an idea (i.e., a potential solution).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify potential entrepreneurial opportunities at home, at school and in the community.

outcomes.statement: Assess design thinking as a process for creating successful and meaningful entrepreneurial solutions.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Design Thinking and Entrepreneurship (Core) · Suggested Time: 7-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 4

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe design thinking, including its human-centric nature.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research proposed benefits (e.g., increased efficiency and return on investment, increased opportunities for collaboration and reduced risk associated with launching new ideas) associated with using the design thinking process in business.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how successful companies such as Netflix, Nike and Airbnb have incorporated design thinking into their business strategies.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the five stages of design thinking (i.e., empathize, define, ideate, prototype and test).

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Explain the non-linear and iterative nature of the design thinking process.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze the role and importance of failure as part of the design thinking process.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research effective brainstorming techniques (e.g., green light thinking, mind maps, rapid ideation, game storming and step-ladder technique).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Establish norms (e.g., defer all judgment, aim for quantity, build on others’ ideas and involve everyone) for group brainstorming.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Apply the design thinking process to find solutions to real-life or given entrepreneurial scenarios.

outcomes.statement: Investigate Indigenous economic reconciliation as an important contributor to reconciliation in Canada.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Economic Reconciliation (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 4

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the state of entrepreneurship among First Nations peoples in Saskatchewan and Canada pre- and post-colonization.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research challenges faced, and contributions made, by First Nations and Métis peoples in helping to shape the entrepreneurial landscape of Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the tenets of Indigenous economic reconciliation including its holistic, values-driven approach to attaining community economic prosperity.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the benefits of Indigenous economic reconciliation for all peoples in Canada.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the concept of economic leakage and the resulting impact on remote, rural, urban and First Nations communities.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate opportunities (e.g., innovation, creating wealth and community issues/problems) that could be addressed by entrepreneurship within the local and/or provincial community.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Define the term urban reserve.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify urban reserves located in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research the history of urban reserves in Saskatchewan including the impact of the Saskatchewan Treaty Land Entitlement Framework Agreement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Assess the economic, social and cultural opportunities provided by the establishment of urban reserves in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Reflect on personal and collective responsibility for supporting Indigenous economic reconciliation within the local and broader community.

outcomes.statement: Explore community initiatives, government and community development agencies, and business associations that support entrepreneurship.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe networking and its importance for entrepreneurial success.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify potential allies (e.g., family, friends, Elders, tribal councils, postsecondary and training institutions) that could be a part of personal and professional networks to support the development of a new venture within the community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe ways (e.g., volunteering, job shadows, attending business trade fairs or business functions and informational interviews) to build and expand personal and professional networks within the local business community

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the mutual benefits of contributing to, and receiving support from, a network.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Propose networking strategies for individuals who are uncomfortable with, or afraid of, the process.

indicators.text: Reflect on personal comfort level with networking.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Construct a plan to develop or grow personal networking skills.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the value of mentorship in entrepreneurship for both mentors and mentees.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the relationship between local entrepreneurial success and the growth and sustainability of communities in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate how business ventures evolve and change over time and how the need for, and kinds of, supports also evolve and change.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Identify incentives or initiatives for new and expanding business development available within the local community.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Research the availability of financial support (e.g., grants and loans) for Saskatchewan entrepreneurs including First Nations and Métis people, newcomers, women and youth.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Describe the processes for accessing financial support available to Saskatchewan and Canadian entrepreneurs.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate common types of business structures.

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Identify examples of each type of business structure within the local community and province.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the features (e.g., ownership, process for establishing, profitsharing, liability protection and longevity) of various types of business structures.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the purpose and benefits of succession planning and the impact each type of business structure has on the process.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Summarize the advantages and disadvantages of each type of business structure.

indicators.text: Discuss how attitudes and beliefs (e.g., community and collective wellbeing) shaped by worldviews inform decisions related to business ownership and structures.
