outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Forestry Partnerships (Optional) · Suggested Time: 7-9 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research how treaty land entitlements, land claims and the spiritual importance of land impacts the forestry industry in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Interpret the message provided by Elders or Knowledge Keepers teaching about their relationship with forests.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research how traditional land use differs within Métis and First Nations communities across Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Summarize forestry industry and First Nations partnerships in Saskatchewan (e.g., Mistik and NorSask).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore contemporary cultural and economic partnerships within forestry (e.g., sawmills, outfitting, ecotourism, development) undertaken by First Nations and Métis peoples.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine how the Indigenous principle of working together and helping each other is being applied to forest management practices and partnerships

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss how long-lasting community-based partnerships that are mutually beneficial enhance all areas of forestry (e.g., risk-management, sustainability and ecosystem-based management).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on the importance and benefits of building relationships and partnerships with neighboring communities at all stages of projects related to land use within forestry.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the partnerships that exist in the forestry industry between organizations like the Canadian Institute of Forestry, Saskatchewan Forestry Association, the Prince Albert Model Forest, and the Association of Saskatchewan Forestry Professionals.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Assess community views on the benefits and disadvantages (e.g., social, economic and environmental) of the forestry industry on families and local communities.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Compare Saskatchewan First Nation and Métis Consultation Policy Framework legislation for duty to consult with Indigenous communities, proponents (e.g., forestry companies), engagement guidelines and other mutually beneficial and trusting partnerships (e.g., environmental, non- government organizations).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explore the relationship between The Natural Resources Transfer Acts and The Saskatchewan First Act and their impact on Indigenous peoples and resource industry stakeholders.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the importance of forest health.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Forest Health (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify natural and anthropogenic factors (e.g., human activity, disease, drought, pollution and climate change) that can affect the health of forests.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe symptoms of forest decline.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how deforestation impacts the ecosystem including soil, water and air.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the impact of forest health on wildlife, habitat, communities and economies.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the benefits and challenges of methods used to improve forest health in Saskatchewan (e.g., cost, tourism and biodiversity).

outcomes.statement: Analyze sustainability of trees, plants, soils, wildlife and water in Saskatchewan forests.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: Forest Sustainability (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the terms ecosystem, niche, habitat, biotic and abiotic as they pertain to forests.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine interrelationships among tree structures and with the soil, water and wildlife involving vital life processes in a forest.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the importance of soil and water in a forest ecosystem.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain succession as it pertains to forest ecosystems.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the different perspectives that community members such as businesses, farmers, consumers and producers have on forest sustainability.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare different models of forest sustainability.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine how forest sustainability impacts the forestry industry, the economy, communities and the environment.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research legislation, regulations, standards and codes put in place by Saskatchewan and Canada to maintain forests and regulate forestry.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss sustainable practices that companies adhere to in maintaining Saskatchewan forests.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect on First Nations and Métis worldviews (e.g., keepers of the land) related to forest sustainability.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine how different worldviews impact human interaction with forests.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the role of humans in forest management and maintaining forests now and into the future.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13: Conservation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare historic and current land use patterns and practices in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify different environmental conservation practices.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine The First Nation and Métis Consultation Policy Framework (which includes the duty to consult) and the consultation process with local communities and Indigenous stakeholders on the environmental impact of a forestry project.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how community-based conservation initiatives can contribute to life-long sustainable use of forests.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore how concepts such as wâhkôhtowin (e.g., good relationship, kinship and responsibility to all creatures and futures) can shape views on conservation of forests (e.g., beyond respecting nature and recognizing we are part of nature).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain why there is an increased demand on forest resources by Canadians and the International community.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Distinguish between misinformation and sensationalized messaging regarding the forestry industry.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the contribution of local and traditional knowledge on forest management.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research the impact of Woodland Caribou conservation and range planning on forestry.

outcomes.statement: Examine the behaviour and impact of forest fires.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14A: Forest Fires (Optional) · Suggested Time: 7-9 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the main causes of forest fires (e.g., lightening and human).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Distinguish among different types (e.g., ground, surface, crown) and characteristics (e.g., severity and intensity) of forest fires.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how fuel type such as surface grass, weather conditions such as wind and rain, and ground conditions such as inclines are used to predict behaviour of a fire.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Review fire history maps and look for long-term and short-term patterns.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Interpret the impact of the types of fires on the ecology of the affected area.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the frequency and impact of fires on different forest regions in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare the annual area affected by forest fires to the amount of area harvested annually.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze the impact of fires on Saskatchewan forests over time (e.g., regeneration, how specific tree and plant species respond after a fire).

outcomes.statement: Investigate forest fire management.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14B: Forest Fire Management (Optional) · Suggested Time: 7-9 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 14A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify language used within forest fire management (e.g., fire status, contained, values protection, monitored and cultural values of the landscape).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the role of a controlled burn in forest fire management (e.g., impact on plant diseases and prevention of wildfires).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the impact forest fires have on wildlife.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify agencies that collaborate and share resources to assist with forest fire management in Canada.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate different forest fire management strategies and factors used to prioritize fires (e.g., location of fire, communities, infrastructure, timber and industry).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe the six levels used to rank forest fires and how they impact response strategies.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research how First Nations and Métis communities have used natural fire management in the past and present day.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the knowledge of Elders and Knowledge Keepers on natural forest fire management used in First Nations and Métis communities in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect on forest fire management techniques (e.g., controlled burn, natural forest fire management) and how these techniques may differ based on worldviews (e.g., First Nations and Métis).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze how public perception or media portrayal of forest fire management has changed over time (e.g., Smoky the Bear campaign).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate the existence of old and very old forests in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain the impact of fire prevention in provincial and national parks.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Discuss how fire history maps from 1945 to the present in Saskatchewan and Canada help inform forest fire management today.

outcomes.statement: Explore methods, planning and processes of harvesting.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15: Harvesting (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the components of harvesting a forest including natural forest patterns, clear cutting, shelter wood, logging, regeneration and environmental protection.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the stages in the harvesting process (i.e., falling, delimbing, skidding, loading and hauling).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore applications of different methods of forest harvest (e.g., clear cutting, selective cutting and shelter wood cutting) and regeneration (e.g., natural, artificial and intensive).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare harvesting methods and the different worldviews that are reflected within them.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the evolution of harvesting methods including techniques and equipment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize factors that influence harvesting methods such as timber characteristics and condition, growth, and utilization.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore the impact of wildfires on the planned area for harvesting trees.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine environmental concerns when planning and conducting harvest.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine harvesting plans for pertinent information such as timber species, quality, allowed cut, volume, age, layout, cutting area, roads and landing sites.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the role of silviculture within the forestry industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16: Silviculture (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 11, 12, 13

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define silviculture and describe how it differs from forestry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Summarize different natural and artificial silviculture techniques.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Practise growing techniques including bare-root, container seedlings or broadcasting seeds.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Conduct an experiment to determine what factors (e.g., soil pH, moisture, sunlight and carbon dioxide) impact growing conditions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research silviculture practices such as natural regeneration, fire, thinning and rotation ages, by different companies in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify reasons for reforestation and afforestation practices used in Saskatchewan (e.g., shelterbelts, wildlife habitat protection, decreasing erosion and increasing biodiversity).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain ecological requirements (e.g., soil and moisture) and management implications (e.g., growth rates, yield, wildlife impact, height and diameter) for a chosen tree species (e.g., spruce, aspen and pine).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss how emulating natural disturbances (e.g., wind, fire, insects and disease) is accomplished in silviculture.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research how harvesting practices have changed over the years (e.g., move from geometric shapes of clear cuts, leaving intact islands or retention structures to maintain diversity, clear cut to maintain even aged and pure stands) because of silviculture.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how the Indigenous worldview (i.e., humans are keepers of the land and all living creatures are connected) relates to current silviculture practices.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the impact of ecosystem-based management on forestry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17: Ecosystem-based Management (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 16

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define ecosystem-based management.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Recognize factors (e.g., human impact, fire, insects, disease and climate change) considered in ecosystem-based management.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the benefits of using ecosystem-based management on forests, the Earth, communities, businesses and economies.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research how ecosystem-based management is used within the forestry industry (e.g., woodland caribou habitat connectivity to forestry).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain how ecosystem-based management contributes to sustainable development and biodiversity protection.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how ecosystem-based management is used within provincial and national parks in Saskatchewan.

outcomes.statement: Explore the use of heavy equipment in the forestry industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18: Heavy Equipment (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify heavy equipment (e.g., buncher, skidder, bulldozer, scraper and rolling equipment) used in various areas of the forestry industry (e.g., harvesting, reforestation, milling and pulping operations).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare levels of training, certification and specialized skills required to operate heavy equipment used in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe safety requirements for heavy forestry equipment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the importance and role of routine inspections and maintenance of heavy equipment in the safety of employees and life of the equipment.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the historical evolution of heavy equipment used in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze the impact of heavy equipment on the forestry industry.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research innovations in heavy forestry equipment.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry on a heavy equipment operator in the forestry industry.

outcomes.statement: Explore the use of light equipment in the forestry industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Light Equipment (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 18

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize the difference between light and heavy equipment in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the types and application of light forestry equipment (e.g., axes, hatchets, winches and water pumps).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare levels of training, certification and specialized skills required to operate light equipment in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe safety requirements (e.g., safety boots, eye and ear protection) of various light forestry equipment.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate storage, transportation and shipping regulations for forestry light equipment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the importance and role of maintenance and routine inspections of light equipment in the safety of employees and life of equipment.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain how light equipment is used in the forestry industry.

outcomes.statement: Explore how mapping and remote sensing are used for forest protection and sustainability.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: Mapping and Remote Sensing (Optional) · Suggested Time: 8-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain how different types of maps (e.g., base, topographic or contour, soil type, geologic, forest stand or type and road) benefit the forestry industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Distinguish between mapping and remote sensing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the importance of using current remote sensing techniques (e.g., GPS, aerial laser 3D mapping and real-time satellite imaging) in forest exploration.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how mapping is part of the planning process in sustainably harvesting forest products.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the benefits of Geographic Information System (GIS) mapping and how it can provide information to the forestry industry.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe how mapping can support the evaluation of forest structure and age.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate how mapping can be beneficial in fire management and prevention.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze how forest mapping can show the relationship between common biogeochemical cycles (i.e., carbon, water, phosphorus and nitrogen).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the three main ways remote sensing and mapping can be applied to the forestry industry (i.e., reconnaissance mapping, commercial forestry and environmental monitoring).

outcomes.statement: Investigate the processes and applications of measuring a forest.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 21: Measuring a Forest (Optional) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 3A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the conducting of a forest survey, the type of information gathered and the purpose for collecting data.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Distinguish between forest samples and forest populations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the goals and techniques for conducting a forestry survey.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss what technology and equipment are used to measure a forest and conduct a forestry survey.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Collect boreal forest measurements (e.g., diameter, circumference and height of trees and distribution of species) accurately and reliably.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply appropriate safety procedures and use of equipment when taking forest measurements.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Select appropriate and efficient ways to organize data collection (e.g., chart, table and technology) for analysis.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze collected data to determine the condition and distribution of tree or wildlife species in the forest.

outcomes.statement: Investigate how forest ecosystems and climate are linked.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 22: Climate Change (Optional) · Suggested Time: 9-11 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze how climate and weather influence Saskatchewan forests.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the history of forests and how glaciation and climate have shaped them to what they are today.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discover how the increase in human population and resources directly impact forests.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how a forest can be a carbon source or a carbon sink and how that can affect climate change.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate how forests store carbon and are an important part of the carbon cycle to balance greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the importance of the earth maintaining a carbon balance.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System (NFCMARS) and its significance in providing information on climate change.

outcomes.statement: Explore the impact forestry has on the Saskatchewan economy.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 23: Forestry Economy (Optional) · Suggested Time: 7-9 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify forestry industry products (e.g., pulp and construction material) that are manufactured in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Define gross domestic product (GDP) as it relates to the forestry industry in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the contribution of forestry on the GDP over the past 50 years.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the role of marketing in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare the marketing of forest products over the past 50 years.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research how technology has impacted marketing, products and production practices within the forestry industry.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine how different worldviews influence marketing, production and profit sharing.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how First Nations forestry partnerships share profits within their communities.

outcomes.statement: Execute a project connected to the forestry industry that includes a trip into the boreal forest.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 24: Forestry Exploration (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Plan an excursion into an area of the boreal forest in Saskatchewan, considering terrain, conditions, wildlife and habitat.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the excursion area by consulting maps, local experts, guidebooks, photographs and weather patterns.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Collect information about a topic within forestry (e.g., treaty education, reforestation, harvesting, wildlife, mapping and forest fires) as it applies to the location being visited or studied.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Complete a planned excursion to compare collected information on a topic in forestry.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect on a personal experience in an area within forestry studies (e.g., harvesting, reforestation, climate change, sustainability, treaty education and land-based education).

outcomes.statement: Complete a project to compare the portrayal of the forestry industry in society with information obtained from a trip to a company, community or organization.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 25: Forestry Excursion (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 24

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Plan an excursion with a company, First Nations community, tribal agency or government organization that is connected to the forestry industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the portrayal of a topic within the forestry industry that will be compared during the excursion.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Collect information about a topic within forestry (e.g., treaty education, reforestation, harvesting, wildlife, mapping, remote sensing, forest fires and conservation) as it applies to the location, community, company or government organization visited or studied.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare how the forestry industry was portrayed with the in-person information gathered.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect on a personal experience in an area within forestry studies (e.g., treaty education, land-based education, harvesting, reforestation, climate change and sustainability).

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III - Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act:
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse - work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one's performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of the mathematics involved in an historical event or an area of interest.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop a rubric or other scoring schema for the assessment of the research and presentation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Collect primary or secondary data (quantitative or qualitative) related to the topic.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Assess the accuracy, reliability, and relevance of the primary or secondary data (quantitative/qualitative) collected by:
- identifying examples of bias and points of view
- identifying and describing the data collection methods
- determining whether or not the data are relevant
- determining whether or not the data are consistent with information obtained from other sources on the same topic.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Interpret data, using statistical methods if applicable.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify controversial issues, if any, and present multiple sides of the issues with supporting data.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Organize and create a presentation (oral, written, multimedia, etc.) of the research findings and conclusions.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of inductive and deductive reasoning including:
- analyzing conjectures
- analyzing spatial puzzles and games
- providing conjectures
- solving problems.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN,PS, R, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Make conjectures by observing patterns and identifying properties, and justify the reasoning.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Provide examples of how inductive reasoning might lead to false conclusions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique the following statement “Decisions can be made and actions taken based upon inductive reasoning”.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify situations relevant to self, family, or community involving inductive and/or deductive reasoning.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Prove algebraic number relationships, such as divisibility rules, number properties, mental mathematics strategies, or algebraic number tricks using deductive reasoning.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Prove conjectures using deductive reasoning.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze an argument for its validity.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify errors in proofs that lead to incorrect conclusions (e.g., a proof that ends with 2 = 1).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Solve situational questions that involve inductive or deductive reasoning.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text:
Determine, explain, and verify strategies for solving puzzles or winning games, such as:
- guess and check
- analyze a pattern
- make a systematic list
- create a drawing or model
- eliminate possibilities
- solve simpler problems
- work backward.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Create a variation of a puzzle or a game, and describe a strategy for solving the puzzle or winning the game.

guidance:
Note: It is intended that:
- proofs NOT be limited to the two column proof style
- analysis and conjectures related to spatial puzzles and games be incorporated throughout the course.

outcomes.statement:
Expand and demonstrate understanding of proportional reasoning related to:
- rates
- scale diagrams
- scale factor
- area
- surface area
- volume.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, PS, R, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and describe situations relevant to one’s self, family, or community that involve proportional reasoning.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create non-symbolic representations for rates, including pictures and graphs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe situations in which a given rate might occur.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the meaning of rates given in context, such as the arts, commerce, the environment, medicine, or recreation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Solve situational questions that require the use of proportional reasoning, including those that involve the isolation of a variable.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze situations in which unit rates can be determined and suggest reasons why the rates would or would not be used to make decisions in each situation (i.e., are other factors in the situation outweighing the importance of the mathematical calculations?).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, the relationship between the slope of a graph and a rate.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify and explain the effect of factors within given situations that could influence a particular rate.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Solve situational questions involving rates, including unit rates.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify and describe situations relevant to one’s self, family, or community that involve scale diagrams of 2-D shapes and 3-D objects and determine the scale factor for the situations.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for solving situational questions based upon scale diagrams of 2-D shapes and 3-D objects, including the determining of scale factors and unknown dimensions.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Draw, with or without the use of technology, a scale diagram of a 2-D shape relevant to self, family, or community to a specified scale factor (enlargement or reduction).

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Solve situational problems involving scale diagrams of 2-D shapes and 3-D objects.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Determine relationships between scale factor and area of 2-D shapes or surface area of 3-D objects; and scale factor, surface area, and volume of 3-D objects.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining scale factors, areas, surface areas, or volumes given the scale factor or the ratio of areas, surface areas, or volumes of 2-D shapes and 3-D objects.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Explain, with justification, the effect of a change in scale factor on the area of a 2-D shape or the surface area or volume of a 3-D object.

indicators.label: q
indicators.text: Solve situational questions that involve scale factors, areas, surface areas, and volumes, including ones that require the manipulation of formulas.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of properties of angles and triangles including:
- deriving proofs based on theorems and postulates about congruent triangles
- solving problems.
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, PS, R, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and describe situations relevant to self, family, or community that involve parallel lines cut by transversals.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, apply, and prove relationships between pairs of angles formed by transversals and parallel lines, with and without the use of technology.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Prove and apply the relationship relating the sum of the angles in a triangle.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Generalize, using inductive reasoning, a rule for the relationship between the sum of the interior angles and the number of sides (n) in a polygon, with or without technology.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply knowledge of angles formed by parallel lines and transversals to identify and correct errors in a given proof.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore and verify whether or not the angles formed by non-parallel lines and transversals create the same angle relationships as those created by parallel lines and transversals.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Solve situational problems that involve:
- angles, parallel lines, and transversals
- angles, non-parallel lines, and transversals
- angles in triangles
- angles in polygons.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for constructing parallel lines.

guidance: Note: It is intended that students be allowed to explore and use different styles of proofs, including paragraph form and two-column proofs. The emphasis should be on the logic used and the communication of that logic and not on the format of the proofs themselves.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of the cosine law and sine law (including the ambiguous case).
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, PS, R]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and describe situations relevant to self, family, or community that involve triangles without a right angle.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining angles or side lengths of triangles without a right angle.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Draw diagrams to represent situations in which the cosine law or sine law could be used to solve a question.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the steps in a given proof of the sine law or cosine law.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Illustrate and explain how one, two, or no triangles could be possible for a given set of measurements for two side lengths and the non-included angle in a proposed triangle.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the number of solutions possible to a situation involving the ambiguous case.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Solve situational questions involving triangles without a right angle.

guidance: Note: This outcome is very similar to P20.5 from Pre-calculus 20. The difference is that in Foundations of Mathematics 20, students are expected to explain steps in a given proof for either the cosine law or the sine law, but not to generate the proof on their own.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate an understanding of normal distribution, including standard deviation and z-scores.
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, PS, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify situations relevant to self, family, or community in which standard deviation and the normal distribution are used and explain the meaning and relevance of each.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the meaning and purpose of the properties of a normal curve, including mean, median, mode, standard deviation, symmetry, and area under the curve.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Calculate, using technology, the population standard deviation of a data set.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique the statement “Every set of data will correspond to a normal distribution”.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze a data set to determine if it approximates a normal distribution.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare the properties of two or more normally distributed data sets and explain what the comparison tells you about the situations that the sets represent.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain, using examples that represent multiple perspectives, the application of standard deviation for making decisions in situations such as warranties, insurance, or opinion polls.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Solve situational questions that involve the interpretation of standard deviations to make decisions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Determine, with or without technology, and explain the meaning of the z-score for a given value in a normally distributed data set.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Pose and solve situational questions relevant to self, family, or community that involve normal distributions and z-scores.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of the interpretation of statistical data, including:
- confidence intervals
- confidence levels
- margin of error.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, R]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and explain the significance of the confidence interval, margin of error, or confidence level stated with respect to statistical data relevant to self, family, or community.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how confidence levels, margins of error, and confidence intervals can be impacted by the size of the random sample used.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Make inferences and decisions with justification about a population from sample data using confidence intervals.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Provide and critique examples from print or electronic media in which confidence intervals and confidence levels are used to support a particular position.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Support a position or decision relevant to self, family, or community by analyzing statistical data, as well as considering other factors.

guidance: Note: It is intended that the focus of this outcome be on interpretation of data rather than on statistical calculations.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of systems of linear inequalities in two variables.
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, PS, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify situations relevant to self, family, or community which could be described using a system of linear inequalities in two variables.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for graphing and solving systems of linear inequalities, including justification of the choice of solid or broken lines.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for verifying solutions to systems of linear inequalities, including the use of test points.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, the meaning of the shaded region in the graphical solution of a system of linear inequalities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Write a system of linear inequalities for a given graph.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Match optimization questions and the graphs of sets of linear inequalities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Apply knowledge of graphing of systems of linear inequalities and linear programming to solve optimization questions.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate an understanding of the characteristics of quadratic functions of the form $y = a(x - p)^2 + q$ , including:
- vertex
- intercepts
- domain and range
- axis of symmetry.
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, PS, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify situations and objects relevant to self, family, or community which could be described using a quadratic function.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the intercepts of the graph of a quadratic function, including factoring, graphing (with or without the use of technology), and use of the quadratic formula.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Conjecture and verify a relationship among the roots of an equation, the zeros of the corresponding function, and the x-intercepts of the graph of the function.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, why the graph of a quadratic function may have zero, one, or two x-intercepts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Write a quadratic equation in factored form given the zeros of a corresponding quadratic function or the x-intercepts of a corresponding quadratic function.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies (with or without the use of technology) to determine the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of a quadratic function.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply a strategy for determining the equation of the axis of symmetry of the graph of a quadratic function when given the x-intercepts of the graph.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of a quadratic function and for determining if the vertex is a maximum or a minimum.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Generalize about and explain the effects on the graph of a quadratic function when the values for a, p, and q are changed.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the domain and range of a quadratic function.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explain what the domain and range of a quadratic function tell about the situation that the quadratic function models.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for sketching the graph of a quadratic function.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Solve situational questions involving the characteristics and graphs of quadratic functions.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Critique the statement “Any function that can be written in the form $y = a(x - p)^2 + q$ will have a parabolic graph.”

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of financial decision making including analysis of:
- renting, leasing, and buying
- credit
- compound interest
- investment portfolios.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, PS, R, T]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of simple interest and compound interest.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify and describe situations that involve compound interest.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Graph and compare the total interest paid or earned over different compounding periods for the same annual interest rate, principal, and time.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the total interest to be paid on a loan given the principal, interest rate, and number of compounding periods for the loan.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine, using technology, the total cost of a loan under a variety of conditions (e.g., different amortization periods, interest rates, compounding periods, and terms).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Solve contextual problems that involve compound interest.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze, using technology, different credit options that involve compound interest, including bank and store credit cards and special promotions, and provide justifications for the credit option.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify and describe examples of assets that appreciate or depreciate relevant to one's self, family, and community.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Compare renting, leasing, and buying of large cost items and generate reasons for considering each choice.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Solve situational questions related to the costs of renting, leasing, and buying (including questions that require formula manipulation).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Solve, using technology, situational questions that involve cost-and-benefit analysis.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze the strengths and weaknesses of two or more investment portfolios, and make recommendations for selection based upon this analysis.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Determine, using technology, the total value of an investment when there are regular contributions to the principal.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Graph and compare the total value of an investment with and without regular contributions.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Apply the Rule of 72 to solve investment problems and explain the limitations of the rule.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Investigate and report possible investment strategies that could be used to achieve a financial goal.

indicators.label: q
indicators.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of long-term and short-term investment options.

indicators.label: r
indicators.text: Investigate and compare small investments over a long term and larger investments over a shorter term.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of inductive and deductive reasoning including:
- analysis of conditional statements
- analysis of puzzles and games involving numerical and logical reasoning
- making and justifying decisions
- solving problems.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, PS, R]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Develop, generalize, verify, explain, and apply strategies to solve a puzzle or win a game such as:
- guess and check
- look for a pattern
- make a systematic list
- draw or model
- eliminate possibilities
- simplify the original problem
- work backwards to develop alternative approaches.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify and correct errors in a solution to a puzzle or in a strategy to win a game.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a variation on a puzzle or game and describe a strategy for solving the puzzle or winning the game.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze an "if-then" statement, make a conclusion, and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Make and justify decisions related to "what-if?" questions, in contexts such as probability, finance, sports, games, or puzzles, with or without technology.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Write the converse, inverse, and contrapositive of an "if-then" statement, determine if each new statement is true, and if it is false, provide a counterexample.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Critique statements such as "If an 'if-then' statement is known to be true, then its converse, inverse, and contrapositive also will be true".

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify and describe situations relevant to one's self, family, and community in which a biconditional (if and only if) statement can be made.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Solve situational questions, using a graphic organizer such as a truth table or Venn diagram, that involve logical arguments based upon biconditional, converse, inverse, or contrapositive statements.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of set theory and its applications.
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, PS, R, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide and describe examples, relevant to one's self, family, and community, of empty set, disjoint sets, subsets, and universal sets.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create graphic organizers such as Venn diagrams to display relationships within collected data or sets of numbers.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Name a specific region in a Venn diagram using the Boolean operators (or, and, not) or set notation, and explain in words what that region represents with respect to a specific situation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, and apply strategies for determining the elements in the complement, the intersection, or the union of sets.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify situations in which set theory is used and explain the role of set theory in each situation. (e.g., specific Internet searches, database queries, data analysis, games, and puzzles)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Solve situational questions that involve sets, including analysis of solutions for errors, using set notation where appropriate.

outcomes.statement: Extend understanding of odds and probability.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide and explain the meaning of statements of probability and odds relevant to one's self, family, and community (e.g., statements of probability found in media, science, medicine, sports, sociology, and psychology).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, the relationship between odds (part-part) and probability (part-whole).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Express odds as a probability and vice versa.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine the probability of, or the odds for and against, an outcome in a situation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, how decisions may be based on probability or odds and on subjective judgments.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Solve contextual problems that involve odds and probability.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify, describe, and justify examples of correct and incorrect use of the words "odds" or "probability" in daily language or in the media.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Critique the statement, "If the odds are close, then the probability of the two outcomes also is close".

outcomes.statement:
Extend understanding of the probability of two events, including events that are:
- mutually exclusive
- non-mutually exclusive
- dependent
- independent.
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, PS, R, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide examples of events relevant to one's self, family, and community that are mutually exclusive or non-mutually exclusive and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze two events to determine if they are complementary.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Represent, using set notation or graphic organizers, mutually exclusive (including complementary) and non-mutually exclusive events.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create and solve contextual problems that involve the probability of mutually exclusive events.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Create and solve contextual problems that involve the probability of non-mutually exclusive events.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Provide examples of events relevant to one's self, family, and community that are dependent or independent and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine the probability of an event, given the occurrence of a previous event.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Determine the probability of two dependent or two independent events.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Solve situational questions that involve determining the probability of dependent and independent events.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of combinatorics including:
- the fundamental counting principle
- permutations (excluding circular permutations)
- combinations.
outcomes.printedWith: [ME, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Represent and solve counting problems using a graphic organizer.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply the fundamental counting principle.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify and justify assumptions made in solving a counting problem.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create and solve situational questions involving the fundamental counting principle.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the number of arrangements of n elements taken n at a time.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, how factorials are related to the determination of permutations and combinations.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine, with or without technology, the value of a factorial.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Solve equations that involve factorials.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the number of permutations of n elements taken r at a time.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the number of permutations of n elements taken n at a time where some of the elements are not distinguishable.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Solve situational questions involving probability and permutations.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, why order is or is not important when counting arrangements.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Identify examples relevant to one's self, family, and community where the number of possible arrangements would be of interest to explain why the order within any particular arrangement does or does not matter.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the number of combinations of n elements taken r at a time.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Critique statements such as "If a question about determining the number of possible arrangements gives the names of the people involved, then it is a permutation question".

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of the representation and analysis of data using:
- polynomial functions of degree ≤ 3
- logarithmic functions
- exponential functions
- sinusoidal functions.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, PS, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze the graphs of polynomial functions and report on the characteristics of those graphs.

indicators.label: b

evidence.observation: The outcomes page lists 6 unit names, with no outcomes under them.

items.text: The intent of this course in geography is to acquaint and explain to the student the basic distributions of physical and cultural phenomena over the earth's surface. Through analysis of these distributions, and some of the societal processes, an understanding of the environment, society and economy of the different regions of the world should be achieved. Further, the study of geography should lead to an appreciation of the fact that the world is one, that no region exists in isolation, that, today, all parts of the world are interdependent. To ensure the attainment of the above, the geography program should foster in the student the development of the following understandings, skills, and attitudes:

There is no split between "physical geography" and "regional geography". Geography is a chorological science (i.e., deals with distribution) which needs and uses the facts of many sciences to arrive at an understanding of differences between regions.

Geography is unified by its method and viewpoint and not by its subject matter. Much of its subject matter may be contained in other disciplines -- in history, in physics, in geology, in economics, etc. -- but its viewpoint is distinctive; it is the regional viewpoint.

The regional viewpoint infers the recognition of differences and of similarities between areas across the earth's surface. Regions are distinguished on the basis of definite criteria, both physical and cultural.

Classification of phenomena (physical or cultural) into categories of greater or lesser degree of generalization should lead to the understanding of areal variation in their occurrence and hence to an appreciation of regional distribution.

In recognizing relationships occurring between different classes of phenomena, e.g., areas of dense population coinciding with great natural resources, one must be careful to differentiate between cause and effect relationships and those relationships which are accidental.
The major device for demonstrating regional differences and distributions is the map. In addition the geographer uses a variety of descriptive devices including statistical diagrams of many kinds.
To read with comprehension in the field of geography.
To analyze, interpret and evaluate data provided in many forms (statistical, map, or other).
To discover geographical relationships and to recognize regional differences.
To present, orally and in writing, in organized fashion, the results of geographical research.
To use, and constuct where possible, the various tools of geography including globes, maps, charts, and graphs.
To make case studies, local or other, and thus develop understanding of relationships between environment and human activities.
To undertake geographical studies, including elementary field work, of the local area to achieve first hand under-standing of the fundamental approach of the geographer.
Recognition that the state of knowledge is not finite, that new methods of research and new concepts are continually enolving, that understanding of the world in which we live is very incomplete.
Willingness to undertake research with an open mind and to arrive at generalizations based on unbiased appraisal.
Willingness to recognize that cultural differences across the world are the result of geographical, historical and societal factors rather than a result of "racial" dissimilarities.

A willingness to recognize that regions of similar physical environment may be occupied by very dissimilar economies and societies and that these dissimilarities are a result of numerous factors including stage of cultural and technical development, together with differences in the objectives of the peoples concerned.
A willingness to understand that no region exists in isolation that al1 parts of the world are inter-related and interdependent.

units.name: Unit I: THE PLANET EARTH: ITS CHARACTER AND PORTRAYAL
units.siteUnitName: The Planet Earth: Its Character and Portrayal

items.text: The earth is one of nine planets which revolve around the sun, a relatively small star, and thus forms part of the solar system.
The positions of the moon relative to the earth and sun account for visible variations in its illumination.

The relationships between sun and earth lead to: timing of 24-hour day;the contrasts between day and night; the period of the year; the differences in the amount of solar energy received latitudinally; the seasons; weather and climatic differences; differences in vegetation and soils and thus to differences in agricultural potential and in habitability from region to region.
The spherical shape of the earth necessitates the use of a special system of angular measurements whereby specific locations may be identified.
A system of standard time zones and an International Date Line are necessary in order to avoid confusion in communications.
Different types of map projections are designed to provide accuracy in shape or area, or to provide for a special use (e.g. the Mercator).

units.name: Unit II: THE FORM OF THE EARTH.

items.text: There is a pattern to the earth's structure.
Rocks are classified according to mode of origin and various properties.
The parts of the earth are in a state of balance. When this balance is disturbed, readjustment, the result of internal movements, takes place.
External processes assist in the sculpturing of the earth's surface.
The hydrological cycle refers to the intimate relationships which exist between atmospheric, surface, and sub-surface waters.
Typical landscapes can be associated with specific agents of gradation, and often with typical climates.
Regional landscapes have developed over great periods of time and should be considered in terms of geological time periods.
Variations in weather are the result of frequent changes in the physical characteristics of the atmosphere.
Climate is a generalization of long-term weather conditions.
The elements of climate include temperature, pressure and winds, and precipitation.
Climatic regions of the world are classified according to temperature and precipitation differences.
Regional patterns of natural vegetation are determined largely by regional patterns of climate.
Climate and natural vegetation determine the distribution of the major soil groups

units.name: Unit IV: CLIMATIC REGIONS AND THEIR EFFECTS UPON MAN.
units.siteUnitName: Climatic Regions and Their Effects Upon Man

items.text: Man's activities are closely related to climatic conditions.
The division of the world into climatic regions is based essentially on temperature conditions, with each region subdivided on the basis of rainfal1.
The type of climate in warm temperate lands is determined by the great seasonal shifts of winds and pressure systems that reflect earth-sun relationships.
The westerly winds and the middle-latitude cyclonic disturbances influence the climate of the cool temperate lands. The interiors of these lands are strongly affected by continental air masses.
Polar and arid lands are sparsely populated because of unfavourable climatic conditions.
Climatic "zones" change with altitude as well as with latitude.
Man has utilized each of the climatic regions in particular ways.
Types of farming and agricultural practices are determined by the natural environment, the culture, technology and the objectives of the people.
The demand for and utilization of minerals are determined by the stage of technological development.

items.text: Man has been classified into races-according to physical traits which can be inherited only. NOTE: Emphasize that race is a purely biological term and has no cultural, religious, or linguistic connotations. Further, there is no "pure race".
People of different skin colour and of different cultures often belong to the same race.
There are several theories to account for the distribution of people over the world.
There is an extreme unevenness of distribution of the world population.
World population is increasing rapidly and the problem of supplying the needs of life is becoming more pressing.
Geographical factors tend to control the presence or absence of people in all parts of the world.
Problems of supplying the needs of life arising from overpopulation can be alleviated.
Cities may be classified according to origin, function, and in other ways.

items.text: THE GRADE XI GEOGRAPHY COURSE

The intention of this course is to provide an under-standing of the geography of North America. The overall approach should attempt to provide understanding of the broad regional differences, physical and cultural, which occur within the continental area. Recognizing that political boundaries sometimes interfere with the full appreciation of geographic relationships the course has been designed to provide a framework of units, some of which may have international distribution while others may occur within a single nation. Nonetheless, it would be wrong to assume that major political boundaries, i.e., the international boundaries, are not geographic boundaries of considerable consequence: they interfere with free movement of men, materials, and even, sometimes, ideas -- and they were so created.

North America has been divided into a number of regions (units) which are not necessarily coterminous with the chapter headings of the text. These regions are broadly based, as far as possible, on groups of common characteristics. Obviously no line separates them but, rather, between them are broad zones of transition. Yet these regions do have validity and are useful as a toolin the analysis of all features which relate to the physical and cultural background of North America.
Basic to description, analysis, and synthesis in terms of the regional separates (units) is the use of maps pertinent to the separation and understanding of the regions.

units.name: Unit I & II
units.siteUnitName: Discovery and Exploration + Cultural Patterns and Economic Geography

items.text: Notth America is typified by north-south trending relief elements while the major political boundary, i.e., between Canada and U.S.A., trends east-west, thereby separating physically similar areas.

As a general characterization, North America can be separated into three main divisions: a northerly area too cold for agriculture; a western area generally too mountainous or/and too dry for agriculture, and an eastern humid area generally suited to agriculture.

These same divisions are applicable to North America as the home of the aboriginal population (map page 9) - the north representing the caribou, and other hunting areas; the western cordilleran area exhibiting specialized economics, not all based on agriculture; the eastern area showing adaptations to hunting in the drier interior and maize growing in the more humid sections.

These broad separates indicated here tend also to provide a gross picture of the distribution of population in North America, recognizing that some coastal and irrigated areas in the far west have developed large nodes of population.

But certain areas have been highly significant. The east, the area of initial settlement, faced Europe, receiving immigrants from the latter and developing trade with it. lajor routeways especially the Hudson-Mohawk, the St. Lawrence-Great Lakes, and the lississippi, provided ingress to the continental interior and funnelled the products of the latter eastward. Early industrial development occurred in the east and with the use of coal from the Appalachians and iron ores of the northeast and Lake Superior regions, the industrial supremacy of this area was ensured. Today the "heart" of North America includes much of the-north-eastern.and-mid-western United States together with the adjacent Great Lakes - St. Lawrence Lowland area of Canada. City development has been great and, today, many of these cities have grown to incorporate or make contact with satellites or other cities: indeed along the east coast from southern New England to Baltimore there is almost continuous urban development, making this the outstanding conurbation in the world -- a megalopolis.

The United States has demonstrated man's abilities to develop continental resources and has achieved the highest standards of living in the world. Canada, with lesser population and with its rather narrow zone of high potential for development, shows many parallels in growth. But in Central America, for many reasons, development has been slower. Both Canada and Central America show considerable emphasis on the export of raw materials and dependence on.foreign, especially American, development capital.

items.text: This is a region of hill lands extending from laritimes into the U.S.A. Here the Atlantic Ocean constituted an important focus, and settlement was early。 But major differences in economic development between the American and the Canadian sections have become increasingly apparent. While there are physical differences between the liaritimes and the North-East United States, differences in economic development cannot be directly attributed to these. Therefore, explanation of economic differences between these two areas must have basis in other factors.

items.text: The development of the lowlands was stimulated by their accessibility to the peoples and markets of Western Europe.
The region possessed a climate which proved fairly well suited to intensive agricultural development within the lowlands.
Huch of the early industrial capacity was a direct outcome of the agricultural production of the region.
The natural waterways in this region have provided a major impetus to the development of this, the industrial heart of North America.
Heavy concentration of population has transformed many features of the landscape.

units.name: Unit V: Region: The Prairies and the Great Plains Region of Canada and the United States.
units.siteUnitName: The Prairies and Great Plains of Canada and the United States

items.text: Variation in climate and topography related closely to differences in farming and rancing activities, some areas specializing, as for example, in Spring wheat. 2。1 Dry climate has necessitated the development of special farming techniques and seed varities. Large farming units and principles of "Big Business" are characteristic of most forms of land-use.

Economic stability has been promoted through crop diversification, irrigation, improved methods of cultivation, government aid, etc.; development of mineral resources (coal, petroleum, natural gas, potash, etc.) and the introduction of industry have also assisted in providing greater economic diversity.

The Plains are sparsely settled. Changes in the economy and in transportation and other facilities have led to rural depopulation and to urbanization. Hajor cities, e.g., Edmonton, Calgary, Winnipeg, Kansas City, Denver, etc., tend to lie on the margins.
The 49th parallel separates politically but does not create essential differences in land-use.
The Western Cordillera is a good example of "Unity in diversity". The variety of landforms, climate and human response gives the whole region a distinctive geographic personality.

The Western Cordillera exhibits the greatest contrasts in human and economic geography found in any part of the North American continent; these contrasts are apparent in agriculture, fisheries, forest industries, minerals, power, and industry.
There is a close relationship between the irrigated lands of the cordilleran region and the distribution of agriculture and population.
The Western Cordillera is an area potentially rich in resources but man has had to overcome natural handicaps in their development.
Tropical climate and its effects on vegetation and land-use.
Geographical location and land forms and their influence on agriculture and settlement.
History of settlement and population characteristics.
Poverty of the masses, riches of the few.
Developpent of resources.
Contrasts between Liddle America and the United States and Canada in products, exports and economic development.
Economic interdependence with northern neighbors.

units.name: Unit VIII: The Canadian Shield and the Northland

items.text: There is a close relationship between peneplenation, uplift, stream rejuvenation, glaciation and permafrost, on the one hand, and the problems of land and water transportation and communication, poor drainage, the scarcity of arable soil, hydro-electric power potential and the accessibility of mineral deposits, on the other.

The physical characteristics - terrain, permafrost, climate of the Canadian Shield and Northland create major obstacles to transportation and communication. These in turn retard the utilization of resources and the extension of settlement.
The nature of rock structure and the effects of glaciation are related to the comparative surface accessibility of mineral deposits.

The Canadian North possesses great potential wealth in furs, forest products, minerals, hydro-electric power, and even agricultural lands (Clay belt). Present and future development of these resources is contingent on over-coming the handicaps of a short growing season, permafrost, muskeg, great distances, difficult climate, difficulties of road and railway construction, the expense of air transport and isolated settlement patterns.
The Eskimo has survived in the northern desert (tundra) by developing skills that enable him to exploit the meagre offerings of his environment, particularly those of the sea。
The location and vast extent of the Northland has given the region a new significance strategically.

This is an area characterized by recent massive economic and political changes.The original pattern·of English settlement, based on the plantation, led to the importation of slave labor and its social consequences. The breakdown of plantation agriculture led to new patterns of land-use and the relocation of some older activities, e.g., cotton to drier areas. This has been a difficult area marked by cleavage in economic and cultural opportunity. Industrial activity is increasing, e.g., Gulf Coast, T.V.A., (as example of change); and forms and types of agriculture are undergoing rapid transformation. The South is no longer the "cotton belt" or the "deep south" but a competitive region within the American complex.

outcomes.statement: Investigate expectations and standards in the hairstyling and esthetics industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Introduction to Hairstyling and Esthetics (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify expectations and standards in the hairstyling and esthetics industry such as sanitation, safety, work ethic and professional image.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Construct a list of skills for an individual entering into a career in hairstyling and esthetics.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of effective communication such as active listening and speaking clearly as it relates to hairstyling and esthetics.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Reflect on the impact of positive and negative non-verbal communication (e.g., smile/frown, body language) when working in the field of hairstyling and esthetics.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Define terminology (e.g., draping, sanitization, massage, cuticle, contour) and identify the chosen profession (e.g., hairstyling, nail technician, skin technician, makeup artist) where the term would be used.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research and present on an area of interest found within hairstyling and esthetics (e.g., how much money annually is spent on the beauty industry, how animal testing impacts use of products, the increase in use of environmentally sustainable products).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the question, “How does dermatology, massage therapy, theatrical makeup, hairstyling and barbering fit under the umbrella of the beauty industry?”.

outcomes.statement: Examine general safety requirements within hairstyling and esthetics.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2A: General Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Distinguish between provincial and federal health and safety rules and guidelines as applied to hairstyling and esthetics.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify potential hazards in salons, appropriate safety equipment (e.g., personal protective equipment (PPE)) and appropriate safety precautions (e.g., public sanitation, trip hazards).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss general safety practices when using common salon equipment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Brainstorm general safety guidelines for a salon such as managing wires on the floor, extension cords, walkways and handling chemicals.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect on the impact that salon cleanliness (e.g., dust, organization) has on safety and business feasibility.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how technician’s choices and behaviours impact safety (e.g., wearing sandals or clothing that exposes skin can cause damage to self or clients).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of ergonomics for the health and well-being of technicians.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify the effects that wellness components such as posture, exercise, rest, stress management, hygiene and nutrition have on the success of a hairstylist or esthetician.
