indicators.text: Define the terms sanitation, disinfection and sterilization.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the three levels of infection control (i.e., sanitation, disinfection and sterilization).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe contamination and decontamination.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate the purpose and application of antiseptic versus a disinfectant.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Classify given scenarios as sanitizing, disinfecting, or sterilizing.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Classify single-use implements versus multi-use tools.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the different levels of disinfection (i.e., high, intermediate and low level) and describe situations when each level is appropriate.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare different techniques for sanitizing, disinfecting and sterilizing instruments and surfaces.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate techniques for sanitizing and disinfecting instruments and surfaces.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate different processes for disinfecting, sanitizing and sterilizing non-porous items (e.g., glass, metal, electric files, linen).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Recognize the difference between a chemosterilant and a high level disinfectant.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Compare labels on chemicals for proper use and disposal.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Critique sanitation practices when performing a service (e.g., manicures, pedicure, facial, makeup application, cut and style).

outcomes.statement: Justify the importance of proper sanitation, disinfection and sterilization.

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: c

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Justify the importance of maintaining a safe and organized workstation throughout a service.

indicators.label: e

indicators.label: f

indicators.label: g

indicators.label: h

outcomes.statement: Examine scope of practice within hairstyling and esthetics.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Scope of Practice (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify hairstylist services such as shampoo, cut, style and chemically treat hair.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify esthetician services such as massage, skin care, nail enhancements and make up.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Define scope of practice and how it applies to estheticians and hairstylists.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize what is appropriate scope of practice for someone who has not received all the necessary training and certification.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore different steps found within scope of practice (e.g., technician, journeyperson apprentice, journeyperson, medical, dermatologist).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss why hairstylists may also provide services such as scalp treatments, hair additions and barbering techniques.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss why successful hairstylists incorporate technical and interpersonal skills.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate appropriate scope of practice within hairstyling and esthetics.

outcomes.statement: Examine professionalism within hairstyling and esthetics.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7A: Professionalism (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define professionalism and ethics in the field of hairstyling and esthetics.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe characteristics of a professional image.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how the choices and behaviours of a hairstylist or esthetician impacts their professional lives.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the importance of mental and physical health and well-being for personal and also professional reasons.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Define and compare non-verbal, verbal and written communication.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss qualities of effective communication such as the role of actively listening and confirming expectations of clients.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze the importance of appropriate communication techniques and tools with clients including telephone and technology.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate behaviours (e.g., politeness, accommodating service, modeling hairstyles, nails, make-up and skin) and atmosphere (e.g., music, linens, comfort) that clientele find the most approachable and the most conducive to return business.

outcomes.statement: Explore the impact of professionalism within hairstyling.

indicators.label: e

outcomes.statement: Examine elements of art and principles of design in hairstyling and esthetics.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8A: Elements of Design (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the elements of art (i.e., colour, form, line, shape, space, texture, tone, value).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the principles of design (i.e., balance, contrast and variety, movement and rhythm, pattern, harmony and unity, emphasis, proportion and scale).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how the elements of art and principles of design apply to artistic expression within the context of hair and esthetics.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Respond critically, using appropriate vocabulary, to examples in the context of hair and esthetics creations considering how the elements of art and principles of design are applied.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Justify why examples of hair and esthetics creations are appealing based on elements of art and principles of design.

outcomes.statement: Initiate and develop ideas for artistic expression, within the context of hair, that incorporate the elements of art and principles of design.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8B: Elements of Design (Hairstyling) (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 8A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how the elements of art and principles of design apply to artistic expression within the context of hair.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Respond critically, using appropriate vocabulary, to examples in the context of hair creations considering how the elements of art and principles of design are applied.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Justify why examples of hair creations are appealing based on elements of art and principles of design.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique artistic examples of hair (e.g., what are you seeing, why are you drawn to it or why was it a successful artistic expression).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Use colour theory principles and tools to customize hair services to meet individual needs (e.g., warm cool colours, complementary colours, monochromatic analogous and triadic colour schemes).

outcomes.statement: Initiate and develop ideas for artistic expression, within the context of esthetics, that incorporate the elements of art and principles of design.

outcomes.statement: Explore the impact of elements of art and principles of design on hairstyling.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8D: Elements of Design (Hairstyling) (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 8B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Respond critically, using appropriate vocabulary, to advanced examples in the context of hair creations considering how the elements of art and principles of design are applied.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Respond to the inquiry question, how are elements of art and principles of design in hair reflective of time, culture and societal influences?

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique examples of hair (e.g., ‘the Rachel’ hairstyle, Elvis Presley’s pompadour, Twiggy’s pixie cut, gender expression) that were influenced by historical art styles or pop culture movements.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique examples of hair (e.g., renaissance braids, sixties long hair, WWI bobs that were easier to manage, Japanese geisha hairstyles) that were influenced by social, cultural, geographical and environmental contexts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Use advanced colour theory principles and tools to customize hair services to meet individual needs (e.g., warm cool colours, complementary colours, monochromatic analogous and triadic colour schemes).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss advanced image development strategies used for artistic expression such as exaggeration, layering and simplifying.

outcomes.statement: Examine how beauty can be an expression of a person’s worldview, culture and self-identity.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9A: Inclusive Beauty (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the meaning of worldview, (e.g., attitude and principles) culture (e.g., ethnic background and subculture) and self-identity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research how techniques and trends in hairstyling and esthetics reflect worldviews, culture and self-identity.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine hairstyles, skin care, nail techniques and make-up examples within the local community.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the impact that worldview and culture have on an individual’s definition of beauty.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research and discuss historical and current societal attempts to control (e.g., government regulations/intervention, school dress code) self- expression (e.g., significance of the braid) of beauty.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore ideals of beauty (e.g., size of earlobes, length of hair, piercings, length of nails and gender expression) across cultures.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the question, how does an individual’s expression of human beauty reflect their worldview, culture or self-identity?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on personal aesthetic choices (e.g., makeup, hair, nails) and their potential to communicate worldview, culture or self-identity.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss how a traditional Western definition of beauty (e.g., hair texture, light-coloured eyes and skin, hetero normativity) excludes and marginalizes expression of identity and culture.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss how cultures that have been historically excluded and marginalized are challenging the stereotypical Western ideal of beauty.

outcomes.statement: Examine how beauty can be an expression of a person’s worldview, culture and self-identity.

indicators.text: Discuss the meaning of worldview, (e.g., attitude and principles) culture (e.g., ethnic background and subculture) and self-identity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research how techniques and trends in hairstyling and esthetics reflect worldviews, culture and self-identity.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine hairstyles, skin care, nail techniques and make-up examples within the local community.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the impact that worldview and culture have on an individual’s definition of beauty.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research and discuss historical and current societal attempts to control (e.g., government regulations/intervention, school dress code) self- expression (e.g., significance of the braid) of beauty.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore ideals of beauty (e.g., size of earlobes, length of hair, piercings, length of nails and gender expression) across cultures.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the question, how does an individual’s expression of human beauty reflect their worldview, culture or self-identity?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on personal aesthetic choices (e.g., makeup, hair, nails) and their potential to communicate worldview, culture or self-identity.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss how a traditional Western definition of beauty (e.g., hair texture, light-coloured eyes and skin, hetero normativity) excludes and marginalizes expression of identity and culture.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss how cultures that have been historically excluded and marginalized are challenging the stereotypical Western ideal of beauty.

outcomes.statement: Examine how beauty can be an expression of a person’s worldview, culture and self-identity.

outcomes.statement: Analyze career opportunities within hairstyling and esthetics.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Career Opportunities (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Classify different community business options in hairstyling and esthetics including nail technician, make-up artist and skin care technician.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the various career opportunities within the hairstyling and esthetics industry (e.g., hairstylists, hair salons, spas, barber shops, schools, hair replacement clinics, health care establishments, hotels, tourism, fashion and entertainment industries).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore career advancement opportunities in the hairstyling and esthetics industry such as salon managers, salon owners, fashion consultants, educators, platform artists and product sales representatives.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss ways hairstylists may be remunerated such as salary, commission, a combination of salary and commission or chair rental agreements.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Interview a community member in a specific field within hairstyling and esthetics.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss how different careers within hairstyling and esthetics complement one another and how often professionals have more than one trade or certification.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Critique different business examples in the field of hairstyling and esthetics.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the qualities (e.g., positive client relationships) of successful technicians.

outcomes.statement: Examine characteristics of a successful salon.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11A: Introduction to Salon (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify relevant laws, regulations and regulatory bodies for a salon that contains hairstyling and esthetics.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify procedures for equipment storage, cleaning and organization in a salon.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe how a salon can ensure safe and productive work practices.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Categorize components that are necessary for business operation of a successful salon (e.g., operation expenses, working environment, profit margin, ethics and client relationships).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research accurate client-scheduling skills including allowing sufficient time for all treatments and services.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe skills salon employees need to recommend and sell products and services.

outcomes.statement: Analyze characteristics of a successful salon.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11B: Introduction to Salon (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 11A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Categorize components (e.g., operation expenses, working environment, profit margin, ethics and client relationships) that are necessary for the business operation of a successful salon.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create responses to customer complaints and examine their potential impact on salon business.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique class created responses to customer complaints including the importance of maintaining professional ethics and positive client relationships.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a salon list of services, determine appropriate pricing for each service and justify the impact on the business operation of the salon.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss economic and environmentally sustainable business practices for a salon.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify techniques used to promote economically sustainable services/treatments.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore how environmentally sustainable products and practices impact salon business.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Design a concept for a salon detailing the services provided.

outcomes.statement: Explore the scope of technicians in esthetics.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: Introduction to Esthetics (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify different treatments performed by skin and nail technicians.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research tools, equipment and maintenance used in esthetics.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe how technicians can ensure safe and productive work practices including employing proper ergonomics and personal protective equipment (PPE) throughout services.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how advancements in technology have impacted esthetics.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the consultation process and its impact on the client’s experience.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13: Client Consultation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify communications skills such as asking clarifying questions used in successful client consultations.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a list of possible questions for client consultations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how respect for a client’s worldview, culture or self-identity should inform the consultation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique appropriate communication skills during a client consultation scenario or within a classroom role play.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss preparations for client consultation such as appropriate salon documents, client allergies and sensitivities, hair textures (e.g., fine, medium, coarse, kinky and curl pattern) and hair characteristics (e.g., density, porosity, elasticity).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Determine, through client consultation scenarios, the type of service, the required time and the total cost.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the question, how important is the client consultation for a successful salon experience?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss how technicians can create an inclusive and welcoming environment for all clients, including the important role language plays in client experiences.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain the importance of confirming the final outcome for the service.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify ways to establish, document, maintain and store records of client services/treatments.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Demonstrate discretion and confidentiality in acquiring and managing client information.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze examples (e.g., potential bias, gender normativity expectations) that could negatively impact the client consultation process.

outcomes.statement: Explore hairstyling and esthetics products.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14A: General Product Knowledge (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define categories such as professional, prestige and drugstore as used to distinguish hairstyling and esthetics products.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the questions: What can certain products offer that others cannot? Why would professionals want to use professional products?

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the benefits of licensed sellers when purchasing hairstyling and esthetics products.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine the qualifications required to work for a licensed seller or within hairstyling and esthetics product distribution.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the reason qualifications are beneficial for those employed within product distribution.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze different products, including following manufacturer’s instructions, to optimize results.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Justify product selection for provided scenarios (e.g., client has a certain skin type, hair texture or desires a specific outcome).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine ingredients used in products (e.g., consumer packaging and labelling act and regulations for Canada) and the potential impact on the health of clients.

outcomes.statement: Analyze hair care products.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14B: Hairstyling Product Knowledge (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 14A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify products and discuss selection criteria based on alignment with client budget and behaviours (e.g., work outside, stay at home).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Categorize different hair care products based on their chemical ingredients or lack of chemical ingredients.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Define potential hydrogen (pH), acidity and alkalinity.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine the pH level of hair and products (e.g., shampoos, conditioners, hydrochloric acid, lye, permanent wave solution).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss what impact drugstore products have on hair compared to professional hair care products.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare ingredient lists of professional products for different hair textures and characteristics.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Recognize how allergies and conditions affect product selection.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the question, how does hair texture (e.g., fine, medium, coarse, kinky, curl pattern or coil configuration) and hair characteristics (e.g., elasticity, porosity, condition and density) influence the selection of hair care products?

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the environmental impact and sustainability of products and packaging.

outcomes.statement: Analyze skin care products.

indicators.label: c

indicators.label: f

indicators.label: g

indicators.label: h

indicators.label: j

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify contraindications and how it could affect skin care product selection.

indicators.label: l

indicators.label: m

indicators.label: n

indicators.label: g

indicators.label: m

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the potential impact nail and foot care products could have on the health of clients.

outcomes.statement: Examine maintenance and use of hairstyling equipment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16A: Hair Styling Equipment and Maintenance (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify single-use and multi-use manual tools, styling tools, cutting tools, electric tools, chemical service tools and equipment used in hairstyling.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe how manual tools, electric tools and equipment are used in hairstyling.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate application of hairstyling manual tools, electric tools and equipment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize how proper ergonomic practices are necessary to maintain the health of stylists.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of sanitation and safety for each tool and piece of equipment used in hairstyling.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe and perform sanitization, sterilization or disinfection of tools and equipment (e.g., spraying disinfectant, wiping and soaking; handling/storing cleaning towels, capes, aprons and smocks).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe and perform an inspection process (e.g., check for product build- up and determine when a tool must be removed from service) to maintain manual tools, electric tools and equipment (e.g., remove debris from filters in hairdryers, clippers and clothes dryer and discard refuse and product waste according to regulations).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss and apply safety practises when using all tools and equipment (e.g., adjust hydraulic chairs and other equipment according to stylist’s ergonomic support, use personal protective equipment (PPE), locate first aid and eye wash stations, discard sharps according to regulations and recognize all hazards).

outcomes.statement: Examine characteristics of hair and scalp.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17A: Hair and Scalp (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify hair structures (i.e., cuticle, cortex and medulla) and sub-scalp structures (e.g., hair root and gland systems).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Summarize factors that affect hair growth such as age, nutrition, health and hormones.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine hair texture (e.g., fine, medium, coarse, kinky and curl pattern) and characteristics such as weight, shape, elasticity, porosity, density and growth patterns.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore techniques (e.g., stretch single hair, feel hair with hands) used to determine elasticity and porosity.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Recognize effects on hair exhibiting a lack of moisture or protein.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Perform hair analysis and recommend products for maintenance, optimal health and condition of hair.

outcomes.statement: Analyze characteristics of hair and scalp.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17B: Hair and Scalp (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 17A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify hair and scalp disorders such as psoriasis, alopecia, dandruff and dry or oily scalp by performing a visual inspection with hands or comb.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss and practice different types of hair and/or scalp treatments.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify infections (e.g., vegetable, animal, staphylococci) on the scalp.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of hair repair products.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss types of treatments for scalp conditions.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Execute a scalp treatment including preparation, draping, safety and sanitation procedures.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze the theory of massage including purpose of scalp massage, massage movements and the benefits of massage.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the questions: What impact does hair texture and hair characteristics have on the analysis of client hair care needs? Why is it important to use industry language (e.g., hair texture and characteristics) when discussing hair?

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Conduct a client consultation for a hair repair treatment.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Perform a scalp massage.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Perform a hair repair treatment.

outcomes.statement: Execute a shampoo and condition tailored to a client’s needs.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18: Shampoo and Rinse (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss with client their current hair care needs and concerns.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze hair to determine which shampoo and conditioner would be suitable for the client.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Experiment with appropriate conditions (e.g., water temperature, detangling techniques, brush and comb selection and water nozzle distance) for washing hair.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Practice proper scalp manipulations and techniques for shampooing and conditioning hair and scalp.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Perform pre-brushing, draping, shampoo (e.g., apply, lather, appropriate pressure to suit client ensuring complete saturation) and conditioner (e.g., ensure hydration, close the cuticle and detangle).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss and apply sanitary procedures when shampooing hair.

outcomes.statement: Investigate hair styles and hair styling techniques.

indicators.label: a

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: c

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Execute braiding techniques including visible, invisible and fishtail.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the significance of braiding in First Nations’ cultures.

indicators.label: g

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

f

- Where are safety notices posted?

outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Generate a list of occupations that require a background in health science through research and/or participation in events such as a career fair or job shadow. (K, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the connection between topics in Health Science 20 and occupations of personal interest. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify which health-science related occupations are facing shortages and which are oversubscribed locally, regionally and/or nationally. (STSE, S, K, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the roles, responsibilities, educational qualifications and personal and professional qualities common to people involved in health-science related jobs. (S, A)

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Examine the role of self-regulating professional bodies (e.g., college, association society, board and council) in the health care field. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess the role of a volunteer, the importance of volunteerism and potential local opportunities to volunteer in the health sector. (K, A)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Communicate research findings related to health-science occupations through a display, brochure, video, presentation software, website or orally. (K, S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Use acquired knowledge to develop a plan to attain a job of the student's interest in the health science field. (S, A)

outcomes.statement: Create and carry out a plan to explore one or more topics of personal interest relevant to Health Science 20 in depth.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Design a scientific investigation related to a topic of study in Health Science 20 that includes a testable question, a hypothesis, an experimental design that will test the hypothesis and detailed procedures for collecting and analyzing data. (STSE, S).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Carry out an experiment following established scientific protocols to investigate a question of interest related to one or more of the topics of Health Science 20. (S, K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assemble and reflect on a portfolio that demonstrates understanding of a health science topic of interest to the student. (S, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate the effectiveness of a device, model or technique that demonstrates the scientific principles underlying a concept related to a Health Science 20 topic. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Debate an issue related to health science, including developing materials to support the arguments for and against a position. (S, A, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop a case study that exemplifies ethical decision making in health care. (S, K, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop a case study of the progression and/or treatment of a specific pathology from the perspective of a Western, traditional, complementary and/or alternative approach to health care. (S, K, A)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create a personal medical history, incorporating information such as family history, baseline data and immunizations. (S, K, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Share the results of student-directed research through a display, presentation, performance, demonstration, song, game, commercial, fine art representation or research paper. (S)

indicators.label: j

outcomes.statement: Analyze how Western, Indigenous, traditional, complementary and alternative approaches to health care can contribute to a holistic (e.g., mental, emotional, physical and spiritual) perspective of health.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify how humanity's beliefs about health, wellness, illness, disease and treatment have changed over time. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of and difficulties in defining terms such as Western, Indigenous, traditional, complementary and alternative approaches to health care within a global context. (K, A, S, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess how practitioners of Western, Indigenous, traditional, complementary and alternative approaches to health care address health, wellness, illness, disease, and treatment through beliefs and practices such as Circle of Life, disharmony of body energies, being symptom free and healthy lifestyle choices. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify where Western, Indigenous, traditional, complementary and alternative approaches to health care are offered in your community and elsewhere in Saskatchewan. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the costs associated with various approaches to health care and the health benefits available to residents of Saskatchewan and Canada. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the intended results of using natural products (e.g., herbs, vitamins, minerals, probiotics, and essential oils), mind and body practices (e.g., acupuncture, various massage therapies, yoga, spinal manipulation, relaxation techniques, meditation, and movement therapies) and other complementary and/or alternative approaches to health care. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the significance of rituals, place-based ceremonies, plants, and traditional herbs in Indigenous and traditional approaches to health care. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess the importance of clinical trial features (e.g., informed consent, randomized control trial, blind and double-blind protocols and placebos) in providing reliable scientific evidence to support Western approaches to health care. (STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Provide examples of how one or more of the major approaches to health care might be implemented together to support the health and wellbeing of an individual from mental, emotional, physical and spiritual perspectives. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss potential health hazards or complications that may arise from combining different approaches to health care to address an individual's health concerns. (K, A, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Examine how personal, cultural and societal beliefs affect ethical decisions regarding health care.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions about ethical dilemmas within health care. (K, S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Understand the core ethical questions to be considered when making health care decisions:
- What can be done for the patient? (intervention technologies)
- Does the patient understand the options? (informed consent)
- What does the patient want? (autonomy)
- What are the benefits? (beneficence)
- Will it harm the patient? (non-maleficence)
- Are the patient's requests fair and able to be satisfied? (justice)
- Are the costs involved fair to society? (economic consequences) (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze a health care issue with respect to the core ethical questions. (K,A, S, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Contrast how procedures to prevent illness, such as immunizations, vitamin supplements, physical activity, nutrition and prayer, might be viewed from the perspective of Western, Indigenous, traditional, complementary and alternative approaches to health care. (K, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine ethical considerations related to various practices and treatments (e.g., chemotherapy, radiation, acupuncture, sweat lodge, blood transfusions, herbal remedies and hirudotherapy) that might be considered in Western, Indigenous, traditional, complementary and alternative approaches to health care. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss individual, community and cultural beliefs regarding issues related to life and death such as home birthing, blood transfusions, contraception, abortions, organ donation, autopsies, euthanasia, cremation, burials and medical aid in dying. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine ethical considerations and perspectives related to issues such as the use of cadavers in professional studies, dissection and raising animals for the purpose of dissection, and public exhibits of plastinated organs and bodies, all of which could provide increased scientific understanding of human anatomy. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Understand a patient's rights in Saskatchewan and in Canada concerning health care decisions such as developing an advance care directive, refusal of treatment, informed consent and the role of a proxy or substitute decision-maker. (K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Recognize the importance of considering linguistic and cultural needs when providing health care services. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Assess how various ethical considerations (e.g., personal beliefs, informed consent, the roles of institutional review boards and regulatory agencies) may influence an individual's decision to participate in a clinical study of a new biomedical intervention (e.g., vaccine, drug, treatment, device or process). (STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Debate a decision related to ethics in health care from the viewpoint of individuals who hold different belief systems. (K, A, S, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Analyze the anatomy and physiology of a healthy human.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine First Nations, Métis and other holistic perspectives of the human body. (K, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the anatomy (structure) and physiology (function) of at least five human body systems (i.e., cardiovascular, endocrine, lymphatic, digestive, urinary, muscular, nervous, respiratory, reproductive, integumentary and skeletal). (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the normal values or ranges for the common vital signs (e.g., heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, O2 saturation and respiratory rate) of a healthy human. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use anatomical terminology, including directional terms, body planes, body regions and body cavities, to locate human anatomical features based on standard anatomical position. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the anatomical locations of organs in mammals such as pigs, rats or cats through dissection or virtual simulation. (K, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Design and carry out an investigation to examine baseline values used for assessing health such as heart rate, O2 saturation, blood pressure, temperature and respiratory rate. (K, S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the interrelationships between the ABO and Rh blood group systems, an individual's blood type and blood donor compatibilities. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the benefits of normal flora, or normal microbiota, on and in the human body. (K, S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research advances in scientific understanding of human anatomy and physiology. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Investigate the effects of various injuries, disorders and diseases on human cells, tissues, organs and systems.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate among the ways in which medical practitioners and the public use terms such as disease, illness, ailment, disorder, infection, medical condition, syndrome and abnormal condition. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate how the immune system uses a layered defense to respond to pathogens, including the difference between the innate and adaptive immune system.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the symptoms, possible causes, stages and scope (e.g., cells, tissues, organs and/or systems) of a pathology that affects one or more body systems. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a representation (e.g., illness narrative, journal, timeline, story, video or diorama) of the progression of a specific pathology from the perspective of a real or hypothetical individual, including impacts on their lifestyle. (K, A, S, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Outline the history of a disease or illness and its causes, including societal and cultural perspectives. (K, A, S, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare prepared slides or digital images of healthy and diseased tissues to identify how pathologies affect cells. (K, A, S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare how bacteria (e.g., Salmonella, Streptococcus, and Escherichia coli) and viruses (e.g., common cold, influenza and herpes) differ in how they are transmitted, their impact on the human body and how each is treated. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze the role of homeostasis in various phenomena such as regulation, heart rate, breathing, urination, sweating, digestion, body temperature, blood composition and stress.

outcomes.statement: Assess the importance of macronutrients (i.e., carbohydrates, proteins and fats) and micronutrients (e.g., vitamins, minerals and phytochemicals) in maintaining human health.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify which macronutrients and micronutrients are commonly found in each food group (i.e., vegetables and fruit, grain products, milk and alternatives, meat and alternatives and oils and fats). (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how the body breaks down and uses simple (e.g., monosaccharide and disaccharide) and complex (i.e., polysaccharide) carbohydrates and dietary fiber. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the role of fats (e.g., saturated, unsaturated and trans fats) in processes such as long term energy storage, supporting vitamin absorption, creating cell membranes, synthesizing hormones, cushioning and protecting organs and helping us feel full. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the roles of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) in managing cholesterol levels.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the role of proteins in the production of antibodies, hemoglobin and insulin, structural support and building and maintaining muscle. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how enzymes (e.g., amylase, pepsin, lipase and protease) found in the mouth, stomach, pancreas and small intestine aid in the chemical digestion of food. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Recognize issues (e.g., hypo/hyperglycemia, high/low cholesterol and denaturation of proteins) that may arise when macromolecules disrupt homeostasis. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Establish the relationships between dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis reactions in relation to the macronutrients (e.g., glucose + fructose = sucrose). (K, S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain how micronutrients (e.g., vitamins A, B, C, D, E and K, and iron, calcium and phosphorous) are necessary for health. (K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research the food source and health claims associated with various phytochemicals (e.g., carotenoids, flavonoids, phenolic acids, phytoestrogens and organosulphur compounds). (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine the connection between undernutrition or overnutrition and development of diseases such as anemia, scurvy, Type 2 diabetes and heart disease. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Investigate the contributions of various people (e.g., Justus von Liebig, Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier, Claude Bernard and Emil Fischer) in advancing scientific understanding of nutrition. (STSE)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explain the role of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) as a molecule indispensable for the functioning of cells and life. (K)

outcomes.statement: Analyze dietary choices based on personal and cultural beliefs and scientific understanding of nutrition.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, CP

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions about the role of nutrition in supporting healthy eating practices. (K, S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how various factors (e.g., activity level, muscle mass, gender, age, weight and height) affect personal energy requirements. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Calculate personal energy requirements and record personal caloric and macronutrient intake for a specified period. (S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare results of personal macronutrient intake to recommended daily intake (RDI) values. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain how analysis of excrement (e.g., Bristol stool chart) and urine (e.g., urine analysis by color, clarity, odor, pH, nitrites, protein, glucose, tinkle test and Pee-O-Meter) serve as indicators of healthy functioning. (STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine how the dietary recommendations in Canada's Food Guide compare with recommendations in food guides from other countries. (S, K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess the value of information from food labels (e.g., ingredient list, nutrition facts table, nutrient content claims and health claims) to guide personal food choices. (A, S, K, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Design a healthful diet based on personal lifestyle choices. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critique the use of tools (e.g., body mass index [BMI], skinfold caliper, BOD POD and hydrostatic weighing) that provide information about body composition. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate the effects of processed foods, nutrition supplements, growth hormones, genetically modified foods and food additives (e.g., caffeine, aspartame, food coloring and monosodium glutamate [MSG]) on human health. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Evaluate physiological and psychological effects of nutritional disorders such as anorexia nervosa, bulimia and obesity and their connection to body image and nutrition deficiencies. (K, A)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Assess whether eating practices such as carbohydrate loading, fad diets, vegetarianism, veganism, fast food, energy drinks, 100-mile diet and fasting provide sufficient nutrition to support healthy functioning. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Examine how various eating practices (e.g., pre-contact First Nations and Métis, kosher, halal and fasting practices during observances such as Lent and Ramadan) are based upon cultural and religious beliefs. (A, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Explore the tools and procedures used to diagnose and monitor medical conditions.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, SI, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Assess the significance of monitoring vital signs in health care, including obtaining accurate medical history and patient perception of pain. (K, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify examples of procedures (e.g., visual inspection) and tools (e.g., stethoscope, octoscope and sphygmomanometer) commonly used for non-invasive diagnostic observations in health care. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Measure and record vital signs (e.g., pulse, respiration, temperature, blood pressure and degree of pain) of self and/or others. (S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the procedures, safety concerns and relevance of common laboratory tests (e.g., blood testing, blood glucose, culture swabs, urinalysis, stool, biopsy and microscopy) used in medical diagnosis. (K,S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the operation, risks, benefits and imaging modalities (e.g., sound, light, radiation and nuclear medicine) of medical imaging tools, including X-ray radiography, magnetic resonance imaging [MRI], computed tomography [CT], ultrasound and positron emission tomography [PET]). (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe technological advances in medical imaging tools (e.g., X-ray, ultrasound, computerized tomography and magnetic resonance imaging). (K, S, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss factors (e.g., severity of illness, dose received, cost and availability) that influence the choice to use a diagnostic tool or procedure. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the responsibility, including preparation and expectations, of the patient in diagnostic and imaging procedures. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify differences in tools and procedures used in diagnosing illness from the perspectives of Western, Indigenous, traditional, complementary and alternative approaches to health care. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of diagnosis in improving the care of patients, protecting the health of clients and improving the economics of health care. (K, STSE, A)

outcomes.statement: Assess the importance of interpreting diagnostic findings to support treatment options for specific pathologies.
outcomes.printedWith: DM, SI, CP

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify tools and procedures that may be used to assist health care providers in monitoring the progression of a specific pathology. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Suggest explanations based on interpretation of data from diagnostic assessment tools (e.g., identifying a broken bone in an X-ray, ultrasound of a pregnancy to determine number of fetuses and identifying high blood pressure based on given values). (K, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Interpret diagnostic results and choose an appropriate course of action based on participation in a role-play, simulation and/or case study. (K, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain why medical practitioners often use multiple tools and procedures to establish a medical diagnosis. (STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss possible implications (e.g., incorrect diagnosis, improper treatment and psychological effect on patient) associated with incorrect interpretation of diagnostic findings for the patient and others. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe some treatment options (e.g., dialysis, radiation therapy, surgery and organ transplantation) which have been designed to address specific health care issues. (STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe various treatment options that might be considered at various stages of a specific pathology from the perspective of Western, Indigenous, traditional, complementary and/or alternative approaches to health care. (K)

units.note: Course-level foundational objectives (not part of any unit).

items.text: understand that humans establish various kinds of organizations as a means of systematically meeting their needs and wants;
items.stem: The knowledge objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: understand that individuals within organizations must have some way of resolving differences and making and enforcing conclusions so that a collective course of action can be carried out;
items.stem: The knowledge objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: understand that industrial societies are based on a complex system of political and economic organizations, which makes possible the production of goods and services;
items.stem: The knowledge objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: understand that whenever groups, societies, or nations interact, they do so according to patterns of beliefs and values which are both implicitly and explicitly accepted by the members of the group; and,
items.stem: The knowledge objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: understand that nations must live within a community of other nations in which the sovereignty of one nation must be reconciled with the sovereignty of another.
items.stem: The knowledge objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: learn to make hypotheses based on reasonable assumptions and inferences;
items.stem: The skills/abilities objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: learn to test hypotheses using established criteria; and,
items.stem: The skills/abilities objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: learn to organize data so that relationships within the data may be analyzed.
items.stem: The skills/abilities objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: appreciate the necessity of interdependence within human relationships;
items.stem: The values objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: appreciate the legitimate constraints that interdependence places on the actions of individuals and nations; and,
items.stem: The values objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: appreciate the need for social organizations to bring order to social life.
items.stem: The values objectives are to help students:
items.heading: Foundational Objectives for the Course Social Organizations

items.text: Know that humans establish various kinds of organizations as a means of systematically meeting their needs and wants.
Know that in order to have security, stability, and predictability, humans tacitly agree to conform to the beliefs, values, and mores imposed on them by the various organizations of society.
Know that any group or organization must decide on some means of decision making that will allow it to function effectively.
Know that groups or organizations must have some way of resolving differences and making and enforcing conclusions so that a collective course of action can be carried out.
Review/learn the skill of categorizing and classifying material according to some system in order to make it meaningful.
Review/learn the skill of drawing inferences from the patterns that emerge from classification systems.
Review/learn the use of criteria as a basis for analysing an event or situation.
Learn the skill of hypothesizing.
Learn to test hypotheses against historical fact.
What are legitimate constraints on human behaviour?
Should the rights of the individual or the group have the higher priority?
What areas of life are appropriate for society to control, through norms and sanctions?
Should some people be given more power and privilege than others?
Should men and women be given the same access to power and privileges?
Is the use of force ever justified in a conflict over social change?
Know that a study of history may be helpful in relating the cumulative human experience of the past to our experiences with reality.
Know that historical events can be chronologically ordered.
Know some of the major events and dates of chronological world history.
Know that an accurate description of "what has occurred where" is fundamental to an interpretation of why these events have occurred.
Know the geographic location of the major places which play a role in the history of this course.
Review the skill of organizing information for analysis.
Practise making generalizations and drawing inferences from classified data.
Practise map interpretation.
Does one's culture influence what is perceived to be a major historical event?
Know that human beings live in society because they can best satisfy their needs and wants by working with other members of society.
Know that social organizations stem from and deal with the basic, universal problems of ordered, social life.
Know that social organizations provide for the needs and wants of Canadians, provide them with meaning and purpose, and give them direction and discipline.
Know that social organizations play a significant role in providing order and direction within a society.
Know that social organizations establish norms or values which legitimize sanctions used to regulate human behaviour.
Know that the regulations of social organizations discipline human behaviour to conform to some definite, continuous, and organized patterns of behaviour.
Know that the freedom to live one's life according to the dictates of one's conscience is a significant value in Canadian society.
Know that social organizations based on the cultural assumptions of one historical tradition may be quite different from the social organizations based on another cultural tradition.
Learn to use their own background knowledge as a source of useful data for understanding concepts.
Review/teach the skills of brainstorming and exchanging information through class discussions.
Learn to use grids as a way of organizing information for analysis.
(See activity guide.)
Review/teach the skill of categorizing material according to some system in order to make it meaningful.
Should social organizations be able to use sanctions to control and direct human behaviour?
Should limits be placed on this power?
Should conformity take precedence over individualism?
Know that the established organizations people live within are part of their cultural heritage.
Know that pluralism is the belief that groups which are distinctly unique should have that distinctiveness recognized and protected.
Know that the basic assumptions on which social organizations are organized come from the prevailing world view.
Know that organizations established by one cultural group in Canada may based on very different values than those established by another cultural group.
Know that organizations establish a system of persons or things ranked one above the other.
Know that women should have the same opportunities within society as men.
Practise using their own background knowledge as a source of useful data for understanding concepts.
Practise the skills of brainstorming and exchanging information through class discussions.
Practise using concepts as criteria for making evaluations.
Would they (the students) wish to live in a world without morality, ethics, or values?
Would a world where people had no constraints on their behaviour be one that you would want to live in?
Should the rights of the individual or the rights of the group have the higher priority?
What areas of life is it appropriate for society to control through norms and sanctions?
Know that a social contract is an agreement between the rulers and the ruled which defines the rights and duties of each explicitly and implicitly.
Know that each social organization will determine its particular purpose, a set of beliefs and values, and an organization and structure which will include a decision making system.
Know that political decision making occurs in every social organization in an attempt to reconcile the different needs and wants within the organization.
Know that societies have to make decisions about how best to reconcile the conflicting interests within society.
Know that politics is the process of conciliating individuals and groups by giving them a share of valued scarce resources according to the amount of power they wield within society.

Know that power may be expressed through:
- the use of force;
- reliance on authority; and
- through the use of influence.
Practise the skill of using their own background knowledge as a source of useful data to apply concepts.
Learn to use concepts in a grid format to analyze the relationships in human behaviour.
On what basis should groups be awarded power within the social contract?
Know that a world view is a comprehensive conception or image of reality and of humanity's relation to it.
Know that a world view is a distinctive way of looking at reality and creates a context for living.

Know that the Sacred Circle represents the belief that "Everything the Power of the World does is done in a circle. The sky is round ... The wind in its greatest powers whirls ... The sun comes forth and goes down again in a circle ... Even the seasons form a great circle in their changing ...
The life of a man is a circle from childhood to childhood, and so it is in everything where power moves" (Black Elk, Oglala Sioux).
Know that Indian cultures start with philosophical assumptions as found in the sacred circle while Eurocentric cultures start with assumptions based on science and technology.
Know that a specific world view is influenced by its immediate environment.
Practise the skill of using their own background knowledge as a source of useful data to understand concepts.
Review/teach the skills of brainstorming and exchanging information through class discussions.
Should the rights of the individual or the rights of the group have the higher priority?
Know that paradigms are patterns of ideas, beliefs, and values which are used to understand reality.
Know that paradigms help humans perceive and understand certain aspects of reality more clearly and limit the perception and understanding of other aspects of reality.
Know that a social contract is an agreement between the rulers and the ruled which defines the rights and duties of each explicitly and implicitly.

Know that patriarchy involves the belief that there should be a clear distinction between the rulers and the ruled with power flowing from the top of the social hierarchy to the bottom of the hierarchy.
Know that the Aboriginal social contract makes very little distinction between the rulers and the ruled with power moving from group to group as the need arises.
Know that liberal democracy believes that power is vested in the people and is awarded to those that can best demonstrate their right to it.
Review/teach the skill of categorizing material according to some system in order to make it meaningful.
Review/teach the skill of using continua as a way of organizing information for analysis.
Review/teach the skill of drawing inferences from the patterns that emerge from the categorized material and from the value issues-implicit in the material.
What areas of life is it appropriate for society to control through norms and sanctions?
What kinds of sanctions may be used to control behaviour?
Know that most traditional societies tended toward a consensus and collaboration model of decision-making.
Know that in most cases societal checks and balances were developed and placed upon political leaders to ensure that group cohesiveness and survival would be maintained.
Know that individuals were allowed the freedom to ignore group decisions provided the individuals did nothing to cause harm to group safety and survival.
Know that women played an important role in the political life of many traditional cultures.
Know that the nations of the Iroquoian Confederacy often fought each other and that a tendency to pursue separate goals and objectives remains today.
Know that officially recognized and elected political leaders within Iroquoian society were designated as sachems.
Review/teach the skill of drawing inferences from the patterns that emerge from the categorized material and from the value issues implicit in the material.
Is order or freedom more fundamental to the well being of society?
Do individuals have the right to question the basic social contract of a group?

Know that the ‘election' of a political leader was a process involving reference to the lineage of a nominee as well as his acceptance by the community based upon his personal values and skills of leadership and mediation.
Know that positive aspects of the traditional Iroquoian political decision making model included the lengthy and well considered deliberations upon issues affecting all members of the Confederacy.
The procedure required that all Council members be allowed to present their views before any decisions would be attempted.
The principle guiding the Council was to maintain collaboration while allowing for individual autonomy.

Know that the decentralization of power within the Confederacy Council and the individual nations' councils sometimes led to factionalism, an inability to resolve issues and problems which placed the Confederacy in a weak position (to be divided and conquered) when dealing with highly united European colonies.
Know that women played a key role within the traditional political decision making process although they were not entitled to hold the position of sachem.
Know that traditional Iroquoian society operated upon a clan system which cut across national lines.
Know that the position of sachem within the Great Council was permanent but that individual sachems could be deposed from office.
Learn to compare and contrast information organized under one paradigm with material organized under another paradigm.
Practise the skill of drawing inferences from the patterns that emerge from the categorized material and from the value issues implicit in the material.
Which is better: a collaborative view of power, or a competitive view of power?
Know that security based on order and predictability is a fundamental need of people.
Know that when a society undergoes fundamental change another set of social relationships must be developed so that individuals understand their relationship to the larger society.
Know that paradigms are patterns of ideas, beliefs, and values which act as criteria for decision making
Know that paradigms help people perceive and understand certain aspects of reality more clearly and limit the perception and understanding of other aspects of reality.

Know that hierarchy is the belief that certain people and/or groups are believed to have special abilities and responsibilities for the well being of society which in turn means that they should have special powers and privileges to carry out these responsibilities.
Know that sovereignty is the power to make and enforce decisions about any matter that is recognized to be within a defined jurisdiction.
Know that gaining and preserving power is the most significant goal a prince representing a state can aspire to.
Review/teach the skills of co-operative group work.
Review/teach the concept of criteria and the skills of using them a way of analysing an event.
Is security or freedom the higher value?
Know that chaos and anarchy is the greatest threat to society because it destroys the ability of the state to maintain sovereignty.
Know that the theoretical justifications for assigning authority and sovereignty within the state may also be applied to social organizations such as marriage and the family.
Know that centralizing power by giving it to an elite is often seen from the standpoint of patriarchy as the most effective way of restoring order to society.
Know that a state is sovereign when it possesses control over the systems of justice and the use of force within a society.
Know that an absolutist state sees all organizations within its jurisdiction as subordinate to its authority.
Know that in an absolutist state sovereignty in embodied in the ruler who is not restrained or checked by any other legal authority.
Review/teach the concept of paradigms and the skill of using them as a way of predicting the choices societies will make.
Teach the skill of hypothesizing by learning to select a proposition that is testable and can be used to guide the search for data.

What is the fair way of evaluating the behaviour of the people of the past:
- on the basis of the reality they faced at the time or on the basis of some fundamental concepts of justice and morality?
Societies are made up of competing interest groups each with a power base (resources, numbers, organization) and each desiring decisions that will satisfy their needs/wants.
Know that societies must manage conflict in some way because unresolved conflict is destructive to the social system.
Know that freedom without responsibilities or limits can results in chaos in a society.
Know that societies have organized their members into a hierarchy in which certain people are able to control more resources, organizations, and or people than others.
Political power is desired as a way of dealing with the tensions between and among individuals and public groups in the decision making process.
Political power can be expressed through the use of force, the support of authority, and/or through the use of influence.
Know that sovereignty is the ultimate and in some cases the unlimited power to command, to judge, and to make laws and enforce them within a society.
Review/teach the skills of co-operative group work.
Review/teach the concept of criteria and the skills of using it as way of analysing an event.
Review/teach the concept of paradigms and the skill of using them as a way of predicting the choices societies will make.
Who has the right to be sovereign in a group?
What are the correct and incorrect ways of using power?
Equality and Hierarchy and Freedom and Order Know that every society/culture defines, based on its paradigms, what it means by equality, hierarchy, freedom, and order.
Know that these definitions are often unspoken and are tacitly accepted by the members/citizens of the social grouping in question.
Know that every society has to establish some fundamental criteria which can be used to justify the allocation of supreme power within society to certain individuals or groups.
Know that in society people live as if there were a social contract which defines the rights and duties of the rulers and ruled explicitly and implicitly.
Know that at-certain times in history, the definitions which had been accepted as defining the rights and duties of the rulers and the ruled will shift significantly.
Understand that some balance between order and freedom is essential if a society is to function in a constructive manner.

Know that societies find it difficult to decide what adjustments are necessary and carry them out in a short period of time.

well-being of the entire society.
Practise categorizing information so that inferences may be drawn from it.

Know that the French economy would not be able to expand unless it took measures that would enable French goods to compete successfully with British goods.
Know that goods that are used to create other goods are labelled capital goods.
Know that capital goods like consumer goods must be created out of the scarce productive resources of an economy.
Know that an economy if it is to grow must divert scarce resources (invest) from consumption to the creation of capital.

creation of wealth?
equitable distribution of wealth?
unite economic and political power?
Know that it is difficult for many to see the possibilities of change that may exist for a society.

Know that the opportunity cost of investing in new industries means sacrificing opportunities for using wealth in other ways.
Know that a technological lead is seldom very long lasting.

Has today's industrial society different priorities than 19th century industrial Europe?
Have all classes of society benefited from industrialization?

Know that paradigms are patterns of ideas, beliefs, and values which are used to understand reality.
Know that the way reality is perceived will have a profound effect on human behaviour.
Know that cultures create and/or accept paradigms as the basis for their world view.

Know that every human has been socialized to accept a certain reality and that the only way to understand this is to use a different world view to examine familiar reality from a different perspective.
Know that paradigms heip people to perceive and understand certain aspects of reality and limit the perception and understanding of other aspects of reality
Know that because we must depend on paradigms to make any sense of reality all perceptions of reality will be somewhat limited in their completeness.
Know that a different culture will select different ideas, beliefs and values, arrange them in different patterns or paradigms and come up with a different world view.
Know that both Indian cultures and European cultures have done this and as a result have come up with different economic world views.

Should the profit motive be the basis for decision making?
Is one of the differing paradigms better than the other?
Do the different paradigms represent dangers to the environment?

items.text: Know that whenever any group, society, or nation interacts, it does so according to understandings which are both implicitly and explicitly accepted by the members of the group.
Know that individuals accept consciously and unconsciously certain claims to sovereignty as being legitimate and reject other claims as illegitimate.
Know that not all members of a group accept all aspects of the common understanding governing the group.
Know that the political process within society is necessary to resolve differences over who should have sovereignty within the group.
Know that industrialization contributed to the urbanization of European societies.
Know that European societies had to deal with new perspectives or ideologies which would lead to new social organization.
Know that industrialization, urbanization, and the perspectives provided by new ideologies would stimulate the reorganization of social, economic, and political institutions.

Know that the conflict over control of decision making would be expressed in terms of controlling the sources of power.
Know that politics is the process of conciliating individuals and groups by giving them a share of valued scarce commodities according to the amount of power they wield within society.

Know that the modern industrial, nation states finds its roots in the changes that occurred in the nineteenth century.
Know that European societies developed a new social and economic infrastructure which led to urbanization.
Know that industrialization contributed to the urbanization of European societies.
Know that European societies had to deal with a new industrial, urban world view which challenged the perspectives or ideologies of the traditional social organizations.
Know that industrialization and urbanization would require the reorganization of the social and political organizations.
Know that many of the traditional paradigms were no longer able to offer adequate solutions to the new social realities.
Know that during this time a number of new paradigms known as ideologies were developed in an attempt to deal with the changes which were occurring.

Know that societies are made up of competing interest groups each with a power base (resources, numbers, organization) and each desiring decisions that will satisfy their needs/wants.
Know that each society will establish based on its world view a decision making system.
Know that political decision making occurs in every social organization in an attempt to reconcile the different needs and wants within the organization.
Know that societies must manage conflict in some way because unresolved conflict is destructive to the social system.
Know that societies have to make decisions about how best to reconcile the conflicting interests within society.
Know that an ideology is a system of ideas that attempts both to explain the world and to change it.

Know that an ideology is similar to a paradigm.

Know that the characteristics common to all ideologies are:
- a set of assumptions,
- an interpretation and explanation the past and present,
- a vision of the future and strategy to achieve that vision, and
- a simple believable picture of reality.
Know that ideologies attract and maintain supporters because they offer predictability, and meaning and purpose as goals.
Know that ideology is a source of identity and also a source of optimism.
Know that what is considered legitimate is based on the assumptions of the particular ideology individuals subscribe to.
Know that the social contract that existed within a rural society did not meet the needs and interests of an urban society and so was looked on with some suspicion.
