evidence.observation: The curriculum document groups its outcomes under 12 headings: “Culture (CU)”, “Strategies (ST)”, “Language Knowledge (LK)”, “Applications (AP)”, “Culture (CU)”, “Strategies (ST)”, “Language Knowledge (LK)”, “Applications (AP)”, “Culture (CU)”, “Strategies (ST)”, “Language Knowledge (LK)”, “Applications (AP)”.

items.text: Explore historical and contemporary elements of the social environment and personal identity.

Explore using Michif French for following protocol when welcoming visitors and Elders/Lii pleu vyeu (e.g., welcoming into a space, offering a gift or tobacco, pulling out a chair, offering tea, serving of food).

Explore using Michif French while completing routine tasks of the home and classroom (e.g., washing dishes, tidying the house/class, laundry, wiping the table, help to prepare a meal, setting the table).
Explore how routine tasks in the home and classroom have changed over time.
Investigate local historical and contemporary spaces, businesses or schools by reaching out to community members for information, stories, and support.
Investigate opportunities in Saskatchewan to participate in Michif French culture with the guidance of a Language Carrier or Lii pleu vyeu.
Begin to develop relationships by visiting with local community members, Language Carriers, Elders, collectives, clubs and local Métis organizations.

Apply, with support, a variety of before, during, and after comprehension strategies to construct meaning in Michif French written texts and oral communications, with the guidance of a Language Carrier or Lii pleu vyeu.
Learn through la manyair dis promnii (e.g., with Lii pleu vyeu, Language Carriers, family, peers or learning circles) both inside and outside of the classroom.

Review interpretation of written texts and oral communications, after reading and listening, using strategies such as:
• discussing key words in oral and written texts;
• making connections between new information, prior knowledge and personal experience; and,
• reacting with emotion (e.g., empathy, surprise, appreciation or dislike).

Begin to develop personal language learning tools (e.g., classroom/personal Michif French Dictionary, self-created pronunciation audio files) on topics such as home items, routines, hobbies and foods.

Consult resources (e.g., Lii pleu vyeu, Language Carriers, peers, family, Michif French dictionaries and mobile apps, anchor charts, websites) and visual aids (e.g., pictures, graphs and drawings) to help construct meaning of written texts and oral communications.
Apply, with support, a variety of strategies to produce Michif French written texts and oral communications.
Learn through la manyair dis promnii (e.g., with Lii pleu vyeu, Language Carriers, family, peers).
Explore how interactions with the land contribute to authentic Michif French language acquisition.
Explore the Michif French language for personal communication on topics, such as introductions, greetings, general interactions, phrases to participate in a discussion.
Use tools such as graphic organizers and outlines to make a plan for speaking or writing.

Consult resources (e.g., Lii pleu vyeu, Language Carriers, peers, family, Michif French dictionaries and mobile apps, anchor charts and websites) and visual aids (e.g., pictures, graphs and drawings) to support the production of oral and written texts.

Discuss how to take risks, try unfamiliar approaches, and experiment with various forms of expression (e.g., reduce anxiety by using mental techniques, such as positive self-talk and humour, to instill confidence).
Identify prior knowledge for personal expression in Michif French.
Describe physical (e.g., gestures and facial expressions) and auditory (e.g., laughter, tone, volume) cues to convey meaning.
Retell (in English) a Michif French oral communication with Lii pleu vyeu, Language Carriers, peers, or family members.
Demonstrate a short dialogue (e.g., practise, rehearse, role-play) with classmates in Michif French.
Reflect on personal strengths and needs with respect to one’s Michif French language and culture learning journey.
Determine personals strengths as a language learner.
Identify personal needs related to speaking, listening, reading, and writing in Michif French.
Recognize that risk-taking and a positive attitude are part of effective language learning.
Identify how la manyair dis promnii helps to meet personal language learning needs.
Celebrate personal Michif French language learning successes.

Reflect on identity through the Michif/Métis worldview and language by considering questions such as:
• How does la manyair dis promnii help to improve my understanding of the Michif French language and worldview?
• How does my use of Michif French shape the way I understand my social environments?
• How does my use of Michif French shape the way I understand my own identity?
• How does my use of Michif French shape the way I understand the Michif culture and community?
Identify, with support, when listening and reading, Michif French language concepts including basic context- specific vocabulary, word order and linguistic conventions.

Recognize context-specific and common vocabulary (e.g., lii zhours – days, lii mwaan – months, lii zoochii a likol – school supplies, paarchu dju korr – parts of the body, lii maanzhii - food, lii noombr - numbers).
Discuss the use of singular personal pronouns (e.g., Ji, Ja, Je, Tchu, Ta, y, il, ell).
Identify appropriate prepositions in context (e.g., annaryayr - behind, annavaan – in front of, dissu – on top of, ennhou - above, akoootii – beside, didaan – inside).
Recognize directional terms in context (e.g., dret - right, goosh - left, nor – north, sud – south, ouest - west, lest – east).
Recognize definite (e.g., le la, lay, lii) and indefinite articles (e.g., aen, de, day, dii).
Explain simple sentences in context (e.g., Netway la taab - Clean the table, Monnom ay – My name is, Je rest a – I live in, Jem sa maanzhii – I like to eat).
Identify, when speaking and writing, Michif French language concepts including basic context-specific vocabulary, word order and linguistic conventions.

Recognize context-specific and common vocabulary (e.g., lii zhours – days, lii mwaan – months, lii zoochii a likol – school supplies, paarchu dju korr – parts of the body, lii maanzhii - food, lii noombr - numbers).
Recognize the use of singular personal pronouns (e.g., Ji, Ja, Je, Tchu, Ta, y, il, ell).
Utilize appropriate body language and tone when speaking.
Respond to prepositions in context (e.g., annaryayr - behind, annavaan – in front of, dissu – on top of, ennhou - above, akoootii – beside, didaan – inside).
Recognize directional terms in context (e.g., dret - right, goosh - left, nor – north, sud – south, ouest - west, lest – east).
Recognize definite (e.g., le la, lay, lii) and indefinite articles (e.g., aen, de, day, dii).
Repeat simple sentences in context (e.g., Netway la taab - Clean the table, Monnom ay – My name is, Je rest a – I live in, Jem sa maanzhii – I like to eat).
Construct meaning, with support, of a variety of simple oral non-fiction and fiction Michif French communications on familiar topics.

Listen to or view a variety of simple oral Michif French communications (e.g., how to videos, storytelling videos, in-person visiting, songs) that address big ideas:
• elements of social environment;
• elements of personal identity; and,
• elements of Michif French culture.
Interpret simple oral communications or conversations.
Respond appropriately in structured interactions with common, simple, short phrases.
Respond to simple questions regarding personal identity (e.g., name, hometown, family names, interests, and hobbies).
Compare information related to others’ personal identity (e.g., name, hometown, family names, interests, and hobbies).
Describe personal reactions to simple oral communications with emotion (e.g., empathy, surprise, appreciation or dislike).
Construct meaning, with support, of a variety of simple written non-fiction and fiction Michif French texts on familiar topics.

Read a variety of simple written Michif French texts (e.g., children’s books, recipes, dictionaries, conversational sentences) that address elements of:
• the social environment;
• personal identity; and,
• Michif French culture.
Comprehend simple labels within the school in Michif French.
Repeat the basic directions of written imperative texts.
Respond to a survey regarding personal identity (e.g., name, hometown, family names, Treaty area, hobbies, age, preferred foods).
Identify the vocabulary words in context in written texts on familiar topics.
Discuss the possible variations within the written orthography of Michif French based on regional variation or language carrier preference.
Describe personal reaction to written texts with emotion (e.g., empathy, surprise, appreciation or dislike).
Produce, with support, a variety of simple oral non-fiction and fiction Michif French communications on familiar topics.

Produce simple oral Michif French communications related to elements of:
• the social environment;
• personal identity; and,
• Michif French culture.
Pose questions to generate conversations on familiar topics such as hobbies, family members and class schedules.
Respond appropriately to other speakers during conversations or discussion.
Express feelings and emotions using simple adjectives, facial expressions and body language.
Convey opinions or personal perspectives on a given topic such as a fashion, music, or food.
Provide basic step-by-step instructions in situations such as cooking and giving directions to a location.
Communicate information about time.
Produce personal greetings (e.g., on the phone, in video recordings, in person).
Explain personal lived experiences or activities.
Use Michif French language for entertainment and personal enjoyment (e.g., express humour, perform skits or songs and create stories).
Produce, with support, a variety of simple written non-fiction and fiction Michif French texts on familiar topics.

Produce simple written Michif French texts related to elements of:
• the social environment;
• personal identity; and,
• Michif French culture.
Write about a variety of daily topics, such as personal details (e.g., name and age), dates (e.g., days of the week, months, seasons) and school/classroom items and routine.
Communicate simple written expressions (e.g., wii - yes, noo - no, sil voo play - please, maarsii –thank you, bonn mataen - good morning, boon apray mijii - good afternoon, Je regret - I’m sorry).
Compose a greeting card (e.g., Bonn Fayt- birthday, maarsii – thank you, Schwettchu vyen bayn - I hope you get well soon) using simple expressions.
Create simple social media posts using basic vocabulary (e.g., personal introduction, homeland).
Provide basic written directions to a place within the school or community using imperative sentences.
Experiment with communicating messages in a variety of written formats (e.g., notes, lists, paragraphs, graphs, emails, blogs and text messages).
Draft descriptions of personal lived experiences or activities related to the big ideas.
Explore the use of Michif French phonetic orthography based on regional variations or language carrier preference.
Explore historical and contemporary elements of the natural environment and kinship.
Recognize personal roles and responsibilities in family and community according to the Michif/Métis core values).
Discuss the traditional and contemporary roles of women in maintaining kinship ties and caring for each other.

Discuss places in Canada where Michif French is and was historically spoken (e.g., St. Laurent, St. Eustache and Saint Ambroise in Manitoba, the St. Louis Batoche, St. Laurent, the Duck Lake region in Saskatchewan, and the Lac la Biche, St. Paul, St. Albert and Bonnyville areas in Alberta).
Investigate opportunities in Saskatchewan to participate in Michif French language revitalization.

Discuss the transmission and endangerment of the Michif French language (e.g., Why was Michif French not always taught at home? Why were people reluctant to speak Michif French? Why and when did this stigma shift?).
Compare Michif languages (Northern, Heritage & Michif French) in terms of their origin, similarities, and differences.
Consider effective ways that local Indigenous language revitalization approaches have been implemented.
Discuss Indigenous language revitalization projects in other parts of the world and how successful strategies can be applied to Michif Language revitalization efforts in Saskatchewan.

Identify institutes and organizations that support efforts (e.g., resources, lesson plans, recordings) to revitalize Michif languages (e.g., Gabriel Dumont Institute, Louis Riel Institute, Métis Nation - Saskatchewan, Rupertsland Institute).
Discuss with representatives of Michif/Métis organizations about their efforts to revitalize Michif languages.
Explore Michif language programs that exist (e.g., Michif Kindergarten, online classes, in-person classes, language nests, post-secondary classes, community-led Michif classes).

Explore Michif /Métis ways to cope with challenges (e.g., visiting, spirituality, meeting with Lii pleu vyeu).
Seek opportunities to communicate in Michif French (e.g., at community events and celebrations).

outcomes.statement: Communicate interactively in Nakoda, with guidance, to experience the natural and constructed environments of the community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Interact with classmates and teacher, with guidance, during learning activities using the Nakoda language.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Interact with classmates in pairs or small groups, with guidance, to plan and complete class projects using the Nakoda language.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Seek and record information to further understanding of Nakoda concepts from Elders and other knowledge keepers within the community.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Participate, with guidance, in developing language and culture during experiential learning opportunities, such as helping at community/cultural events, volunteering with child care children, visiting and conversing with Elders in the community, planning cultural camps/activities.

indicators.text: Discuss and promote positive interactions and relationships in the school (e.g., how to engage with Elders).

indicators.text: Respond to a variety of text forms including storytelling in a variety of media (e.g., recorded instructions or events, creating illustrations, respond in learning logs or questioning the author).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Respond to representation of ideas, events and information by creating a chart, illustrations or using technology.

outcomes.statement: Construct meaning, with guidance, of a variety of Nakoda simple oral fiction and non-fiction texts on familiar topics.

indicators.text: Explain digitally or in person, short and simple oral excerpts from the oral tradition of the people, relating to areas of local lifestyles in the past and present (e.g., histories, biographies, moral stories, songs, entertainment stories).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Use language creatively and for a variety of purposes (e.g., listening to music, listening to jokes, viewing dances, personal enjoyment).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Share and explain examples of short and simple excerpts using stories from the oral tradition.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Respond to the main point and some supporting details of oral texts on a variety of familiar topics.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss selected topics providing some details to support main idea.

outcomes.statement: Produce, with guidance, simple oral texts on familiar topics in Nakoda.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Express some emotions and feelings familiar to the classroom (e.g., role-playing, talking circles).

indicators.text: Explain and follow rules, routines, and procedures related to a specific activity (e.g., playing a sport, preparing a meal, planning a meeting).

indicators.text: Retell parts of oral narratives using a variety of traditional and contemporary mediums to support the retelling such as drama, dance, music or visual art.

indicators.label: h

indicators.text: Identify and produce uses of common regional or other variations in the Nakoda language.

indicators.text: Use politeness conventions in a variety of contexts (e.g., using suitable language to engage listeners’ attention when beginning to speak).

indicators.text: Use nonverbal communication in a variety of contexts (e.g., shrugging shoulders, pointing with lips).

indicators.text: Use Plains Sign Language along with Nakoda language.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Participate in ceremonies or feasts by extracting the words known and then discuss the meaning.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Explore outdoors to become familiar with the weather and environment to strengthen vocabulary.

(There is an appropriateness to asking questions when someone is speaking, and therefore essential that unless you know the language there are cultural protocols to follow - many of these indicators are practised in prayer.)

items.text: Apply previous knowledge to a group project. Aboriginal worldviews are as diverse as they are complex. Aboriginal peoples in Saskatchewan, like all other Canadians, have divergent cultural backgrounds and innumerable experiences that shape the ways in which they see the world. Saskatchewan Education acknowledges the complexity of Aboriginal worldviews. However, it is important for teachers to explore and expand their understanding of Aboriginal worldviews because they are so closely linked to Aboriginal identity. Such knowledge aids in dispelling stereotypes and enhances our ability to empathize. Seeing the world from another person’s perspective is an invaluable skill that can enhance all the relationships we have in life. Teachers and students need a guide or benchmark from which to begin discussions and learning. Therefore, the following model of a traditional Aboriginal worldview is presented. It is important to remember that the Aboriginal students in Saskatchewan classrooms may or may not have this worldview and that their own is just as important as anyone else’s, even those expressed in this curriculum guide. Within Aboriginal philosophy, four dimensions of human nature (spiritual, mental, emotional and physical) are identified and viewed as interrelated.

Students will explore how cultural heritage shapes understanding and how moral values influence behaviours. (PSVS) Have students read the Ethics Common to First Nations. Where else have the students heard or seen these maxims stated or applied? Relate the Ethics to your school's code of behaviour or that stated in the Education Act under the sections detailing the responsibilities of principals, teachers, and students. Have students relate the 12 Principles Common to First Nations Philosophies to the Ethics common to First Nations which are the subsequent behaviours and attitudes. Relate the Ethics to the 10 Commandments of the Hebrews in the Bible's Old Testament, the Codification of Roman Laws by Julius Caesar, the Canada Act and Charter of Rights and Freedoms, 1982. Relate the Ethics Common to First Nations to the Saskatchewan Human Rights Code, or the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights, 1976. Have students determine the human needs that give rise to legislated human rights and First Nations' ethics. Most of these documents appear in the Social Justice Unit of the Student Resource Guide and are suitable subjects for further investigation and discussion, as they define what is acceptable behaviour before the Creator, and in society. It is appropriate to utilize materials from the Social Justice Unit, or any other unit if they are relevant to the issue or concept being discussed. A holistic perspective is necessary to fully understand and appreciate the implications of facts and concepts arising from the case studies.

Students will explore how moral principles and cultural philosophy influence peoples' behaviours and practises. (PSVS) Invite an Elder or Aboriginal spiritual teacher into the classroom to speak about aspects of Indian philosophy and spirituality. Refer to the Inviting Elders to the School.

items.keyUnderstanding: Key Understanding: A major aim of Native Studies is to develop personal and cultural awareness in all students through a focus on contemporary Canadian issues. Native Studies fulfils the vision to provide a course of study which focuses on Canadian Aboriginal peoples. The course is intended for all schools and the foundational objectives may be adapted to accommodate local needs according to the adaptive dimension of Core Curriculum. Through thoughtful examination of contemporary Aboriginal issues, it is hoped that students will gain a broader understanding of cross cultural relationships. Communities, comprised of individuals with differing racial or cultural identities, may need to develop strategies for harmonious relationships. Cultural representation in all aspect of the school environment empowers children with a positive group identity. describe the factors which affect identity.
items.keyUnderstanding: Key Understanding: Factors of diversity of Aboriginal nations of Canada. To determine identity, criteria may be categorized as objective or subjective. Objective criteria may include those qualities which are deemed characteristic of a specific identity and by the boundaries of identity as determined by legislation or practice. Subjective criteria may be more difficult to determine because the boundaries are not conducive to measurement. In most instances, self-determination and community acceptance are major tenets of subjective criteria. In Canada, Indian peoples have been defined according to objective criteria as set out in The Indian Act. The criteria which defines who is Métis results from community and government directives. Key issues to consider are the implications and consequences of who has the power to legally define Indian and Métis peoples in Canada. The Métis struggle for self-determination can be traced back to the earliest days of contact between the Indigenous peoples and the newcomers. The Métis viewed themselves as a new people and did not identify with either First Nations, nor European peoples. During the fur-trade, many Métis people lived in the Red River Settlement where they developed their own traditions, laws and lifestyles. To protect their way of life, the Métis organized themselves under the leadership of Louis Riel. Since the 1869-70 Red River Resistance and the 1885 Riel Resistance, Métis people have been recognized, as acknowledged in The Constitution Act, 1982. The identity of Aboriginal peoples in political and legal terms has been largely created by acts of government. Changes to these terms through subsequent legislation have created a complex, categorized system that is often difficult to understand. Teachers may review the different ways the identity of Aboriginal peoples in Canada has been categorized: Legal Distinctions

The Métis struggle for self-determination can be traced back to the earliest days of contact between the Indigenous peoples and the newcomers. The Métis viewed themselves as a new people and did not identify with either First Nations, nor European peoples. During the fur-trade, many Métis people lived in the Red River Settlement where they developed their own traditions, laws and lifestyles. To protect their way of life, the Métis organized themselves under the leadership of Louis Riel. Since the 1869-70 Red River Resistance and the 1885 Riel Resistance, Métis people have been recognized, as acknowledged in The Constitution Act, 1982. The identity of Aboriginal peoples in political and legal terms has been largely created by acts of government. Changes to these terms through subsequent legislation have created a complex, categorized system that is often difficult to understand. Teachers may review the different ways the identity of Aboriginal peoples in Canada has been categorized: Legal Distinctions

items.text: describe how worldview shapes peoples lives.
items.keyUnderstanding: Key Understanding: Influences of worldview on daily life. The way in which we see the world is influenced by a number of factors including cultural background, experience, values, and personal preferences. In Canada, worldviews are expressed in a variety of ways. Some groups express their particular philosophy of life privately and quietly, while others seek to convert others to their ways. When discussing worldview it is important not to over-generalize. Although common elements do exist, it is not always appropriate to seek a single statement of worldview. Individual variances within groups are affected by ethnicity, or the degree to which people identify with their cultural heritage. Within Aboriginal communities, the spectrum of worldviews ranges from the traditional to the mainstream. Key definitions relevant to this section include: Worldview: a particular philosophy or view of life. Philosophy: the use of reason in seeking truth and knowledge, especially the causes of the principles governing existence. Values: involve one's principles or standards or judgements about what is valuable or important in life. Value judgement: a subjective estimate of quality. Elder: the title given to a respected individual from the Aboriginal community who is a keeper of tradition and worldview; age may be a factor, but not a prerequisite. It is critical to create a climate for learning that reflects respect for the procedures and protocols involved in the sharing of worldviews, values and philosophy. Consider the complexity of Aboriginal identities, including the degree to which individuals identify with their cultural heritage. Do not assume that all Aboriginal peoples ascribe to, live by, or believe in the same philosophical approach to life. Individuals who are authentic sources of information are available in the community. It is critical to involve them meaningfully in the Native Studies classroom according to local protocols. Historically in Canada, considerable efforts have been made to eradicate the traditional perspective from Aboriginal existence; for example, through restrictions on use of language, conversion to Christianity and outlawing ceremonies. These practices were reflected in the residential school period and through The Indian Act. Teachers should seek a balance of traditional and assimilated perspectives of Aboriginal worldview; taking into account the great diversity among Aboriginal peoples themselves.

items.text: define the concepts of Aboriginal rights, nation, sovereignty, and treaty.
items.keyUnderstanding: Key Understanding: The basis of Aboriginal rights. The term Aboriginal is comprised of the Latin prefix ab meaning from, and the Latin word originalis meaning origin. The concept of Aboriginal rights literally derives from these Latin forms. Aboriginal rights are those rights which Aboriginal peoples have because of their Indigenous status in the place now known as Canada. Aboriginal peoples’ historical position as self-governing peoples who occupied and used the land prior to the arrival of the European colonists further confirms special status. Aboriginal rights include everything necessary for survival, including rights to land, language, economic and cultural practices and forms of law and government. An important perspective to consider is presented by Soifer, (1992): "Indian rights to land, resources, culture, language, a livelihood and self-government are not something conferred by treaties or offered to Indians as concessions by a beneficent government. These are the rights which Indian Nations enjoy from time immemorial. These rights are pre-existing and inviolable. A Canadian constitution can accommodate Indian rights, it cannot diminish, alter or eliminate them (p.293)." The Métis inherited Aboriginal rights by virtue of their Indian ancestry. As descendants of the original people, the Métis have had their special status accepted in custom and statute, as having an Aboriginal claim to the land and the right to benefit from natural resources. The Manitoba Act, 1870 acknowledges the rights of the Métis nation to land. To fully comprehend the implementation of Aboriginal rights, students require understanding of the interrelated concepts of nation, sovereignty and treaty. Nation: A group of people with a common history, language, and culture, that occupy a particular territory. To belong to a nation means sharing a common heritage, beliefs and worldview. The word nation comes from the Latin word meaning birth. A nation is born from common stock and shares a common heritage. The concept of nation has similar meanings in the Mohawk and English languages. The Mohawk word for nation is kanakerahsera. Naker is the root of the word "to be born". Therefore, the Mohawk concept of nation means "to be born from". Sovereignty: Possessing s_preme authority. A nation that is sovereign is indepenent and free, with the right to a territory of its own. Treaty: A solemn agreement negotiated between sovereign nations.

items.text: define the concept of confederation.
items.keyUnderstanding: Key Understanding: The effects of Canada's expansionism of the 1800s. A confederation is a group of people or organizations brought together for a common purpose. The Confederation of Canada brought together a number of colonies. In the early 1860s, Canada consisted of seven separate British colonies and a large area owned by the Hudson's Bay Company. On July 1, 1867, the new country of Canada came into being. The British North America Act, 1867 created the Dominion of Canada. The British North America Act (BNA) stated the powers each level of government would hold and outlined the way in which the government of the new dominion would be structured. Section 91(24) has particular significance to Aboriginal peoples as it provided for the federal government to make laws in relation to "Indians, and Lands reserved for Indians". The National Policy was the economic paradigm that dominated the actions of Canadian decision makers. The plan assigned an economic role for each region of the nation, determined by resources readily available in that region. The nation's manufacturing and industrial heartland would be located in central Canada. The west and Atlantic regions would serve two functions: supply the industries of central Canada with raw resources and serve as markets for the productions of those industries. This economic paradigm provided a need to secure resources for the domestic and export markets. Acquisition of Rupert's Land was a priority of the first Canadian government. items.text: describe the concept of civilization in relation to colonialism.
items.keyUnderstanding: Key Understanding: The impact of colonial rule on authority and sovereignty of traditional Aboriginal governments. Civilization: accumulation of the traditions and culture of a people; their ability to express civilization in a variety of ways--in dance, music, philosophy, art, law, religion and storytelling. Colonialism: the process of one sovereign nation asserting control over another sovereign nation without informed consent of that nation. Sovereignty: the authority to override all other authorities. Identity: the community self-definition in the creation of a distinctive identity among Aboriginal peoples. Institutions: the structures of government present in the community, and the acceptance of the principles which underlie their existence. Interactions: the pattern of interaction between the Aboriginal community and other communities, later the ‘state'. North and South America were inhabited by diverse civilizations, which ultimately endured colonialism by newcomers. International laws confirm the right of indigenous nations to maintain their own traditions and culture. Each nation exercised self-determination within its own lands and boundaries and under its own sovereignty. As self-governing nations, laws were made and enforced.-These-included laws-governing use of the land and its resources. A key concept of European imperialism was the doctrine of discovery. Upon the "discovery of a new" territory, the newcomers assumed they could obtain title to the "discovered" land. This ignored the principle of long possession applicable to Indigenous peoples. European nations, assumed political control of nations without acknowledging existing social orders. Traditionally Indian leaders were servants to their people. However, under colonial structures, based on hierarchical authority Indian leaders were cast in the role of managers of their people, A second concept of imperialism was that of trusteeship. The Europeans considered themselves better able to look after the affairs of Indigenous peoples. This concept justified a takeover of Indian peoples' lives and lands. This responsibility was vested in the British Crown with the enactment of the Royal Proclamation, 1763. Since the first contact between European peoples and the Indian peoples, the relationship between governments has generally evolved through several distinct stages (dates are approximate). Alliance (1600-1814): From early settlement to the Royal

items.text: Educational Aspects

Sections 114-122 of The Indian Act (1985) allow the Minister to provide educational services to Indian students from ages six to eighteen who are living on reserve or Crown land. In addition, post-secondary education is available through grants made to certain eligible Indian students. Under the terms of The Indian Act, the Minister responsible for Indian affairs has influence over most schools where students attend and over the nature of contents of any education agreement.

Nonetheless, since the 1972 position paper by the National Indian Brotherhood, there have been many changes and progress has been made. In 1973, the federal government reached an agreement with the National Indian Brotherhood to transfer control of Indian education to Indian people. Despite this agreement struggles still go on over a legal basis for the transfer, funding arrangements, and parameters of decision-making authority.
Political Life - Status and Band Membership

Since 1850, the federal government has enacted legislation to define and determine Indian status and band membership. Over the years, amendments to this legislation, which became known as The Indian Act, have significantly changed the ways in which status and membership are determined.
Historical Legislation: 1850-1951

Interaction with, and connection to the land, is shaped by the philosophical ideals of Aboriginal peoples. The concept of land ownership was introduced to this continent by the newcomers. In traditional times, the land was viewed as something which existed for the use of the people. Traditional peoples viewed themselves as caretakers of the land for future generations. items.text: illustrate the social and political origins of Métis land claims.
items.keyUnderstanding: Key Understanding: Basis and various procedures employed for settlement of Métis land claims. In Canada, the existing inherent rights of Indian, Métis and Inuit peoples are recognized in the Constitution Act, 1982. Although the three groups are grouped together in acknowledgement of their special rights, the basis, content and implementation of these rights differs between all three nations. Like other Aboriginal peoples, the Métis of western Canada felt threatened by the arrival of settlers. Most had lived in the Red River area for generations, but they had no official title to their land. In 1869, the Métis were concerned when government surveyors arrived to measure lots for new settlers. The surveying was done so the Canadian government could purchase the area for the Hudson's Bay Company. The Métis believed that their way of life, based largely on the buffalo hunt, was at risk. They knew that the arrival of farmers would mean the end of the buffalo. Moreover, most of the new settlers were Englishspeaking Protestants, whereas most Métis were French-speaking Catholics. Not only were Métis lands threatened, but also their culture and religion. Adapted from: Multiculturalism in Canada: Images and Issues (1997). It is important to note that the Aboriginal rights of the Métis peoples derive from a different source and are different than the Aboriginal rights of Indians. While the federal government deals with Indian peoples, the responsibility for Métis peoples lies within provincial jurisdictions. Varying approaches have historically been used when addressing Métis interest in land: Separate treaty with Métis - "Half-Breed Adhesion to Treaty No. 3" In 1875, near Fort Francis in the northwestern area of Ontario, an entire Métis community was signed on to Treaty No. 3 whereby they were recognized as a distinct people entitled to treaty benefits, including their own reserve. In time, this community was recognized as a band under The Indian Act and its citizens were treated like registered Indians.

describe and summarize the factors which affect social relationships in Canada.
items.keyUnderstanding: Key Understanding: There are many factors which have affected social relationships among Aboriginal peoples. Interrelated factors affecting social relationships in Canada may be categorized as: Personal: How individual preferences and personalities affect our relations with others. Geographical: How we respond to the influence of our physical environment. Cultural: How cultural norms and protocols affect our response to others and our willingness to engage in cross cultural interactions. Political: How various levels of government influence our lives and the nature of special political relationships in Canada. Economic: How we use and access resources to meet our needs. Educational: How we are socialized. Historical: How past events shape the kinds of relationships between peoples. Sociological: How we relate to others. Spiritual: How our core values are expressed. Canada could be described as a "community of communities," a place where the concept of pluralism influences social relationships. Pluralism exists within a society where all peoples are able to maintain independent cultural traditions. Unlike the melting pot theory, where it is expected that all peoples assume a single common identity, Canada is more like a mosaic, where diverse peoples come together to form a Canadian identity. Historically, the policies and practices affecting Canadian Aboriginal peoples have not lived up to the promise of pluralism. Assimilation and integration were primary objectives in the newcomers' relationship with Canada's first peoples. Residential schools, childwelfare policies, and enfranchisement are examples of attempts to convert Aboriginal peoples to the lifestyles of the newcomers. Undoubtedly, Aboriginal peoples have been profoundly affected by these attempts. The quality and nature of social relationships between Aboriginal and non-Native people continues to be influenced by events of the past. Issues such as racism, discrimination, stereotyping, and segregation are a manifestation of the deterioration of positive human interaction. The goal of cross-cultural education is to build bridges of understanding between all peoples. Opportunities for students to define, describe, explain and illustrate factors affecting social relationships in Canada provide for local priorities and areas of interest to serve as the focus of study. The teacher is advised to approach discussions dealing with the impact of factors affecting social relationships with caution.

outcomes.statement: Recognize and document the potential of photography as a communication medium through the exploration of a variety of images.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Introduction to Photography (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe and compare the aspects of a variety of purposes for photography (e.g., news report, wedding, advertising, hobby, art).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare a snapshot to a photograph with an impact that has endured through time (e.g., World Trade Centre, the Hindenburg Disaster, Terry Fox).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss and categorize different styles of photography (e.g., journalism, portraiture, landscape) given a series of photographs.

outcomes.statement: Identify and demonstrate the controls and functions of a camera.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2A: Camera Controls and Functions (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Demonstrate and explain the proper procedures to:
- hold a camera securely to reduce camera shake
- turn the camera on and of
- manipulate the modes and/or settings on the camera
- preview the image that the camera will take using the viewfinder or display
- focus the lens
- take, review, and delete images
- turn flash on and off (if available)
- connect accessories such as tripod, flash, and cables.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify similarities and differences between controls of various cameras including examples of film and digital devices.

outcomes.statement: Capture images that demonstrate advanced camera functions and controls.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2B: Camera Controls and Functions (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 2A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Select and display tools that can be manipulated (e.g., white balance, histogram, exposure compensation, automatic bracketing).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Select and adjust a variety of camera functions when shooting pictures including:
- metering modes
- focus modes and points
- frame rates
- flash settings (e.g., rear and front curtain sync, manual vs. ttl).

outcomes.statement: Assess and demonstrate the effects of utilizing the photographic triangle (i.e., shutter speed, aperture, and ISO) when capturing an image.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3A: Basic Photographic Skills (Core) · Suggested Time: 15-20 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the relationships of exposure values on a camera to the amount of light for the exposure.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create images to demonstrate the effects of different shutter speeds, aperture settings, and ISO settings.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a wide variety of images by combining techniques and principles of shutter speed, aperture, and ISO.

outcomes.statement: Utilize and extend skills from Module 3A to capture images of increasing quality and refinement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3B: Basic Photographic Skills (Core) · Suggested Time: 15-20 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 3A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a variety of images demonstrating planning, including awareness of aspects such as focus, light manipulation, framing, and the photographic triangle.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a log of camera settings, personal reflections, and knowledge regarding increasing skill level.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Load and unload the storage media from the camera.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate proficiency of image capture through manipulation of camera settings.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3C: Basic Photographic Skills (Core) · Suggested Time: 15-20 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 3B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Consistently create quality images through control of the exposure triangle.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Consistently create quality images that are in focus, demonstrate basic composition rules, and have a clear focal point.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a log of camera settings which includes a personal assessment of each image based on the above criteria.

outcomes.statement: Describe safe and sustainable practices connected to the field of photography.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Safety and Sustainability (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: List safety issues and produce a plan for personal safety when taking photographs.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a list of safety practices to protect both equipment and self when using photographic equipment such as cameras, flash, external lighting.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify environmentally sustainable ways to use and dispose of equipment and accessories such as batteries and chemicals.

outcomes.statement: Create images through demonstration of visualization and composition.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Composition (Core) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 3A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research and define elements of photographic critique.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Critique various photos on their compositional merit.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Visualize and describe or illustrate techniques to compose a photograph.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create images demonstrating aspects of composition such as rule of thirds, negative space, lines, contrast, and colour.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Recognize when normal rules of compostion can be broken.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the effect of focal length on the image.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6A: Focal Length and Camera Lenses (Core) · Suggested Time: 6-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Show the effects on a series of images produced by changing the focal length (i.e., zoom).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a series of images to demonstrate how perspective is changed by altering the camera position relative to the subject.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Produce a series of images to show the apparent change in depth of field resulting from a change in focal length.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate an understanding of selecting various lenses and focal lengths to create a variety of effects on the image.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6B: Focal Length and Camera Lenses (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 6A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Illustrate how different lenses affect an image (e.g., fast versus slow, zoom versus prime).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate the change in image as a result of using a variety of lenses (e.g., fisheye, wide angle, telephoto).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Understand and illustrate, through providing examples, the concept of how a resulting image is affected by focal length and/or format size.

outcomes.statement: Create a series of images showing the effect of the quality, quantity, and direction of light.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7: Understanding Light (Core) · Suggested Time: 7-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 3A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Explore and demonstrate the effect of changing:
- the direction of light on a subject
- the quality of light on a subject including diffuse light, natural light, colour, temperature, and types of light sources
- the quantity of light on a subject.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Manipulate light to change the resulting image through the use of tools such as reflectors, diffusers, coloured gels, and additional light sources.

outcomes.statement: Explore and evaluate the career training and occupational opportunities in the field of photography in Saskatchewan, Canada, and globally, including post-secondary education programs.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Career and Occupational Opportunities (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify specific examples of occupational skills required in photography occupations.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate programs offered by universities and technical institutes in photography.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the career opportunities for professional photographers.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify local opportunities for being paid as a freelance photographer.

outcomes.statement: Create images demonstrating the use of an electronic flash.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Electronic Flash (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 7

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare images that demonstrate the effects of using an electronic flash.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate the effects of changing the flash technique (e.g., bounce, using diffusers, or using coloured gels on the flash).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Show the effects of manipulating flash through power settings (e.g., full power, half power).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate the use of mixed lighting and fill-in flash.

outcomes.statement: Optimize colour values when capturing an image.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Colour Balance/White Balance (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 7

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate how changes in white balance can be manipulated to produce different effects.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Adjust the colour balance on a camera to achieve different visual impacts in different lighting situations to represent what you see.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate how to set a custom white balance for specific locations, light sources, and conditions.

outcomes.statement: Develop a workflow to improve digital images using software.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11A: Image Adjustment (Core) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 5

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Crop images to create a better composition.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Resize images for various outputs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate and explain why and how files are saved in different formats.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate and explain how and why files are saved with different resolutions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Adjust brightness, colour, and contrast to enhance a photograph.

outcomes.statement: Continue to develop proficiency with software to improve digital images.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11B: Image Adjustment (Core) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 11A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Use curves to adjust brightness, contrast, and colour saturation and tone.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Apply various types of filters when adjusting an image (e.g., sharpening, texturizing, blur, black and white).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Use software tools to retouch an image.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate increasing expertise using software to improve digital images.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11C: Image Adjustment (Core) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 11B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Manipulate original images to enhance their appearance.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Apply advanced editing effects to create images such as:
- selection tools
- masking
- brushes
- vignetting
- dodging and burning
- temperature adjustment.

outcomes.statement: Investigate and articulate legal issues related to photography such as copyright and consent.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12A: Legal and Ethical Issues (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the term “copyright” as used in the Canadian legal system and assess its impact on a photography class.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the three factors that place some works in the public domain and cite some examples of these works along with reasons for their inclusion.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate and report on current issues and resources connected to copyright law such as “open source”, “creative commons”, and stock resources.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate and report on the need for consent in various circumstances such as location, appearance, and material.

outcomes.statement: Discuss and reflect on the need for societal standards (e.g., legal, ethical, and community norms, and values) and cultural sensitivity in photography.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12B: Legal and Ethical Issues (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 12A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Formulate a list of societal standards in relation to issues such as sexism, racism, and homophobia, and support the list with positive media examples.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compose a strategy for inclusion of appropriate content and images reflective of societal standards in personal, class, and school projects and assignments.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify and discuss issues regarding posting of images on the web including safety, possible consequences, and permanence of web postings.

outcomes.statement: Identify through research the positive and negative aspects of creative, artistic, and intellectual works receiving ownership protection.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12C: Legal and Ethical Issues (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 12B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Utilize the Canadian Intellectual Property Office to distinguish between copyright, a patent, and an industrial design, and identify some common examples pertaining to photography.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Collect and categorize a number of articles from various sources regarding intellectual property that reflect opposing points of view.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain and support a personal stance on intellectual property.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the ownership rights of personal work and how to protect and sell usage rights of personal work using techniques such as watermarking.

outcomes.statement: Develop skills using basic image editing software to manipulate photographs.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13A: Image Manipulation (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 11A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate a variety of manipulation techniques such as compositing, distorting, and perspective control.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare original and manipulated images to examine the different messages of each.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize and discuss some of the ethical implications in image manipulations.

outcomes.statement: Continue to develop skills using basic image editing software to manipulate photographs for a defined purpose.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13B: Image Manipulation (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 13A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate techniques such as retouching, skin correction, contrast, layering, panoramas, stitching, and masking as examples of manipulation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Provide personal and ethical justification for choosing manipulation procedures to enhance an image.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate increasing expertise using software to perform advanced manipulation of digital images.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13C: Image Manipulation (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 13B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Apply software/editing effects to create personally satisfying images.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Manipulate an image to alter the appearance (e.g., colour, apparent age, masking).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Restore old or damaged photographs.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Apply tone-mapping using multiple images.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore high dynamic range (HDR) photography.

outcomes.statement: Develop abilities to critique photographic work as a means of evaluation and self-reflection of personal, peer, and public work.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14: Critiquing Images (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 5

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research and discuss various aspects of critiquing work (aesthetic and technical merits).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a critique of acquired images produced by self and peers.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Express an opinion based on knowledge of composition, genre, design, style, message, presentation, and target audience.

outcomes.statement: Explore and demonstrate a variety of presentation formats that photographers use to display work.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15A: Presentations/Sharing of Images (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-20 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 14

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Maintain a personal portfolio reflecting growth in understanding and skills involved in image creation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compile personal images for display.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Select a style and venue for a school or public showing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Practise aspects of presentations such as matting, mounting, and framing.

outcomes.statement: Create and display a digital or print gallery of completed images along with photographer’s notes and descriptions of the process involved.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15B: Presentations/Sharing of Images (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-20 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 15A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a plan for an exhibition including time, space, intended audience, and purpose.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a personally satisfying photography presentation through the use of matting, mounting, and/or framing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Engage classmates and/or the public in a display of personally created photographs.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create an assessment of the exhibition through personal reflection and feedback from others.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate skills and processes used by photojournalists.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16: Photojournalism (Optional) · Suggested Time: 6-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 8

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate and report on what a photojournalist does.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Choose a theme and document an event through the use of images and captions in the style of a photojournalist.

outcomes.statement: Develop skills and processes used in commercial photography to promote a product or service.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17: Advertising and Product Photography (Optional) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 8

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Critique an existing advertisement on the effectiveness of the photography.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a series of images of various products.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a fictional draft advertisement using an existing campaign or a personal example.

outcomes.statement: Develop and demonstrate techniques employed by portrait photographers.
outcomes.printedWith: Develop and demonstrate techniques employed by portrait photographers. (Optional) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 7

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the effects of lighting on subjects (e.g., supplementary lighting, reflectors).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how various poses create emphasis.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Practise group arrangements to produce an effective group portrait.

outcomes.statement: Develop required skills to operate a variety of photographic businesses.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Entrepreneurship (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 8

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and interview an entrepreneur to investigate how he/she started out in business and what advice he/she can provide.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze the differences between photojournalism, social photography (e.g., weddings, parties), portrait photography, assignment photography and stock photography and create a statement about your personal business preference.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the costs of starting a photography business such as buying equipment, obtaining a business licence, paying taxes, pricing your product, and purchasing insurance.

outcomes.statement: Explore and articulate the major historical developments in photography.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: History of Photography (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate a photographic process (e.g., camera obscura, daguerreotype, tintype) and share the knowledge through a photographic presentation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a visual presentation to present the work of a single noted phototgrapher or to compare the styles of two or more photographers including how they contributed to advancements in the art or science of the field.

outcomes.statement: Service Learning – Explore how participation in activity-based service learning benefits self and community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how participating in service learning develops positive citizenship and community involvement, including relationship building to support reconciliation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate a variety of fitness-related opportunities (e.g., coaching/officiating minor sports, helping seniors who are housebound, senior centre fitness class, Special Olympics and walking school bus) that can benefit the well-being of self and/or community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess personal interests and skills to determine the most appropriate role (e.g., coach, instructor, manager, official, volunteer) in a specific activity-based service learning opportunity.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore requirements (e.g., safe contact standards in football, concussion protocol and criminal record check) for individuals seeking a role in activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Participate in activity-based service learning such as local, provincial and national cultural (e.g., pow wow, children's festival and multicultural celebrations) and sporting (e.g., rodeo, track and field and national championships) events.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Document participation in activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on perceived benefits for self and community from participation in activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore careers in your community related to physical activity, health and wellness.

outcomes.title: Service Learning

outcomes.statement: Health- and Skill-Related Fitness – Explore components of health- and skill-related fitness through physical activity.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Reflect on questions such as:
- How might participation in physical activity affect my lifestyle?
- What factors might influence how I pursue personal fitness goals?
- How might my physical activity interests change based on my fitness goals?
- What organizations and events exist to support my fitness?

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify how to measure components of health- (e.g., cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, muscular strength and endurance) and skill-related (e.g., agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed) fitness.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research how to use fitness appraisal tools (e.g., fitness apps, sit and reach board and stop watch) to collect data on specific components of health- and skill-related fitness.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how to apply principles of training such as FITT (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type), overload, progression, reversibility and specificity to improve health- and skill-related fitness.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess, through participation, how different training styles and approaches (e.g., cross fit, pilates, plyometrics, weight training and yoga) improve components of health- and skill-related fitness.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the drawbacks of overemphasizing specific components of fitness when engaging in physical activity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify personal aerobic thresholds, such as maximum and target heart rates, while participating in physical activity.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Collect and analyze health -and skill-related data, using fitness appraisal tools and available equipment (e.g., free weights, medicine balls, stability balls and wobble boards), to identify personal strengths and weaknesses.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop a personal fitness plan with a focus on improving components of health- and skill-related fitness.

outcomes.title: Health- and Skill-Related Fitness

outcomes.statement: Body Management – Explore and participate in body management activities as pathways towards personal well-being.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Participate in body management activities (e.g., aquatics, dance, gymnastics, karate, pilates, weight training and yoga) to enhance personal well-being.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze how fundamental movement skills transfer between different body management activities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss physical, emotional, mental and spiritual benefits that can result from participating in body management activities.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Propose solutions to potential challenges (e.g., cultural, financial, safety, motivation and time) that might restrict an individual's participation in body management activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply knowledge of a body management activity from another culture by teaching it to peers or other members of the community.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the physical, emotional, mental and spiritual benefits of participation in First Nations and Métis body management activities (e.g., jigging, hoop dance, pow wow and hand games).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Evaluate the influence of current societal trends (e.g., CrossFit and yoga) on individuals' participation in body management activities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the benefits of technology (e.g., apps, fitness watches and heart rate monitors) when engaging in body management activities.

outcomes.title: Body Management

outcomes.statement: Complex Skills – Demonstrate improvement in performance of complex skills.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate complex skills within various activities and/or games in multiple environments (e.g., air, land, snow/ice and water).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate First Nations and Métis perspectives on holistically developing complex skills (e.g., throwing a ball using either hand).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the components of a specific complex skill.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine, through feedback, which components of a complex skill to target in order to improve performance.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply principles of practice (e.g., part-whole and whole-part-whole) to improve performance of complex skills.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify how improved performance in a complex skill can influence proficiency in other complex skills.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Document progress (e.g., blog, journal, photos and video) of improved performance of one or more complex skills.

outcomes.title: Complex Skills

outcomes.statement: Physical Activity within Multiple Environments – Investigate how physical activity within multiple environments contributes to the well-being of self and others.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the benefits for well-being of self and others that can result from participating in physical activities within multiple environments (e.g., air, land, snow/ice and water).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify opportunities to participate in outdoor physical activities within your community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Participate in fitness, leisure and/or competitive activities in multiple environments.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design and/or participate in an outdoor experience (e.g., biking, canoeing, geocaching, hiking, ice-fishing, skiing and trapping) that promotes personal well-being.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate respect for the environment when participating in physical activities.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate, and follow when appropriate, First Nations and Métis protocols, traditional knowledge and practices when interacting with the environment.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Use technology (e.g., backpack, compass, fitness and activity apps, global positioning satellite, hiking boots, maps and satellite phone) appropriately and responsibly when participating in physical activities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Propose potential solutions for challenges (e.g., cultural, financial and geographical location) that might limit individual's participation in physical activities.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Document and reflect on how participation in physical activities within multiple environments contributes to the well-being of self and others.

outcomes.title: Physical Activity within Multiple Environments

outcomes.statement: Games, Tactics and Strategies – Compare how effective tactics and strategies enhance performance and enjoyment in physically active games.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize how prior knowledge of tactics and strategies can transfer to different games.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify tactics and strategies used in traditional First Nation and Métis games (e.g., double ball, knuckle hop, lacrosse, leg wrestling and snow snake).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Incorporate effective tactics and strategies in target, invasion/territorial, net/wall, striking/fielding, low organization and inventive games to enhance performance and enjoyment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between individual and team tactics and strategies used in individual/partner and group/team games.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate an understanding of effective tactical and strategic decisions used in a variety of game situations while participating in individual/partner and group/team games.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess personal use of effective tactics and strategies incorporated in game situations.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Modify tactics and strategies to enhance participation in games for all students.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss and apply different models (e.g., teaching games for understanding, sport-model and Long-Term Athlete Development) for teaching games, tactics and strategies.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Present a game from another culture, including its tactics and strategies, to peers or members of the community.

outcomes.title: Games, Tactics and Strategies

outcomes.statement: First Nations and Métis – Examine First Nations and Métis worldviews regarding learning through physical activities.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine how First Nations and Métis ways of knowing inform people's interactions with self, others and the environment through physical activity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss how First Nations and Métis people use story-telling to convey knowledge about learning through physical activity.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how the benefits of physical activity (e.g., endurance, flexibility and social skills) serve a purpose to meet the demands of activities such as hunting, observation skills or learning social values.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify, and follow when appropriate, First Nations and Métis protocols, traditional knowledge and practices when engaging in physical activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Incorporate local, traditional First Nations and Métis ways of relating to and using the environment when participating in activities (e.g., orienteering and navigation, setting fishing nets and traps, and snowshoeing).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Participate in traditional First Nations and Métis games (e.g., snowsnake, double ball, lacrosse, leg wrestling and knuckle hop), dance (e.g., jigging, hoop and pow wow) and activities (e.g., snowshoeing and archery).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore how skills developed in traditional games, dance and activities could be transferable to other contexts.

outcomes.title: First Nations and Métis

outcomes.statement: Nutrition – Examine how healthy nutritional choices support a physically active lifestyle.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare personal nutritional practices to the recommendations in Canada's Food Guide.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify how an individual's nutritional choices may be influenced by factors such as cultural eating practices, finances, advertising and marketing and/or geographical location.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze personal daily caloric intake to determine if it meets energy requirements (e.g., basal metabolic rate calculation) of a physically active lifestyle.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the limitations of calorie counting as a method of determining how much food to eat to support a physically active lifestyle.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the role of macro and micronutrients and hydration in supporting a physically active lifestyle, before, during and after activity.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine how nutrition-related illnesses (e.g., cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes) may be impacted by participation in physical activity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine how nutritional trends (e.g., ketogenic, gluten free and high protein diets) compare with the recommendations in Canada's Food Guide.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify how a specific nutritional trend can influence personal nutrition practices.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Create or evaluate a nutrition plan that supports a physically active lifestyle considering food availability, cost, likes and dislikes.

outcomes.title: Nutrition

outcomes.statement: Skeletal and Muscular Systems – Investigate the effect of physical activity on the skeletal and muscular systems of the human body.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the major bones, joints and muscles that are affected by participation in a specific physical activity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate the three types (i.e., concentric, eccentric and isometric) of muscle contractions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the impact of the three types of muscle contractions on muscle development.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate and perform isolated and compound movements that target major muscles.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify and perform different exercises that increase the efficiency of slow and fast twitch muscle fibres.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how various types of exercise incorporate specific joint actions (e.g., abduction, adduction, circumduction, eversion, inversion, pronation and supination).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research common injuries (e.g., fracture, sprain and tear) to bones, joints and muscles that result from physical activity.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the cause and treatment of injuries (e.g., stress fracture, tendonitis and muscle strain) that result from over-use of a bone, joint and/or muscle during physical activity.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze the impact of a sedentary lifestyle on skeletal and/or muscular systems in the short and long-term.

outcomes.title: Skeletal and Muscular Systems

outcomes.statement: Personal Mental Health – Investigate the benefits of physical activity on mental health.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the short- and long-term effects of physical activity on factors that can affect mental health such as anxiety, body image, depression, self-esteem and stress.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the interrelationship between physical activity, hormone levels (e.g., dopamine, cortisol, endorphin and serotonin) and physical, emotional, mental and spiritual health.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss First Nations and Métis understandings of the interrelationships between physical, emotional, mental and spiritual health.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Incorporate physical activity as a strategy to enhance personal positive mental health.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Document personal perceptions of how physical activity affects mental health over an extended period of time.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Reflect on how participation in individual (e.g., jogging, meditation and yoga) and group (e.g., cooperative games, fitness classes and team sports) activities may provide mental health benefits.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Communicate (e.g., brochure, display, oral, presentation software, video and website) research findings on community resources (e.g., Kids Help Phone and Sask Health) designed to support individuals and raise mental health awareness.

outcomes.title: Personal Mental Health

outcomes.statement: Student-Directed Study – Create and implement a plan to explore one or more topics of personal interest relevant to Physical Education 20.

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Assemble and reflect on a portfolio that demonstrates understanding of a Physical Education 20 topic of interest to the student.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Share the results of student-directed study through a display, presentation, performance, demonstration, song, game, commercial, fine art representation or research paper.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form or peer-evaluation form) to assess the process and products involved in a student-directed study.

outcomes.title: Student-Directed Study
