outcomes.statement: Leadership through Service Learning – Assess, through participation, how leadership in activity-based service learning benefits self and community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize the contributions that young adults have made to their community and province through activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss what is known about leadership within physical activity (e.g., what leadership means; why it is important to give back to the community and province; what it means to be a mentor or an advocate in the community/province).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess personal strengths and weaknesses in communication and building relationships with others.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how First Nations and Métis ways of knowing guide the development of relationships with others and the environment through activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate leadership roles in a variety of activity-based service learning opportunities in the community.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore the requirements (e.g., safe contact in football, concussion protocol and criminal record check) for individuals seeking certification in a specific leadership role (e.g., coaching, officiating and volunteering).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Participate, in a leadership role, in activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Document personal leadership in activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect on how participation in activity-based service learning has enhanced personal leadership skills.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect on perceived benefits for self and community from leadership in activity-based service learning.

outcomes.title: Leadership through Service Learning

outcomes.statement: Lifelong Fitness – Explore methods and opportunities for sustaining lifelong fitness.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Reflect on questions such as:
- How might my lifestyle change after graduation?
- What factors after graduation might influence how I pursue personal fitness goals?
- How might my physical activity interests change as I age?
- What organizations and events exist to support my lifelong fitness?

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Implement various principles of training (e.g., specificity, progression and reversibility, overload and FITT: Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type) and reflect on how they address health- and skill-related components of fitness.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate how to incorporate suitable technologies (e.g., heart rate monitor, fitness and activity tracker, pedometer and video) to enhance physical activity goals.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recommend physical activities that maximize an individual's ability to improve aerobic thresholds (e.g., target and maximum heart rate).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify events (e.g., annual winter games, fun run, yoga in the park, cycling, Spartan race and pow wow) in the community that support lifelong fitness.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify organizations in the community (e.g., fitness facilities, recreational sport leagues and community-based leisure services) that promote lifelong fitness.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Create a plan to identify events and organizations in a community that promote lifelong fitness.

outcomes.title: Lifelong Fitness

outcomes.statement: Body Management – Explore how participation in body management activities affects the wellbeing of self and community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Participate in body management activities (e.g., dance, pilates, yoga, aquatics, karate, walking, spinning/cycling, Zumba, Tai Chi and aerobics classes) that are available in the community.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore potential use of community space (e.g., rink, golf course, community green space, parks, walking/bike path, recreation center and public/private gyms) for body management activities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Propose body management activities that address a community need.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the physical, emotional, mental and spiritual benefits of participation in First Nations and Métis body management activities (e.g., jigging, hoop dance, pow wow and hand games).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate leadership through organization and participation in a chosen community-based body management activity.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Document your leadership role in a community-based body management activity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on how participation in community-based body management activities has enhanced personal leadership skills.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compile the participants' perceptions of the impact of a community-based body management activity on their well-being.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss how self and community may benefit physically, emotionally, mentally and spiritually from participation in body management activities.

outcomes.title: Body Management

outcomes.statement: Movement in Multiple Environments – Investigate how movement in multiple environments promotes lifelong physical activity for self and others.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the potential lifelong benefits, for self and others, from participating in physical activities within multiple environments (e.g., in the air; on the land; on snow and ice; and in and on water).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Participate in physical activities (e.g., fitness, leisure and/or competitive) in multiple environments.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Construct first aid and safety plans that support physical activity in multiple environments.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the advantages and disadvantages of technology (e.g., global positioning satellite, adjustable dumbbells, fitness and activity tracker, exercise ball and clothing/footwear) used during physical activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate, and follow when appropriate, First Nations and Métis protocols, traditional knowledge and practices when engaging in experiences within the outdoor environment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate respect for the natural environment through stewardship.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Document and reflect on how participation in physical activities within multiple environments contributes to the lifelong well-being of self.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research and design a group physical activity outside of the community while considering logistical and financial details (e.g., destination, budget, equipment, nutrition and transportation).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Propose potential solutions for challenges (e.g., certifications, resources and geographical location) that may limit participation in physical activities outside of the community.

outcomes.title: Movement in Multiple Environments

outcomes.statement: Complex Skills, Tactics and Strategies – Assess, through participation, the proficiency of skills, tactics and strategies in target, invasion/territorial, net/wall, striking/fielding and low organization and inventive activities.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare at least two complex skills (e.g., swinging a baseball bat and swinging a golf club) that have similar transferrable, basic movement patterns, strategies and performance cues.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate a complex skill in a specific activity and compare execution to that of a proficient performance.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: View the execution of complex skills, performed by self or others, and provide feedback to increase proficiency.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Receive and incorporate feedback to improve skill proficiency in a variety of activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply modifications to complex skills, tactics and strategies in activities and games, considering age and developmental stage, to enhance the confidence and competence of participants.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop strategic plans and tactics for individual and multi-player activities and games, including First Nations and Métis games and activities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Design and implement a plan to teach skills, tactics and strategies required to participate in an individual or multi-player activities and games.

outcomes.title: Complex Skills, Tactics and Strategies

outcomes.statement: First Nations and Métis – Examine how First Nations and Métis perspectives and ways of knowing support lifelong learning through physical activity.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine how First Nations and Métis ways of knowing inform people's interactions with self, others and the environment through physical activity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how the benefits of physical activity (e.g., endurance, flexibility and social skills) serve a purpose to meet the demands of lifelong activity such as hunting, observation skills or learning social values.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate, and follow when appropriate, First Nations and Métis protocols, traditional knowledge and practices when engaging in physical activities.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Incorporate local, traditional First Nations and Métis ways of relating to and using the environment when leading physical activities (e.g., setting traps and fishing nets, snowshoeing, orienteering and navigation).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Plan and facilitate traditional First Nations and Métis games (e.g., snowsnake, double ball, lacrosse, leg wrestling and knuckle hop), dance (e.g., jigging, hoop and pow wow) and/or activities (e.g., snowshoeing and archery).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore how leadership skills developed by planning and facilitating traditional games, dance and activities could be transferable to other contexts.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the long-term physical, emotional, mental, and spiritual benefits of participation in First Nations and Métis games, dance and activities.

outcomes.title: First Nations and Métis

outcomes.statement: Nutrition – Analyze the role of nutritional choices to support participation in self-selected physical activities.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Assess how nutritional choices (e.g., vegetarianism, carbohydrate loading, intermittent fasting and high protein meal) might impact participation in a physical activity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify how an individual's nutritional choices for a self-selected physical activity may be influenced by factors such as type of activity, cost and geographical location.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Apply a basal metabolic rate formula with an activity factor to determine the daily caloric requirements when participating in an activity.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess whether an individual's daily caloric intake meets the daily energy requirements for participating in an activity.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the limitations of calorie counting as a method of determining how much food to eat to support participation in a physical activity.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe how nutrient timing (e.g., what and when to eat and drink) impacts participation and performance in an activity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research the positive and negative effects of supplements (e.g., protein powder, creatine, branched-chain amino acids and steroids) and nutritional products (e.g., meal replacement drink, sports drink, energy gel and protein bar) on physical performance.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Critique how current nutritional trends (e.g., ketogenic, gluten free and high protein diets) might influence nutritional choices when participating in physical activity.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Design a nutrition plan using informed nutritional choices and nutrient timing, to enhance performance in a self-selected physical activity.

outcomes.title: Nutrition

outcomes.statement: Physiology and Biomechanics – Analyze physiological and biomechanical principles of movement.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze the physiological benefits of short- and long-term training programs.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify, through participation, how to execute self-selected movement patterns and complex skills.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique, for self and others, various movement patterns and complex skills for proper biomechanical (e.g., rotation of a wrist, flexion of a joint and body position) execution.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify, through participation, the movement patterns required to execute self-selected weight training exercises (e.g., proper form for bench press) and fitness activities (e.g., proper foot plant for long distance running).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Critique, for self and others, various weight training exercises and fitness activities for proper biomechanical execution.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the potential long-term effects of using improper movement patterns in a specific activity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the importance of rest and active recovery as part of a fitness or training plan.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the possible short- and long-term effects (e.g., lack of muscle growth and degeneration of joints) of over-training on an individual's physiology.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the importance of participating in multiple activities to support physical development.

outcomes.title: Physiology and Biomechanics

outcomes.statement: Exercise Psychology – Investigate psychological factors that impact participation in physical activities.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate personal motivations for participating in physical activity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the interrelationship between physical activity and physical, emotional, mental and spiritual health.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss First Nations and Métis understandings of the interrelationships between physical, emotional, mental and spiritual health.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine psychological factors (e.g., self-talk, imagery/visualization, regulation of arousal, anxiety and relaxation, motivation, goal setting and concentration) that impact enjoyment, participation and performance in physical activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the role of external (e.g., audience, weather and teammate expectations) and internal (e.g., fatigue, mental toughness and making a mistake) factors on an individual's enjoyment, participation and performance in physical activity.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Incorporate a psychological factor to improve participation, enjoyment and/or performance in a self-selected physical activity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on the effectiveness of psychological factors in supporting and maintaining participation in physical activities.

outcomes.title: Exercise Psychology

indicators.text: Assemble and reflect on a portfolio that demonstrates understanding of a Physical Education 30 topic of interest to the student.

indicators.text: Share the results of student-directed study through a display, presentation, performance, demonstration, song, game, commercial, fine art representation or research paper.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form and peer-evaluation form) to assess the process and products involved in a student-directed study.

outcomes.statement: Analyze and explore physical science related occupations in Saskatchewan, Canada and the world.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Generate a list of occupations that require a background in physical science through research and/or participation in events such as a career fair or job shadow. (K, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore connection between topics in Physical Science 20 and occupations of personal interest. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify which physical science related occupations are facing shortages and which are oversubscribed locally, regionally and/or nationally. (STSE, S, K, A)

indicators.label: d

legacyEvidence.reason: 1992 guide; not in the site's menus; its 30-level part is replaced by the renewed Physics 30 (id 72)
evidence: Status on the site (2026-11-21): the course page has no notice that the guide is superseded; it offers only the PDF (its 'Outcomes & Indicators' page is empty). The course is reachable only through the site's search list: the 'Browse by Subject' → Sciences menu lists Science 10, Computer Science 20/30, Environmental Science 20, Health Science 20, Physical Science 20, Biology 30, Chemistry 30, Physics 30 and Earth Science 30, and not the 1992 'Biology/Chemistry/Physics 20, 30' entries.

The renewed Health Science 20 curriculum (CurriculumFile?id=74, Health_Science_20_2020.pdf, p. 3) says: 'Saskatchewan has developed science courses at Grade 11 that provide students with opportunities to learn core biology, chemistry and physics disciplinary ideas within interdisciplinary contexts.' and 'The current credit requirements for graduation from Grade 12 are one 10-level credit and one 20-level credit in science.' Neither document names Biology 20, Chemistry 20 or Physics 20 or says they were withdrawn; the authoritative list of courses in effect is the Registrar's Handbook for School Administrators (not checked).
The 30-level parts of this guide are superseded on the site by the renewed Biology 30 / Chemistry 30 / Physics 30 (ids 68, 69, 72), which have outcomes in sk.json.

evidence.observation: The curriculum document groups its objectives under 14 headings: “Core Unit I: The Physics of Everyday Things”, “Core Unit II: Waves”, “Core Unit III: Light”, “Core Unit IV: Heat”, “Optional Unit V: Sound”, “Optional Unit VI: Optics”, “Core Unit I: Kinematics and Dynamics”, “Core Unit II: Mechanical Energy”, “Core Unit III: Electricity”, “Core Unit IV: Nuclear Physics”, “Optional Unit V: Applications of Kinematics”, “Optional Unit VI: Fluid Mechanics”, “Optional Unit VII: Electromagnetism”, “Optional Unit VIII: Atomic Physics”.

Solve problems to determine the relative index of refraction between any two given media.
Calculate the distance, in metres, that light travels in one light year, based on its speed in metres per second.
Explain why the light year is used to measure astronomical distances.

Define the following terms: interface, ray, incident ray, point of incidence, normal, reflected ray, angle of incidence, angle of reflection, specular reflection, diffuse reflection, indirect lighting, direct lighting.
State the laws of reflection.
Compare and contrast specular and diffuse reflection.
Explain why the laws of reflection still apply for diffuse (irregular) reflection.
List some different kinds of surfaces which produce either specular or diffuse reflection.
Compare the effects produced by direct and indirect lighting.
Apply the laws of reflection in problem solving.
Define the following terms: real image, virtual image, plane mirror, magnification, ray diagram.
Identify the characteristics of an image formed by a plane mirror.
Distinguish between a real and a virtual image.
Identify some optical systems which produce either a real or a virtual image.
Draw ray diagrams neatly, accurately, and to some appropriate scale.
Apply the correct use of solid and dotted lines on ray diagrams.
Interpret solid and dotted lines on ray diagrams.
Label ray diagrams correctly, using conventional symbols.
Determine appropriate scales to use when drawing ray diagrams.
Apply the magnification formula and the mirror equation in problem solving.
State the four important image characteristics which need to be considered for any type of optical system.
Recognize and explain the importance of ray diagrams in geometric optics.
Demonstrate an understanding of important principles of drawing ray diagrams.
Draw ray diagrams for analysis and for solving problems dealing with optics.
Recognize the combined use of ray diagrams and equations in solving problems related to optics.
Use ray diagrams, along with other experimental or theoretical methods, to determine the characteristics of an image in an optical system.
Describe the location and number of images formed by two perpendicular plane mirrors.
Suggest some applications of multiple images formed by more than one mirror.

Define the following terms: converging mirror, concave surface, diverging mirror, convex surface, vertex, principal axis, focal plane, centre of curvature, radius of curvature, focal length, paraxial rays, axial point, principal focus, spherical mirror, cylindrical mirror, aberration, spherical aberration, parabolic mirror, conjugate points.
Explain the Principle of Reversibility.
Distinguish between a concave and a convex surface.
Draw diagrams of converging and diverging mirrors, showing the principal axis and important points located on the principal axis for each.
Explain the difference between a focal point and a focal plane.
Explain one way that spherical aberration can be corrected in a curved mirror.
Express the relationship between the focal length and the radius of curvature of a curved mirror.
Apply the relationship between the focal length and the radius of curvature of a curved mirror in solving problems.

Use the rules for drawing ray diagrams for converging and diverging mirrors (parallel-ray method) to position an object on the principal axis and locate the position and other characteristics of the image.
Interpret the characteristics of an image from a ray diagram.
Demonstrate an understanding of the importance and use of a procedure of verification when using ray diagrams and equations.
Observe and explain that the image position in either a converging or a diverging mirror depends on the location of the object.
Observe and explain that except for the image position, all other characteristics of an image formed in a diverging mirror are independent of the object position.
Observe and explain that the characteristics of an image formed in a converging mirror depend on the object position.
Apply mirror equations to solving problems.
Apply the sign conventions for mirror equations correctly when solving problems.
Recognize that ray tracing and the use of equations are techniques that developed from experimentation.

Define the following terms: refraction, boundary, partial reflection, point of incidence, refracted ray, angle of refraction, spectrum, dispersion, dispersive medium, chromatic aberration, lateral displacement, angle of deviation.
Explain why refraction occurs.
Explain that no bending of the incident ray occurs if it strikes the boundary while travelling along the normal.
Draw and label a diagram which illustrates the way in which light behaves when it undergoes refraction.
State the three laws of refraction.
Apply Snell's Law to solve problems relating to refraction.
Recognize the direction that a refracted light ray will bend, depending on the relative index of refraction for the two media.
Explain what causes chromatic aberration.
Solve problems relating to the refraction of light.
Identify several applications or examples from common experience which illustrate the refraction of light.
Define the following terms: total internal reflection, critical angle.
Solve problems involving the refraction of light.
Recognize situations in which total internal reflection could occur.
Determine the critical angle for light travelling from any medium into some other medium.
Recognize that the critical angle depends on the relative index of refraction between two media.

Explain how an incident ray, travelling towards a medium with a lower index of refraction, would behave if the angle of incidence were smaller than the critical angle, the same size as the critical angle, or larger than the critical angle.

items.text: Demonstrate an understanding of the kinetic molecular theory.
Explain how theories are used in science.
Perform experiments to investigate heat energy.
Develop an enthusiastic pursuit of learning as a life-long endeavour.
Recognize the need to control variables in experiments.
Demonstrate the need for precision in measurement and careful observation in experiments.
Recognize that both qualitative and quantitative analysis of data have important roles in scientific investigations.
Demonstrate respect for the environment and for all forms of life.
Use a wide range of possibilities for developing knowledge of the major concepts within physics. (COM)
Develop understanding of the uses and abuses of mathematical concepts in everyday life. (NUM)
Promote both intuitive, imaginative thought and the ability to evaluate ideas, processes, experiences and objects in meaningful contexts. (CCT)

Access information. (IL)
Define the following terms: thermal energy, heat, temperature, convection, conduction, radiation, thermal expansion, linear expansion, coefficient of linear expansion.
Identify some important postulates of the kinetic molecular theory.
State what is meant by a theory.
Explain that, as new information accumulates, a theory could be supported, modified, or rejected in favour of new theories which better help to explain the evidence.
Describe the difference between a theory and a law.
Give an example of an observable phenomenon which lends support to the kinetic molecular theory.
Explain the difference between heat and temperature.
State the correct units used to measure heat energy and temperature.
Explain that heat can not be measured directly whereas temperature can.
State that a thermometer, like any other measuring instrument, must be calibrated in some way.
Recognize the limitations of certain materials that are used in making thermometers.
Explain the reference points that were used to calibrate the Celsius temperature scale.
Compare the Celsius and Kelvin temperature scales.
Convert a temperature reading from degrees Celsius to Kelvin and vice versa.
State that substances vary in their amount of thermal expansion.
State three important factors which determine the linear expansion of a material.
State the correct units for the coefficient of linear expansion.
Recognize that the coefficient of linear expansion is based on the unique physical properties of different substances.
Suggest some applications in which an understanding of thermal expansion would be extremely useful.

Recognize any potentially hazardous situations that could arise from the thermal expansion of materials, especially those involving an increase in pressure from the expansion of gases in closed containers.
Solve problems involving heat and temperature, and thermal expansion.

items.topic: B. Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat
items.text: Identify several unique physical properties of water.

items.topic: B. Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat

Define the following terms: calorimeter, heat engine, heat pump.
State the Law of Conservation of Energy.
Give a practical example which illustrates the Law of Conservation of Energy.
State the Principle of Heat Exchange.
Give a practical example which illustrates the Principle of Heat Exchange.
State the Zeroth, First, Second and Third Laws of Thermodynamics.
Give examples to illustrate the Laws of Thermodynamics.
Explain that it is impossible to build a perfect heat engine.

units.name: Optional Unit V: Sound

items.text: Select areas of study, develop learning goals, identify and comply with project tasks, and develop time management skills to meet given time lines.
Investigate the characteristics of sound experimentally.
Appreciate the roles that science and technology play in understanding sound.
Synthesize ideas from a variety of sources.
Identify and clarify key issues.
Make decisions systematically after careful deliberation.
Describe some important applications of sound.
Appreciate that an understanding of the basic principles of physics can be useful in understanding common and practical life experiences.
Use a wide range of possibilities for developing knowledge of the major concepts involved in the understanding of sound. (COM)
Strengthen their understanding within physics through applying knowledge of numbers and their interrelationships. (NUM)
Develop an understanding of how knowledge is obtained, evaluated, refined, and changed within physics. (CCT)
Develop appreciation of the value and limitations of technology within society. (TL)
Support the development of a positive disposition to life-long learning. (IL)
Define the following terms: meatus (auditory canal), tympanic membrane (eardrum), cochlea, auditory nerve, Eustachian tube.
Identify some important physical principles involved in human hearing such as: amplification, levers, accelerometers, resonance, longitudinal waves, and pressure.
Explain the physical process by which sound signals reaching the ear are transferred from the outer ear to the middle ear.
Define the following terms: sound, pressure, longitudinal waves, compression, rarefaction, vacuum, echo, reverberation, damping.
Describe some of the ways in which sound illustrates wave behaviour.
Explain that sound is produced by vibration.
Determine some vibrating sources which produce different sounds.
Explain that the vibrations cause a change in pressure near the vibrating source.
Explain that the changes in pressure can create a series of longitudinal sound waves which are transmitted from the source.
State that sound can not travel in a vacuum.
Explain that sound can travel through different types of solids, liquids, and gasses.
Define an echo and reverberation and state similarities and differences between them.
Identify two important damping principles.
Give examples of different kinds of damping devices.
Explain that the speed of sound varies in different types of media.
Make generalizations comparing the speed of sound in solids, liquids, and gases.
State that the temperature of air (or any other gas) affect the speed of sound in that medium.
Calculate the speed of sound in air at different temperatures.
Solve problems relating to the speed of sound in air, or any other given medium.
Suggest an experimental procedure which could be used to determine the speed of sound.
Define the following terms: intensity, bel, decibel, logarithmic scale.
State the units commonly used to measure sound intensity.
Illustrate the relationship between sound intensity values expressed in W/m2 and in multiples of 10 on the dB scale.
flags: sub/superscript flattened inline in "intensity values expressed in W/m2 and in" (PDF p142)

items.text: Compare logarithmic and arithmetic scales.
State that 0 dB has been arbitrarily set to correspond to the threshold of human hearing.
State that the threshold of pain lies somewhere between 120 and 130 dB.
Explain that minimum threshold levels of human hearing vary with frequency.
Estimate the approximate intensity of sounds emanating from various different sources.
Recognize that sound intensity diminishes with increased distance.
Explain why instruments which measure sound intensity must be placed at some standard distance away from a sound source.
Interpret inverse square law relationships, as illustrated by the dependence of distance from the source on sound intensity.
Solve problems relating to the intensity of sound.
Explain why extremely loud sounds may cause a perforation of the eardrum.
Explain that repeated exposure to loud sounds may cause permanent hearing damage.
Explain that the intensity of a sound, as well as its duration, determine the extent of hearing damage that could occur from it.
Realize that hearing damage is usually irreparable.
Recognize that partial hearing loss first begins with certain frequencies, then extends to other frequencies until total deafness occurs.
Realize that a "ringing" sensation in the ears may be an indication that permanent hearing damage has occurred.
Realize that there are few pain receptors in the ears to warn us when hearing damage may be taking place.
Recognize that permanent hearing loss is usually irreparable.
Explain that hearing protectors can be used to help protect the ears from loud noises.
Recognize that hearing protectors can not protect the ear adequately from sounds which travel through the skeleton into the bones of the middle ear.
Explain that hearing loss tends to become more pronounced with age.
Explain that in certain developed parts of the world hearing loss among people tends to be more severe.
Explain some things which may be of assistance to people who have experienced hearing loss.
Appreciate the role that both science and technology play in helping people who have experienced hearing loss.
Recognize that noise pollution poses a serious threat to the quality of life.
Suggest a variety of factors which are contributing to noise pollution in both urban and rural environments.
Explain how the term "quality of life" relates to the issue of noise pollution.
Suggest various ways in which the amount of noise pollution experienced in any given situation might be reduced.

Explain that pitch is a term used to describe the frequency of sound waves.
State the approximate range of audible frequencies for humans.
State some important applications for ultrasonic and infrasonic sound.
Explain that doubling the frequency will raise the pitch of a sound by one octave.
Explain that only certain devices, such as a tuning fork, are capable of producing sounds having a single frequency.
Explain that when a sound source generating waves moves relative to an observer, or when an observer moves relative to a source, there is an apparent shift in frequency.
Explain that the frequency apparently decreases when the distance separating the source and the observer increases.
Explain that the frequency apparently increases when the distance separating the source and the observer decreases.
Apply mathematical relationships describing the Doppler Shift to problem solving.
Describe a situation or an application which involves the Doppler Effect.
Transfer an understanding of the Doppler Effect to practical examples and common experiences.
Define the following terms: natural frequency of vibration, mechanical resonance, fundamental frequency, overtones, harmonics, beat frequency.
Explain that all objects have a unique natural frequency of vibration.
Explain that a periodic force occurring at the same frequency as the natural frequency of vibration of an object may cause the object to begin to vibrate.
Explain that the periodic force and the object being affected must come into contact for mechanical resonance to occur.
Explain that mechanical resonance may cause objects to undergo failure.
Suggest ways in which the failure of an object due to mechanical resonance can be prevented.
Transfer an understanding of mechanical resonance to practical examples and common experiences.
Explain that mechanical resonance must be taken into account when selecting and designing materials for a specific application.
State that the fundamental frequency is the lowest frequency which will produce a standing wave pattern in a one dimensional medium.
State that the first overtone has twice the frequency of the fundamental frequency.
Explain that a closed pipe does not exhibit first (or any odd number) overtone, but only even numbered overtones (or odd harmonics).
State that overtones have whole number multiples of the fundamental frequency.
Identify different variables which will affect the frequency produced by a vibrating string.
Apply mathematical relationships governing the frequency of vibrating strings in problem solving.
Recognize that musical instruments are designed based on important underlying physical principles.
Suggest how an understanding of standing wave interference patterns can help to explain resonance in air columns.
State that an air column will resonate if certain specific frequencies of sound pass through it.
Recognize that resonance will occur when an antinode (loop) is allowed to form at the end of the air column from which sound is escaping.
Explain that an adjustable air column can be made to resonate at several different lengths for a given frequency of sound.
Solve problems relating to the resonance of sound in open and closed air columns.
Explain why a vibrating tuning fork produces an interference pattern.
Explain why the placement of one or more speakers in a room affects the quality of sound produced.
Explain that beats are produced when two sound sources vibrate at slightly different frequencies.
Explain that the beat frequency depends on the difference in the frequencies of the two vibrating sources.
Apply an understanding of beat frequency in problem solving.
Define the following terms: accommodation, near point.
Describe the function of the following parts of the human eye: cornea, lens, ciliary muscles, suspensory ligaments, iris, aqueous humour, vitreous humour, sclerotic, retina, rods, cones, optic nerve.

Research the causes and known treatments of any of the following defects in human vision: myopia (nearsightedness), hypermetropia (farsightedness), presbyopia, astigmatism, colour blindness, cataracts.
Describe how the rods and cones on the retina respond to light differently.
Explain why binocular vision is necessary for correct depth perception.
Explain the differences between regular eye glasses, bifocals, and trifocals.
Define the following terms: converging (positive) lens, diverging (negative) lens, optical centre, principal axis, principal focus, focal length, focal plane, achromatic lens, virtual object.
Distinguish between a converging (positive) lens and a diverging (negative) lens.
Draw diagrams of converging and diverging lenses, showing the principal axis and important points on the principal axis for each type of lens.
Draw neat, properly labelled, accurate, scaled ray diagrams for single thin lenses.

Apply the rules for drawing ray diagrams for converging and diverging lenses (parallel-ray method) to draw an object on the principal axis and locate the position and other characteristics of its image.
Use a ray diagram to interpret the characteristics of an image formed by a lens.
Demonstrate an understanding of the importance and use of a procedure of verification.

Recognize that, even though light rays are refracted at both surfaces by a lens, for thin lenses the incident rays can be shown refracting at the construction line passing through the optical centre of the lens.
Explain why light rays travelling over a long distance are effectively parallel when they reach a lens (or other type of optical system).
Apply lens equations, in conjunction with ray diagrams and other methods, to solve problems in optics dealing with lenses.
Explain one method that can be used to correct for spherical aberration in lenses.
Distinguish between a real object and a virtual object.
Identify various useful applications of lenses, and show their importance to society.

Describe a mechanical model which helps to conceptualize the polarization of light.
Give examples of reflecting surfaces which are capable of polarizing light.
Explain that scattering in the atmosphere produces polarization.
Describe the diffraction pattern produced by a single slit.
Explain why the diffraction of light is most pronounced when the slit is narrow, within the same order of magnitude of the wavelength(s).
Describe the interference pattern produced by Young's double slit experiment.
Suggest why Young's double slit experiment gave support to the wave theory of light.

Explain how Michelson's interferometer produced an interference pattern.
Define the following terms: electromagnetic spectrum, electromagnetic radiation, monochromatic light, continuous spectrum, line spectrum, visible light, infrared light, ultraviolet light.
State what predictions Maxwell made about the nature of electromagnetic waves.
State the range of wavelengths for visible light.
Describe the infrared and ultraviolet regions of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Investigate several practical applications of infrared and ultraviolet light.
Describe regions of the electromagnetic spectrum on both sides of the visible spectrum and state several applications that arise from them.
Explain that different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum vary in their frequency, wavelength, and the amount of energy possessed.
Define the following terms: additive primary colours, secondary colours, filter, complementary colours, colour filter.
State the three additive primary colours.
Explain that "white light" contains at least the three additive primary colours.
Explain that usually nonluminous objects appear to be a certain colour because they reflect light at those wavelengths that combine to produce the resulting colour observed.
Suggest what causes some nonluminous surfaces to appear to be black or white.
Explain that by combining red, green, and blue light at varying intensities, a wide range of other colours can be produced.
Suggest some applications of the additive theory of light.
State the three secondary colours of light.
Give examples to illustrate what is absorbed and what is transmitted by various different types of filters.
Suggest some important applications of colour theory.

Conduct risk analysis to explore the impact of technology on society and on the environment.

Recognize that periodic motion can be used to measure time.
Compare uniform and non-uniform motion.

Make reasonable numerical estimates when solving problems.

Calculate speed, average speed, velocity and average velocity.
Recognize the situations in which it is essential to differentiate between speed and velocity.

Determine the average velocity of an object graphically and algebraically.

The 30-level parts of this guide are superseded on the site by the renewed Biology 30 / Chemistry 30 / Physics 30 (ids 68, 69, 72), which have outcomes in sk.json.
Physics 20 Optional Unit VI: no unit opening page; first seen as running header on PDF page 151.

outcomes.statement: Create and carry out a plan to explore one or more topics of personal interest relevant to Physics 30 in depth.
outcomes.printedWith: DM, SI TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Design a scientific investigation related to a topic of study in Physics 30 that includes a testable question, a hypothesis, an experimental design that will test the hypothesis and detailed procedures for collecting and analyzing data. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Carry out an experiment following established scientific protocols to investigate a question of interest related to one or more of the topics of Physics 30. (S, A, K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assemble and reflect on a portfolio that demonstrates an understanding of a topic of interest related to physics. (S, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate the effectiveness of a device, model or technique that demonstrates the scientific principles underlying concept related to a Physics 30 topic. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Debate an issue related to physics, including developing materials to support the arguments for and arguments against a position. (A, K, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Share the results of student-directed research through a display, presentation, performance, demonstration, song, game, commercial, fine art representation, video or research paper. (S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form or peer-evaluation form) to assess the process and products involved in a student-directed study. (S, A)

outcomes.statement: Analyze the importance of relativistic principles and quantum mechanics in our world.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the development of quantum mechanics and relativity, including perspectives of key scientists such as Albert Einstein, Maxwell Planck, Erwin Schrödinger, Werner Heisenberg, Thomas Young and Stephen Hawking. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate how Newtonian mechanics, quantum mechanics, relativity and emerging theories describe the universe on different scales. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Distinguish between the theories of general and special relativity with respect to space and time (e.g., curvature of space-time, time dilation, length contraction and relativistic mass). (K, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Consider the implications of inconsistent time with respect to a frame of reference (e.g., time travel and the twin paradox). (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the impact of scientific understanding of relativity on the development of technologies such as the Global Positioning System, atomic clocks and communication systems. (K, S, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the importance of phenomena such as the photoelectric effect, Young's double slit experiment, black body radiation and Compton scattering to understanding the quantum nature of light. (S, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the implications of conducting observations while investigating wave-particle phenomena and objects at a quantum-scale. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Determine Planck's constant experimentally or using simulations and discuss its implications for quantum mechanics. (S, K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the photoelectric effect including the influence of various frequencies and energies of electromagnetic radiation. (S, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the ongoing debates within physics regarding contradictory and differentiated interpretations (e.g., Collapse, Pilot Wave, Many Worlds and Copenhagen) of quantum mechanics. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Assess the effects of radioactivity and applications of nuclear technology on society and the environment.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the contributions of women (e.g., Harriet Brooks, Marie Curie, Lise Meitner, Chien-Shiung Wu, Mileva Maric and Ida Noddack) from various cultures to the development of scientific understanding of radioactivity. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify natural and artificial sources of radiation on Earth and throughout the universe. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the characteristics (e.g., composition, penetrating power, speed and potential danger) of alpha, beta and gamma radiation. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Represent nuclear reactions involving alpha, beta and gamma decay using words, diagrams and equations. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain that some isotopes undergo natural radioactive decay, and that half-life is a measure of the rate of radioactive decay. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the short- and long-term implications of radiation on living things, including the effects on different types of tissues and cells. (A, K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss how the difficulties in detecting effects of radiation on living things lead to lack of agreement among scientists and others about those effects. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the characteristics of the weak nuclear force and its role in beta decay. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Model the process of nuclear fission, including conditions necessary for a chain reaction. (K, S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Compare the amount and rate of energy released in various man-made fission reactions (e.g., nuclear energy production, nuclear weapons, nuclear propulsion and satellites). (K)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine the process of nuclear fusion and the difficulties in harnessing nuclear fusion as an energy source. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain the characteristics of the strong nuclear force and its role in maintaining atomic stability. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of mass defect and $e=mc^2$ and why this particular equation has gained such prominence in society. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Analyze societal and environmental impacts of applications of nuclear technologies such as medical isotopes, food irradiation, smoke detectors, industrial radiography, pesticide tracers, nuclear weapons, nuclear reactors and nuclear waste disposal. (A, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Analyze motion in one- and two-dimensions, including uniform motion, uniformly accelerated motion, circular motion and projectile motion.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide examples of situations in which everyday objects undergo uniform motion, uniformly accelerated motion, circular motion and projectile motion. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Critique examples of realistic and non-realistic motion in popular culture such as movies, TV shows and comics. (STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Solve problems involving different types of motion in one- and two-dimensions, including relative motion, using graphical methods, vector analysis and kinematics equations. E.g. $v ↖ {→} = {\Δd}/t$, $v ↖ {→}_f = v ↖ {→}_i+a ↖ {→}\Δt$, $v ↖ {→2}_f = v ↖ {→2}_i+2a ↖ {→}\Δd ↖ {→}$, $\Δd ↖ {→} = v ↖ {→}_i \Δt + 1/2a ↖ {→} \Δt^2$, and $\Δd ↖ {→} = 1/2(v ↖ {→}_i+v ↖ {→}_f)\Δt$. (S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Experimentally determine the value of the acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface. (K, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the horizontal and vertical components of a projectile's motion using tools such as video analysis and/or online simulations. (K, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Solve problems involving projectile motion and objects in free fall using graphical (e.g., scale diagrams) and/or mathematical (e.g., vector components, sine law and cosine law) methods. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Design and perform an experiment that includes collecting, analyzing and interpreting data from objects that undergo projectile motion or uniform circular motion. (STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Determine the characteristics (e.g., speed, velocity, period, distance travelled and acceleration) of uniform circular motion. (K, S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the orbits (e.g., geosynchronous, elliptical and/or circular) of satellites and celestial bodies using uniform circular motion concepts. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Predict the path an object (e.g., shot put, discus, hammer throw, bolo, particles in a synchrotron and rocket undergoing gravity assisted space travel) will follow once released from uniform circular motion. (K, S, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the challenges in representing real world motion using models of ideal motion, which normally treat objects as a single center of mass and which disregard frictional forces. (STSE)

notes: Indicator labels (b), (c) printed more than once on the official page.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the effects of forces on objects undergoing uniform motion, uniformly accelerated motion and circular motion.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions related to practical examples of the effects of forces on objects. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Provide examples of how Newton's three laws of motion can describe the movement of objects in the real world. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of the concepts of inertia and inertial mass with respect to the development of Newton's laws of motion. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the effect of changing the mass of an object and/or force applied to an object on the acceleration of that object. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Solve problems involving force, mass and acceleration, using free-body diagrams and Newton's second law of motion $F = ma ↖ {→}$. (K, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe the effect of friction and air resistance, including terminal velocity, on objects in motion (e.g., rollercoasters, skydiving, snowboards, meteors entering Earth's atmosphere, inclined plane situations, rolling balls, spacecraft and satellite re-entry, aircraft, race cars and artillery). (K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Predict and investigate the effect of balanced or unbalanced forces, including the effect of friction, on an object that is at rest, undergoing uniform motion or undergoing uniformly accelerated motion. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Solve problems involving forces acting in one- and two-dimensions using graphical (e.g., scale diagrams) and mathematical (e.g., vector components, sine law and cosine law) methods. (K, S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the limitations of Newton's laws of motion in relativistic and quantum situations (e.g., objects moving at or near the speed of light and subatomic particles). (K, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the vertical and horizontal forces involved in various types of circular motion (e.g., roller coaster, Ferris wheel, merry-go-round and figure skater) with reference to the concepts of centripetal and centrifugal. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine the horizontal and vertical forces that act on a projectile throughout its trajectory. (K)

outcomes.statement: Investigate the nature of mechanical energy and efficiency in mechanical systems in relation to the law of conservation of energy.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize work as the transfer of energy that takes place when a force acts over a displacement. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the conditions required for positive, negative and zero mechanical work and their relation to the angle between the applied force and displacement. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how common usage of the terms work, energy and power differ from their operational definitions in physics. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the properties (e.g., boundaries, inputs and outputs) of a system with respect to total mechanical energy. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the law of conservation of energy in terms of isolated and non-isolated systems and conservation of mechanical energy. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Solve problems related to kinetic, potential and total mechanical energy using relevant equations. E.g. $W=Fd \cosθ$,$W=\ΔE$,$E_k={mv ↖ {→2}}/2$,$E_p=mg ↖ {→}h$, and $TME=E_k+E_p$. (K, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Design and perform experiments and/or simulations, including collecting, analyzing and interpreting data, to determine the kinetic energy involved in elastic and inelastic interactions (e.g., curling stones, billiard balls, bouncing ball, seatbelts and automobile collisions). (STSE, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the challenges in modeling conservation of energy in real-life situations. (STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the efficiency of energy transformations in various technologies with reference to useful work, friction and the production heat, sound and light. (K, STSE)

notes: Indicator labels (b), (c), (d) printed more than once on the official page.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the motion of objects and interactions between objects using momentum concepts, including the law of conservation of momentum.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore how impulse and momentum concepts apply to motion-related technologies in fields such as sports science, transportation and space science. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Derive the formula for impulse from Newton's second law of motion. (S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how changing the net force applied to an object or the amount of time the force is applied affect the momentum of an object, with reference to the formula $F\Δt=m\Δv ↖ {→}$. (S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Provide examples that show how momentum is or is not conserved in everyday situations. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Conduct an experiment or simulation, including collecting, analyzing and interpreting data, to determine the extent to which momentum is conserved in elastic and inelastic collisions. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Solve problems using the law of conservation of momentum in one- and two-dimensional interactions (e.g., head-on collisions, glancing collisions, rocket launches and explosions). (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze applications (e.g., neutrino detection, Large Hadron Collider, crash test dummies and personal safety devices) of the law of conservation of momentum. (STSE)

notes: Indicator labels (b), (c) printed more than once on the official page.

outcomes.statement: Investigate gravitational fields and their interactions with matter.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the value of the concept of fields and field theory and the meaning of field strength in understanding the effects of non-contact forces (i.e., action at a distance). (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the characteristics of the gravitational force and its effect on large-scale phenomena throughout the universe. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore phenomena such as gravitational lensing, dark matter, universal expansion and contraction and time dilation as they relate to gravitational fields within the universe. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Relate gravitational field strength near Earth's surface, and variations in that field strength, to the accepted value of acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface. (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Distinguish, qualitatively and quantitatively, between weight and mass. (K, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain variations in gravitational field strength as a function of inverse-square dependence. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the relation between common misconceptions about perceptions of weightlessness in microgravity environments and people's understanding of gravitational field strength. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research how scientists use an understanding of microgravity environments to further scientific understanding in fields such as biotechnology, fluid physics, materials science, combustion science and fundamental physics. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Solve problems involving gravitational field strength using $g={Gm}/r^2$ and Newton's law of universal gravitation $F=G{m_1m_2}/r_^2$. (K, S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explore the nature of scientific collaboration and contribution in researching questions related to emerging topics such as gravitational waves and the graviton. (STSE, S)

outcomes.statement: Investigate electric and magnetic fields and their interactions with matter.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize that electric fields act on point charges, including action at a distance and following the inverse-square law to determine strength of field. (S, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Draw and describe electric field lines for like and unlike point charges and plates separated by a distance. (K, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how the electric field strength at a point varies according to the inverse square of the distance between two charges, with reference to the equation $E={kQ}/d^2$. (K, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Solve problems related to Coulomb's law $F = k{q_1q_2}/d^2$, including electrostatic equilibrium in one- and two-dimensions. (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe current scientific thinking regarding the electromagnetic force, one of the four fundamental interactions. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize how our understanding of the interrelationships between magnetic and electric fields has led to the development of technologies such as generators and electromagnets (e.g., moving charged particles create a magnetic field, interaction of electric and magnetic fields). (K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Represent magnetic fields using magnetic field lines. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Represent the direction of the magnetic field around current-induced conductors, including linear wires and wire coils, using the right hand and/or left-hand rules. (K, S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research the characteristics of Earth's magnetic field, including the effects of short- and long-term changes to the field. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze the direction of positive, negative and neutral charges moving in natural (e.g., solar flares and aurorae) and man-made (e.g., particle accelerators and MRI's) magnetic fields. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate a prototype of a technology (e.g., electric motor, generator or electromagnet) to demonstrate principles of electromagnetism. (K, S)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze ways in which natural and technological sources of electric and magnetic fields can influence society and the environment (e.g., changes in animal migration, health concerns and increased communication). (K, STSE, A)

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of the absolute value of real numbers and equations and functions involving the absolute value of linear and quadratic functions.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide examples relevant to one’s life, family, or community that illustrate different situations in which quantities referenced are positive, negative, or an absolute value and justify.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Determine the distance of two real numbers of the form $±a,a∈R,$ from 0 on a number line, and relate this to the absolute value of a $(|a|)$.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine the absolute value of a real number.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Order, with justification, a set of real numbers that includes the absolute value of one or more of the quantities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain, with the use of examples, how absolute value fits into the order of operations used on expressions involving real numbers.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Determine the value of numerical expressions involving absolute value(s).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Simplify expressions involving absolute value(s).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze, describe, and explain the relationship between the graph of $y = f(x)$ and $y = |f(x)|$.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Create a table of values for $y = |f(x)|$ given $y = f(x)$.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Sketch the graph of $y = |f(x)|$ given $y = f(x)$ and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Develop and apply strategies for determining the intercepts, domain, and range of $y = |f(x)|$ given the equation of the function or its graph.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain what the range of the function $y = |f(x)|$ reveals about the graph of the function.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for graphically determining (with and without the use of technology) the solution set of an equation involving absolute values of algebraic expressions.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for algebraically determining the solution set of an equation involving absolute values of algebraic expressions.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Analyze and generalize conclusions about absolute value inequalities of the form $ |f(x)| < 0 $.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Identify and correct errors in a solution to an absolute value equation.

indicators.label: q
indicators.text: Solve situational questions involving absolute value functions or equations.

indicators.label: r
indicators.text: Analyze and generalize the relationship between $| x |$ and $√x^2$ and between $| f(x) |$ and $√(f(x))^2$.

outcomes.statement:
Expand and demonstrate understanding of radicals with numerical and variable radicands including:
- computations
- solving equations (limited to square roots and one or two radicals).
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, PS, R, T]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for expressing an entire radical (with numerical or variable radicand) as a mixed radical.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for expressing a mixed radical (with numerical or variable radicand) as an entire radical.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Order a set of real numbers which includes radical expressions with numerical radicands.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for simplifying radical expressions (with numerical and/or variable radicands).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for rationalizing the denominator of rational expressions with monomial or binomial denominators.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe the relationship between rationalizing a binomial denominator of a rational expression and the product of the factors of a difference of squares expression.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Verify and explain, using examples, that $(-x)^2=x^2$, $√x^2=|x|$, and $√x^2≠ ∓ x$

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Solve situational questions that involve radical expressions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining the values of a variable for which a given radical expression is defined.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining non-permissible values (restrictions on values) for the variable in a radical equation.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply algebraic strategies for determining and verifying the roots of a radical equation.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain why some roots determined in solving a radical equation are extraneous.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Model and solve situational questions that involve radical equations.

outcomes.statement:
Expand and demonstrate understanding of rational expressions and equations (up to and including degree 2 numerators and denominators) including:
- equivalent forms of expressions
- operations on expressions
- solving equations that can be simplified to linear or quadratic equations.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, R]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop, verify, explain, and apply strategies for determining equivalent rational expressions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare the determining of equivalent rational expressions to determining equivalent rational numbers.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Verify, with explanation, whether or not a given value is permissible for a given rational expression.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining the non-permissible values of a rational expression.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for simplifying rational expressions.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain why the non-permissible values of a simplified rational expression must be stated as those of the original rational expression.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Apply understanding of rational expressions to locate and correct errors in the simplification of a rational expression.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop, verify, explain, and apply strategies for adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing rational expressions, including the determination of non-permissible values.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Compare the performing of operations on rational expressions to performing the same operations on rational numbers.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for simplifying rational expressions that involve two or more operations on the rational expressions.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply algebraic strategies for determining the solution, including non-permissible values, of equations involving rational expressions.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain why a value obtained in solving a rational equation may not be a solution of the equation.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Model and solve situational questions involving rational expressions.

outcomes.statement: Expand and demonstrate understanding of the primary trigonometric ratios including the use of reference angles (0° ≤ θ ≤ 360°) and the determination of exact values for trigonometric ratios.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, ME, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide examples relevant to one’s self, family, or community that illustrate the need to define a standard position for angles.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Sketch an angle in standard position given the measure of the angle.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine and justify, with or without sketching, the quadrant in which an angle in standard position terminates.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine the reference angle for an angle in standard position.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze, describe, and generalize the relationship between the reference angles for angles (in standard positions) that are reflections of each other across both the $x-$ and $y-$ axes (e.g., $30°$ and $150°$, or $-60°$ and $60°$).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Sketch an angle in standard position given a point $P(x,y)$ on the terminal arm of the angle.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining a point on the terminal arm of the angle in each quadrant that has the same reference angle as the angle with $P(x,y)$ on its terminal arm.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining the distance between the origin and a point $P(x,y)$ on the terminal arm of an angle.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the value of $sinθ$, $cosθ$, and $tanθ$ when given a point $P(x,y)$ on the terminal arm of $θ$.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining $sinθ$, $cosθ$, and $tanθ$ for quadrantal angles.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the sign (without calculation or the use of technology) of $sinθ$, $cosθ$, or $tanθ$ for a given value of $θ$.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for solving, for all values of $θ$, equations of the form $sinθ = a$ or $cosθ =a$, where $-1 ≤ a ≤ 1$, and equations of the form $tanθ = a$, where $a$ is a real number.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Analyze $30°- 60°- 90° \and 45°- 45°- 90°$ triangles to generalize about the relationship between pairs of sides in such triangles in relation to the angles.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the exact value of the sine, cosine, or tangent (without the use of technology) of an angle with a reference angle of $30°, 45°, \or 60°$.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe and generalize the relationships and patterns in and among the values of the sine, cosine, and tangent ratios for angles from $0° \to 360°$.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create and solve a situational question relevant to one’s self, family, or community which involves a trigonometric ratio.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify angles for which the tangent ratio does not exist and explain why.
