outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of the cosine law and sine law, including the ambiguous case.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, PS, R, T]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide a diagram or picture to illustrate a situation relevant to one’s self, family, or community that involves a triangle without a right angle.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for solving a non-right angle triangle using the primary trigonometric ratios.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Derive and explain a proof of the sine law or cosine law.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Provide an example of a situation relevant to one’s self, family, or community that involves the need to consider the ambiguous case and provide a diagram or picture to illustrate the situation and explain why the ambiguous case needs to be considered.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply the sine law and/or cosine law to solve situational questions.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Critique the statement “For every possible pair of angles (whose sum is less than $180°$) and line segment, a triangle can be constructed”.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Critique the statement “The sine law and the cosine law only apply to non-right triangles”.

outcomes.statement:
Expand and demonstrate understanding of factoring polynomial expressions including those of the form:
- $a^2x^2-b^2y^2, a ≠ 0, b ≠ 0$
- $a(f(x))^2-b(f(x))+c,a ≠ 0$
- $a^2(f(x))^2-b^2(g(y))^2, a ≠ 0, b ≠ 0$
where a, b, and c are rational numbers.
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, ME, R]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for factoring polynomial expressions of the form:
- $a^2x^2-b^2y^2,a ≠ 0, b ≠ 0, \text "a and b are real numbers"$
- $ca^2x^2-cb^2y^2,a ≠ 0, b ≠ 0, \text "a, b, and c are real numbers"$
- $a(f(x))^2-b(f(x))+c, a ≠ 0, \text "a, b, and c are real numbers"$
- $da(f(x))^2-db(f(x))+dc, a ≠ 0, \text "a, b, c, and d are real numbers"$
- $a^2(f(x))^2-b^2(g(y))^2, a ≠ 0, b ≠ 0, \text "a and b are real numbers"$
- $da^2(f(x))^2 - db^2(g(y))^2, a ≠ 0, b ≠ 0, \text "a, b, and d are real numbers"$

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Verify, with explanation, whether or not a given binomial is a factor for a given polynomial.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of quadratic functions of the form $y=ax^2+bx+c$ and of their graphs, including:
- vertex
- domain and range
- direction of opening
- axis of symmetry
- x- and y-intercepts.
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, ME, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Generalize a rule from sets of graphs, using inductive reasoning, and explain about how different values of a (including 1, 0, and -1) transform the graph of $y = ax^2.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generalize a rule from sets of graphs, using inductive reasoning, and explain about how different values of q (including 0) transform the graph of $y = x^2 + q$.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Generalize a rule from sets of graphs, using inductive reasoning, and explain how different values of p (including 0) transform the graph of $y = (x - p)^2$.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the coordinates of the vertex, the domain and range, the axis of symmetry, x- and y- intercepts, and direction of opening of the graph of the function $f(x) = a(x-p)^2 + q$ without the use of technology.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for graphing functions of the form $f(x) = a(x - p)^2 + q$ by applying transformations related to the values of a, p, and q.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies (that do not require graphing or the use of technology) for determining whether a quadratic function will have zero, one, or two x-intercepts.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for writing a quadratic function in the form of $y = a(x - p)^2 + q$ that represents a given graph or set of characteristics of a graph.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, verify, and apply a strategy (including completing the square) for writing a quadratic function in the form $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ in the form $y = a(x - p)^2 + q$.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Using knowledge about completing the square, identify and correct errors in a given example of completing the square.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the coordinates of the vertex, the domain and range, the axis of symmetry, x- and y- intercepts, and direction of opening of the graph of a function in the form $y = ax^2 + bx + c$.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Sketch the graph of a quadratic function given in the form $y = ax² + bx + c$.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Write a quadratic function that models a given situation and explain any assumptions made.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Analyze quadratic functions (with or without the use of technology) to answer situational questions.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of quadratic equations including the solution of:
- single variable equations
- systems of linear-quadratic and quadratic-quadratic equations in two variables.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: $ \text "Note: It is intended that the quadratic equations be limited to those that correspond to quadratic functions."$

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, the relationship among the roots of a quadratic equation, the zeros of the corresponding quadratic function and the x-intercepts of the graph of the quadratic function.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Derive the quadratic formula, using deductive reasoning.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Apply strategies for solving quadratic equations of the form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ including:
- determining square roots"
- factoring"
- completing the square"
- applying the quadratic formula"
- graphing its corresponding function, with and without the use of technology"

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain different strategies for verifying the solution to a quadratic equation.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, how the discriminant may be used to determine whether a quadratic equation has two, one, or no real roots; and relate this knowledge to the number of zeros that the corresponding quadratic function will have.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Apply knowledge of quadratic equations and functions to identify and correct any errors within a solution to a quadratic equation.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Solve situational questions involving the writing and solving of quadratic equations.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Match systems of linear-quadratic and quadratic-quadratic functions to situations.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text:
Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for solving systems of linear-quadratic and quadratic-quadratic functions, including:
- graphically
- algebraically
- with the use of technology.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explain the meaning of the intersection point of a system of linear-quadratic or quadratic-quadratic equations in terms of the situation being modeled.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Illustrate and explain how a system of linear-quadratic or quadratic-quadratic equations may have zero, one, two, or an infinite number of solutions.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Solve situational questions by using systems of linear-quadratic or quadratic-quadratic equations.

outcomes.statement:
Expand and demonstrate understanding of inequalities including:
- one-variable quadratic inequalities
- two-variable linear and quadratic inequalities.

indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the solution region for two-variable linear or two-variable quadratic inequalities.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, how test points can be used to determine the solution region that satisfies a two-variable inequality.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Solve a situational question that involves a two-variable inequality.

indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies, such as case analysis, graphing, roots and test points, or sign analysis, to solve one-variable quadratic inequalities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Interpret the solution to a situational question that involves a one-variable quadratic inequality.

Demonstrate understanding of reciprocal functions of:

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop and apply strategies for sketching the inverse of a relation, including reflection across the line $y=x$ and the transformation $(x,y)⇒(y,x)$.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Sketch the graph of the inverse relation, given the graph of the relation.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining if one or both of a relation and its inverse are functions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Determine what restrictions must be placed on the domain of a function for its inverse to be a function.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critique statements such as "If a relation is not a function, then its inverse also will not be a function".

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Determine the equation and sketch the graph of the inverse relation, given the equation of a linear or quadratic relation.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explain the relationship between the domains and ranges of a relation and its inverse.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Develop and apply numeric, algebraic, and graphic strategies to determine if two relations are inverses of each other.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate an understanding of logarithms including:
- evaluating logarithms
- relating logarithms to exponents
- deriving laws of logarithms
- solving equations
- graphing.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the relationship between powers, exponentials, logarithms, and radicals.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Express a logarithmic expression as an exponential expression and vice versa.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine, without technology, the exact value of a logarithm such as $log_2 8$.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how to estimate the value of a logarithm using benchmarks (e.g., since $log_2 8 = 3$ and $log_2 16 = 4$, $log_2 9$ is approximately equal to $3.1$ ).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Derive and explain the laws of logarithms.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply the laws of logarithms to determine equivalent expressions for given logarithmic statements.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine, using technology, the approximate value of a logarithmic expression (e.g. $log_2 9$).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Solve exponential equations in which the bases are powers of one another.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Solve exponential equations in which the bases are not powers of one another.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for solving logarithmic equations and verify the solutions.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explain why a value obtained in solving a logarithmic equation may be extraneous.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Solve situational questions that involve exponential growth or decay, such as loans, mortgages, and investments.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Solve situational questions involving logarithmic scales, such as the Richter scale and pH scale.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Analyze graphs of exponential functions of the form $y=a^x,x>0$ and report about the relationships between the value of a and the domain, range, horizontal asymptote, and intercepts.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Sketch, with or without the use of technology, the graphs of exponential functions of the form $y=a^x,x>0$.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Explain the role of the horizontal asymptote for exponential functions.

indicators.label: q
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for sketching transformations of the graph of $y=a^x,x>0$.

indicators.label: r
indicators.text: Analyze graphs of logarithmic functions of the form $y=log_b x,b>1$ and report about the relationships between the value of b and the domain, range, vertical asymptote, and intercepts.

indicators.label: s
indicators.text: Sketch, with or without technology, the graphs of logarithmic functions of the form $y=log_b x,b>1$.

indicators.label: t
indicators.text: Explain the role of the vertical asymptote for logarithm functions.

indicators.label: u
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for sketching transformations of the graph of $y=log_b x,b>1$.

indicators.label: v
indicators.text: Demonstrate graphically that $y=log_b x,b>1$ and $y=b^x,b>0$ are inverses of each other.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of polynomials and polynomial functions of degree greater than 2 (limited to polynomials of degree $≤ 5$ with integral coefficients).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply long division for dividing polynomials by binomials of the form $x-a,a∈I$.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare long division of polynomial expressions by binomial expressions to synthetic division, and explain why synthetic division works.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Divide a polynomial expression by a binomial expression of the form $x-a,a∈I$ using synthetic division.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the relationship between the linear factors of a polynomial expression and the zeros of the corresponding polynomial function.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Generalize, through inductive reasoning, the relationship between the remainder when a polynomial expression is divided by $x-a,a∈I$ and the value of the polynomial expression at $x=a$ (The Remainder Theorem).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain and apply the factor theorem to express a polynomial expression as a product of factors.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Categorize, with justification, a set of functions into polynomial functions and non-polynomial functions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze graphs of polynomial functions to determine the impact of changing the values of the constant term and leading coefficient in the equation of a polynomial function with respect to the graph of the function.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Generalize and apply strategies for graphing polynomial functions of an odd or even degree.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text:
Explain the relationship between:
- the zeros of a polynomial function,
- the roots of the corresponding polynomial equation,
- the x-intercepts of the graph of the polynomial function.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explain and apply strategies for determining the behaviour of the graph of a polynomial function at zeros with different multiplicities.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Sketch, with or without the use of technology, the graph of a polynomial function.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Solve situational questions by modelling the situations with polynomial functions and analyzing the graphs of the functions.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of radical and rational functions with restrictions on the domain.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Sketch the graph of the function $y=√x$ using a table of values, and state the domain and range of the function.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply transformations to the function $y=√x$ to sketch the graph of $y-k=a√{b(x-h)}$.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Sketch the graph of the function $y=√{f(x)}$ given the graph of the function $y=f(x)$, and compare the domains and ranges of the two functions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the relationship between the roots of a radical equation and the x-intercepts of the graph of the corresponding radical function.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine, graphically, the approximate solutions to radical equations.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Sketch rational functions, with and without the use of technology.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the behaviour (shape and location) of the graphs of rational functions for values of the dependent variable close to the location of a vertical asymptote.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze the equation of a rational function to determine where the graph of the rational function has an asymptote or a hole, and explain why.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Match a set of equations for rational and radical functions to their corresponding graphs.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Describe the relationship between the roots of a rational equation and the x-intercepts of the graph of the corresponding rational function.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Determine graphically an approximate solution to a rational equation.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Critique statements such as "Any value that makes the denominator of a rational function equal to zero will result in a vertical asymptote on the graph of the rational function".

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of permutations, including the fundamental counting principle.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop and apply strategies, such as lists or tree diagrams, to determine the total number of choices or arrangements possible in a situation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain why the total number of possible choices is found by multiplying rather than adding the number of ways that individual choices can be made.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide examples of situations relevant to self, family, and community where the fundamental counting principle can be applied to determine the number of possible choices or arrangements.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create and solve situational questions that involve the application of the fundamental counting principle.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Count, using graphic organizers, the number of ways to arrange the elements of a set in a row.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies, including the use of factorial notation, to determine the number of permutations possible if n different elements are taken n or r at a time.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain why $n$ must be greater than or equal to $r$ in the notation $_nP_r$.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Solve equations that involve $_nP_r$ notation such as $_nP_2=30$.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the number of permutations possible when two or more elements in the set are identical (non-distinguishable).

outcomes.statement: PC30.13 Demonstrate understanding of combinations of elements, including the application to the binomial theorem.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain, with examples, how to distinguish between situations that involve permutations and those that involve combinations.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the number of ways that a subset of $k$ can be selected from a set of $n$ different elements.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies to determine combinations of $n$ different elements taken $r$ at a time in situational questions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain why $n$ must be greater than or equal to $r$ in the notation $ _nC_r $ or $ (\table n; r) $.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Prove or explain using examples $_nC_r = _n C _(n-r)$ or $(\table n; r) = (\table n; n-r)$.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Solve equations involving combinations e.g. $_nC_2=15$ or $(\table n; 2)=15$.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore and describe patterns found within Pascal's triangle, including the relationship between consecutive rows.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore and describe the relationship between the coefficients of the terms in $(x+y)^n$, and the combinations.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for expanding $(x+y)^n,n≤4$.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining specific terms within a particular expansion of $(x+y)^n$ given $n∈\ℕ$.

indicators.label: c

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research and compare validity, reliability and ethical issues in various research methods (e.g., interview, observation, case study) used in psychology.

outcomes.statement: Explore how biological, cognitive, emotional and spiritual dimensions and social factors influence the way we think and feel about the world.

indicators.text: Examine the influences of the four dimensions of being (biological, cognitive, emotional and spiritual), as they are presented in Indigenous Ways of Knowing as well as their link to behaviors and interpersonal relationships.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze the role of socio-cultural influences such as customs, lifestyles and values, on physical and social development.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine how the brain processes sensory information and distinguish the differences among sensation, perception and subliminal perception.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the role and function of the endocrine system and the effects stimulants, depressants and hallucinogens have on the body’s ability to process information.

indicators.text: Investigate and evaluate ethical and moral issues (e.g., genetic engineering, organ donation, organ transplants).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore the challenges (e.g., language, lifestyle, customs, laws) a newcomer might face when integrating into a new culture.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine how the perception of one’s physical and cultural environment can influence the behaviours, relationships and life goals of a person.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze differences among motivation, attitude and emotions and determine the roles each plays in performance (e.g., sports, academics, arts).

indicators.label: l

outcomes.statement: Investigate socioemotional development from early childhood through adolescence.

indicators.text: Analyze differences between emotions and feelings regarding social and cultural influences on emotional expression.

indicators.text: Discuss socioemotional development that takes place during mid-childhood throughadolescence.

indicators.text: Examine the role that birth order may play in the socioemotional development of a child.

indicators.text: Differentiate among parenting styles and their possible influences on youth.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Creatively represent different parenting styles (e.g., role play scenario, cartoon or comic strip, mock interview).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate attachment development in children, types of attachments and short and long-term effects of social deprivation (e.g., neglect, abuse, removal from home).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze how children learn values, develop moral and ethical behaviour and potentialimpact on decision making in adolescence.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine sociocultural influences of economic and social status on childhood and adolescent development.

indicators.text: Analyze influences of friendships, peer pressure and bullying on socioemotional development and own lives.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate the theory of emotional intelligence and its role in socioemotional development of youth.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine one’s ability to interpret the perception of others' emotions in order to understand and adjust one's behaviour accordingly.

indicators.label: l

indicators.text: Analyze contributions of social-cognitive theories to understanding of personality.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess strengths and limitations of dispositional approaches to personality.

indicators.text: Investigate the development of various temperaments (e.g., thoughts, feelings) as they apply to own life.

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: h

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate ways individuals’ support systems (e.g., parents, foster parents, extended family caregivers, social, religious and cultural organizations, worldviews) influence thoughts, feelings and behaviour.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how different cultures and perspectives view lifespan development (e.g., First Nations, Métis and Inuit, Black, Asian).

outcomes.statement: Investigate factors that influence development of the four dimensions (i.e., biological, cognitive, emotional, spiritual) from conception to five years.

indicators.label: g

indicators.label: h

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the influence of biological, cognitive, emotional and spiritual dimensions on the development of identity in childhood.

outcomes.statement: Investigate factors that influence development of the four dimensions (i.e., biological, cognitive, emotional, spiritual) from adolescence to early adulthood.

indicators.text: Summarize and discuss key changes (e.g., biological, cognitive, emotional and spiritual) in development from adolescence to early adulthood.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine issues and challenges in adolescence (e.g., substance misuse, eating disorders, teen parenting, gender identity, teen violence, crime, bullying, self-harm, suicide).

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: e

indicators.label: f

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine development of agency (i.e., acting independently and making own choices) and co-agency (i.e., interactive, mutually supportive relationships) in adolescence.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze how an individual or groups may encounter obstacles (e.g., racial or gender privilege, ideals of beauty) within mainstream society that can impact their sense of agency and ability to achieve personal goals.

indicators.text: Examine emotional and social issues and challenges involved in becoming a parent (e.g., values, family genetic history, parenting styles, relationship stability, spiritual beliefs, parent age, finances).

indicators.label: k

outcomes.statement: Investigate ways in which biological influences affect thoughts, feelings and emotions in relation to development.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify parts and functions of the central nervous system (e.g., brain, spinal cord, neurons) and the endocrine system (e.g., thyroid, pituitary pancreas).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine ways emotions are connected to biological influences.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the roles of nutrition and physical activity on thoughts, biological and emotional development.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze the effects of traditional food diets (e.g., Western, Indigenous, South Asian, African, Mediterranean) vs. processed food diets and their impact on health and emotional well-being

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how injuries, health conditions affecting the nervous and/or endocrine system and substance misuse can influence thoughts, feelings, perceptions and behaviour.

outcomes.statement: Examine cognition as it applies to lifespan development.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine various historical and current cognitive development theories (e.g., Vygotsky, Piaget) and traditional Indigenous views of cognitive development.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the development of the nervous system and the brain from birth to five years.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine developmental changes in cognition from childhood through adolescence.

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine connections between cognition and memory (e.g., memory tools, dementia, Alzheimer’s, muscle memory).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Distinguish differences among learning styles theories (e.g., visual/spatial, logical/mathematical, kinesthetic) and examine their roles in learning and surrounding controversies.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Create a representation (e.g., mind map, cluster diagram, 3D model, mobile, game, song) depicting one’s learning style strengths.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate explanations for elements of cognition (e.g. learning, memory, imagination, judgement, decision-making) shared through oral storytelling.

outcomes.statement: Examine interconnectedness of the four dimensions (i.e., biological, cognitive, emotional, spiritual) of the whole person through lifespan development.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate historical and contemporary perspectives (e.g., First Nations and Métis traditional worldviews, psychoanalytic, behavioural, sociocultural, psychosocial) on human development.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the benefits of holistic approaches (i.e., interconnected mind, body, spirit, emotion) to lifespan development.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine biological, cognitive, emotional and spiritual changes, challenges and benefits during the aging process.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the impacts of change as one transitions through different experiences (e.g., moving away from home, entering the work force, becoming a parent, retiring) in a lifespan.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Create a written piece (e.g. interview of a senior citizen about their current life, series of personal daily journal entries 50 years in the future, letter to one’s future senior self) that details daily life as a member of the older generation.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create a representation (e.g., essay, letter, comic strip, magazine advertisement) that supports a positive quote about aging (e.g., “Getting old is like climbing a mountain; you get a little out of breath, but the view is much better!”, Ingrid Bergman), based on two dimensions.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess influences of childhood traumas (e.g., war, violence, abuse, neglect, attachment issues, exposure to or witnessing substance misuse, family isolation, poverty) on adult development and lifestyle.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze relationships between personality, lifestyle and health and discuss implications for own life.

outcomes.statement: Investigate various sociocultural factors that influence adulthood.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze the influences of various lifestyle choices (e.g., nutrition, exercise, substance abuse, how one chooses to handle stress, deceitfulness in a relationship) on the four dimensions (i.e., biological, cognitive, emotional, spiritual) during adulthood.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research influence of substance misuse on cognitive, biological, spiritual well-being and identify reasons why some people may be susceptible to addiction.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research various relationship trends, processes and moral and legal commitments.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore how adverse childhood experiences (e.g., abuse, death of caregiver, divorce, caregiver incarceration, abandonment) influence choices and behaviour in adult life.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine causes and affects of divorce on couples and their families.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into various cultural influences on one’s perceptions of death and dying.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore the meaning of the phrase “living beyond one’s means” and the effects this can have on one’s physical and mental well-being.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine some issues and challenges (e.g., financial, mental and physical well-being, cognition, retirement, relationships) seniors face and consider potential solutions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Determine stressors parents face and research resiliency and coping skills they can develop to maintain balanced and healthy lives.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the strengths and challenges of becoming new parents at different stages (e.g., 20s, 40s, 60s) of life.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explore the emotional and physical effects of grandparents becoming primary care givers for their grandchildren and research available community supports

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze the pros and cons (e.g., medical, emotional) of postponing motherhood/pregnancy to establish one’s career.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Debate when old age starts and discuss various cross-cultural attitudes towards aging.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the definition of personality and determine if aspects of one’s personality continue to develop during a lifespan.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Determine the connections between one’s personality, lifestyle, health and relationships.

outcomes.statement: Investigate contemporary developmental psychology issues.

indicators.label: a
b

indicators.text: Explore issues involved in transitioning from dependent child into independent adult (e.g., living on your own, post-secondary schooling and/or work responsibilities, financial stresses, boomerang children, establishing adult relationships, responsibility to parents/caregivers versus self-responsibility).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate and compare current and past studies which reflect various viewpoints and/or theories regarding nature and nurture.

indicators.label: e

outcomes.statement: Apply principles and techniques for injury prevention to ensure safety in the work area.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: General Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify personal protective equipment (PPE) such as eyewear, clothing, footwear and ear wear that may be needed for the work site, school or home.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Apply accident prevention principles and techniques, and discuss appropriate actions in case of an injury or accident, such as whom to contact, fire extinguisher locations, emergency exit routes and first-aid procedures.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of ventilation in a confined environment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Practice good housekeeping and avoid obvious hazards (e.g., touching live wires, extending cords over walking spaces and leaving objects on the floor).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Complete an assessment of all safety and robotics equipment and, in consultation with the instructor, perform maintenance to repair or replace defective or worn parts.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize and apply safe and fair work practices including freedom from violence, harassment and bullying.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the historical development of robotics and autonomous technologies.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: History of Robotics (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the history of robots and robotics.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify characteristics common to all robots and robotic devices.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research and create a representation (e.g., timeline, infographic) of important dates in the history of robotics and autonomous devices.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the criteria generally associated with autonomous devices, including different levels of autonomy.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Provide examples of contemporary applications of robotic and autonomous devices, used in industry, manufacturing, agriculture, mining, healthcare, military and for general purposes.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research a recent development in robotics or autonomous devices.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe tasks that are suitable for robotics and autonomous devices.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Predict future trends in robotics and autonomous devices.

outcomes.statement: Explore ethical, moral and legal issues relevant to robotics and autonomous devices.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Ethics and Laws (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how the ethics of robotic and autonomous devices have been portrayed in the media, particularly in science fiction (e.g., 2001: A Space Odyssey).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss legal and/or ethical perspectives with regards to fault when a robotic or autonomous device causes harm to a person, property or nature.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the theoretical relevance of Asimov’s Laws of Robotics to contemporary applications of robotics and artificial intelligence.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze case studies (e.g., The Case of the Killer Robot by Richard G. Epstein) or news reports of accidents involving death or injury caused by industrial robots and discuss who is considered at fault.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research current and proposed legislation involving the personal and commercial use of drones.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Hypothesize about the possibility that robots or devices with artificial intelligence will be able to make their own decisions and the potential ramifications of this ability.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss moral implications (e.g., racial profiling, choosing who lives or dies, unemployment and robot rights, the Trolley problem and unintended consequences) related to artificially intelligent robotic and autonomous devices.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate historical and contemporary impacts of robotics and autonomous devices on society.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Societal Impact (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the uses of robotics in the field of medicine for applications such as surgery, rehabilitation and remote diagnosis.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze how movies (e.g., “I, Robot” and “ShortCircuit”) about robots portray the effects of robot interaction on humanity and the role of work in the future.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore societal implications of the increasing prevalence of robotic and autonomous devices in our daily lives and routines.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess potential positive and negative impacts of robotics on various industries (e.g., automotive manufacturing, agriculture and mining).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze how artificial intelligence can impact robotics and autonomous devices.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Evaluate the impact of a specific application of artificial intelligence.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Debate an issue related to autonomous devices such as the viability of driverless vehicles of varying levels of autonomy on public highways and private worksites.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the prevalence and societal impacts of automation.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Introduction to Automation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between robotics and automation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the use of automation in a variety of fields, such as retail, healthcare, food services, mining, waste management, industry, manufacturing, logistics, automotive and in the home.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the main advantages of automation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique the use of automation in our society, including current and potential effects of automation on society and the environment.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore issues (e.g., human input, mechanical wear, technical programming) arising with automation.

outcomes.statement: Examine applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in robotics and automation.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Artificial Intelligence (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the evolving understanding of the concept of artificial intelligence.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss how to identify whether a robotic or automated device is considered to have or display artificial intelligence.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze how devices with artificial intelligence work differently than controlled or autonomous devices and robots.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the interrelationships between automation, machine learning and artificial intelligence, within the context of robotics and autonomous devices.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the extent to which artificial intelligence can or cannot exceed or replace human ability in regards to certain tasks (e.g., game-playing computers, self-driving cars and personal assistants).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine current limitations of artificial intelligence (e.g., machine learning is based on human instructions and data sets, data sets can perpetuate bias, learning must be supervised).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the ways in which machine learning applications make use of different types of datasets (e.g., image data and facial recognition, text data and news article searches, physical data and astronomy).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore potential applications for machine learning and artificial intelligence in robotics and automation.

indicators.text: Test one’s prototype against end-user generated success criteria and identify areas for improvement.

outcomes.statement: Incorporate empathy into engineering design processes.

indicators.label: a

outcomes.statement: Incorporate appropriate strategies and conventions for debugging circuits.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Debugging Circuits (Optional) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Follow a standard colour convection (e.g., white is signal, negative is black and red is positive) when assigning wires for different purposes.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Organize electrical and electronic components and make all connections in a neat and tidy manner.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop and follow a test strategy for debugging each sub circuit.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Debug a non-working circuit, following a step-by-step process and considering questions such as:
- Did you build the circuit as described in your circuit diagram or schematic?
- Is there power to your circuit?
- Have you exceeded the limitations of any component?
- Are all terminals receiving the correct voltage and polarity?
- Are there any short circuits?
- Is the logic of the circuit correct?

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of gears, sprockets and chains and pulleys and belts in robotics and automation applications.

indicators.text: Examine how gears can be used to change the direction of rotation of a drive shaft.

indicators.text: Compare the suitability of different types (e.g., flat, round, Vee, and toothed) of belts for various robotics and automation applications.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Calculate gear ratios using the following formulas:
- gear ratio = # of driven gear teeth/# driving gear teeth
- gear ratio = diameter of driven pulley/diameter of the driving pulley

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Calculate torque and speed changes using the following formulas:
- output torque = input torque x gear ratio
- output speed = input speed/gear ratio

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Convert angular speed of a drive shaft (e.g., rpm) to linear speed (e.g., cm/s) using the formulas:
- revolutions per second (rps) = revolutions per minute (rpm) x 60
- Angular speed (radians per second) = 2 x pi x rps
- Linear speed = radius of wheel x angular speed

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe some of the challenges associated with using pulleys and belts, gears, or chains in robotic and automation applications.

indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: g

indicators.label: h

indicators.label: i

units.name: Force and Motion in Our World

outcomes.statement: Investigate career paths related to various branches and sub-branches of science.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a representation that demonstrates interrelationships between various branches and sub-branches of science. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the breadth of science-related work roles and who is engaged in those work roles in the community. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop a profile of a specific individual involved in a science career, addressing factors such as their educational and personal background, what drew them to their career, the focus of their work and their advice for others who wish to pursue a similar career. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research the range of science-related programs offered by post-secondary institutions in Saskatchewan and across the country. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the ways in which professional societies and organizations provide support to those engaged in science-related careers in Saskatchewan. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the educational qualifications of people engaged in science-related careers. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Attend a science-related career fair and analyze career choices based on information gathered. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify how personal activities and interests relate to topics in secondary science curricula. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Represent the range of career options available related to a specific branch or sub-branch of science. (STSE, S, A)

outcomes.statement: Assess the implications of human actions on the local and global climate and the sustainability of ecosystems.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions or problems relating to the effects of human actions on global climate change and the sustainability of ecosystems that arise from personal research. (A, S, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect upon your personal view of humanity's relationship with the environment. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research how people from Aboriginal and other cultures view relationships between living organisms and their ecosystems, and the role of humans in those relationships. (STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the positions of First Nations and government agencies responsible for the stewardship and management of resources, including the duty to consult. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate changes in the scientific worldview of sustainability and human's responsibility to protect ecosystems, considering key milestones and publications such as Our Common Future, Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, Agenda 21, Convention on Biological Diversity and the Bonn Declaration. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss why it is important to consider economic, social justice and environmental perspectives when examining sustainability. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Select, integrate and analyze the validity of information from various human, print and electronic sources (e.g., government publications, community resources and personally collected data), with respect to sustainability, sustainable development and education for sustainable development. (S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Provide examples of human actions that have contributed to the anthropogenic greenhouse effect. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research how scientists examine changes to the key indicators of climate change (e.g., CO2 concentration, global surface temperature, Arctic sea ice area, land ice mass and sea level) to support the scientific understanding of climate change. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon individual and societal behavioural and lifestyle choices that can help to minimize anthropogenic sources of global climate change. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Develop, present and defend a position or course of action based on personal research related to mitigating the effects of global or local climate change or to enhancing the sustainability of an ecosystem, taking into account human and environmental needs. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Assess the current and potential future effects of ongoing changes to Earth's climate systems on the people and the environment in Saskatchewan and Canada's Arctic region. (K, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Investigate factors that influence Earth's climate system, including the role of the natural greenhouse effect.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between weather and climate, and the impacts of each on daily life. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Understand that Earth's climate system results from the exchange of thermal energy and moisture between the sun, ice sheets, oceans, solid earth and the biosphere over a range of timescales. (K, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how Earth's axial tilt, rotation and revolution around the sun cause uneven heating of Earth's surface, resulting in global convection currents, the Coriolis effect, jet streams, thermohaline circulation of the oceans and climate zones. (S, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Hypothesize how energy transfer, weather and climate might be different if Earth had a different axial tilt, diameter, period of rotation and/or period of revolution. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain how greenhouse gases (e.g., water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, sulphur dioxide and ozone), particles, clouds and surface albedo affect the amount of solar energy absorbed and re-radiated at various locations on Earth. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the role of natural sources (e.g., volcanoes, fire, evaporation and living organisms) of the primary greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere and how they contribute to the natural greenhouse effect. (K, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate the effectiveness of a model used to illustrate the natural greenhouse effect, the reflectivity of Earth's surface or the relationship between Earth's axial tilt and the seasons. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate, through laboratory activities or simulations, heat transfer in air and water, including heat involved in phase changes. (S, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine how interactions between heat, pressure and the Coriolis Effect result in global wind patterns, ocean currents, jet streams and severe weather (e.g., hurricanes, tornadoes, blizzards and thunderstorms). (S, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze weather and atmospheric data to identify patterns in temperature and atmospheric pressure, and changes in those patterns locally, regionally and globally. (S)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Provide examples of positive and negative feedback mechanisms in Earth's climate system. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Provide examples to show how scientific understanding may be refined in light of new evidence. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Examine biodiversity through the analysis of interactions among populations within communities.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of biodiversity and maintaining biodiversity. (S, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Understand that scientists describe biomes as resulting from the interaction of biotic and abiotic factors such as temperature, precipitation, insolation, latitude, altitude and geography. (A, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the biodiversity and climatic characteristics of several of Earth's major biomes. (S, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Estimate the abundance of organisms in a local ecosystem using random (e.g., quadrat), systematic (e.g., line transect and belt transect) and/or stratified sampling techniques. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine the population density, percentage frequency and/or percentage cover of one or more organisms in an ecosystem using primary or secondary population data. (S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss ethical and cultural perspectives related to studying biotic components of ecosystems, including the potential benefits and consequences of technologies (e.g., radio collar) and techniques (e.g., mark and recapture) used to collect data. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine ways in which scientists collaborate with Elders, knowledge keepers and other community members to gather and interpret data related to biotic components of ecosystems. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Construct and/or interpret graphs of population dynamics of humans and other species to determine population trends within an ecosystem. (S, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate various ways in which natural populations attempt to maintain equilibrium, and relate this equilibrium to the resource limits of an ecosystem with reference to concepts such as carrying capacity, natality, mortality, immigration and emigration. (S, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the relationship between the biodiversity of an ecosystem, its primary productivity and ecological resilience. (K, S)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine how factors such as invasive species, habitat loss and climate change affect biodiversity within an ecosystem, and can result in species becoming at-risk (i.e., vulnerable, threatened and extirpated). (K, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze how the bioaccumulation and biomagnification of human-made substances can affect the viability and biodiversity of organisms and populations in an ecosystem. (K, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Investigate the role of feedback mechanisms in biogeochemical cycles and in maintaining stability in ecosystems.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain systems in terms of their type (e.g., open, closed and isolated), equilibrium (e.g., dynamic, static, stable and unstable) and their associated feedbacks (e.g., positive and negative). (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a representation of a feedback mechanism that is relevant to a specific biogeochemical (e.g., carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and water) cycle. (S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore Indigenous ways of understanding the role of matter and energy in the environment. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how human actions can affect the cycling of matter and flow of energy through ecosystems. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the role of photosynthesis, respiration and sinks in the cycling of carbon through the environment. (K, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Design and carry out an investigation to determine the effect of carbon dioxide levels on photosynthesis and/or to determine the effect of nitrogenous-based fertilizer on plant or algal growth. (S, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare the processes of nitrification and denitrification in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research the short-term and long-term effects of small-scale and large-scale agricultural practices on the cycling of phosphorus, nitrogen and other nutrients in an ecosystem. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze the interdependence between the water cycle and other biogeochemical cycles. (K, S)

outcomes.statement: Explore the properties of chemical reactions, including the role of energy changes, and applications of acids and bases.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a representation about the prevalence of chemistry in our lives. (A, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the ways in which people, including First Nations and Métis, from various times and cultures have applied their understanding of the transformation of materials to produce new substances. (STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Observe and describe a variety of chemical reactions, including synthesis, decomposition, combustion, single replacement and double replacement. (S, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate knowledge of Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS 2015) standards by selecting and applying proper techniques for handling and disposing of lab materials and interpreting Safety Data Sheets (SDSs). (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain why it can be difficult to classify changes as physical or chemical, including reference to the reversibility of the reaction. (K, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate between reactants and products in chemical reactions. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the properties of endothermic and exothermic chemical reactions, including identifying where or how energy is absorbed or released in the reaction and identifying potential benefits and consequences of the reaction. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research practical examples of chemical reactions involving acids and bases, including neutralization reactions such as those involved in chemical spills, soda-acid fire extinguishers and antacids. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Provide examples of the importance of pH measurements in areas such as biology, chemistry, food science, environmental science and water treatment. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research the operation of technologies designed to monitor and manage pH in various applications such as swimming pools, consumer products, agriculture and horticulture. (K, S, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Name and write formulas for common ionic and molecular chemical compounds, including acids and bases.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the relationship between an element's position on the periodic table, the number of its valence electrons and its chemical properties. (K, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of valence electrons, and whether they are shared or transferred, in determining bond type in chemical compounds. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Name and write formulas for common ionic compounds, including compounds involving polyatomic ions, using the periodic table and a list of common ions. (S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the relationship between the structure of ionic compounds, their chemical formulas and their common names. (K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Classify substances as ionic or molecular, based on their properties and the results of student conducted tests (e.g., melting/boiling point, electrical conductivity and solubility). (S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Relate the properties (e.g., solubility, conductivity in solution or gaseous form, high melting point and brittleness) of ionic compounds to their uses. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Name and write formulas for common molecular and organic compounds (e.g., methane, propane, butane, octane, methanol, ethanol and glucose), using the periodic table and a list of numerical Greek prefixes. (S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Design and carry out investigations to determine the properties of acids and bases, including selecting and using appropriate instruments for safely collecting evidence. (S, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Classify substances as acids, bases or salts, based on observable properties, name and chemical formula. (S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate how certain substances, including those traditional to First Nations and Métis cultures, can serve as acid-base indicators. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Describe how the pH scale is used to classify substances as acidic, basic or neutral. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Name and write formulas for common acids and bases, using the periodic table, a list of ions and rules for naming acids and bases. (S)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explain the importance of scientific nomenclature systems such as the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) naming conventions in communicating information about chemical compounds. (STSE, A)

outcomes.statement: Represent chemical reactions and conservation of mass symbolically using models, word and skeleton equations and balanced chemical equations.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Design and safely carry out an experiment to confirm the law of conservation of mass, identifying and controlling major variables. (A, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the importance of the concept of conservation of mass in understanding, interpreting and predicting results of chemical reactions. (K, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Represent chemical reactions, organic compounds and conservation of mass using models and word equations. (S, K, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Represent chemical reactions and conservation of mass using skeleton equations and balanced equations. (S, K, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Translate word equations to balanced chemical equations and balanced chemical equations to word equations. (S, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate between the use of subscripts and coefficients in representing the numbers of atoms and molecules present in chemical reactions. (S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Categorize chemical reactions as synthesis, decomposition, combustion, single replacement and double replacement, including acid base neutralization. (S, K, A)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Verify whether a chemical equation is correctly balanced, and correct any errors. (S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the value of representing chemical reactions using models, word and skeleton equations and balanced chemical equations. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Investigate the rates of chemical reactions, including factors that affect the rate.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide examples of chemical reactions that occur over a range of time scales. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Predict how factors such as temperature of the reactant(s), concentration of the reactant(s), surface area of the reactant(s) and the presence or absence of catalysts or inhibitors might affect the rate of a chemical reaction. (S, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Formulate scientific questions about the rates of chemical reactions and the factors that affect rates of chemical reactions. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design and perform an experiment to determine how various factors affect chemical reaction rates, including identifying and controlling major variables. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compile and organize data, using appropriate formats and data treatments to facilitate interpretation of data related to rates of chemical reactions. (S, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Interpret patterns and trends in data, and infer or calculate linear and nonlinear relationships among variables related to chemical reaction rates. (S, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect upon data collection and analysis procedures, and suggest improvements to increase precision and accuracy. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Use the collision model to explain differences in chemical reaction rates. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Value the processes for drawing conclusions in science. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research how the rates of chemical reactions are controlled in everyday situations as well as in agricultural and industrial applications. (STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Work co-operatively with team members to develop and carry out a plan, and troubleshoot problems as they arise when investigating rates of reactions. (S, A)

outcomes.statement: Explore the development of motion-related technologies and their impacts on self and society.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a representation of different types of motion and motion-related technologies from various cultures, including First Nations and Métis. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe how motion that may appear imperceptible to humans (e.g., continental drift, subatomic particles, light, blood circulating and galaxies) can be measured using appropriate technologies. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Evaluate the historical development of a motion-related technology, including the role of continued testing in the development and improvement of the technology. (STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate a prototype of an object that meets a student-identified need related to motion. (STSE, S, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate the design and function of a motion-related technology using student-identified criteria such as safety, cost, availability and impact on everyday life and the environment. (STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe examples of Canadian contributions to science and technology in motion-related fields such as transportation, sport science or space science. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Investigate and represent the motion of objects that travel at a constant speed in a straight line.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide examples of objects that exhibit, or appear to exhibit, uniform motion. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the concept of 'frame of reference' in determining whether an object is in motion and in constructing representations of an object's motion. (S, K, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Construct scale diagrams of displacement vectors (i.e., collinear, non-collinear [perpendicular], and non-collinear [non-perpendicular]) to represent changes in an object's position. (S, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design and carry out experiments to determine the properties of uniform motion, using technologies such as photogates, motion detectors, ticker timers and stopwatches to collect distance and time data effectively and accurately. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of distinguishing between scalar (e.g., distance, speed and time) and vector (e.g., position, displacement, velocity and acceleration) quantities when studying motion. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Construct and analyze graphs (i.e., distance-time, position-time, speed-time and velocity-time) using student-collected data obtained from objects undergoing uniform motion or through computer simulations. (S, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe quantitatively the relationship among distance, time and speed for everyday objects that undergo uniform motion. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Derive the relationship between speed, distance and time (i.e., $v={\Δd}/{\Δt}$) and between velocity, displacement and time (i.e., $v ↖ {→}={\Δd ↖ {→}}/{\Δt}$) using student-collected data from objects undergoing uniform motion.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Solve problems related to the motion of objects that travel at a constant speed in a straight line. (S)

notes: Indicator label (b) printed more than once on the official page.

outcomes.statement: Investigate and represent the motion of objects that undergo acceleration.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop and carry out experiments to determine the properties of accelerated motion, including identifying variables to be tested, developing appropriate sampling procedures for data collection, collecting and recording data and analyzing data to generate conclusions. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Evaluate the relevance, reliability and adequacy of data and data collection methods, including identifying and explaining sources of error and uncertainty in measurements. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Apply the concept of 'rate of change' to operationally define speed, velocity and acceleration. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate the importance of converting measurements to the same units when solving motion problems. (K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate between the concepts of instantaneous and average as they relate to speed and velocity. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Construct and analyze graphs (i.e., distance-time, position-time, speed-time and velocity-time) that represent the motion of objects that undergo acceleration. (S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Solve problems related to acceleration using the equations of motion (e.g., $a^ ↖ {→}={\Δv ↖ {→}}/{\Δt}$, and $\Δd ↖ {→}=v ↖ {→}_it+1/2{a ↖ {→}\Δt^2}$). (S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Value the role and contribution of science and technology in understanding phenomena that are directly observable and those that are not. (A)

notes: Indicator label (b) printed more than once on the official page.

outcomes.statement: Explore the relationship between force and motion for objects moving in one and two dimensions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose and refine scientific questions about the ways in which forces cause objects to move or change their motion. (A, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the effects of applying constant forces to objects at rest and to objects moving at a constant velocity in a straight line. (S, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Add force vectors in one and two dimensions (i.e., collinear, non-collinear [perpendicular] and non-collinear [non-perpendicular]) using vector diagrams to determine the net force acting on an object. (S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate the role of friction in changing the position and/or motion of an object. (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Provide examples of technologies that have been developed to increase or decrease frictional forces between two or more surfaces. (STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze student-collected data to verify the relationship between the acceleration of an object and the net force acting on it. (S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe and provide examples of Newton's three laws of motion in practical situations such as sports, flight and transportation. (K, A)
