indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe what tourism is and what it means to be a tourist.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss reasons (e.g., leisure, education, personal interests, disposable income and business) why people travel as tourists.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate among outbound (i.e., Saskatchewan residents travelling out of province), inbound (i.e., out-of-province tourists travelling to and within the province) and domestic (i.e., Saskatchewan residents travelling within the province).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess the relationship between culture and tourism.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research what is meant by the term visitor economy.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Discuss reasons (e.g., economic and job opportunities) why tourism is important to an area and specifically the local area.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain potential negative impacts (e.g., wear and tear, pollution, rising costs for local residents and overcrowding) of tourism on a community.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the five industries (i.e., food and beverage, accommodation, recreation and entertainment, transportation, and travel services) within the tourism sector.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify examples of the five industries found within the community and the surrounding area.

outcomes.statement: Investigate types of tourism found within the local community, Saskatchewan and/or Canada.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Types of Tourism (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Research the prevalence of, and provide examples for, each type of tourism found within the local community, Saskatchewan and/or Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Reflect on personal preference for a specific type of tourism and how that preference may evolve and change over time.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a plan, including anticipated expenditures, for a vacation to a destination of choice within Canada that supports one’s preferred type of tourism and references the five industries of tourism.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the importance of environmental, economic, cultural and social sustainability to the tourism sector.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Sustainable Tourism (Core) · Suggested Time: 8-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss what sustainability is and why it is an important consideration for all tourism industries at the local, provincial, national and global level.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the four components (i.e., environmental, economic, cultural and social) of sustainable tourism.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate between mass and alternative tourism.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate potential positive and negative impacts of mass and alternative tourism on the environment, economy, culture and society.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the origin, development and resulting impact of the Palau Pledge.

indicators.label: f

outcomes.statement: Explore the role and impact of tourism on the local community and surrounding area.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Local Tourism (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of tourism to the local community and surrounding area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the connection and relationship of First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples to the land in the local community and the surrounding area and the resulting impact on tourism.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the local area, including ecosystems, landscape, climate, history, culture and people and their relationship to tourism.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Brainstorm reasons why tourists visit the local community and surrounding area.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss common characteristics (e.g., families with young children, hunters, sports enthusiasts, adults, artisans, Saskatchewan residents and residents from other provinces or countries) of tourists who typically visit the local community and surrounding area.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Construct plans (i.e., for one and several days) for being a tourist within the local community and surrounding area, referencing all five industries in the tourism sector.

outcomes.statement: Examine the role and impact of tourism in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Tourism in Saskatchewan (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the evolution of tourism in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Classify tourism businesses within the local community and surrounding area as family-owned and operated or as franchises.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of owning and operating a family-owned and operated business to owning and operating a franchised business.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss evolving expectations (e.g., experiencing nature and the outdoors, and enjoying local flavours and traditions) of travellers to the province and the resulting trends in tourism opportunities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze regional differences in tourism in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Assess the attitudes and habits of Saskatchewanians pertaining to tourism in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Propose factors (e.g., pandemic, economic downturn or economic boom) that may contribute to periods of growth and decline in the tourism sector in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: List examples of urban and rural tourism experiences in Saskatchewan for each of the five industries.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain strategies used by tourism industries to increase customer count.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Research how the tourism industry has capitalized, or could capitalize, on Saskatchewan’s natural capital (e.g., diversity, culture and natural landscape).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Discuss the concept of competitive advantage.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Summarize Saskatchewan’s competitive advantage in the tourism sector compared to other provinces and neighbouring American states.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Investigate the connection and relationship of Métis, First Nations and Inuit peoples to the land in Saskatchewan and the resulting impact on tourism.

indicators.label: o

outcomes.statement: Examine the role and impact of tourism in Canada.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Tourism in Canada (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the evolution of tourism in Canada.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify trends in tourism within Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze regional differences in tourism in Canada.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the attitudes and habits of Saskatchewanians and Canadians pertaining to tourism in Canada.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the reasons why Canada may or may not be considered a destination of choice for people in other countries around the world.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Discuss factors (e.g., pandemic, economic downturn, lack of skilled workers and economic boom) that may contribute to periods of growth and decline in the tourism sector in Canada.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research strategies that tourism industries can utilize to remain resilient and thrive during times of adversity and/or an economic downturn.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the work of organizations such as Destination Canada that market Canada as a tourism destination internationally.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine once-in-a-lifetime travel experiences that are found only in Canada through programs such as Destination Canada Signature Experiences.

outcomes.statement: Examine the role and impact of global tourism.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7: Global Tourism (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss what is meant by the term global tourism.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the evolution of global tourism.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the impact of the tourism sector on the global economy.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify trends (e.g., sharing economy, sustainability, eco tourism, business/leisure travel, robots and automation, artificial intelligence and virtual reality) that may impact global tourism.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the attitudes and habits of Saskatchewanians and Canadians pertaining to global tourism.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Identify countries where tourism is a major industry or is on the rise.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the reasons why tourism is a major industry or on the rise in specific countries and the factors that have contributed to its prominence and growth.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine the work of organizations such as the United Nations World Tourism Organization that promote responsible, sustainable and accessible tourism.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: List examples of United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) World Heritage Sites found within Canada and other parts of the world.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Summarize potential positive and negative impacts on tourism and the local community when a location attains World Heritage Site designation.

outcomes.statement: Explore the food and beverage industry and its interrelatedness to other industries within the tourism sector.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8A: Food and Beverage Industry A (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe common types of food service (e.g., fast food service, fine dining, drive through service, pick up and delivery, catering, cafeteria, buffet style and family style) and provide examples of when each might be used.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Classify examples of food establishments within the community and surrounding area or province according to market segments (e.g., banquet service, buffet and smorgasbord, haute cuisine; family, speciality and chain restaurants; franchise; catering; entertainment; and institutional food service).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research characteristics of artisanal food (e.g., made locally using traditional methods and tools and local ingredients, and produced on a small-scale or in small batches).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify food artisans within the community and surrounding area or province.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate between commercial and non-commercial food service operations.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the interrelatedness among the food and beverage and other tourism industries (e.g., food and beverage as well as accommodation, transportation and/or travel services may be accessed by visitors attending an event).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify trends (e.g., plant-based meat alternatives, gluten-free diet and 100-mile diet) within the food and beverage industry.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain the potential impact (e.g., economic and human) of unforeseen events such as a global pandemic, natural disaster (e.g., earthquake or tornado) or man-made catastrophe (e.g., 9/11) on the food and beverage industry.

outcomes.statement: Examine the evolution and importance of culinary tourism in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8B: Food and Beverage Industry B (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 3 and 8A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify milestones/factors (e.g., field to table, fast food restaurants using better quality oils, food/safety legislation and no smoking bylaws) in Saskatchewan that have impacted the food and beverage industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the evolution of the food and beverage industry in Saskatchewan and Canada over the past decade or more.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the influence of culture on Saskatchewan’s culinary history.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze Saskatchewan statistics and facts (e.g., the number of people employed in the industry, the demographics of those employed in the industry and annual spending on food and beverages) to determine the impact of the food and beverage industry on the local and provincial economies and labour market.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of culinary tourism within the food and beverage industry.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine examples of culinary tourism in the province.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Propose ideas for incorporating culinary tourism, including Indigenous culinary experiences, as part of unique visitor experiences in Saskatchewan.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the elements of quality customer service within the food and beverage industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8C: Food and Beverage Industry C (Optional) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Modules 8B and 14A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect on what it means to provide quality customer service within the food and beverage industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research ways that the food and beverage industry can accommodate customers with diverse backgrounds (e.g., cultural, social and demographic) and with diverse needs (e.g., accessibility, communication and mobility).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate between front-of-house (e.g., maître d’, waiter, greeter, host, bartender, busser, food runner and cashier) and back-of-house (e.g., chef, sous chef, prep cook, line cook, dishwasher and kitchen crew) positions within a food and beverage business and describe their respective roles.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of safety, good communication between front-of- house and back-of-house staff and interpersonal skills for workers in the food and beverage industry.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Role-play scenarios for providing good table service (e.g., greeting/seating customers, taking reservations, pouring water, taking customer orders, serving courses and presenting the bill) and bussing tables (e.g., changing tablecloths, clearing the table, loading a bus pan/trays and carrying a bus pan).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate setting a dinner table using the North American place setting arrangement.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze differences between the North American place setting and a variety of international table settings such as Moroccan, French, Japanese and Mexican.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship among the menu, type of restaurant and ambience for determining how to set a table in a particular venue.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of a risk mitigation plan including communication strategies to ensure the safety and security of both employees and patrons in response to unforeseen events (e.g., customer experiencing an allergic reaction, natural disaster or security threat).

outcomes.statement: Explore the accommodation industry and its interrelatedness to other industries within the tourism sector.

outcomes.statement: Examine the importance of professionalism for workers in the tourism sector.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13: Professionalism (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe personal qualities and behaviours (e.g., demonstrating a positive attitude; showing responsibility; being adaptable; showing respect for self and others; demonstrating communication skills; and being an ambassador for one’s school, community and province) that demonstrate professionalism as it relates to working in the tourism industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Discuss:
- the importance of professional appearance, good personal hygiene and conduct for a career in tourism;
- professional etiquette in using a variety of communication tools such as email, telephone, social media and smart phone applications both on- and off-the-job while employed in the tourism industry; and,
- common ethical standards (e.g., confidentiality and privacy) related to customer service in the tourism industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the contributions of employees and volunteers and how their actions and attitudes can positively or negatively shape the identity of a business, community, province and country.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess the importance of acknowledging and respecting customer diversity.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect on the potential impact of personal beliefs and unconscious bias on relationships and interactions with clients and co-workers in the workplace.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss what it means to be a good ambassador for a community.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on and commit to undertaking personal actions that demonstrate professionalism and being a good ambassador for one’s school and/or community.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the impact of customer service on the visitor experience.

indicators.label: a

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of a first impression and its impact on the visitor experience.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe ways to provide a good first impression when serving a customer in a tourism job.

indicators.label: c

indicators.label: h

d

outcomes.statement: Analyze the purpose and benefits of tourism marketing.

indicators.text:
Research answers to questions related to the geography of the community or area, such as:

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

courses.name: Treaty Education

evidence.observation: The curriculum document groups its outcomes under 3 headings: “Grade Ten: Examining the Canadian context for Treaties”, “Grade Eleven: Assessing Treaty Making from a Global Perspective”, “Grade Twelve: Applying Treaty Understandings to One’s Life”.

units.name: Grade Ten: Examining the Canadian context for Treaties

items.text: Examine contemporary economic implications of Treaties for all the people of Saskatchewan and other Canadian jurisdictions.

Investigate the economic impact that First Nations have on the provincial and territorial economies and the resulting benefits for all people (e.g. natural resources; hunting, fishing and gathering; tourism; hospitality; gaming).
Evaluate the impact that First Nations have on local economies.
Investigate the cost of fulfilling treaties within Saskatchewan and other Canadian jurisdictions.
Analyze the spirit and intent of Treaties and investigate the extent to which they have been fulfilled.
Identify spirit and intent of the terms of treaty.

Imagine and describe what our society would look like today if all treaty obligations had been completely fulfilled and what it could look like into the future (e.g., Maori influence on New Zealand institutions).
Investigate opportunities and challenges faced by First Nations and the Government of Canada in relation to governance issues.
Examine the impact of federal, provincial, and municipal government policies on the fulfillment of Treaties.
Research public policy as it relates to self-government.
Investigate issues related to resource development and Treaties.
Research crown and private corporations that are involved in resource development to investigate the relationship they have with First Nations.
Investigate court rulings that have set the stage for resource development in Saskatchewan.
Examine the positions of First Nations and Government agencies responsible for the stewardship and management of resources (e.g., duty to consult process).

units.name: Grade Eleven: Assessing Treaty Making from a Global Perspective

items.text: Examine how Canada’s process of treaty making could be applied to situations in other parts of the world where Indigenous people have struggled to have rights recognized.
Apply the principles of Canadian treaty making as a means for resolving conflict and represent it (e.g. dramatization, visual, dance, oral representation, multi media presentation).
Investigate how the United Nations addresses issues regarding the self-determination of Indigenous peoples.
Analyze how the unfulfilled aspects of treaties, with international indigenous people, have resulted in inequities.
Analyze international examples of treaties involving indigenous peoples that have resulted in inequities.
Research how the Indian Act and its implementation differ in practice from First Nation governance structures.
Explore legal, political, ethical, and social impacts within Canada where Treaties do not exist.
Evaluate specific treaties that have been, or currently are, in place globally to determine their effectiveness.
Conduct an inventory of the various treaties that currently exist.
Assess the various motives for entering into treaty.
Construct a recommendation as to the effectiveness of treaty as a means for addressing conflict (e.g., a motion, passing of a law).
Research UN resolutions and initiatives in relation to self-determination of indigenous peoples.
Analyze the impact Canadian treaties could have on resolving global conflict.
Assess Canadian treaty making processes and compare to treaty processes from around the world.
Assess the leadership role Canada plays internationally in treaty making.

units.name: Grade Twelve: Applying Treaty Understandings to One’s Life

items.text: Examine one’s position regarding the importance of the treaty relationship for the social, cultural and economic prosperity of all Saskatchewan and Canadian people.

Analyze data from multiple sources (e.g., oral tradition, National Council on Welfare, Assembly of First Nations, Statistics Canada, Indian and Northern Affairs Canada) to inform personal beliefs regarding the effectiveness of treaties in addressing social, cultural and economic inequities.
Analyze how the media currently depicts the treaty relationship and determine the effects this has on public perception.
Analyze what you believe about treaty relationships, why you believe it, and how you came to believe it.
Investigate the values and beliefs of self, family, community, and society in relation to the importance of honouring the Spirit and Intent of treaties.
Interview family, friends and community members to determine values and beliefs in relation to treaties.
Describe ways people could demonstrate the spirit and intent of treaties and treaty principles (e.g., honour, respect, honesty, fairness, ethical space).
Reflect on and discuss personal experiences in honouring treaty principles.
Examine how treaties within contemporary society impact on individual’s lives.
Describe the principles of treaty and understand the importance those principles play.
Evaluate one’s actions according to personal beliefs nurtured through their understanding of treaty making.
Analyze responses to treaties in current federal and provincial government policies.
Synthesize knowledge and appreciation of treaties.
Represent personal understanding of the concept, We Are All Treaty People.
Examine the benefits of treaties as a way of defining and honouring relationships between nations.
Describe various worldviews represented by the signing of treaty.
Examine the importance of decolonization as a process that supports the understanding that We Are All Treaty People.

notes: Treaty Education is organised by grade (10, 11, 12), not by course level, and is meant to be taught within other subjects. `level` gives the matching course level (Grade 10 = 10-level, 11 = 20-level, 12 = 30-level) only so the course can sit beside the others.
Outcome codes are printed with a superscript goal number (TR¹, SI², HC³, TPP⁴, per the page's KEY); the superscript is kept in `superscript`, and `code` is the code as the Ministry CSV lists it.

outcomes.statement: Critically respond to art work by Canadian artists whose subject matter is related to resistance and/or resilience.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how art works can be acts, or representations, of resistance and resilience (e.g., What is the relationship between art and resistance and resilience? Does art have power to inspire social and political change? How does art contribute to individual or collective resilience? How can art-making support mental health and wellness?).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine how artists over time, and in various parts of the world, have responded to events involving acts of resistance and demonstrations of resilience (e.g., visual documentation of wars and genocide, African apartheid, Latin American artists’ responses to political injustices).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Respond to traditional and evolving work of First Nation, Métis and Inuit artists whose subject matter speaks to experiences of resistance and resilience (e.g., Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls art works and projects, treaty education outcome TR12 - examine one’s position regarding the importance of the treaty relationship for the social, cultural and economic prosperity of all Saskatchewan and Canadian people.).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how concerns about the abuse of power are represented in works by Canadian artists (e.g., subject matter related to anti-racism, environmental sustainability, gender equity, political cartoons, comic book illustrations).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Use one or more approaches for responding critically to the visual art examples studied (e.g., write a formal critique or research paper using proper format including citations, create own work in response).

outcomes.statement: Critically reflect on choice of discipline, content and media in the development of own voice and style.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Review and discuss portfolios (e.g., own and peers, physical folder or digital collection) and write artist biographies and statements for individual works and/or a series of works.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect on own work and select examples to include in a portfolio (e.g., documentation of creative process, sketches showing idea development, photos of works in progress and resolved, collection of various techniques or different media).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain, using visual art terminology, how one’s portfolio is demonstrating ideas, style and voice (e.g., How is the work related to a big idea?).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research, deconstruct, and discuss various approaches to the creative process and apply that understanding to own work.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Document and assess personal development in the creative process.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Document how an artist develops a style and voice over time including development of cultural, Western and personal narratives.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss how groups within societies have determined definitions of art throughout history leading to the exclusion or inclusion of specific voices (e.g., How have artists, minorities and their allies challenged definitions of art and promoted inclusion of diverse voices?).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine artistic influences and describe the impact of those influences on own work.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Search for inspiration through a variety of sources (e.g., music, fashion, other artists) to extend ideas and techniques to apply to future works.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate Indigenous perspectives and ways of knowing to appreciate sources of inspiration (e.g., memory, history, story) and range of artistic styles, and describe how personal worldview, voice and style are demonstrated in own artistic development.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Conduct an investigation into the connections between place, territory and/or identity (e.g., research Canadian artists whose work reflects a sense of place and identity).

outcomes.statement: Investigate how visual art in Canada can support and build relationships and deepen understanding that we are all treaty people.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Engage with Elders and/or community members to gain understanding of ways that visual art in Canada can support relationship building.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze and communicate how artists have responded to colonization.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the meaning of We are all Treaty People, considering its importance for Saskatchewan’s First Nations, Métis and non-Indigenous peoples.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how some art works and images promote stereotypes while other art works represent the truth and lived experiences of First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine issues surrounding cultural appropriation and stereotypes (e.g., images, sports logos).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Use research, discussions, experiences and ideas about treaties as inspiration for creating own work (e.g., treaty education outcome SI122 - investigate the values and beliefs of self, family, community, and society in relation to the importance of honouring the Spirit and Intent of treaties).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research and share findings about the work of contemporary Indigenous artists and curators in Canada.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine, respect and honour traditional, historical and contemporary connections to the land and the natural world (e.g., treaty education outcome TPP12 - represent personal understanding of the concept, We Are All Treaty People).

outcomes.statement: Examine how visual art expressions have changed over time and/or inspired change in individuals, communities and societies.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research key changes in art and design throughout history (e.g., furniture, jewelry, architecture, functional art, fashion, album covers).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the influence of the evolution of digital media on the creation of art expressions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how artists from various cultural backgrounds draw on their historical traditions in different ways as contemporary art practices evolve over time.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine various approaches to communicate (e.g., humour, story, irony, satire, metaphor, symbol, using beauty to depict challenging subject matter) and respond visually in ways that can influence perspectives and contribute to change in communities and societies.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how visual art, and the other arts, contribute to personal and social wellbeing in communities (e.g., fostering connections, sharing stories, creating empathy).

outcomes.statement: Engage with communities to collaborate and build relationships beyond the classroom through visual art experiences.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Interact with other classrooms, professional artists, art shows or community events to improve own growth.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine visual art careers and opportunities to learn from individuals who work in the arts sector (e.g., participate in Work Study* experiences with professional associations, provincial and community arts and cultural organizations; independent study mentorships with individual artists or collectives).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research artists and examine examples of artist biographies, resumes and artist statements as exemplars for own art practice.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss opportunities and challenges of working in various visual arts careers.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Use technology to connect with community (e.g., website, social media) to further own development in visual art.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine issues often encountered by visual artists (e.g., protecting own and others’ intellectual property, copyright, cultural appropriation of images, music, fashion) and ways of addressing these issues.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate artist collectives, alternative gallery environments, artist run centers, or student run art pop-up center, and consider opportunities to volunteer in own community.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Engage with artists on collaborative projects through such means as artists in schools or artist in communities’ programs.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research provincial and community arts organizations as resources to make connections within communities.

indicators.label: b
c
d

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Take personal and musical risks by trying new ways to express oneself in the jazz idiom, using new ides, new concepts and a variety of styles.

outcomes.statement: Recognize, with assistance as necessary, the importance of musical text in personal musical performance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Prepare, rehearse and perform music in jazz style in solo, small group and/or large ensemble settings.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Explore text through creating original text to pre-existing melodies and improvisations (vocalese)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the conventions regarding jazz articulation and use those conventions in performance.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Recognize jazz vocabulary and use this vocabulary to describe personal musical practise, learning, theory and performance.

outcomes.statement: Identify the elements of music and apply these to create a musical product.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate the knowledge of standard notation conventions (e.g., note durations up to eighth notes, repeats, codas, D.S.s and dynamic markings). Identify jazz conventions that differ from traditional classical notation (e.g., falls, glisses, slides, inflection marks and hats).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Sing a variety of vocal jazz styles (e.g., swing, funk, ballad) accompanied and a cappella.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the relationship of form and text in music, particularly blues and ABA, AABA song forms.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In groups, design, implement and evaluate a plan to improve individual performance and to enhance the knowledge and uderstanding of vocal jazz. As part of this process of improvement, include recording and listening back to performances, practices and/or rehearsals.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify different elements of music such as articulation, rhythm, beat, metre, time placement and tone that help create a jazz style and apply this knowledge while music making.

outcomes.statement: Identify personal vocal techniques and apply these to create or show a musical product.

indicators.text: Recognize a vocal tone appropriate to the style and personal development.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the connection betrween the breath and the voice.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Establish the key concepts related to singing expressively (e.g., work painting, phrasing, motion and dynamics). Show the knowledge of these concepts through singing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Sing a known tune(e.g., O'Canada) a cappella maintaining key centre.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Sing a one octave chromatic scale, scending and descending, unaccompanied

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Sing the chord tones of major and minor triads and scale triads.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Sing a jazz standard (with recorded or live acoompaniment) exploring scat singin and other appropriate jazz stylings.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Sight-read a melodic line written in stepwise motions

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Compare and contrast vocal jazz style to other vocal styles.

outcomes.statement: Identify the skills and abilities required to listen and respond as a vocal jazz performer when singing jazz.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Respond to qualities of personal tone such as pitch, dynamics, style, colour, blend, rhythm, time, and consistent vowel use.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Respond to the rest of the ensemble (e.g., its tone, colour, pitch, dynamics, style, rhythm, time, balance, consistent vowel use and blend).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Immediately respond to the ensemble's response (e.g., When singing, does the student match and change vowel sounds and shapes to match the group?).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Respond to the conductor/leader, including gestures, cues, tempo, expressions and body language.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Listen to the acoustic properties of the performing space, including the sound, tone, loudness, and reverb of the room and adjust singing and microphone technique accordingly.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: React to the audience, their presence (or nor), body language, expressions and reaction to the music (e.g., applause, cheering, being asked to sing louder or quieter).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Know the history, culture, style, form and tempo of the music being performed and respond to the music by reading it and/or performing the notes and/or changes appropriately

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Recall previous experiences and knowledge (in music and in life) and integrate these into solo group vocal jazz performances.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Know any special emotional context that may apply to the music, generate the appropriate emotional feeling or energy and/or synchronize the personal emotional state of the performer with the emotional context of the music being performed.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Know, predict and/or anticipate what is next or might bve next in the music and prepare for that while performing in the moment of the music.

outcomes.statement: Identify skills and abilities necessary to listen to a jazz performer.

indicators.text: Listen to jazz music and with assistance analyze form, tone, style, era, dynamics, articulation, time signature, characteristic rhythms, time, balance, blend, key, monde and/or pitch.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Analyze the development of the jazz music(melody, arrangement, changes, or improvisation) as a whole or in smaller sections.
;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: In groups, analyze the characteristic sounds, licks, tone and other elements of well-known singers and/or groups. Identify these singers and/or groups. Identify these singers and/or groups on recordings aurally, only by listening to the characteristic sounds or ideas presented in the music.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze and reflect on just one voice or instrument from the beginning to the end of a musical selection (e.g., Does the singer or player perform the same way all the way through? How was it different or the same? What did he/she sing or play that the student also might be able to sing or play?)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Listen to music analyzing and reflecting on the melody, other voices, bass line, drums and percussion, background lines, background vocals, roots and chord progression and sing with the recording.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the history, cultural heritage and effect of current events as these apply to the musical selection.

outcomes.statement: Identify the skills and abilities to analyze vocal jazz music in real time while making or listening to the music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: In groups, identify, discuss and apply strategies to solve different challenges related to music making.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine common chord structures such as triads in music performed and/or listened to.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create strategies to identify the time signature on first hearing a piece of music, in simpler time signatures such as 2/4, 3/4, 4/4.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop strategies to identify the types of scales being used (pentatonic, blues, major, etc.) in music performed and/or listened to.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develp strategies for hearing 2 and 4 on first hearing a piece of music in an appropriate time signature.

outcomes.statement: Listen to performances of vocal jazz music and with assistance, develop and apply critical criteria to use in critical exaluation of one's own work and other's work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to the music of the great jazz and vocal jazz performers.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate criteria of excellence through listening to the music of the great performers (e.g., What is it that makes the music great? what do the great performers do that the student or student's ensemble does no do?)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: In groups, design and implement a plan for improvement (personal and ensemble) based on the criteria generated from listening to the great performers.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: When listening to a musical selection, as a group develop the ability to describe and classify the music using appropriate jazz language (e.g., style, period, compose, culture and performer).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the skills and components of listening actively, continue to develop these listening skill and recognize that listening contributes to the authenticity of performances.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize and discuss the value of original thought, technical proficiency, place, era and other concepts in the music of the great jazz performers.

outcomes.statement: Describe the skills, techniques and attitudes necessary for successful ensemble performace.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the role of each of the parts within the student's ensemble by demonstrating the ability to perform those specific tasks that are particular to the vocal part or instrument that the student sings or plays in the ensemble (e.g., bass part in the choir, comping for guitar and piano, walking lines for the bass, solo parts in the choir and position in a section).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: With assistance, identify the importance of and begin to implement, melodic phrasing, rhythmic accuracy and articulation in perparation and performance of vocal jazz.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the challenges and importance of singing in tune with good balance and tone and learn the capabilities of the student's own voice (e.g., range, where the break in the student's voice is).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the components of a professional attitude towards conduct, focus and communication skills in rehearsal, preparation of materials and presentation of products.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Begin to apply the learned characteristics of different styles, eras, etc. to the performance of the student's music.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Show respect for the personal work of self and others through appropriate critique.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: With assistance, critically examine and assess the student's individual work and personal contribution to group projects/performances.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Know the value of individual practive, know how to practice, conduct an ongoing evaluation of the student;s personal practice skills and implement a plan for improvement.

outcomes.statement: Explore the different eras, genres, styles and feels of vocal jazz through listening to and.or performing the representative music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: As a group, listen to recording of vocal jazz, develop a list or understanding of the basic characteristics of different jazz styles, genres, periods and place and implement that knowledge into practice and performance.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss aspects of vocal jazz such as history, performers, styles and eras through a variety of media, with a focus on Canadian or Saskatchewan jazz artists.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate an awareness of key historical and artist developments and trends as the relate to the eras and styles of vocal jazz.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop a jaz history timeline from about 1890 through the present, including developments in jazz music, major figures and styles along with important world historical events.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the most influential jazz sings (e.g., Ella Fitzgerald, Frank Sinatra). Investigate why these performers are identified as influentional and listen to their music.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: A number of vocal jazz artists have First Nations or America Indian heritage (e.g., Mildred Bailey, Lena Horne, Joe Williams and Juila Keefe). Discuss possible resons why their heritage is not widely known.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the influence of jazz (and other musics) on contemporary First Nations music.

outcomes.statement: Discuss the influence of vocal jass on other types of music, with an emphasis on the music of Canada and Saskatchewan and assess possible careers in vocal jazz and music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the influence of vocal jazz in Canadian musical culture (e.g., Was jazz ever the "pop" music in Canada?).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the different peoples that made up the culture of New Orleans at the start of the 20th century and the ways that these cultures influenced the development of jazz. Are there parallels in Canada?

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research career pathways in vocal jazz and music in general.

indicators.text: Know the role of each of the parts within the student's ensemble by demonstrating the ability to perform those specific tasks that are particular to the vocal part or instrument that the student sings or plays in the ensemble (e.g., bass part in the choir, comping for guitar and piano, walking lines for the bass, solo parts in the choir and position in a section).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Attend to melodic phrasing, rhythmic accuracy and articulation in perparation and performance of vocal jazz.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Sing in tune with good balance and tone and be aware of the qualities of the student's own voice (e.g., range, where the break in the student's voice is).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop leadership as a performer by offering help, ideas and guideance to other performers during rehearsals and sectionals.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate a professional attitude towards conduct, focus and communication skills in rehearsal, preparation of materials and presentation of products.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Employ the learned characteristics of different styles, eras, etc. to the performance of the student's music.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore understanding of PA systems including set up, tone and level settings for microphones, and so on.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Show respect for the personal work of self and others through appropriate critique.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critically examine and assess the student's individual work and personal contributions to group projects/performances, with assistance as necessary.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Be accepting ofappropriate critiques from others, and work towards implementing the solutions to those critiques.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: With assistance as necessary, demonstrate and record technical development, and from that, develop strategies to improve.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Know the value of individual practice, know how to practive, conduct an ongoing evaluation of the student's personal practice skills, and implement a plan for improvement.

outcomes.statement: Develop knowledge of the different eras, genres, styles and feels of vocal jazz through listening to and.or performing the representative music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Individually and in groups, listen to recording of vocal jazz, develop a list or understanding of the basic characteristics of different jazz styles, genres, periods and place and implement that knowledge into practice and performance.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Individually and as a group listen to recordings of vocal jazz and catagorize the music into styles, genres, periods and/or place.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore aspects of vocal jazz such as history, performers, styles and eras through a variety of media, with a focus on Canadian or Saskatchewan jazz artists.

outcomes.statement: Explore jazz music and its performers and educators and their influence in the world.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate some of the challenges that vocal jazz artists with African America, First Nations, and/or mixed race heritage may have had in their daily lives, and compare to the situations faced by many groups of people today.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research how vocal jazz artists may raise or have raised awareness of local, national and international issues (e.g., Billie Holiday singing "Strange Fruit" or Manhattan Transfer singing "Aqua").

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the influence of jazz (and other musics) on contemporary First Nations music.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate the degree of influence that vocal jazz has had on other types of music with an emphasis on the music of Canada and Saskatchewan, and assess possible careers in vocal jazz and music

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify influential vocal ensembles, investigate why these performers are so influential and listen to their music. Give special attention to performers from Saskatchewan and Canada

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the relationship between instrumental and vocal jazz, with particular emphasis on vocal performers who "imitate" insturmental sounds (e.g., Bobby McFerrin, Mark Murphy, Giacommo Gates, Louis Armstrong, Ella Fitzgerald).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe how Canadian and international copyright laws affect the lives of those who work in the jazz field.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research career pathways in vocal jazz and music in general.

outcomes.statement: Improvise in a jazz style, integrating understanding of applicable jazz theory.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: To deepen understanding of jazz style, analyze musical events within a solo or composition(e.g. introduction, shout chorus, form, dynamics, pitches, changes, articulation).

indicators.label: b
c
d
e
indicators.text: Demonstrate improvement and growth in the presentation and construction of improvised solos in a performance setting.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Take personal and musical risks by trying new ways to express oneself in the jazz idiom, using new ideas, new concepts and a variety of styles.

outcomes.statement: Infuse, independently, the understanding of the muscial text into a personal musical performance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Prepare, rehearse and perform music in jazz style in solo, small group and/or large ensemble settings.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Create original text to pre-existing melodies and improvisations (vocalese)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Integrate knowledge of conventions regarding jazz articulation and use those conventions in performance.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Show proficient use jazz vocabulary and use this vocabulary to describe personal musical practise, learning, theory and performance (see Jazz Glossary).

outcomes.statement: Identify the elements of music and apply these to create a musical product.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Individually design, implement and evaluate a plan to improve individual performance and to enhance the knowledge and uderstanding of vocal jazz. As part of this process of improvement, include recording and listening back to performances, practices and/or rehearsals.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Integrate into performance the knowledge of standard notation conventions (e.g., note durations up to eighth notes, repeats, codas, D.S.s and dynamic markings). Identify jazz conventions that differ from traditional classical notation (e.g., falls, glisses, slides, inflection marks and hats).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Sing a variety of vocal jazz styles (e.g., swing, funk, ballad) accompanied and a cappella.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Integrate an understanding of the relationship of form and text in music, particularly blues and ABA, AABA song forms.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify different elements of music such as articulation, rhythm, beat, metre, time placement and tone that help create a jazz style and apply this knowledge while music making.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Integrate an understanding of the different elements of music such as articulation, rhythm, beat, metre, time placement and tone that help create a jazz style, and apply this knowledge while music making.

outcomes.statement: Model individual vocal techniques and apply these to create or show a musical product.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Consistently sing with a tone appropriate to the style and personal development.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Model a consistent connection between the breath and the voice.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Internalize and consistently the key concepts related to singing expressively (e.g., work painting, phrasing, motion and dynamics). Show the knowledge of these concepts through singing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Individually generate technical inquiry questions and take action on the findings of the inquiry (e.g., "What can I do to get better?" or "How could I improve this performance, paper, or arrangement?").

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Consistently use good microphone techniques in rehearsals and the performance of music.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Sing harmony a cappella maintaining key centre.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Sing a one octave chromatic scale, scending and descending, unaccompanied.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Sing one octave major, harmonic minor, dorian, mixolydian and blues scales, ascending and descending, unaccompanied.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Sing the chord tones of major and minor triads, dominant and major 7ths, major and minor 6ths and 9ths, and scale triads.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Sing a jazz standard (with recorded or live acompaniment) demonstrating scat singin and other appropriate jazz stylings.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Sight-read a simple 2 - 4 part composition

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Compare and contrast vocal jazz style to other vocal styles.

outcomes.statement: Listen and respond as a vocal jazz performer when singing jazz.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Respond to qualities of personal tone such as pitch, dynamics, style, colour, blend, rhythm, time, and consistent vowel use.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Respond to the rest of the ensemble (e.g., its tone, colour, pitch, dynamics, style, rhythm, time, balance, consistent vowel use and blend).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Immediately respond to the ensemble's response (e.g., When singing, does the student match and change vowel sounds and shapes to match the group?).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Respond to the conductor/leader, including gestures, cues, tempo, expressions and body language.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Listen to the acoustic properties of the performing space, including the sound, tone, loudness, and reverb of the room and adjust singing and microphone technique accordingly.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: React to the audience, their presence (or nor), body language, expressions and reaction to the music (e.g., applause, cheering, being asked to sing louder or quieter).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Know the history, culture, style, form and tempo of the music being performed and respond to the music by reading it and/or performing the notes and/or changes appropriately

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Recall previous experiences and knowledge (in music and in life) and integrate these into solo group vocal jazz performances.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Know any special emotional context that may apply to the music, generate the appropriate emotional feeling or energy and/or synchronize the personal emotional state of the performer with the emotional context of the music being performed.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Know, predict and/or anticipate what is next or might bve next in the music and prepare for that while performing in the moment of the music.

outcomes.statement: Listen to jazz as a jazz performer when not personally performing the music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to jazz music and independently analyze form, tone, style, era, dynamics, articulation, time signature, characteristic rhythms, time, balance, blend, key, monde and/or pitch.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Analyze the development of the jazz music(melody, arrangement, changes, or improvisation) as a whole or in smaller sections.
;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the characteristic sounds, licks, tone and other elements of well-known singers and/or groups. Identify these singers and/or groups. Identify these singers and/or groups on recordings aurally, only by listening to the characteristic sounds or ideas presented in the music.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze and reflect on just one voice or instrument from the beginning to the end of a musical selection (e.g., Does the singer or player perform the same way all the way through? How was it different or the same? What did he/she sing or play that the student also might be able to sing or play?)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Listen to music analyzing and reflecting on the melody, other voices, bass line, drums and percussion, background lines, background vocals, roots and chord progression and sing with the recording.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the history, cultural heritage and effect of current events as these apply to the musical selection.

outcomes.statement: Independently analyze vocal jazz music in real time while making or listening to the music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Individually identify, experiment with, and purposefully use strategies to solve different challenges related to music making.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine common chord structures including, but not limited to, triads, seventh and ninth chords in music performed and/or listened to.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the time signatures on first hearing a piece of music, including 6/8, in addition to simpler duple time signatures. Demonstrate the patters of strong and weak beats that are identified with the time signatures

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use strategies to identify the types of scales being used (pentatonic, blues, major, etc.) in music performed and/or listened to.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop strategies for hearing 2 and 4 on first hearing a piece of music in an appropriate time signature.

outcomes.statement: Listen to performances of vocal jazz music and individually or with assistance develop and apply critical criteria to use in critical evaluation of one's own work and other's work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to the music of the great jazz and vocal jazz performers.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate criteria of excellence through listening to the music of the great performers (e.g., What is it that makes the music great? what do the great performers do that the student or student's ensemble does no do?)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Design and implement a plan for improvement (personal and ensemble) based on the criteria generated from listening to the great performers.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Upon first hearing a musical selection, describe and classify the music using appropriate jazz language (e.g., style, period, compose, culture and performer).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Broaden knowledge of skills and components of listening actively, continue to develop these listening skill and recognize that listening contributes to the authenticity of performances.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize and discuss the value of original thought, technical proficiency, place, era and other concepts in the music of the great jazz performers.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine roles that vocal jazz artists might have beyond being performers, and identify individuals who fit those particular roles (e.g., Bobby McFerrin, Phil Mattson, and Gene Puerling).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: A number of jazz artists have First Nations or American Indian heritage (e.g., Mildred Bailey, Lena Horne, Joe Williams and Julia Keefe). Discuss possible reasons why this is not widley known and the effect that this heritage may have had on their music and lives.

outcomes.statement: Apply principles and techniques for unintentional injury prevention to ensure safe work performance in the welding area.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: General Shop Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the purpose and demonstrate the proper use and fit of personal protective equipment (PPE) including eye protection (lens shades), clothing, hearing protection, and footwear while identifying the hazards from which they protect individuals.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze potential risk situations and solutions that apply specifically to slips and falls, as well as lifting heavy material, and identify safe solutions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize hazards associated with oxy-acetylene welding equipment (i.e., tanks, hoses, gauges) and take the necessary measures to avoid unintentional injuries, including those caused by flashback and backfire.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize hazards associated with electric welding processes and take necessary measures to avoid unintentional injuries.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate the fire plan for the shop, including components such as fire alarms, fire extinguishers, exits, and procedures; and make recommendations for improvements.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate the proper procedures to follow when reporting an unintentional injury.

outcomes.statement: Work safely with properly maintained safety equipment in an organized environment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Intermediate Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Express knowledge of safe handling of materials according to WHMIS, using materials safety data sheets (MSDS).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research and discuss Occupational Health and Safety regulations which apply to the welding industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize and apply safe and fair work practices including freedom from violence and harassment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Complete an assessment of all safety and welding equipment and, in consultation with the instructor, perform maintenance to repair or replace defective or worn parts.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate and explain the correct procedures for the safe use, care, and handling of the hand tools and power equipment used in a welding shop.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Hand and Power Tools (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-15 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and define the safe use of hand tools such as hammers, pliers, wire brushes, strikers, anvils, files, tip cleaners, hand shears, hacksaws, clamps, vices, and marking tools.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate and articulate the correct procedures for operating power tools such as grinders (stationary and portable), buffers (stationary and portable), power shear, power hacksaw, band saw, and drill press.

outcomes.statement: Assess the condition of and the maintenance of tools used in the welding shop.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Intermediate Hand and Power Tools (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate the proper method for cleaning weld-spattered tools.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess and report any potential faults with electrical cords and receptacles.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Repair or replace welding-distorted surfaces on benches or table tops in consultation with the instructor.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate the proper techniques to remove and replace saw blades.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify potential maintenance issues with hand and power tools and consult with the instructor to determine a solution.

outcomes.statement: Develop and apply a systematic routine for setting up and putting away oxy-acetylene equipment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Oxy-acetylene Start-up, Shut-down, and Cutting (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe and perform the accepted start-up and shut-down procedures for the oxy-acetylene system which includes valves, regulators, torches, tips, types of flames, and safety precautions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Understand and describe how to cut 3⁄8” mild steel including the correct flame, flame distance, angle of the tip, direction of travel, speed of travel, and motion of tip.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate safe and effective cutting using an oxy-acetylene torch after determining the proper tip size and gas pressure for the gauge of metal.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Introduction to Oxy-acetylene Cutting (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 5

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify precautionary procedures to limit the danger to others in the shop.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the relationship between the tip size, metal thickness, and gas pressures.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate the specified cuts on the provided material using an oxy-acetylene cutting torch.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate use of an oxyacetylene torch to make specified cuts.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7A: Oxy-acetylene Cutting Skills (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 6

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Cut straight lines on 3⁄8” mild steel.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Complete bevel cuts on 3⁄8” mild steel.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Cut holes and circles on 3⁄8” mild steel.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate cuts to fit a given template to increase accuracy to within 1⁄16” tolerance.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7B: Oxy-acetylene Cutting Skills (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 6 and 7A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Complete round and/or curved cuts specified by the instructor.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Complete square and/or rectangular cuts specified by the instructor.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate cutting with an oxy-acetylene torch on a variety of metal thicknesses to achieve a high quality cut.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Oxy-acetylene Cutting Practice (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate the correct settings for the oxygen and the acetylene regulators and explain the relationship between the settings and the metal thickness.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate and evaluate oxy-acetylene cutting torch work on a variety of thicknesses and types of metal.

outcomes.statement: Use oxy-acetylene equipment to complete the specified welds and analyze the results.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Oxy-acetylene Welding (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 5

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Run lines of fusion without the use of filler rod in the flat position on gauge mild steel.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess the quality of personal work on practical assignments including butt weld, edge weld, and lines of fusion.

outcomes.statement: Effectively use oxy-acetylene equipment to increase the quality of the specified welds.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Intermediate Oxy-acetylene Welding (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 9

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Perform and analyze a variety of specified welds, including butt weld, edge weld, and lines of fusion.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare and chart personal progress to identify increasing skill.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess personal technique and document results in consultation with the instructor.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate an increasingly high quality of both welding skill and self-assessment of that skill while using oxy-acetylene equipment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11A: Oxy-acetylene Welding Practice (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 10

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create examples of basic oxy-acetylene welding practices, including beads with no filler, edge weld, corner weld, beads with filler, butt weld, and lap weld.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Perform an outside corner weld, no filler rod, in the flat position, on gauge mild steel.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Run lines of fusion using filler rod, in the flat position, on gauge mild steel.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Perform a butt weld using filler rod, in the flat position, on gauge mild steel.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess personal technique and results in consultation with the instructor.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate increasing proficiency in oxy-acetylene welding skills.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11B: Oxy-acetylene Welding Practice (Core) · Suggested Time: 20-25 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 10

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Perform a butt weld using filler rod, in the flat position, on gauge mild steel ensuring 100% penetration.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Perform a butt weld using filler rod, in the vertical position, on gauge mild steel.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Perform a lap weld using filler rod, in the flat position, on gauge mild steel; overlap by half.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess personal technique and document results in consultation with the instructor.

outcomes.statement: Select, complete, and assess an approved oxy-acetylene welding project to demonstrate welding proficiency.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12A: Advanced Oxy-acetylene Welding Projects (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 11A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a drawing and develop a cutting list of materials.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Use organized and practised skills to construct a project using appropriate technical language. Utilize the following guidelines to complete a project:
- Generate different project ideas
- Plan and manage the project including assessment criteria in consultation with the instructor
- Plan and use drawings with appropriate symbols
- Set a procedural sequence
- Prepare a material list and cost estimate
- Create a timeline
- Determine fabrication techniques
- Cut material and set up in the proper sequence
- Complete each part as specified
- Interpret and follow directions
- Adhere to timelines
- Work cooperatively
- Follow all safety requirements
- Follow all handling and storing procedures
- Fulfill cleanup and tool maintenance responsibilities
- Present the completed project and complete a self-assessment based on the criteria for the project.

outcomes.statement: Plan, complete, and assess an oxy-acetylene welding project to demonstrate increasing welding proficiency.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12B: Advanced Oxy-acetylene Welding Projects (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 11B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a scale drawing of the project using appropriate symbols including a cutting list.

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Categorize and explain the difference between alternating current and direct current with straight and reverse polarity.

indicators.label: f

indicators.label: g

- Communication.

outcomes.printedWith: Module 33C: Work Study Follow-up (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 32C

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Design and participate in an exit interview with the workplace.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Prepare and present a report on the work study experience including aspects such as:
- Expected hours of work
- Dress code and personal protective equipment (PPE)
- Job description
- Employer expectations
- Absence and late policies
- Problem solving
- Communication.

outcomes.statement: Determine personal skills and interests that could lead to a career in the welding trade through an apprenticeship, technical school training, or paid work.

indicators.text: Compare the transition from high school to apprenticeship to that of high school to further classroom instruction at university or college.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop a list of career opportunities related to the field of welding.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify entrepreneurial opportunities available to people in the welding profession.

indicators.label: d

outcomes.statement: Investigate the apprenticeship and trade certification process and the role of the Saskatchewan Apprenticeship and Trade Certification Commission (SATCC), opportunities that apprenticeship offers, and the relationship between secondary level courses and apprenticeship training.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 88: Apprenticeship in Saskatchewan (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Use and understand the appropriate terminology related to apprenticeship including but not limited to:
- Journeyperson
- Indenture
- Pre-employment training
- Designated trade and sub-trade
- Advanced standing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine the steps involved in becoming an apprentice from the perspective of the specific trade, including length of apprenticeship, annual training requirements, and Red Seal certification.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop an understanding of the programs available to help make the transition from secondary school to apprenticeship.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Conduct research such as interviewing employers to identify the qualities of a successful apprentice.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate one's understanding of wellness while participating in various learning opportunities that balance the dimensions of wellness (i.e., physical, psychological, social, spiritual, environmental).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Participate in a variety of learning experiences that positively influence and balance one's well-being (e.g., exercising, smudging, recycling, gardening).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect on personal beliefs (e.g., being healthy takes work) while addressing common misconceptions about wellness (e.g., if one is not sick, then one must be well).

indicators.label: c
