indicators.text: Explore how wildlife can become a vector for transmission of diseases to humans (e.g., rabies, lyme disease, West Nile virus and coronavirus disease).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain the significance of biodiversity in preventing disease.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate the role of public and private organizations, including wildlife sanctuaries and rescue facilities, in mitigating threats to wildlife.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Examine different levels of wildlife protection legislation (i.e., provincial and federal) and their connection to non-profit organizations.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explain how the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada (COSEWIC) influences legislation.

outcomes.statement: Investigate wildlife rescue and rehabilitation practices in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the purpose and function of wildlife rescue and rehabilitation organizations in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Define “capture myopathy” and identify its symptoms.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Outline steps that can be taken to prevent capture myopathy from occurring in wildlife.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the negative impact of imprinting on young wildlife and the risks (e.g., no fear of humans, territorial behaviour and difficulty interacting with their own species) when young wildlife imprint on humans.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Explore humane ways of coping with “nuisance” wildlife, such as:
- deterring or hazing the animals with unpleasant smells (e.g., cider vinegar), sounds (e.g., music, air horn) or bright lights;
- sealing off any denning areas; and,
- using repellants.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Explain why relocation of wildlife is an ineffective method for dealing with “nuisance” wildlife, including:
- wild animal babies left orphaned when their mother is trapped and removed;
- danger to the relocated animal in other animals' territory; and,
- difficulty finding food, water and shelter in unfamiliar areas.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe how seeking alternatives to euthanizing an injured animal is an act of stewardship.

outcomes.statement: Employ cooperative group living skills.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: Group Living and Leadership Skills (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore examples of teamwork in nature (e.g., geese's flying formation).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Participate in a variety of team-building activities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of cooperative living in communities in different cultures (e.g., Indigenous, Asian and Nordic), including a shared sense of responsibility for the good of the collective.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore examples of how group cooperation was employed in Indigenous ways of living (e.g., hide tanning, rope making and shelter building).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the various roles required to work effectively as a group in outdoor living situations, such as meal preparation and shelter building.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Implement constructive problem-solving strategies, including eliciting input from each group member.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify rules and norms (e.g., sharing responsibility, contributing to the group’s activities and respecting others) for effective group living.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze the importance of establishing group norms.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Exhibit cooperative behaviour in partner recreational activities (e.g., wall climbing and canoe paddling).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain the importance of effective communication in group living.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Employ effective communication skills (e.g., active listening and positive body language) in various situations.

outcomes.statement: Plan and facilitate an outdoor excursion in the local community.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 21A: Outdoor Excursion - Local (Optional) · Suggested Time: 6-12 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 1 and 2A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of land acknowledgements (e.g., naming the traditional peoples of the area, identifying the treaty and partnerships with local Indigenous people) when participating in local excursions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect upon the traditional stories of the land where the local excursion will take place.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Investigate the principles of layering clothing and appropriate fabric choices depending on the season, weather conditions and activity.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify which supplies are required for the excursion.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Establish communication routines (e.g., whistle commands and carry contact information) in emergency situations both within and outside of cell phone range.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify the route, possible exit points and muster point for the excursion.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Evaluate possible risks (e.g., weather, terrain, animals and plants) that may be encountered.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Plan for hydration and nutrition requirements appropriate to the excursion.

outcomes.statement: Plan and facilitate an overnight outdoor excursion.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of land acknowledgements (e.g., naming the traditional peoples of the area, identifying the treaty and partnerships with local Indigenous people) when participating in overnight excursions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect upon the traditional stories of the land where the overnight excursion will take place.

indicators.text:
Explain and demonstrate use of the principles of layering clothing, including:

- mid layer (i.e., insulates to preserve body warmth); and,
- outer layer (i.e., protection from weather).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Select and collect appropriate equipment for the excursion.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Conduct an equipment check prior to excursion to ensure functionality, including:
- operating Naptha gas stoves (i.e., lighting and unflooding);
- erecting tents; and,
- verifying stock in First Aid kit.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of carrying a personal survival kit (e.g., compass, personal medications, knife and emergency blanket).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Practise communication routines (e.g., whistle commands and satellite phone) in emergency situations both within and outside of cell phone range.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Establish plans for emergency situations such as extreme weather conditions, fire, injury, illness, becoming lost or animal threats.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify factors (e.g., pain, cold, hunger, fatigue and fear) that affect the ability to cope with emergency conditions in the outdoors.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Plan appropriate menus for the excursion and group.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Develop a budget for the menu and other excursion costs.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain the risks of consuming untreated water and methods (e.g., filters, chemical treatment and boiling) of water purification.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Prevent food from spoiling and attracting wildlife by using safe food storage practices (e.g., appropriate containers, bear-proof containers and hanging food).

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Plan and prepare a meal cooked over a fire or gas stove.

outcomes.statement: Plan and facilitate a multi-night outdoor excursion.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of land acknowledgements (e.g., naming the traditional peoples of the area, identifying the treaty and partnerships with local Indigenous people) when participating in multi-night outdoor excursions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect upon the traditional stories of the land where the multi-night outdoor excursion will take place.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore possible activities appropriate for the season and group, such as hiking, canoeing, cycling, skiing or snowshoeing into camp.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss ideas for topics, questions or issues pertaining to wildlife species and habitats.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III - Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse - work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement. These may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one's performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of the preservation of equality including solving problems that involve the manipulation and application of formulas related to:
- perimeter
- area
- the Pythagorean Theorem
- primary trigonometric ratios
- income.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, PS, R, T]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Verify, using examples, and explain why different forms of the same formula are equivalent.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Verify if given forms of the same formula are equivalent and justify the conclusion.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe, using examples, how a given formula is used in a trade or an occupation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create, solve, and verify the reasonableness of solutions to situational questions relevant to self, family, or community that involve the use of a formula.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze solutions to questions that involve formulae to verify the preservation of equality and correct, with explanation, if necessary.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Solve situational questions that involve the application of a formula that:
- does not require manipulation
- does require manipulation.

guidance: (It is intended that this outcome be integrated with other outcomes throughout the course.)

outcomes.statement: Analyze puzzles and games that involve spatial reasoning using problem solving strategies.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, PS, R]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Determine, explain, and verify strategies to solve a puzzle or to win a game such as:
- guess and check
- look for a pattern
- make a systematic list
- draw or model
- eliminate possibilities
- solve a simpler problem
- work backwards

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Observe and analyze errors in a solution to a puzzle or in a strategy for winning a game and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a variation on a puzzle or a game, and describe a strategy for solving the puzzle or winning the game.

guidance: (It is intended that this outcome be integrated throughout the course by using sliding, rotation, construction, deconstruction, and puzzles and games such as Tetris, Rubik’s cube, Blokus, chess, checkers, Backgammon, Mastermind, Tic-Tac-Toe, Connect Four or Five, Battleship, and Cathedral World).

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate using concrete, and pictorial models, and symbolic representations, understanding of measurement systems including:
- The Système International (SI)
- The British Imperial system
- The US customary system.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Research and present about a topic related to measurement systems such as:
- how the SI system and the Imperial system were developed
- the adoption of the SI system in Canada
- development of the US customary system and the relationship between the units of this system and those of the Imperial measurement system (e.g., units for length and area are the same; there are differences, however, for mass, weight, and capacity)
- early systems of measurement in Canada and contexts in which some are still used today (e.g., hand span and thumbs for measuring horses from the ground to its withers).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe situations relevant to self, family, or community in which the SI and/or Imperial systems are used.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Analyze the relationships between:
- the base units of the metric system of measurement and the base ten number system
- the prefixes used in the metric system and powers of ten
- the related units for length, area, volume, capacity, mass, and temperature for each of the two systems of measurement.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Explain, using examples, how and why:
- decimal numbers are usually used for SI units
- fractions are usually used for Imperial units.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Provide an approximate measurement in:
- SI units for a measure given in Imperial units (e.g., 1 inch is approximately 2.5 cm, 1 kg is a little more than 2 lbs)
- Imperial units for a measurement given in SI units (e.g., 1 litre is approximately 1/4 US gallon, 250 mL is approximately 1 cup).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Develop (using proportional reasoning), generalize, explain, and apply strategies (including formulas) to convert measurements from:
- SI to Imperial units (e.g., Celsius to Fahrenheit, centimetres to inches, kilograms to pounds, litres to quarts)
- Imperial to SI units (e.g., Fahrenheit to Celsius, inches to centimetres, pounds to kilograms, quarts to litres).

guidance:
It is intended that students explore, analyze for patterns, and develop understanding of many units in all three systems of measurements. The units used should be those that are appropriate to the workplace or apprenticeship context being considered. These units include:
- metres, grams, litres, and seconds along with appropriate prefixes such as kilo, hecto, deci, centi, and milli, as well as hectare, tonne, and degrees Celsius (SI system).
- inch, foot, board foot, yard, mile, acre, teaspoon, tablespoon, cup, pint, quart, gallon, bushel, ton, and degrees Fahrenheit (British and US systems where appropriate).

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate, using concrete and pictorial models, and symbolic representations, understanding of linear measurement, including units in the SI and Imperial systems of measurement.
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, ME, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Justify the choice of referents for units in both the SI system and the Imperial system (e.g, the width of the thumb for an inch and the width of the little finger for 1 centimetre).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Estimate, using personal referents for SI and Imperial units, linear measurements such as the dimensions of regular 3-D objects or 2-D shapes found in the classroom, at home, or in the community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Explain why and how the same linear measurement can be expressed using:
- equivalent SI units (e.g., 10 centimetres, 0.1 metres, and 100 millimetres)
- equivalent Imperial units (e.g., 6 inches, $1/2$ foot, $6/36$ or $1/6$ yard).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Measure and record (using Canadian spelling and abbreviations for SI or Imperial units) using a variety of instruments such as trundle or surveyor’s wheels, height gauges, metric and Imperial tapes and rulers, carpenter’s squares, micrometers, fractional or electronic callipers, and pedometers:
- distances at school, at home, and in the community
- inside diameters, outside diameters, lengths, and widths of personally relevant 3-D objects.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies to convert units of linear measurements within the same system (e.g., feet to yards, or metres to millimetres).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply knowledge and skills with linear measurement to create and solve or verify the reasonableness of solutions to situational questions relevant to self, family, or community (including perimeter, circumference, and the length + width + height measurement used in shipping and air travel).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine the operation that should be used to solve a linear measurement problem and explain the reasoning (e.g., Write the equation that could be used to determine how many lengths of $1/3$ of a yard can be cut out of a log measuring $5 1/2$ yards).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies to determine the midpoint of a linear measurement, such as the length, width, height, depth, diagonal length, or diameter of a 3-D object (e.g., A wall measures 5 yards and $6 7/8$ inches. If a painting is to be hung centered on the wall, how far is the centre of the painting from each of the adjacent walls?).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critique the statement “the distance between Regina and Saskatoon is 2 hours”.

guidance: It is intended that contextual situations involve the four arithmetic operations on decimals or on fractions, and that students do not convert from one to the other when performing calculations unless required within the particular question.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate using concrete and pictorial models, and symbolic representations, understanding of area of 2-D shapes and surface area of 3-D objects including units in SI and Imperial systems of measurement.
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, ME, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe situations relevant to self, family, or community in which SI and/or Imperial units for area measurement are used.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Justify the choice of referents for area measurements in both the SI and Imperial units (e.g., a dime or a small fingernail is about one cm² and the thumb nail is about 1 in²).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Estimate, using strategies such as personal referents or grids, area and surface area measurements in SI or Imperial units including regular, composite, and irregular 2-D shapes and 3-D objects found in the classroom, at home, or in the community.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies (including measuring and applying formulae) for determining areas and surface areas of:
- regular, composite, and irregular 2-D shapes, including circles.
- 3-D objects, including right cylinders and right cones.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Create, solve, and verify the reasonableness of solutions to situational questions relevant to self, family, or community that involve area or surface area measurement of:
- regular or irregular 2-D shapes including circles.
- 3-D objects, including right cylinders and cones.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies to convert, within the same system of measurement, area measurements expressed in:
- an SI unit squared to another SI unit squared
- an Imperial unit squared to another Imperial unit squared.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze, with and without the use of dynamic geometry software, the effect of changing the measurement of one or more dimensions on area and perimeter of rectangles and surface area of rectangular prisms.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Critique the statement “Area involves one face of a 2-D object while surface area is the sum of the areas of all the faces of a 3-D object”.

outcomes.statement: Apply understanding of the Pythagorean Theorem to solve problems.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, PS, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Model, including the use of drawing, concrete materials, and technology, the meaning, role, and use of the Pythagorean Theorem, using examples and non-examples.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Observe and analyze a set of triangles to judge if the Pythagorean Theorem could be used to determine an unknown side length and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe historical and contemporary applications of the Pythagorean Theorem, including the 3:4:5 ratio (e.g., Explain the relationship between a circle of string that has 13 equidistant knots or beads forming 12 spaces of equal length on it to the Pythagorean Theorem).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Relate, using examples, ratios equivalent to 3:4:5 and other Pythagorean Triples to the Pythagorean Theorem.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, apply, and explain strategies to verify if a corner of a 3-D object is square (90°) or if a parallelogram is a rectangle.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Observe and analyze the lengths and intersections of diagonals of various quadrilaterals and draw conclusions.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine if given triangles are right triangles and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create, solve, and verify the reasonableness of solutions to problems relevant to self, family, or community, for which the Pythagorean Theorem can be used.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of similarity of convex polygons, including regular and irregular polygons.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, PS, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Analyze and generalize about the relationships between:
- the corresponding sides of two or more polygons that have corresponding angles of equal measure
- the corresponding angles of two or more polygons that have corresponding sides that are proportional.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining if two or more convex polygons (regular or irregular) are similar.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Verify whether two or more given polygons are similar.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Draw polygons that are similar to a given polygon using measuring tools and technology, explain the strategies used, and justify why the polygons are similar.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply knowledge and skills related to similar polygons to solve situational questions relevant to self, family, or community that involve right triangles with a shared acute angle (e.g., determining the height of a tree).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create and solve situational questions relevant to self, family, or community that involve similarity of polygons.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Critique the statement “All congruent polygons are similar and all similar polygons are congruent”.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate an understanding of primary trigonometric ratios (sine, cosine, and tangent).
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Observe a set of similar right triangles and analyze and draw conclusions about the ratios of the lengths, with respect to one acute angle of the:
- side opposite to the side adjacent
- side opposite to the hypotenuse
- side adjacent to the hypotenuse.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify situations where the trigonometric ratios can be used for indirect measurement for angles and lengths.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply formulae for the primary trigonometric ratios (cosine, tangent, and sine).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze solutions to situational questions that involve primary trigonometric ratios to determine if they are reasonable and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply knowledge and skills related to the solving of right triangles using the primary trigonometric ratios to create and solve situational problems relevant to self, family, or community.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of angles including:
- drawing and sketching
- replicating and constructing
- bisecting
- relating to parallel, perpendicular, and transversal lines
- solving problems.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, ME, PS, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Justify the choice of personal referents for angles measuring $22.5°$, $30°$, $45°$, $60°$, $90°$, and $180°$ and use them to estimate angle measurements (e.g., a corner of a sheet of paper is $90°$ so $1/2$ of a corner is $45°$).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Sketch or draw angles of various measures, including acute, right, straight, obtuse, and reflex angles, and justify the choice of sketching or drawing in relation to the situation.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, how to measure angles in different orientations using a variety of instruments such as a protractor, carpenter’s square, or dynamic software.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain and illustrate how angles can be replicated (e.g., Mira, protractor, compass and straightedge, carpenter’s square, and dynamic software).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Replicate angles in various orientations, with and without the use of technology.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, the relationship between the bisecting of angles and axial symmetry.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Bisect angles in various orientations and explain the strategy used.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Observe and sort a set of pairs of lines as perpendicular, parallel, or neither, and justify.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Relate complementary and supplementary angles to parallel, perpendicular, and transversal lines.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Observe and identify in a situation relevant to self, family, or community adjacent angles that are complementary, supplementary, or neither, and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text:
Generalize, develop, explain, and apply relationships between pairs of angles formed by parallel lines and a transversal, inclu
- corresponding angles
- vertically opposite angles
- alternate interior angles
- alternate exterior angles
- interior angles on the same side of the transversal
- exterior angles on the same side of the transversal.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Provide concrete and pictorial examples that show that there are no angle relationships (excluding vertically opposite angles) when two lines that are not parallel are crossed by a transversal.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Describe and apply strategies for determining if lines or planes are perpendicular or parallel in situations relevant to self, family, or community (e.g., are the walls perpendicular to the floor? Are the corners square? Are the seams on the duvet parallel? Are the joists parallel?).

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Analyze personally relevant situations for the impact if lines or planes that are meant to be perpendicular or parallel are not (e.g., What would it be like if the stairs in a staircase were not parallel?).

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Create and solve relevant situational questions that involve angles and/or parallel lines and transversals, including perpendicular transversals, and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Critique the statement “If two or more lines are perpendicular, then each is a transversal of the other and if two or more lines are transversals of each other, they are perpendicular”.

indicators.label: q
indicators.text: Critique the statement “All lines are either parallel or transversals”.

indicators.label: r
indicators.text: Analyze and describe the role of angles, parallel lines, perpendicular lines, and transversals in games and sports (e.g., chess, curling, pool, hockey, soccer, and basketball).

outcomes.statement: Apply proportional reasoning to solve problems involving unit pricing and currency exchange.
outcomes.printedWith: [CN, ME, PS, R, T]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create and solve problems relevant to self, family, and community that involve best buy, and explain the solution in terms of the cost as well as other factors, such as quality and quantity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe and analyze, using relevant examples taken from print and other media, different sales promotion techniques (e.g., deli meat at $2 per 100g seems less expensive than $20 per kilogram).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine the percent increase or decrease from an original price to a new price and explain the reasoning for the method

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Develop (using proportional reasoning), explain, and apply strategies for:
- comparing the unit price of two or more items
- solving situational problems involving currency exchange
- determining percent increase or decrease for a given situation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop using proportional reasoning and mental mathematics strategies, explain, and apply strategies for estimating the cost of items or services in Canadian currency while in a foreign country or when making purchases via the Internet, and explain why this may be important.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Convert between Canadian currency and foreign currencies, such as Mexican or American currencies, using formulas, charts, or tables, and explain how to know if the solution is reasonable

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze solutions to situational questions that involve unit pricing or conversions of currency to determine if they are reasonable and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research advantages and disadvantages for individuals, groups, businesses, and communities of having differences in currency rates between Canada and the United States.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of income including:
- wages
- salary
- contracts
- commissions
- piecework
- self-employment
- gross pay
- net pay.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, R, T]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe, using examples, various methods of earning income.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research and record jobs that commonly use different methods of earning income, including hourly wage, wage and tips, salary, commission, contract, bonus, and shift premiums.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the advantages and disadvantages for a variety of methods of earning income, such as hourly wage, tips, piecework, salary, commission, contract work, and self-employment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Read and explain the information provided on pay stubs.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine in decimal form, from a time schedule, the total time worked in hours and minutes, including time and a half and/or double time and explain the strategies used.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Determine gross pay for different situations, including:
- base hourly wage, with and without tips, from given or calculated hours worked
- base hourly wage, plus overtime (time and a half, double time) from given or calculated hours worked
- base wage, plus commission
- single commission rate
- graduated commission.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine the Canadian Pension Plan (CPP), Employment Insurance (EI), and income tax deductions for a given amount of gross pay.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify and describe deductions that may be relevant to self in the future which are used when calculating net pay (e.g., health plans, uniforms, union dues, charitable donations, payroll tax).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate, using technology, “what if ...” questions related to changes in income (e.g., “What if there is a change in the rate of pay?”, “What if there is a change in the method of earning income?”, “What if I can qualify for deductions?”, “What if I work 80% time instead of full time?” , “What if I am sick for a long period of time?”).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Create, research, and solve situational questions relevant to self, family, and community that involve income.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Critique the statement “When planning for a budget, it is important to calculate net pay rather than rely only on gross pay”.

outcomes.statement: Expand and apply understanding of the preservation of equality including solving problems that involve the manipulation and application of formulae for volume and capacity, surface area, slope and rate of change, simple interest, and finance charges.
outcomes.printedWith: C,CN,ME,PS,R,T

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Verify, using examples, and explain why different forms of the same formula are equivalent.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Verify whether given forms of the same formula are equivalent and justify the conclusion.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe, using examples, how a given formula is used in a trade or an occupation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create, solve, and verify the reasonableness of solutions to situational questions that involve the use of a formula relevant to self, family, or community.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze solutions to questions that involve formulae to verify the preservation of equality, correct if necessary, and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Solve, with or without the use of technology, situational questions that involve the application of a formula that:
- does not require manipulation
- does require manipulation.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate the ability to analyze puzzles and games that involve numerical reasoning and problem solving strategies.
outcomes.printedWith: C,CN,PS,R

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Determine, explain, and verify strategies to solve a puzzle or to win a game such as:
- guess and check
- look for a pattern
- make a systematic list
- draw or model
- eliminate possibilities
- formulate and simplify a problem that is similar to the original problem
- work backwards
- develop alternative approaches.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Observe and analyze errors in solutions to puzzles or in strategies for winning games to identify and correct errors, if necessary, and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a variation of a puzzle or a game, and describe a strategy for solving the puzzle or winning the game.

outcomes.statement: Extend and apply understanding of surface area, volume, and capacity using concrete and pictorial models and symbolic representations (SI or imperial units of measurement).
outcomes.printedWith: C,CN,ME,PS,V

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Observe, analyze, generalize, and explain using examples including nets, the relationships between area, surface area, and volume.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Observe, analyze, and compare volume and capacity using examples.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique the statement: "Volume and capacity represent the same attribute to measure so the same units of measure can be used for either volume or capacity".

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify and describe situations in which given SI or imperial volume or capacity units would be used.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Justify and compare the choice of personal referents for surface area, volume, and capacity measurements in both SI and imperial units, (e.g., The bottom half of a two-litre carton of milk has a capacity of one litre, a surface area of 500 cm² or if a top was added to make a prism it would have a surface area of 600 cm² and a volume of about 1000 cm³, or the volume of a box for hockey helmets is approximately 1 ft³ [1800 in³] and the surface area is about 6 ft² [900 in²]).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Justify and apply strategies including use of personal referents to estimate the surface area and volume of 3-D objects, and the capacity of containers.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Solve situational questions that involve:
- the volume of 3-D objects and composite 3-D objects in a variety of contexts
- the capacity of containers.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Convert given volume, surface area, and capacity measurements:
- expressed in one SI unit to another SI unit (including units squared and units cubed)
- expressed in one imperial unit to another imperial unit (including units squared and units cubed).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Determine the surface area and volume of prisms, cones, cylinders, pyramids, spheres, and composite 3-D objects, using a variety of measuring tools such as rulers, tape measures, callipers, and micrometers and explain the strategy used including the manipulation of formulae.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Determine the capacity of prisms, cones, pyramids, spheres, and cylinders, using a variety of measuring tools and methods, such as graduated cylinders, measuring cups, measuring spoons, and displacement and explain the strategy used.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text:
Analyze and generalize the relationship between the volumes of:
- cones and cylinders with the same base and height
- pyramids and prisms with the same base and height.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze and illustrate, using examples, the effect of dimensional changes on area, surface area, and volume.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text:
Solve using a variety of strategies, including the manipulation of formulae, situational questions that involve:
- the surface area of 3-D objects, including spheres
- the volume of 3-D objects, including composite 3-D objects
- the capacity of containers.

outcomes.statement: Solve problems that involve at least two right triangles.
outcomes.printedWith: CN,PS,T,V

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze and sort a set of illustrations of triangles in a given context according to whether they are right triangles or not, and justify the sort.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Apply personal strategies to determine, with justification, if solutions to problems that involve two or three right triangles are reasonable.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Sketch representations of 2-D shapes or 3-D objects from given contexts or situations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Apply personal strategies including the primary trigonometric ratios to solve situational questions that involve:
- angles of elevation or angles of depression, and explain the reasoning
- more than two right triangles and explain the reasoning.

outcomes.statement:
Extend and apply understanding of 3-D objects including:
- top, bottom, and side views
- exploded views
- component parts
- scale diagrams.
outcomes.printedWith: CN, R, T, V

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and sketch or draw, with or without technology, using a variety of strategies including the use of isometric paper:
- 2-D representations of 3-D objects relevant to self, family, and community
- 3-D objects, given the top, front, and side views
- a one-point perspective view of given 3-D objects
- the components of given exploded diagrams, and explain their relationship to the original 3-D objects
- 2-D representations of 3-D objects, given their exploded view.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Draw to scale:
- top, front, and side views of given actual 3-D objects
- the components of a 3-D object.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Construct models of 3-D objects, given the top, front, and side views.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze a set of views of 3-D objects to determine if they represent a given object and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify and justify the point of perspective of given one-point perspective drawings of 3-D objects.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of personal budgets and their importance for financial planning.
outcomes.printedWith: CN,PS,R,T,V

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and justify income and expenses that could be included in a personal budget.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain considerations that must be made when developing a budget (e.g., prioritizing, recurring and unexpected expenses).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a personal budget based on given income and expense data or from personally collected data and justify the reasoning.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Modify a budget to achieve a set of personal goals.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate and analyze, with or without technology, "what if ¿" questions related to personal budgets.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, the advantages of creating personal budgets.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of compound interest.
outcomes.printedWith: CN, ME, PS, T

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Solve situational questions that involve simple interest, given three of the four values in the formula I=prt and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze and generalize the relationship between simple interest and compound interest.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Solve, using a formula, situational questions that involve compound interest.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, the effect of changing different factors on compound interest such as different compounding periods, different interest rates, and starting at a younger age.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Estimate, using the Rule of 72, the time required for a given investment to double in value and explain the reasoning.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of financial institution services used to access and manage personal finances, including credit options.
outcomes.printedWith: C,ME,CN,PS,R,T

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research and present orally, with the aid of visuals (electronic or other), various types of banking services available from various financial institutions, such as online services, different types of accounts, telephone banking, mobile banking, ATM banking, or credit cards.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze given or personal situations to determine the type of account that best meets the needs of the criteria for each of the situations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research and explain various automated teller machine (ATM) service charges.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Describe the advantages and disadvantages of:
- online banking
- debit card purchases
- different types of credit options, including bank and store credit cards, personal loans, lines of credit, and overdraft.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe ways that try to ensure the security of personal and financial information (e.g., passwords, encryption, protection of personal identification number (PIN) and other personal identity information).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research, compare, and report on credit card options from various companies and financial institutions.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze credit options related to the use of credit, such as service charges, interest, payday loans, and sales promotions, to make informed decisions and plans and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe strategies to use credit effectively, such as negotiating interest rates, planning payment timelines, reducing accumulated debt, and timing purchases.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Solve situational questions that involve credit linked to sales promotions, credit cards, or loans.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Critique the statement, "It is always better to have the lowest possible limit on a credit card."

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate concretely, pictorially, and symbolically (with and without the use of technology) an understanding of slope with respect to:
- rise over run
- rate of change
- solving problems.
outcomes.printedWith: C, CN, PS, V

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research and present contexts that involve slope including the mathematics involved (e.g., ramps, roofs, road grade, flow rates within a tube, skateboard parks, ski hills).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze and generalize relationships between slopes in given contexts such as 3:1 and a 1:3 roof pitch or slopes that are usually described by a colour for downhill skiing and snowboarding, and explain implications of each slope including safety and functionality.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe conditions under which a slope will be either 0 or undefined and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique the statement, "It requires less effort to independently use a wheelchair to climb a ramp of a certain height that has a slope of 1:12 rather than a slope of 1:18."

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Justify, using examples and illustrations:
- slope as rise over run
- slope as rate of change.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze slopes of objects, such as ramps or roofs, to determine if the slope is constant and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze, generalize, and explain, using illustrations, the relationship between slope and angle of elevation (e.g., for a ramp (or pitch of a roof, grade on a road, slope in pipes for plumbing, azimuth in the sky) that has a slope of 7:100, the angle of elevation is approximately 4 degrees).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Solve situational questions that involve slope or rate of change, verify and explain why solutions are reasonable or not.

outcomes.statement: Extend and apply proportional thinking to solve problems that involve unit analysis and scale.
outcomes.printedWith: C,CN,PS,R,T,V

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the process of unit analysis used to solve a problem (e.g., given km/h and time in hours, determine how many km; given revolutions per minute, determine the number of revolutions per second).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Solve situational questions, using unit analysis, and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain, using examples, how unit analysis and proportional reasoning are related (e.g., to change km/h to km/min, multiply by 1h/60min because hours and minutes are proportional or have a constant relationship).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Solve, using personal strategies such as applying proportions or interpreting tables, situational questions that involve conversions of units within and between SI and/or imperial systems of measurement (e.g., km to m or km/h to ft/sec).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe, using examples, contexts in which scale representations are used.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Determine, using proportional reasoning, the dimensions of objects, given scale drawings or models.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Construct models of 3-D objects, given the scale.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Draw, with or without technology, a scale diagram of 3-D objects.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Solve situational questions that involve scale and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain the importance of scale in mathematical drawings and/or in situational applications.

outcomes.statement:
Extend and apply understanding of representing data using graphs including:
- bar graphs
- histograms
- line graphs
- circle graphs.
outcomes.printedWith: C, CN, PS, R, T, V

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions that could be answered using histograms, construct the histogram, and draw conclusions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze and compare sets of bar graphs and histograms.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze sets of data in a variety of contexts to determine and create, with or without technology, possible graphs that could be used to represent the data and explain the advantages and disadvantages of each graph.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique the statement, "All histograms are bar graphs and all bar graphs are histograms."

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze graphs including bar graphs, histograms, line graphs, and circle graphs to determine and describe trends.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Explain, using examples:
- how the same graph can be used to justify more than one conclusion
- how different graphic representations of the same data set can be used to emphasize a point of view
- what happens if the graph is drawn to the wrong scale
- why the graph selected is not reflective of the data set.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Solve, using a variety of strategies including interpolation and extrapolation, contextual problems that involve data analysis and graphs.

outcomes.statement: Analyze puzzles and games that involve logical reasoning using problem-solving strategies.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, PS, R]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Determine, explain, and verify strategies to solve a puzzle or to win a game such as:
- guess and check
- look for a pattern
- make a systematic list
- draw or model
- eliminate possibilities
- formulate and simplify a problem that is similar to the original problem
- work backwards
- develop alternative approaches.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Observe and analyze errors in solutions to puzzles or in strategies for winning games, and explain the reasoning.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Create a variation on a puzzle or a game, and describe a strategy for solving the altered puzzle or winning the game.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate concretely, pictorially, and symbolically an understanding of limitations of measuring instruments including:
- precision
- accuracy
- uncertainty
- tolerance.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain, using concrete models and pictorial representations, the difference between precision and accuracy.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Analyze given contexts to generalize and explain why:
- a certain degree of precision is required

- look for patterns and relationships to help identify the meanings of related phrases (e.g., 工gōng → 工gōng人rén, 工gōng作zuò, 工gōng资z ī); and,
- use mnemonics to help remember the eight basic strokes in Standard Chinese writing (e.g., 永yǒng字z ì八b ā法f ǎ).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Recognize and distinguish the following elements:
- the remaining 12 finals (i.e., four triphthong finals and eight nasal compound finals); and,
- the formation of related syllables with specific tones in hanyu pinyin (see Appendix A).

indicators.text: Infer the meaning of new Standard Chinese words created from familiar and newly-learned radicals.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:

- ‘工gōng’ means ‘work’ (verb);
- ‘工人gōngrén’ means ‘worker’ (noun); and,
- ‘工gōng作zuò’ means ‘work’ (noun).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Comprehend common sight words:
- Standard Chinese characters that sound alike, such as (音yīn 似shì 字zì) (e.g., 目mù，木mù，墓mù ；鸡jī 机jī，肌jī); and,
- Standard Chinese characters that look alike, such as (形xíng似sì字zì) (e.g., 人rén，八bā，入rù ; 士shì，土tǔ ；千qiān，干gàn).

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text:
Discuss differences in formal and informal Mandarin, such as:
- the number “1” is pronounced differently by some; instead of pronouncing “1” as “yī” like in pinyin, it is read as “yāo”. The reason is to clearly distinguish “1” from “7” because “7” in pinyin is “qī”, which may sound alike over the crackling of a telephone conversation.

- researching Canadian organizations, events and festivals (e.g., Salsa on St. Claire, Hispanic Fiesta and Latin America Festival Latino); and,
- exploring Spanish-speaking communities in Canada.
